And in the mind-door process, it is stated: "Eleven mind-moments have passed, then when there is a remaining lifespan of five mind-moments..."

Here, regarding the static sub-moment (ṭhiti-kkhaṇa) of the mind that is mentioned, it should be investigated whether it exists or not. In the Citta-yamaka, the Buddha taught only this much as an answer: "Is a phenomenon that has reached the three sub-moments (khaṇattaya) currently arising? A phenomenon that has reached the dissolving sub-moment (bhaṅga-kkhaṇa) is not currently arising." He did not teach that a phenomenon that has reached either the static sub-moment or the dissolving sub-moment is not currently arising. Likewise, He taught only this much as an answer: "Is it not that a phenomenon which is not currently arising has not reached the three sub-moments? It is not that a phenomenon which is not currently arising at the dissolving sub-moment has not reached the three sub-moments." He did not teach by including both the static sub-moment and the dissolving sub-moment.

Similarly, in fully answering the question, "Is a phenomenon that has not yet ceased not currently ceasing? Is a phenomenon that is not currently ceasing not yet ceased?", the fact that He taught "the arising sub-moment is future" and did not mention "the static sub-moment," and in the section on past time (atikkanta-kāla-vāra), the fact that He taught "at the dissolving sub-moment, the mind has passed the arising sub-moment" and did not mention "the static sub-moment," shows the non-existence of the static sub-moment (ṭhiti-kkhaṇa) of the mind. Also, in the Sutta Pāḷi, it is stated: "The alteration of what is present (ṭhitassa aññathattaṃ) in conditioned phenomena is evident." Since there cannot be an alteration of that very same single conditioned phenomenon, it is possible to say that the "presence" (ṭhiti) whose alteration is evident is only the presence of a continuity (santati-ṭhiti).
23:
Only this much of an answer was spoken [by the Blessed One]: "It is not arising." He did not say, "In the moment of presence (ṭhitikkhaṇa) and the moment of dissolution (bhaṅgakkhaṇa), it has reached the triad of moments, but it is not arising." Furthermore, to the question, "Is it not arising? Has it not reached the triad of moments?" only this much of an answer was spoken: "In the moment of dissolution, it is not arising, but it is not the case that it has not reached the triad of moments." He did not say, "In the moment of presence and the moment of dissolution [it is not arising, but it is not the case that it has not reached the triad of moments]."

Similarly, in providing a full answer to these problems: "Is it not ceased, is it not ceasing?" and "Is it not ceasing, is it not ceased?" by saying "In the moment of arising (uppādakkhaṇa), it is future," and by not mentioning "in the moment of presence," and also in the section on past time (atītakālavāra), by saying "In the moment of dissolution, the mind has passed the moment of arising," and by not mentioning "in the moment of presence," He shows the non-existence of the moment of presence for the mind. Indeed, even in the Sutta texts, in the passage "The alteration of that which is present (ṭhitassa aññathattaṃ) is evident," since there is no alteration of that single conditioned thing itself, it is possible to say, "The alteration of which presence is evident, that presence is the presence of continuity (santati-ṭhiti)." Or else, it is possible to call a conditioned thing "present" (ṭhita) when it is endowed with the combination of the two evident moments: the moment of arising and the moment of dissolution.

In explaining this [topic of] simultaneous arising and different cessation (ekuppāda-nānānirodha) etc., the arising of certain matter (rūpa) at the moment of the mind's dissolution (bhaṅgakkhaṇa) is stated; that arising of matter at the mind's moment of dissolution should also be examined. Why? Because to the question, "Or else, for whom the truth of the origin (samudayasacca) is ceasing, for him is the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca) arising?" He answered, "No." The cessation of certain matter at the mind's moment of arising is stated; that cessation of matter at the mind's moment of arising should also be examined. Why? Because to the question, "For whom wholesome states (kusalā dhammā) are arising, for him are indeterminate states (abyākatā dhammā) ceasing?" He answered, "No," and so on.

It cannot be said that the rejection "No" was made referring only to mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa). Why? Because it is not the domain of mind-produced matter alone, and because the term "indeterminate" (abyākata) does not apply only to mind-produced matter. If it is argued that "by the term indeterminate, only mind-produced matter is taken here" because in the Saṅkhāra Yamaka it is stated that the bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāra) arises and ceases together with the mental formation (cittasaṅkhāra), that reason is not valid. For by that statement, the simultaneous arising and simultaneous cessation of kamma-born (kammaja), temperature-born (utuja), and nutriment-born (āhāraja) matter—other than mind-born matter—is not rejected; nor is their separate arising and separate cessation permitted; nor is the indeterminate nature of matter other than mind-produced matter prohibited. Therefore, the cessation of kamma-born matter etc., which are indeterminate and have simultaneous arising and cessation etc., and which are not so rejected, permitted, or prohibited, is rejected by this canonical text and logical reasoning. Thus, it is not possible to assert the cessation of kamma-born matter etc. at the mind's moment of arising.

When following the Citta Yamaka text with wisdom, it is understood that the mind is ceasing immediately after arising. Therefore, at that moment of dissolution, because the mind is ceasing, it cannot cause matter to arise, nor can it become a companion to temperature and nutriment which cause other matter to arise. Therefore, the temperature (utu) that arises together with the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta) can cause matter to arise only at the moment of arising of the first life-continuum (bhavaṅga) consciousness, which is immediately following that rebirth-linking consciousness. In this way, since mind and matter can cause matter to arise simultaneously at the beginning of life, this aspect to be seen (daṭṭhabbākāra) as "preceding and following" no longer exists.
24:
The mind has an extremely rapid change. Therefore, it is said that the matter (rūpa) which arises together with a certain mind is only in the state of arising (uppajjamāna) at that mental sub-moment. Because the mind is so rapid (or because matter is slow), that mind cannot support the non-mind-produced matter (acittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa) that arises with it from the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) onwards by any condition. In the moment immediately following that mind, that matter reaches the stage of presence (ṭhiti); at that time, the subsequent mind supports that matter by way of post-nascence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya), and not by way of conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya).

If it were so (that matter is only in the state of arising throughout the mental sub-moment), if one were to ask, "For one to whom the bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāra) is arising, is the verbal formation (vacīsaṅkhāra) ceasing for that person?", should one not answer "No" (no)? (Should one not rather answer "Yes" (āmantā)?). If such an objection is raised, it is not so (it is proper to answer "No"). This is because there is no beginning of the arising of matter at the moment of the mind's dissolution (nirodhakkhaṇa).

In the ultimate sense (nippariyāyena), matter is in the state of arising only at the moment of the mind's arising (uppādakkhaṇa). However, before the mental sub-moments (arising and dissolution) have passed, that matter cannot yet perform its function of producing its own matter (rūpasamuṭṭhāpana) and the function of the pre-nascence condition (purejāta-paccaya). Mental states (nāma) also cannot yet become the post-nascence condition for that matter. Intending this lack of special benefits that are obtained only upon reaching the stage of presence (ṭhiti), this was said figuratively (pariyāyena).

The phrase "Tato paraṃ pana" is connected with the statement "From then on, the succession of kamma-born matter does not proceed," after the conclusion of the summary discussion (saṅgahakathā) beginning with "Ettha pana yadetam" and the determination of the previous discourse. Therefore, it means "after the death-consciousness (cuti-citta)."

As stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) with the words "Rūpaṃ pana rūpena saha," etc., because matter does not have the nature of simultaneous arising and simultaneous cessation (ekuppāda-ekanirodha) with mental states, and mental states do not have it with matter, matter is associated only with matter, and mental states only with mental states.

The matter of the body is a component part. "Ghanapuñjabhāva" means being a solid mass or aggregate. It means it is not a loosely connected aggregate like a heap of sesame or green grams. By the term "Ekuppādāditā," the three aforementioned modes are referred to.

"Heṭṭhā" refers to the description in the Section on Matter (Rūpakaṇḍa). In saying "Parinipphannāva honti," it is said because the change-matter (vikāra-rūpa), etc., are also figuratively called "produced" (parinipphanna) in the description of the Section on Matter. What is the difference between "parinipphanna" and "nipphanna"? An ultimate reality (sabhāva-dhamma) that is delimited by a beginning (arising) and an end (dissolution), produced by conditions, and marked by the three marks (tilakkhaṇa) is called "parinipphanna." "Nipphanna," however, can also be a non-ultimate reality (asabhāva-dhamma/paññatti) that is produced by way of naming or the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), etc. By this statement "Nirodhasamāpatti pana," it should be understood that the entire concept of derivative designation (upādā-paññatti) is shown by way of that single part, the attainment of cessation.

## The Explanation of the Miscellaneous Discussion is finished.
25:
## Explanation of the Discussion on the Determination of Sequence, etc.

The teaching of the states to be abandoned first with the words "Dassanena pahātabbā" (to be abandoned by vision), etc., is the sequence of abandonment (pahānakama). The teaching by way of the planes (bhūmi) because the noble planes are determined in successive order is the sequence of planes (bhūmikama). The sequence such as "Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā" (the four foundations of mindfulness) is only a sequence of teaching (desanākama), because the foundations of mindfulness, etc., can occur even in a single moment. Although the discourse on generosity (dānakathā), etc., is spoken in a sequence of increasing excellence, since there is no determination by way of arising, etc., the mention of generosity, etc., here is called the sequence of teaching. The sequence of teaching means that because it is impossible to utter many words simultaneously due to the absence of the aforementioned determinations, they must be taught in some order of priority; thus, it refers only to the sequence of the teaching itself according to various intentions.

"Abhedena hi" means by taking them as a whole without making a distinction between the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha), etc. It refers to the aggregate of matter, which is the whole, by way of a part—the matter that is the object of the eye, etc. "Evaṃ" here means by the method already mentioned. Because of the sayings, "The King who is the lord of the six doors (is the mind)," and "Mental states have mind as their forerunner," consciousness (viññāṇa) is the predominant (adhipati).

In the aggregate of matter, the statement "with taints and subject to clinging" (sāsavaṃ upādāniyaṃ) is meant to exclude the nature of being taintless (anāsava) from the aggregate of matter, since there exist taintless states; it is not to exclude taintless matter (as there is no such thing). In the phrase "Anāsavāva khandhesu vuttā," the word "eva" should be seen as misplaced; the meaning is that taintless states are taught only within the (five) aggregates (as the aggregate of Dhamma).

The collection of all conditioned things into one by way of similarity is the "single collection of all conditioned things by way of similarity" (sabbasaṅkhatasabhāgeka-saṅgaha). Indeed, when collected according to their respective similar groups, all conditioned things such as contact (phassa), etc., become the five aggregates. Therein, groups that are similar by way of the general characteristic of being deformed (ruppana), etc., should be known as "similar" (sabhāga). Among those contact, etc., because the function of constructing conditioned things is powerful in volition (cetanā), which has the function of accumulating (āyūhana-rasa), that volition is called the "aggregate of mental formations" (saṅkhārakkhandha). Other states like contact, etc., which lack the specific characteristics of being deformed, etc., should also be understood as the aggregate of mental formations by way of the general nature of constructing conditioned things. It should be understood that the Tathāgata, who knows the nature of things, did not teach an "aggregate of contact," etc., because natures such as touching (phusana), etc., are not worthy of being called by the separate term "aggregate" (khandha).

By the power of such suttas as, "Monks, whatever recluses or brahmins who are eternalists describe the world and the self as eternal, all of them do so depending on and starting from these five aggregates of clinging, or one of them," it should be understood that the object of the grip of 'self' and 'belonging to self' has these five aggregates as its limit. By the power of this sutta and the suttas to be mentioned later, wrong view (diṭṭhi), which cannot be described as having a limited object (parittārammaṇa), etc., also arises depending only on the aggregates. This is because there is no other ultimate reality apart from the aggregates and Nibbāna.
26:
Ascetics and brahmins designate the 'self' based on the five aggregates; according to the discourses, it should be noted that the basis for the clinging to 'self' is limited to these five aggregates. Based on those aggregates, through the power of limited objects (pariṭṭārammaṇa) and so forth, there arises a wrong view that is indescribable (na vattabbā). This is the intended meaning because there is no ultimate reality (sabhāva-dhamma) other than the five aggregates and Nibbāna. To dispel the objection: 'Why are there only five, when other things that can be called aggregates, such as the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), clearly exist?', it is said: 'Because other things are also included within these five aggregates.'

The oppressive nature of feeling (vedanā) should be understood through the suffering of pain (dukkha-dukkhatā), the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-dukkhatā), and the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkhatā). Perception (saññā), which takes the form of male, female, etc., in the suffering of change associated with lust (rāga) and so forth, and which is the root of various thoughts, is the origination (samuṭṭhāna). Just as bile and so forth are the proximate causes of a disease, the proximate cause of feeling is the samuṭṭhāna. Just as the imbalance of seasons and food are the root causes, the root cause of feeling is the source (nidāna). Because it is said, 'Mental factors are the components of the mind,' the mind is said to be like a patient. Because perception is the cause of the oppression known as feeling through the power of the perception of pleasure (sukha-saññā) and so forth, and because it makes the 'food' of feeling savory, perception is said to be like a crime and like a condiment. In the Āsīvisūpama Sutta, it is taught: 'Monks, "five murderers who are enemies" is a name for these five aggregates of clinging.' In the Bhāra Sutta, they are called 'the burden.' In the Khajjanīya Sutta, they are called 'devourers' through the teaching: 'In the past, I was devoured by form; now in the present, I am being devoured by form; if I were to delight in future form, I would be devoured by form in the future, just as I am being devoured now.' In the Yamaka Sutta, they are taught as 'impermanent' (anicca) and so forth through the words: 'He does not truly know impermanent form as "impermanent form".' Although in this Vibhaṅga the aggregates are mentioned generally without distinction, it should be understood that because they are most prevalent, only the five aggregates of clinging included therein are to be noted.

'Desitādiccabandhunā' means taught by the Buddha, who is of the Solar Lineage (Ādiccabandhu). In the verse, the nasal (niggahīta) or the syllable 'ni' is dropped for the sake of euphony.

'Cannot be grasped' means it is not proper to grasp them as permanent (nicca) and so forth.

Although a water bubble, which resembles a shield in shape, is seen, it cannot perform the function of a shield because it lacks hardness; thus it is said, 'It is not possible to take that bubble and make a shield or a seat.' 'It does not remain so' means it does not become permanent and so forth. Alternatively, it means that because it breaks immediately after arising through the power of grasping it as permanent by way of craving (taṇhā) and wrong view (diṭṭhi), it does not remain in the form it was grasped. The number 'one hundred thousand crores' should be understood as merely indicating a great quantity.
27:
This number 'one hundred thousand crores' is not to show a limit by counting, but should be understood as showing abundance. 'Udakajallaka' means the scum (or slime) of water. Just as the wind produced by the falling of water drops on the surface of the water gathers the water scum, makes it into a mass, and creates what is called a bubble (pupphuḷa); in the same way, contact (phassa) produced by the arrival of an object at the physical base gathers the uninterrupted scum of defilements (kilesa-jalla) through its role as a co-operating condition (sahakārī-paccaya) and creates what is called feeling (vedanā). It should be understood that this is said with reference to the feeling involved in the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa), which arises due to the defilements as the root cause and the enjoyment of the object. Alternatively, the four conditions are mentioned as a maximum limit; however, feeling certainly arises even with fewer than four conditions.

'Nānālakkhaṇa' (various characteristics) means having diverse natures such as color, smell, taste, and touch. A figure shown by magic is called 'illusion' (māyā). The five aggregates of clinging should also be seen as having the nature of being unattractive (asubha) and so forth, because they are the basis for the impurities of defilements. Even though they are seen as such, because certain aspects of unattractiveness in certain aggregates are easily perceived, it is said 'and specifically' (visesato ca) and so forth. In that context, because the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) can abandon the four perversions (vipallāsa), it is said that the aggregates of form and so forth, which are the objects of mindfulness, should be viewed in terms of unattractiveness and so forth.

One is no longer oppressed by the aggregates because their nature has been fully understood. Even a practitioner of insight (vipassanā) does not fall into suffering when the aggregates perish; as for the Arahants (khīṇāsava), it goes without saying. Indeed, they will not be oppressed by the aggregates in the future either. In the statement 'He fully understands the nutriment of solid food (kabaḷīkārāhāra),' since it is taught that 'with the arising of nutriment, there is the arising of form,' a person who abandons desire and lust (chanda-rāga) for the internal form also abandons desire and lust for the solid food which is its cause; this is 'full understanding as abandonment' (pahāna-pariññā). One who discerns the internal form also discerns the solid food which is its condition; this is 'full understanding of the known' (ñāta-pariññā). Observing the arising and passing away of that form is to be applied as 'full understanding by investigation' (tīraṇa-pariññā). With reference to covetousness (abhijjhā) which is sensual lust (kāma-rāga), it is called 'the bodily tie of covetousness' (abhijjhākāyagantha). This is because sensual lust is abandoned through the meditation on unattractiveness (asubha-nupassanā). Alternatively, it refers to the abandonment of all greed, starting with sensual lust. Since it is taught that 'with contact as condition, feeling arises,' the full understanding of contact should be applied in the same manner as described for the full understanding of nutriment.

Because the longing for existence (bhava) occurs only for the sake of happiness, a person who abandons craving (taṇhā) for feeling crosses over the flood of existence (bhavogha). One who sees all feeling as suffering [does not regard] the new suffering inflicted by others upon oneself...
28:
He no longer perceives the (new) suffering caused by others upon himself, nor the (already obtained) happiness that has been destroyed. Because of not perceiving in this way, he is able to abandon the objects of malice (āghātavatthu) such as 'He has done me harm,' and thus destroys the bodily tie of ill-will (vyāpāda-kāyagantha). One who wrongly assumes that 'purity will occur in the happy realms of existence where there is much pleasure' and misapprehends purity through bovine habits and so forth, misapprehends only by the power of longing for happiness. Therefore, one who abandons craving for feeling does not cling to the clinging to rules and rituals (sīlabbatupādāna). Mental volition (manosañcetanā) is simply the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), while perception (saññā) is a state associated with that mental volition. Thus, one who sees perception and formations as non-self (anatta) simply abandons desire and lust (chandarāga) for mental volition. Because of defining and determining that mental volition, it is said: 'He fully understands perception and formations...'

Due to ignorance (avijjā), the grasping of 'compactness' (ghana) occurs in consciousness. Having broken down that compactness and seeing that consciousness as impermanent (anicca), one is able to cross over the flood of ignorance (avijjogha). It is by the power of delusion (moha) that the misapprehension of rules and rituals (sīlabbataparāmāsa) occurs. One who abandons that delusion is able to destroy the bodily tie of misapprehension of rules and rituals.

'Bhikkhus, regarding this which is called "mind" (citta), "intellect" (mano), or "consciousness" (viññāṇa), the uninstructed worldling (puthujjana) is unable to become disenchanted with it, unable to become dispassionate toward it, and unable to be liberated from it. For what reason? For a long time, bhikkhus, the uninstructed worldling has been attached to, has cherished, and has misapprehended this consciousness as "This is mine, this I am, this is my self"'—according to this teaching, one who sees consciousness as permanent clings to the clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna). Therefore, one who sees consciousness as impermanent no longer clings to that clinging to views.

## The explanation of the analysis of Kamādi etc. is finished.
## The explanation of the Suttanta-bhājanīya is finished.
## 2. Explanation of the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya

Having thus spoken of the state of feelings being knowable by way of the singlefold classification and so forth through the planes (bhūmi), the phrase 'Furthermore' (api ca) and so forth is stated to again speak of the various ways of being knowable, such as the state shown by way of association (sampayutta). In the phrase 'therein by the eightfold way' (aṭṭhavidhena tattha), the word 'therein' (tattha) should be applied only by way of the sevenfold division. This is because if it were applied by way of the sixfold division, it would not reach the state of being eightfold.

The phrase 'stated only for the purpose of completion' (pūraṇatthameva vutto) means it is taught only for the purpose of completing the tenfold division. It is not for the purpose of providing a method (naya) as in the ninefold division. Why? Because the method has already been given in that ninefold division. Indeed, the analysis of what should be analyzed is the giving of a method, and that analysis has already been done there. Just as in the Triad of the Wholesome (kusalatika), so it is here...
29:
The statement 'There is feeling born of body-contact that is pleasant, and there is that which is painful' also indicates that this pair is taught only for the purpose of completing (the tenfold division). The reason is that the method of distinction by way of pleasure and pain has already been given in the eightfold division.

Taking other dyads and triads besides those previously taken is called 'expansion' (vaḍḍhana) by way of expanding the taking. It is not a taking by way of accumulating other things while the previously taken ones remain. Alternatively, the word 'vaḍḍhana' has the meaning of 'cutting,' as in 'cutting hair' (kesavaḍḍhana) and so forth. Therefore, not taking again the dyads and triads previously taken, but cutting them off, is called 'vaḍḍhana.' The expansion of both dyads and triads is 'expansion of both' (ubhayavaḍḍhana). Or, the expansion proceeding from both sides is 'ubhayavaḍḍhana.' That itself is 'ubhatovaḍḍhanaka.' The extraction of the method in that way is the 'method of extraction of expansion from both sides' (ubhatovaḍḍhanakanīhāra). Or, the method that causes expansion is 'vaḍḍhanakanīhāra.' The method of expansion proceeding from both sides is 'ubhatovaḍḍhanakanīhāra.'

In those [methods] of expansion from both sides based on dyads and triads, there is a distinction only in the twofold and threefold divisions. Other divisions are not distinct. Even though they are not distinct, it should be understood that the other divisions are also taught for the purpose of generating specific wisdom, for the purpose of preventing useless thoughts such as thoughts about relatives by means of thoughts connected with the Dhamma, for the purpose of generating joy connected with the Dhamma for one who contemplates this Pali text, because each section (vāra) is a gateway to deliverance from the round of suffering, and by way of the distinction of the twofold and threefold divisions. This is because among divisions that depend on one another, if one division is distinct, the others are also distinct. Not only is it singlefold, but it is also twofold. Not only is it singlefold and twofold, but it is also threefold. Not only is it singlefold... up to ninefold, but it is also tenfold. In this way, these divisions are interdependent. Therefore, one division distinguishes the other division that it depends on, and also distinguishes the other division that depends on it. It should be understood that by the power of that dependent division, those other divisions are also worthy of being taught.

The sections (vāra) such as 'by the sevenfold way' are taught without depending on other divisions, simply to show the state of having many modes. Therefore, by all those modes, it is said: 'He showed the aggregate of feelings by way of many modes.' Just as a king with a vast domain is unobstructed in his own realm, so too the Blessed One, because of the vastness of His range of objects, is unobstructed and able to teach in whatever way He wishes. This is because He is endowed with the Knowledge of Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) and the Knowledge of Unobstructedness (anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa). It is appropriate to say that the triads are included in the dyads because the triads are taught after the dyads. But how are the dyads included in the triads? Because the dyads are applied by way of the 'dependent' and the 'depended upon' in those respective triads taught later.

It is said that the functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu) is obtained by way of adverting (āvajjana). However, adverting does not occur with body-contact as a condition. This is because a later state in the same cognitive process (vīthi)...
30:
A preceding state cannot be a condition for a succeeding state in a certain way. Some teachers say, "The feeling in adverting is said to be thus because it arises from the impact of the visible object on the eye-sensitivity," but this is not appropriate. The reason is that it is not stated in any Sutta or Commentary that "the impact of eye-sensitivity and visible object is eye-contact." If that impact were eye-contact, then the feeling arising together with eye-consciousness would also arise because of eye-contact; that feeling should not be excluded in this Commentary. Also, in the Pali text, since it is already included as "There is indeterminate feeling due to eye-contact," it should not be stated again as "feeling born of eye-contact."

The intended meaning here is: Since eye-contact does not arise without the feeling in adverting, that feeling in adverting, which causes eye-contact, can be figuratively called "eye-contact condition" because it serves that purpose. However, in the primary sense, feelings are obtained only after eye-contact.

Regarding "by way of the 34 consciousness-arisings," the exclusion of fine-material sphere and immaterial sphere (resultants) is because they themselves are the mind-door. All life-continuum (bhavaṅga) consciousness is the mind-door, and death (cuti) and rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) are not different from that life-continuum. In this 24-fold division, the Commentary states that wholesome states etc. having eye-contact as a condition are found in the same thought-process (vīthi). However, in the Pali text, the 19-fold and 24-fold divisions are summarized, stating: "There is a feeling aggregate born of eye-contact which is not clung to and not favorable to clinging, unsoiled and not favorable to being soiled, without initial and sustained application," etc. Since this describes states found in various thought-processes, it should be applied to the Wholesome Triad (Kusala Tika) as being found in various thought-processes as well.

In the Commentary, the occurrence of eye-contact as a condition etc. in the same thought-process is shown as being certain; however, it does not reject the possibility of it being found in different thought-processes. Therefore, it is said: "These states may be explained by standing at any point among the sevenfold divisions etc." This is because it is not only in the same thought-process that they are obtained through decisive support (upanissaya), transcending the limit (koṭisamatikkama), and development (bhāvanā). Intending that they can be obtained in all three ways, it is said: "They may be explained by standing at any point."

"Etāni" refers to the wholesome etc. consciousness already shown. In this explanation of feeling (vedanāniddesa), the connection with consciousness is made because it is easy to explain by way of the preceding consciousness. Therefore, since consciousness is shown by way of triads and planes in the sevenfold division, by way of doors and triads in the 24-fold division, by way of doors and planes in the 30-fold division, and by way of doors, triads, and planes in the many-fold division, it is said: "Among those divisions, they may be explained by standing at any point."
31:
It is said: "Without making a specific mark, it is appropriate to explain by standing at any point." The presentation of the wholesome etc. triads should be done by way of the planes such as the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). These four planes are directly included in the 30-fold division. Unlike the sevenfold division where the door is not mentioned, here it is mentioned. In this 30-fold division, the availability of consciousness in both the same and different thought-processes is very clear; thus it is said: "In the 30-fold... they are shown clearly."

Why explain by standing only at the 30-fold division? Since doors, triads, and planes are directly mentioned, shouldn't they be explained by standing at the many-fold division? No, because that would exceed the appropriate place for explanation. Indeed, the sevenfold division is not a place for explanation because the door is not mentioned. In the 24-fold division, the mentioned doors and triads are not placed with regard to the planes. In the 30-fold division, however, the doors and planes are mentioned. Those triads that were left out can be shown in this 30-fold division as pure triads along with the planes, independent of the doors. Therefore, this 30-fold division is the proper place for explanation. To go beyond these doors and planes would be to exceed the appropriate place for explanation.

In the term "upanissayakoṭiyā," natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya) is taught in various thought-processes, such as "depending on faith, one gives a gift." Therefore, for wholesome states etc. in a single thought-process, the doors like eye-contact—since those wholesome states cannot arise without that eye-contact—it is appropriate to say they condition by a trace of decisive support (upanissaya-lesa), just as birth (jāti) conditions aging and death (jarāmaraṇa). However, in this Commentary, it will be said: "Feelings such as preparatory work (parikamma) arising due to the seeing of a kasiṇa object occur because of eye-contact." Therefore, these consciousnesses like preparatory work that arise in various thought-processes can be obtained due to eye-contact. Thus, a mere trace of decisive support is not the "limit of decisive support" (upanissaya-koṭi). In fact, the eye-contact which is the beginning of all decisive supports for the increasingly powerful preparatory work etc. is called the "limit of decisive support" (the edge/beginning of decisive support). Just as in passages like "the tip of a hair (vālakoṭi) is not known," the word koṭi means either the beginning or a part.

Since the strong decisive support (upanissaya) for feelings of sense-sphere wholesome states etc. begins from the moment of seeing the kasiṇa object, that seeing of the kasiṇa object is called the "limit of decisive support." Alternatively, because the seeing of the kasiṇa object is not yet a powerful decisive support like the preparatory work etc., it is called the "limit of decisive support" in the sense of being the inferior end (upanissayanta) of that decisive support. In explaining this limit of decisive support, the Commentator, by stating that the limit of decisive support is not obtained in the three doors starting with the nose (ghāna), shows that the same thought-process is not taken. Indeed, just as seeing and hearing are powerful supports for kasiṇa preparatory work etc., smelling etc. are not such decisive supports. Therefore, the non-obtaining of the limit of decisive support in the nose, tongue, and body doors is shown. Although the air-kasiṇa (vāyo-kasiṇa) can be grasped by touch, without the prior hearing, that touching itself generally does not become the original root decisive support. Therefore, the state of being a limit of decisive support is not attributed to the touching of the air-kasiṇa.
32:
One who has attained perfection in disposition is called ajjhāsayasampanna or sampannajjhāsaya (one with a perfected disposition). Vattappaṭivatta refers to minor and major duties. Alternatively, the practice performed before is called vatta, and the practice performed after is called paṭivatta.

By the words "thus, eye-consciousness," the eye-consciousness that arises at the beginning is meant. Those that arise thereafter, such as seeing the kasiṇa form, seeing a good friend (kalyāṇamitta), and seeing an object of urgency (saṃvegavatthu), are also indeed decisive support conditions (upanissayappaccaya). Therefore, it should be understood that this eye-consciousness is shown to be their decisive support.

Not contemplating the true nature is called asamapekkhanā. (This refers to) the attachment to form and so on as "I am," the misapprehension of the inherent nature in a different way, and the defilement that has become firm because of repeated arising through the excessive grasping of the object, or one who has unabandoned sensual lust and so on. "Established in grasping" (pariggaha) means being established in the knowledge of investigation (vīmaṃsā). Here, by "non-contemplation" (asamapekkhanā) and so on, the investigation of the arising of delusion (moha) and so on through their manifest functions should be noted. Feeling (vedanā) that occurs by way of overcoming defilements arisen from seeing a visible form is said to be "born of eye-contact" (cakkhusamphassaja) because it has eye-consciousness, which sees the visible form, as its cause. Here, the status of eye-contact as a decisive support for feeling occurring in the four planes is stated in another way. Likewise, the same applies to the phrase "by the power of development" (bhāvanā).

Having attributed the three characteristics through group-comprehension (kalāpasammasana), and having comprehended the visible object by first delimiting it in the sequence of insight (vipassanā) such as the contemplation of arising and passing away (udayabbayānupassanā), or because all comprehension rooted in that visible object occurs in the initial visible object, it is said "having comprehended the visible object." Here, all comprehension such as the delimitation of mind and matter (nāmarūpapariggaha) should be understood as development (bhāvanā). "Having comprehended the visible object" refers only to the visible object that is the object of the aforementioned eye-consciousness, not just any visible object. This is because eye-contact is shown by way of the object. The same should be understood in the phrase "defilement arisen in the visible object."

In the phrase "On what does this tangible object depend?", just as in the case of the eye-door, the dependence on the great elements (mahābhūta) should be applied according to what is possible, by way of the water element (āpodhātu) and by way of mutual dependence.

By the words "Birth... etc... is a strong condition," it shows the status of being a strong condition for the mind-contact (manosamphassa) that arises together with the knowledge that sees birth and so on as fearful, or for the life-continuum mind-contact (bhavaṅgamanosamphassa) which is the door for that seeing.
33:
Mental object (dhammārammaṇa) does not only refer to the mental objects of birth and so on mentioned previously; rather, it occurs when all mental objects that are the basis for lust (rāga) and so on become manifest. In the phrase "dependent on the basis" (vatthunissita), by taking the delimitation of a portion of the mental object called feeling and so on as the starting point, it shows the delimitation of the entire mental object.

By the term "mind-contact" (manosamphassa), consciousness (viññāṇa) is taken as the cause of contact. It is not appropriate to speak of that same consciousness as the result of contact, which is its own result. This is because it would cause confusion for the listeners due to the mixing up of cause and effect. Therefore, it is said, "It is not possible to point out consciousness as being born of mind-contact." This is not said because consciousness does not arise together with mind-contact. Or rather, according to the statement "The meeting of the three is contact," just as the sense-faculties and objects are, consciousness is also a specific condition for contact; however, contact is not a specific condition for consciousness. Therefore, it should be understood that this was not done because consciousness, like the sense-faculties and objects, does not deserve to be called "born of eye-contact" and so on.

## The Explanation of the Abhidhamma Classification is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Questioning Section

Treating each group according to the collection of thought-arisings (cittuppāda) and matter (rūpa) as a single state, it is said, "the fifty-five sense-sphere states." In the words "of one who is lusting" (rajjantassa) and so on, lust (rāga) and so on, and in the six doors, the five restraints (saṃvara) such as virtue (sīla) and so on, should be applied as far as possible. Comprehension-knowledge (sammasana-ñāṇa), however, occurs only in the mind-door. Since there is the arising of covetousness (abhijjhā), displeasure (domanassa), and so on in the fine-material and immaterial sphere states, the restraint of mindfulness (sati-saṃvara), the restraint of knowledge (ñāṇa-saṃvara), and the restraint of energy (vīriya-saṃvara) which guard against those unwholesome states should be applied as appropriate. By the word "grasping" (pariggaha), comprehension-knowledge and reviewing-knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa) are included. By the word "those very ones" (teyeva), the four aggregates mentioned are meant.

While the Dhamma taught is the same, the mere variation in the method of teaching is called a "rotation" (parivaṭṭa). Because there is no deficiency or excess in any place within all three rotations, it is said, "there is only a single delimitation."

## The Explanation of the Questioning Section is finished.

## The Explanation of the Analysis of the Aggregates is finished.
34:
## 2. Āyatanavibhaṅga
## 1. Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā
'Visesato' means that, unlike the general meaning of the word 'āyatana', it refers to the specific meanings of words such as 'cakkhu' (eye) and so forth, which are not common to all. 'Assādeti' (relishes/enjoys) is said because the word 'cakkhati' has the meaning of tasting a flavor, as in "he tastes (cakkhati) honey, he tastes the curry"; thus, the meaning is stated by the power of that sense. According to the teaching, "Māgaṇḍiya, the eye delights in forms, rejoices in forms, is thrilled by forms" (M. Ni. 2.209), the eye relishes the visible form. Although the ear (sota) and others also have delight in sounds and so forth, the word 'cakkhu' is established and prominent only for the eye; it should be understood that the word 'cakkhu' arises only for the eye, just as the word 'pankaja' (mud-born) is used specifically for the lotus and such.

'Vibhāveti' (makes manifest) is also stated as an interpretation by the power of the word 'cakkhati' as established in grammatical science. For 'cakkhati' means to tell, to speak very clearly. Just as a speaker makes manifest the evenness or unevenness, the eye's making manifest the evenness or unevenness of the ground is itself the 'telling'; with this in mind, it was said, "it means it makes manifest." Alternatively, because roots have many meanings, the word 'cakkhu' should be understood in the sense of making manifest.

At times of lust, anger, etc., like the color of a chameleon or the color of an otter, the visible form (rūpa), reaching a particular change of color, manifests the desire born in the heart. It makes manifest the internal state as if it were the visible form itself; it means it shows it as if it had a physical body. Alternatively, the meaning of the word 'rūpa' is 'vitthāraṇa' (expansion/detailing), and expansion is indeed making manifest; thus it was said, "pakāseti" (makes manifest). Or, because roots have many meanings, the word 'rūpa' should be understood simply in the sense of making manifest. The derivative definition (nibbacana) of the word 'rūpa' denoting color/form is 'rūpayati' (it manifests), while the derivative definition of the word 'rūpa' denoting matter is 'ruppati' (it is deformed/affected); this is the distinction between the two.

In the word 'udāhariyati' (is uttered/pronounced), if the meaning 'vuccati' (is spoken) is taken, it would imply only the speech of living beings. However, 'sadda' (sound) here is not merely speech, but rather all sounds cognizable by ear-consciousness. Therefore, 'sappati' means it is brought to the state of being an object in ear-consciousness by its own conditions; it means it is made to reach the state of being cognizable by ear-consciousness. 'Sūcayati' (indicates) means that it makes manifest the source-object which is unmanifest through the power of smell, as in "this object has a good smell, or a bad smell." Alternatively, it is as if it acts as an informer (pesuñña) regarding hidden objects like flowers, saying, "here there is a flower such as campaka, here there is a fruit such as mango."

Because the taking of taste is the basis for swallowing nutriment, and because it inclines towards the taste of nutriment which is the cause of life, it is called 'jivhā' (tongue) by way of linguistic derivation (nirutti), as if it calls out to life (jivita). It is specifically called 'kāya' (body) because it is the abode (āya) of the despicable taints (āsava). Here, among the nose (ghāna), tongue (jivhā), and body (kāya), which are produced by kamma rooted in sensual desire and do not reach the state of being causes for the supreme (anuttariya) qualities, the body is a more prominent cause for the taints. This is because beings who greatly relish the tangible objects (photthabba) through that body even indulge in sexual intercourse. 'Uppattideso' means the cause of arising. Alternatively, the four mental aggregates (nāma-khandha) which have the body-faculty as their support are specifically called 'sāsava' (with taints) because they are the causes for strong taints like the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava); the place where those taints arise is 'uppattideso'.
35:
Among the nose, tongue, and body, which are special causes, the body is a more prominent cause for the taints (āsava). Indeed, beings who relish tangible objects through that body even indulge in sexual intercourse. "Uppattideso" means the cause of arising. Alternatively, the four mental aggregates which have the body-faculty as their support are specifically called "sāsava" because they are the causes for strong taints like the taint of sensual desire; it means the place where those taints arise. Those things such as the eye, which are said to "bear their own characteristics," are spoken of by placing the word 'āyatana' after them (as cakkhāyatana, etc.) by way of their specific characteristics. Other things that are the range of the mind (manogocara) are spoken of by being brought into a single base (dhammāyatana) only by way of the general characteristic of bearing their own nature. The former bases are clear through the states of object and subject, known as gross bases, objects, and cognitions. Similarly, other things that are the range of the mind, which are not clear, are not such that they do not bear their own nature (they do bear it); the word "dhamma" is used to demonstrate this meaning.

"Vāyamanti" means simply that they perform their own function. In this sense, the word 'āyatana' expresses the locative sense (adhikaraṇa) as in "āyatananti ettha"; in the second and third meanings, it expresses the sense of the agent (kattu). "Te ca" refers to the mind and mental factors (citta-cetasika). Indeed, those mind and mental factors come (āyanti), arrive, and occur at their respective doors and objects; therefore, they are called "āyā". "Vitthārenti" means that they expand, make manifest, and produce things that were previously unarisen and thus obscure and unmanifest, from the very beginning onwards.

To state the meaning of the word 'āyatana' by way of usage (ruḷhī), the section beginning with "Api ca" is commenced. In the phrase "taṃ nissitattā", the mind (mind-door) is not the support condition (nissaya-paccaya) for mind-consciousness and other mental factors; therefore, it should be understood that its state as a door is itself its state as a support (nissaya) for them. "Atthato" means by way of the derivative meaning (vacanattha) of the word, not by way of the thing signified (vacanīyattha). Here, the derivative meaning is stated by "cakkhati" and so forth, not the thing signified as in "the eye which is the sensitivity (pasāda) derived from the four great elements" (Dhs. 597).

"Tāvatvato" shows the state of being neither less nor more. In that regard, since there is no dhamma that is exempt from the twelve bases, there is no objection (codanā) by way of excess. However, since bearing one's own characteristic is the general characteristic of all, an objection by way of deficiency is possible; showing this, he said "cakkhādayopi hi" and so forth. "Asādhāraṇaṃ" means not being shared with eye-consciousness and others. Although physical sensitivities like the eye are specific objects, they should be understood as not being included in the mental-base (dhammāyatana) because they have already been taken as doors. Alternatively, "asādhāraṇa" is said in reference to not being shared by way of the states of door and object.
36:
It should be noted that the order of teaching according to the sequence of arising (uppattikkama) and so forth is inappropriate, mostly because of simultaneous arising and other reasons. By the words "Ajjhattikesu hi," it is shown that the six internal bases (ajjhattikāyatana) should be taught first (before the external bases) because they are internal and because they are the subjects (visayī) that experience the objects. Among those internal bases that should be taught first, the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) was taught first because it is the most prominent.

In the phrase "Tato ghānāyatanādīni," it means that since the nose, tongue, and body bases do not have as much benefit and thus should not be taught before the eye and ear bases, and since it is impossible to teach them all at once, they are taught in the sequence starting with the nose-base, as they must be taught in a specific order. It is not that objections could not be raised if they were taught in a different order (indeed, objections could be raised). However, it is also not possible to leave untaught those things that ought to be clarified. Because this mind (mana) has a range of objects, it is called gocaravisaya. If it is asked, "Whose range of objects is this mind?" the answer is that it is the range of objects for the five, such as the eye and so forth. By the statement "because of the determination of the causes for the arising of consciousness," the reason for teaching visible forms (rūpa) and so forth immediately after the eye (cakkhu) and so forth is shown.

Distinction of conditions (paccayabheda) refers to the distinctions of kamma and so forth. Distinction of destination (gatibheda) refers to the differences in destinations such as hell and the differences in beings such as those without feet. Distinction of group (nikāyabheda) refers to the differences in groups such as elephants and horses, or social classes such as the khattiya. Distinction of individuals (puggalabheda) refers to the differences in the continuities of various beings. The infinite distinctions mentioned regarding the bases such as the eye are also the distinctions of the heart-base (hadayavatthu). Therefore, the infinite variety of the mind-base (manāyatana) should be understood through the distinctions of the heart-base, through factors such as the painful practice (dukkhapaṭipadā), and through distinctions such as the object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati).

Since insight (vipassanā) is taught in this Suttanta-bhājanīya method, the mind-base is taught by taking the consciousness that has attained insight and showing its 81-fold distinctions in detail. A blue color is similar (sabhāga) only to a blue color; other colors are dissimilar (visabhāga). In this way, it should be understood in the distinctions such as those arising from wholesome states (kusala-samuṭṭhāna). The previously mentioned statement "by the power of mental objects (dhammārammaṇa) belonging to the three planes" refers to mental objects excluding the eye and so forth.

Striving through an action accompanied by movement is called īhā (effort). Exercising concern through thinking is called byāpāra (activity). Between these two, to show byāpāra, it is said, "The eye does not occur thus to visible forms." To show īhā, it is said, "And those states also," and so forth. However, since both īhā and byāpāra are possible, the order is stated in reverse. Dhammatā (natural law) is simply nature (sabhāva), or the efficacy of causes. The occurrence of the doors (dvāra) and so forth, devoid of īhā and byāpāra, is called dhammatā. In this sense, the word "yaṃ" takes the meaning of "yasmā" (because). In the previous sense, the word "yaṃ" is a modifier of the verb of possibility (sambhavana). According to the teaching, "Monks, 'empty village' is a designation for the six internal bases," the internal bases should be viewed like an empty, deserted village.
37:
In a deserted village that is perceived (or thought) to be well-stocked with food and drink, whichever pot or vessel one handles (or opens), that very pot is found to be empty of food and drink. Similarly, when these internal bases (ajjhattikāyatana), which are taken to be permanent and so forth, are investigated with wisdom, they are seen to be only void and empty of substance and so on. Because they cause greed (abhijjhā) and distress (domanassa) to arise at the doors such as the eye, visible forms and so forth are said to be strikers of the eye-sensitivity and so on. There are six animals: a snake, a crocodile, a bird, a domestic dog, a jackal, and a monkey. Their respective domains are uneven ground, a hole (or water), the sky, a village, a cemetery, and a forest. In this context, the internal bases such as the eye, which have inclinations toward uneven places and so forth, should be correlated with external bases such as visible forms, which are like those uneven places. This is because the internal bases are clung-to phenomena (upādinnadhamma) similar to the snake dwelling on uneven ground, the crocodile in a hole, the bird in the sky, the domestic dog in a village, and the jackal in a cemetery; and also because the mind is like a monkey that delights in the forest.

The phrase "in the sense of not being after having been" is stated separately because it encompasses the other four modes. This is because the mode of "not being after having been" is itself the mode of arising and passing away, and so forth. By the word 'hutvā' (having been), it shows the state of being present in the middle, preceded by non-existence in the prior end. After saying 'hutvā', by the word 'abhāva' (non-being), it shows the state of non-existence in the subsequent end, preceded by being present in the middle. By both of these, it is shown that constant non-existence is the characteristic of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa). Abandoning one's own nature is called change (vipariṇāma). Alternatively, transformation through aging and dissolution, or the occurrence of alteration in the continuum, is called change. Although there is constant non-existence, there might be the assumption that things endure for a long time; to prevent that notion of long endurance, it is said "because of being temporary" (tāvakālikato). A phenomenon that is devoid of arising, passing away, and alteration is called permanent (nicca). Because it is not so, it is called impermanent (anicca) by way of rejecting permanence, meaning it is the opposite of permanent.

Being undesirable due to the nature of birth and so forth is called oppression (paṭipīḷana). "In the sense of oppressing" means that in whichever person's continuum that suffering arises, it oppresses that person; or it has the sense of oppressing because it is itself oppressed by aging and so forth. Even for a phenomenon with a brief duration, because it is constantly and intensely oppressed by arising and so forth at the very moment of its existence, the previously mentioned general characteristic is specified as "due to constant and intense oppression." Because it oppresses the person, it is called suffering (dukkha), which is hard to endure. Because it is the opposite of happiness (sukha), suffering rejects or prevents happiness. Alternatively, because the word "suffering" by its meaning rejects happiness, it is said "due to the rejection of happiness."

For this phenomenon, there is no self that can bring it under its control, nor is this phenomenon itself a self that can bring things under control; therefore, it is called "uncontrollable" (avasavattanaka). Alternatively, the state of exercising control by oneself over others, or by others over oneself, is called "controllability" (vasavattanaka); since this state does not exist in this phenomenon, it is called "uncontrollable." The nature of a phenomenon that cannot be brought under control is the "sense of uncontrollability" (avasavattanakaṭṭha). This is a general characteristic. For that reason, it is void of any mode of being brought under control by another. In this sense, as a specification of the word "void" (suññato), it is said "because of being ownerless" (assāmikato). Or...
38:
Otherwise, for someone thinking, "May this eye... not reach [such a state]," there is no state of being under control (vasavattanabhāva) in the three stages [of arising, presence, and dissolution]. It means that the eye is empty of that mode of being under one's control. This eye is not something to be done or possessed according to anyone's will, nor does it have the nature of acting according to its own will; thus it is called "akāmakāriya" (not acting according to will). By this word "akāmakāriya", the meaning of not being under control (avasavattanattha) is specifically shown.

To reach destruction is called "vibhavagati". In the sequence of continuity, the very arising in another existence is called "reaching the transition of existence" (bhavasaṅkantigamana). Abandoning the usual mode of the sequence of continuity is called "abandoning the natural state" (pakatibhāvavijahana). When it is said, "The eye is impermanent," because the words "eye" and "impermanent" have the same meaning, does it not follow that other impermanent things also become the eye? To prevent this objection, and to show the distinction in understanding the part and the whole of words that express specific and general characteristics, the phrase beginning with "api ca" is stated.

What is shown? This means: what characteristic does the Blessed One, while teaching the occurrence of insight-knowledge, show? "Ānanda, what is the perception of non-self? Here, Ānanda, a monk, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects: 'The eye is non-self... mental phenomena are non-self.' Thus, he dwells frequently contemplating non-self in these six internal and external bases" (Aṅguttara Nikāya, Dasaka Nipāta, Girimānanda Sutta). Because the contemplation of non-self is taught regarding the bases without distinction, the teaching on the bases (āyatana-desanā) is intended to clarify the nature of non-self and the mark of non-self, as the eye etc., which are causes, and eye-consciousness etc., which are effects, are merely cause and effect. Thus it is said, "dvādasannaṃ... anattalakkhaṇaṃ". Although the marks of impermanence and suffering are shown here, the intention is specifically to show the mark of non-self through those marks.

In the word "veti ca", the word "iti" has the sense of completion (samāpanattha). In the word "iccassa", the word "iti" has the sense of pointing out the fault that should be attributed to what has been completed (nidassanattha). "Evaṃ" means "when there is such a view as 'the eye is the self'". Alternatively, in the word "iccassa", the word "iti" has the sense of pointing out the characteristic mode of the fault of the proponent of another view, as in "to one who speaks thus". The word "evaṃ" has the sense of pointing out the manner of reaching the fault. If it is asked: "In the self that is form, does it not reach the designation of ownership, as in 'May my form be thus,' as if it were one's property?" No, because it is taken as "my self". Indeed, if form taken as "my self" were to be as desired, "May my form be thus," because of being under control, then it should be so according to that desire. However, even though one desires it, the self called form belonging to that person is simply not under control. "Ābādhāya" means "for the sake of (oppression by) such suffering".
39:
Paññāpana means making known to others. Since making known the mark of non-self (anattalakkhaṇa) is not within the scope of wise ones other than an Omniscient Buddha, it follows that making known the marks of impermanence and suffering, which illustrate the mark of non-self, is also not within their scope.

Thus, the difficulty in making these bases known is because they are difficult to manifest by nature. Therefore, wishing to ask the reason for the non-manifestation of those bases in knowledge, the phrase beginning with "imāni pana" is stated. The meaning of being constantly oppressed without interval in arising and so on has been mentioned below. Because the bases such as the eye are merely elements, the differentiation from the collection is called "nānādhātuvinibbhoga" (differentiation of various elements). By the singular word "ghanena", all four types of compactness (continuity, mass, function, and object) are spoken of as a single group in the form of compactness. It should be understood that wisdom alone destroys the continuity (santati). "Yāthāvasarasato" means occurring according to the true and unerring nature. Indeed, when the manifest nature is experienced by penetrating it without error, it is called "rasa" (essence/function). The separate mention of the modes such as the mark of impermanence from the five aggregates which are impermanent is because there exists a distinct knowledge of impermanence etc., which is superior to the knowledge of form etc., occurring by way of "ruppana" (deformation) and so on. Indeed, the task of insight-knowledge is not completed merely by the discernment of mind and matter. One must still contemplate the impermanence etc., of form and feeling, and the modes such as the mark of impermanence of form and feeling. Those modes such as impermanence do not exist in the ultimate sense but are merely modes of form and feeling. For this reason, it is said in the Atthasālinī Commentary that insight-knowledge which has the mark as its object has the aggregates as its object. Therefore, one should remain within the intention of the commentator and not over-interpret. A person who contemplates "impermanent" does not simultaneously contemplate "suffering" or "non-self". Likewise, when contemplating suffering etc., one does not contemplate the other two, impermanence and non-self. The contemplations of impermanence etc., are capable of preventing and abandoning the perception of permanence and so on. They are associated with predominant faith, concentration, and wisdom, and they constitute the three doors to liberation (vimokkhamukha). Therefore, because there is a mutual distinction between these modes that are discerned, the three marks are taught.

## The Commentary on the Suttanta-bhājanīya is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya

The discourse that discerns mind and matter is the Abhidhamma discourse. Therefore, unlike in the Suttanta-bhājanīya where it is taught by way of the pairs of causes (doors and objects), in the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya, the bases that should be known with higher knowledge are taught by way of internal and external bases without mixing them. The meaning of the word "āgamma" is "by means of the realization through the Path" by a practitioner whose mind is weary of all formations, inclined towards Nibbāna, and turned away from formations by change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa). Indeed, having attained that Nibbāna which is being realized...
40:
The Path, known as exhaustion (khaya), which is established upon that Nibbāna—which is an object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), an object-predominance condition (ārammaṇādhipati-paccaya), the cause of great relief, the liberation from formations (saṅkhāra), and the foundation as a resting place—exhausts the defilements such as lust (rāga). If one cannot realize that Nibbāna, one cannot reach the cessation where lust and others do not arise again; therefore, it is said, "Depending on that Nibbāna, lust and others are exhausted." "Setting aside the Sutta" means setting aside the words of the Sutta. Just as in the verses beginning with "Having killed mother and father" (Dhammapada 294-295), there is no other meaning to be brought in apart from the direct meaning of the Sutta; it means the meaning is conveyed only by the words of the Sutta themselves.

"Is it one or is it distinct?" is said with disregard for the fine distinction. "Do you not know the one or the distinct?" means "Do you not even know this much?" "Is it not known?" is a way of binding with words someone who is concealing their own knowledge and creating distraction, saying, "Even if it was not known before, is it not good if it is known now?" "Having analyzed" means not stopping at the mere literal meaning of the letters, but distinguishing, extracting, and bringing out the hidden meaning. To the one who says that the exhaustion of lust and others is merely non-existence, and that non-existence does not have multiplicity because it is itself non-existent, the question is asked to cut off their speech: "Is the exhaustion of lust merely the exhaustion of lust itself?" and so on. For if the exhaustion of lust were not the exhaustion of hatred and so on, then the exhaustion of hatred and others would be distinct and different from the exhaustion of lust, which would lead to the danger of there being many Nibbānas. Since distinction from one another does not exist in what is without intrinsic nature (concept/designation), Nibbāna simply has its own intrinsic nature. Among the nine things rooted in craving, such as "Depending on craving, there is seeking," seeking and others should be understood as the defilements that perform the seeking. The one thousand five hundred defilements are mentioned in the Nidānakathā.

"It is made in a coarse manner" means that the extremely subtle Nibbāna is made known, or rebuked, by the fault of making it coarse. "Object" (vatthu) refers to sexual intercourse, which is the tangible object of the grasped (upādinnaka-phoṭṭhabba). Why is the attainment of Nibbāna mentioned even for animals such as bears and others? If one asks, "In the view of one who desires that only the permanent cessation of defilements is Nibbāna, is the temporary non-occurrence of defilements not Nibbāna?" the answer is "No." This is because they are similar in terms of non-existence (abhāva). Indeed, permanent non-occurrence and temporary non-occurrence are both merely non-existence, so there is no difference. Or, in the view of one who speaks with a distinction, it would lead to being a mere designation of non-existence. Because it can be reached even by animals, it is coarse and thick like a prominent ear-ornament for them. However, he rebukes them as if mocking, saying they are unable to wear it in the ear, or they cannot wear it because it is coarser than an ear-ornament.
41: Thinking that the attainment of the destruction of defilements occurs at the moment of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) by taking Nibbāna as an object, he says: 'While you have not yet destroyed defilements, you have reached the destruction of defilements' and so on. Is it not the case that one cannot say the destruction of defilements is reached merely by taking it as an object? For the mind can take everything, such as the past and future, as an object; it does not take only what is already accomplished. Will change-of-lineage also occur by taking as an object the nature of the non-arising of defilements to be brought about by the path? No, because for one who has not reached Nibbāna, there can be no knowledge having Nibbāna as its object. Nibbāna is not like other dhammas; because it is extremely profound, it cannot be taken as an object by one who has not reached it. Therefore, the Nibbāna to be reached by that change-of-lineage must be of a profound nature that transcends the nature of the three periods of time. Or, in the view of one who desires only the destruction of defilements, the destruction of defilements must have been accomplished prior to change-of-lineage. Therefore, it is said: 'While you have not yet destroyed defilements, you designate Nibbāna as the destruction of defilements.' If one could take as an object the destruction of defilements that has not yet been reached, then the states of consciousness prior to change-of-lineage could also take it as an object. The meaning is: 'What is the Nibbāna that is the object of the path?' By the words 'The path' (maggo) and so on, he explains the two previous questions. They say that among forms and so on, Nibbāna is not any [conditioned] object, nor does it ever arise, and it should not be spoken of in terms of being past and so on. The meaning that is appropriate is: because of taking that Nibbāna as an object, not even a single part of ignorance and craving remains; because of that very Nibbāna, those ignorance and craving never exist again. ## The explanation of the Abhidhamma classification is finished. ## 3. Explanation of the Question Section Just as things with objects take some object that cannot be described as limited (paritta) and so on, similarly, by taking some undeclared (navattabba) dhamma as an object, it does not fall into the undeclared category. This is the meaning. ## The explanation of the question section is finished. ## The explanation of the Analysis of the Bases is finished.
42:
## 3. Dhātuvibhaṅga
## 1. Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā
In the Pali texts such as the Dhātusaṃyutta, it is stated: "Bhikkhus, I will teach you the diversity of elements. And what, bhikkhus, is the diversity of elements? The eye element... the mind-consciousness element," and so on (SN 2.85). Although these eighteen elements appear there, it should be understood that the Suttanta classification (Suttantabhājanīya) is analyzed by taking the three sets of six elements that appear only in the Suttanta Pali, rather than taking the eighteen elements because they are common to the Abhidhamma as well. "All elements" refers to the eighteen elements. The term 'element' (dhātu) should be understood as a term established for a mere phenomenon that is empty of a self or soul and is evident in the ultimate sense. "Asamphuṭṭhadhātu" (untouched element) means the state of not being pervaded by the four great elements.

In the Commentary, the lemma is given as "paṭhavīdhātudvayaṃ" (the pair of earth elements), but in the Pali text, only "dvayaṃ" (a pair) appears. However, the meaning is exactly as previously stated. If the reading is "dvayaṃ," this meaning is also possible: it is called "dvayaṃ" because this collection of earth elements has two parts. The collection consisting of two parts of the earth element is called "paṭhavīdhātudvayaṃ." It means the collection of the two earth elements. Alternatively, the two parts themselves when combined are called "dvayaṃ," and the combined two parts of the earth element are called "paṭhavīdhātudvayaṃ." He answers briefly: "Therein, what is the earth element? It is the two types (collection) of earth element; this is the earth element." In the passage "There is the internal element, there is the external element," the terms 'internal' (ajjhattika) and 'external' (bāhira) do not refer to the internal and external sense bases (āyatana) as in the Ajjhattika-duka (Internal Dyad), nor are they identical in meaning to the terms 'internal' (ajjhatta) and 'external' (bahiddhā) mentioned in the Ajjhatta-tika (Internal Triad). Rather, these terms refer to things that are attached to the faculties (indriyabaddha—sentient) and not attached to the faculties (anindriyabaddha—non-sentient). Therefore, it is said, "included within the continuity of beings," and so on. The phrase "one's own internal" is not said with reference only to what is born within oneself as an individual, but should be understood as referring to what is born within the continuity of all beings. Indeed, by the words "internal, within oneself," he shows the state of being internal because it is included within the continuity of beings, not because of individual personality. "By way of natural mode" (sabhāvākārato) means by way of a mode that is distinct from the water element and so on, which is one's own nature and is to be grasped by wisdom.

"Hairs have the characteristic of hardness" is said because the state of hardness is predominant. "A separate portion" means it is merely a collection of earth elements and is empty of a self or being. It should be understood that the brain (matthalunga) is not mentioned separately here because it is included under the term 'bone marrow' (aṭṭhimiñja).
43:
By the words "Thus, the hairs," and so on, [it is shown]. "Having done the work" (kammaṃ katvā) means having applied effort (payoga), energy (viriya), or exertion (āyūhana). Just as one desiring wealth performs plowing and so on, one desiring the fruit of Arahantship should apply effort in this mindfulness. Major obstacles such as the dwelling (āvāsa) are called "previous obstacles" (pubba-palibodha), while minor obstacles such as long hair are regarded as "subsequent obstacles" (apara-palibodha).

Mindfulness by way of the five factors such as color (vaṇṇa) is the preliminary stage common to the mindfulness of elements, the mindfulness of loathsomeness, and the mindfulness of color. Therefore, to show the mindfulness of the element that has arisen, he said, "In the end, mindfulness should be practiced in this way." By the words "devoid of mutual concern or reflection," he shows that they are merely elements because of the lack of agency (avyāpāra) in both cause and effect. The lack of agency in mindfulness, reflection, and so on should also be understood in this same way. This is because those acts of mindfulness and their causes do not arise or act by thinking or reflecting. "By way of characteristic" (lakkhaṇavasena) is said with reference to words such as "the state of hardness, the state of roughness."

Vekantaka is a type of metal. Nāganāsika metal is similar to copper but is a distinct type of metal, just as there are types of turmeric that are not the common turmeric. Because it is produced by mixing lead, copper, and so on, it is called "artificial metal" (kittima-loha). Morakkha and others are simply names of such things. "Pearls produced in the ocean" is merely an illustration; in reality, all pearls are simply pearls.

It is called 'water' (āpo) because it reaches (āp-eti) the other three great elements; it means it reaches or adheres to the remaining three elements by way of binding (ābandhana). "Being liquid" (yūsabhūta) means being of the nature of fluid. In the passage "moistens the gorge, heart, liver, and lungs," it moistens the liver by filling the lower part, while it moistens the other organs by dripping slightly from above them. The simile "as if moistening clods of earth below" should be understood only to illustrate the common lack of agency in the moistener and the moistened, not to illustrate a similarity in spatial position. The fact that some things moistened by accumulated blood are below the blood and some are above will be explained in the Satipaṭṭhāna-vibhaṅga. Thus, the connection should be made: the lower part of the liver does not know, "Blood is staying in me," and the gorge and so on do not know, "Blood is staying, moistening us." Just as in the Bhesajja-sikkhāpada there is a rule, "To whom meat is allowable, to them milk is allowable," there is no such rule here. "By way of sharpness" (tejanavasena) means by way of intensity or heat. The state of heat that exceeds the normal nature of the body is called 'fever' (santāpa). By way of burning the body...
44:
The great burning that has arisen is called paridāha (distress). This is the distinction between santāpa (burning) and paridāha. In the phrase "yena jīrīyati" (by which one decays), the meaning "decayed by fevers such as the quotidian fever" is also appropriate.

Ghee that has been heated a hundred times (or many times), placed in water, and then extracted is called satadhota-sappi (ghee washed a hundred times). Fluid, blood, fat, flesh, sinew, bone, and marrow are called rasā and so on. Some teachers, excluding sinew, speak of semen as the seventh element. Pākatika (natural) refers to the fire element (tejo-dhātu) that is always present without being disturbed. In this discussion of the external fire element (bāhira-tejo-dhātu-kathā), only the fire coming out of the mouths of nijjhāmatanhika pretas is taken.

Vāyana-vasena means (it is called vāyo) because of its power to move with momentum or its power to cause movement all around.

This statement, "In which space... and so on... it is spoken," is said to show that the space resulting from the removal of a kasina (kasiṇugghāṭimākāsa) is not specifically taught, while unobstructed space (ajaṭākāsa) is directly taught.

The spreading nature of pleasant and painful feelings is stated in terms of the ability to spread to a part of the body or the whole body according to strength, because the temperature (utu) residing in the body is the cause for the arising of pleasant and painful tangibles. Similarly, feelings of joy (somanassa) and grief (domanassa) have the power to spread by producing pleasant and unpleasant mind-born matter. Thus, because these feelings spread in the body, it is shown that they are mutually opposed, such that one (pleasure, joy, etc.) can strike or afflict the place of the other (pain, grief, etc.), and vice versa. Alternatively, the distinct arising of these feelings in opposition to each other is itself called spreading (pharaṇa). The bases and objects, which are the causes for continuous occurrence, should also be understood as the place of spreading. This opposition is shown through the experience of a person who has both pleasure and pain, so that it may be easily understood.

Intending the defilement-based sensuality (kilesa-kāma), the commentary says: "Intention is sensuality, passion is sensuality." This refers to intention (saṅkappa or vitakka). That thought also oppresses and burns. Therefore, it is classified as kilesa-kāma because of its association with defilements or because it is the basis for defilements. Kāma-paṭisaṃyutta (connected with sensuality) refers to states associated with or related to sensuality, known as sensual lust (kāma-rāga). Although there are other states connected with sensuality, the term dhātu with the prefix kāma is well-known only in the case of thought (vitakka), because thought is excessively attached to sensuality. This same method applies to the element of ill-will (byāpāda-dhātu) and so on. Wishing for the suffering of others and oneself is called vihiṃsā (cruelty). "Vihiṃsanti" means they desire to harm.

Although it occurs in both beings and formations, sensual thought (kāma-vitakka) is called "kamma-patha-bheda" (breach of the path of action) because it generates a path of action through association with covetousness (abhijjhā) and because it destroys the path of action of non-covetousness (anabhijjhā).
45:
...is stated. By the word byāpāda (ill-will), the thought of ill-will (byāpāda-vitakka) is shown. This is because the thought of ill-will is the element of ill-will (byāpāda-dhātu).
