Likewise, in the case of cruelty (vihiṃsā) and the element of cruelty (vihiṃsā-dhātu), the breach of the path of action should be applied according to the power of ill-will and, as appropriate, according to the power of killing (pāṇātipāta) and so on.

Here, "ettha" refers to the two triads (tika). The "comprehensive discourse" (sabba-saṅgāhika-kathā) refers to the teaching that includes the remaining two pairs of elements by using the term kāma-dhātu (sensual element), which includes all sensual-sphere states, and nekkhamma-dhātu (renunciation element), which includes all wholesome states. If it were said "in this group of six," there would be the fault of including sensual-sphere states as well as renunciation elements and so on by the term kāma-dhātu.

By extracting and showing the states that have attained the nature of the eye element (cakkhu-dhātu) and so on, they are made to be attained. Because it occurs in this collection of states, it is called "cāra" (range). What occurs? It is contemplation (sammasana - insight). "Sammasana-cāra" (the range of contemplation), which is the place where contemplation occurs, is a designation for the states belonging to the three planes.

## 2. Explanation of the Abhidhamma Classification

By the word "cakkhussa" (of the eye), it is indicated as a master in an uncommon sense, being a specific cause. For that eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) is not shared with other persons, but it is shared with all visible forms such as blue and so on. "Vidadhāti" means it produces as if it were being commanded, "You must occur in this and that way." The meaning of the root vidadhāti is specifically shown by the prefix vi-. Therefore, it should be understood that even without the prefix, the word "dhātu" expresses that meaning. Since the word dhātu can be established in the sense of agent, object, state, instrument, and location, these five meanings are stated. Elements such as gold and silver refer to stones and so on, which are the source of gold and so on.

In the statement "they are called elements (dhātu) because they bear (dhārenti) their own nature," the derivation of the word should be understood as: it bears, thus it is an element (dhāti ti dhātu). This is because the word dhātu itself has the meaning of bearing. This sense of agent is also different from the previous one. Bearing a mere nature without a being (nissatta-sabhāva) is the primary meaning of the word dhātu, and thus it is stated separately. In the phrase "elements like elements," just as the word "lion" (sīha), which is well-known for the maned beast, is used metaphorically for men, so the word dhātu, which is well-known for parts of stone, should be understood as being used metaphorically for the eye and so on. Knowledge (ñāṇa) and the knowable (ñeyya) are called ñāṇa-ñeyya. The varieties that are parts of those knowledge and knowable are called elements as parts of knowledge and the knowable (ñāṇa-ñeyyāvayava-dhātu). Among those parts of knowledge and the knowable, the varieties of knowledge are a portion of the dhamma-dhātu. The varieties of the knowable are all eighteen elements. Thus, the elements which are merely parts of knowledge and the knowable...
46:
Elements exist. Alternatively, when the nature to be known by wisdom is expressed by the word 'dhātu', it means the nature that should be known by wisdom (ñāṇañeyya) in an unerring way. It means it is not a nature to be known through wrong views such as diṭṭhi, which grasp erroneously. The parts of that nature to be known by wisdom are the elements such as the eye (cakkhu). The word 'dhātu', which is well-established in parts with dissimilar characteristics such as rasa (realgar, orpiment, etc.), should be understood as being applied metaphorically to other such parts like the eye. Or, just as in rasa and so on, the word 'dhātu' is indeed primarily established in the eye and so forth. By the statement "This word dhātu is a designation for a mere non-living nature," the well-established use of the word 'dhātu' in the sense of being non-living is shown. Because this person has six elements, he is called 'cha dhātu' (six-elemental). In the world, what is called a 'person' (purisa) is a mere collection of dhammas; that person is just a collection of the six non-living natures such as earth (pathavī). The meaning is that herein, there is no soul (jīva) or person.

The order of the eye and so forth has been mentioned before. Here, wishing to show the order of the three elements in each triad, it is said, "by way of the determination of the sequence of cause and effect." The determination of the sequence of cause and effect is simply the state of being cause and effect. Therein, 'cause' (hetu) refers to the condition (paccaya). 'Effect' (phala) refers to the conditioned (paccayuppanna), as stated by "eye-element" and so forth. The causal state of the mind-element (mano-dhātu) and mental-object element (dhamma-dhātu) over the mind-consciousness element (mano-viññāṇa-dhātu) should also be applied as appropriate. Or, the causal state of that mind-element should be applied by way of the mind being the door.

"By way of all" means by way of the thirty-five elements such as the light-element (ābhā-dhātu) mentioned before. Because a non-ultimate nature can never be included within ultimate natures (paramattha), it is said, "which exist by way of their own nature (sabhāva)." Since moonlight, sunlight, and so forth are merely color (vaṇṇa), it is said, "the light-element is indeed only the visible-data element (rūpa-dhātu)." Intending that the mode to be grasped as the basis of lust is the beautiful sign (subha-nimitta), it is not said "only visible data and so forth," but rather "connected with visible data and so forth." Even in the absence of being a basis for lust, the second method is stated: "the beautiful element (subha-dhātu) which is the object of wholesome resultant (kusala-vipāka)." The cruelty-element (vihiṃsā-dhātu) is volition (cetanā) or the desire to harm others. Non-cruelty (avihiṃsā) is compassion (karuṇā).

"Both" refers to the mental-object element and the mind-consciousness element. Regarding the low and so forth, according to the previous method, the eye and so forth which are despised are called 'low' (hīna); those which are esteemed are 'superior' (paṇīta); and those which are neither much despised nor much esteemed are 'middle' (majjhima). Thus, it should be understood that the middle element is stated by extracting it from the 'low dyad' (hīna-duka) that appears in the Khandha Vibhaṅga. Although the consciousness element is divided by way of the six consciousness elements, because it is said, "by taking the consciousness element, the mind-element is already taken due to its being the precursor and the follower..."
47:
The teacher of the Saṅgaha says that, in brief, the consciousness element (viññāṇa-dhātu) is just a summary of the seven consciousness elements. Because there are many elements such as the eye-element, and because each of those elements has various aspects, the world of many elements and various elements (anekadhātu nānādhātu loko) was taught; thus it is said, "merely the distinction of the eighteen elements."

It is written in the Commentary: "By the distinction of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and mind-consciousness elements." In that text, it is not intended to connect the words eye and so on solely with the word 'dhātu' without the word 'viññāṇa', because the intention is to state the distinction of consciousness which has various natures. If connected with the word 'viññāṇa-dhātu', the mention of 'mind' (mano) should not be made twice, because there are not two mind-consciousness elements. Or, it should be said "eye... body-consciousness, mind-consciousness, and mind-element," because a dvanda compound cannot be formed if the members are not of equal status. However, the reading here should be: "by the distinction of eye... body-consciousness, mind, and mind-consciousness elements."

The teachings on the aggregates (khandha) and bases (āyatana) are brief teachings, and the teaching on the faculties (indriya) is a detailed teaching; in view of both of these, the teaching on the elements (dhātu) is a teaching that is neither too brief nor too detailed. Alternatively, the teaching on elements in the Suttanta Bhājanīya is an extremely brief teaching, and the teaching to be given by way of the elements ending with 'many elements and various elements' such as the light-element is an extremely detailed teaching; in view of those two, this teaching on elements is said to be "neither too brief nor too detailed."

The eye-element should be seen like a drum-head because it is the support for consciousness, just as the drum-head is the support for sound. By these similes, just as non-living sounds and so forth arise when non-living drum-heads, drum-sticks, and so forth meet, so too, because non-living eye-consciousness and so forth arise when non-living eyes, visible objects, and so forth meet, the causes and effects are mere elements; this shows the absence of a doer (kāraka) and an experiencer (vedaka).

"Like a precursor and a follower" means they should be seen as some non-living things being precursors and followers of another non-living thing. Alternatively, although the state of being a precursor and a follower does not exist in the eye-consciousness and so forth which do not outlast their own moment, even while the mind-element itself has not outlasted its own moment, they should be seen as precursor and follower because of their occurrence in preceding and succeeding times. They should be seen as being like an arrow or a stake because of their connection with the three types of suffering. Expectation (āsā) itself is suffering (āsā-dukkha), or the distress caused by expectation is suffering. Indeed, because perception (saññā) perceives even the non-existent 'suffering of suffering' (dukkha-dukkha) as beautiful and so forth, it causes that suffering of expectation and the distress of that expectation through the non-fulfillment of the desired beauty and so forth.
48:
It causes distress (vighāta) because of the non-accomplishment of the desired beauty (subha) and so forth. Formations (saṅkhāra) have kamma as their primary cause; thus it is said, "because of depositing in rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi)," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "because of being followed by the suffering of birth (jāti-dukkha)," it is because the suffering of birth, which is produced by oneself, follows along. Birth (jāti) which arises due to the cause of existence (bhava) is indeed the suffering of birth. The aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha), though appearing like a lotus, is actually like a razor-wheel (khuracakka); appearing in the form of a woman and so forth, it produces various kinds of dangers and misfortunes. All things such as lust (rāga) which cause harm, and birth (jāti) and so forth, should be viewed as the Deathless (amata/Nirvāṇa) and so forth, which are their opposites, because they are like poison, are restless, and are accompanied by danger.

By the words "either by releasing or by grasping another," it shows the similarity to a monkey; just as a monkey, having released the branch it was holding, cannot remain in the air, so too the mind, after releasing a grasped object, cannot arise without grasping another object. A bad horse that does not reach docility even when struck to the bone is called a "scoundrel horse" (assakhaḷuṅka). A dancer who has entered the stage is called a "stage-actor" (raṅganaṭa).

By the words "dependent on the eye and forms," the designation of singular and plural in the doors (dvāra) and objects (ārammaṇa) is because the door existing in a single continuity and the objects existing in various continuities are the conditions for the consciousness existing in a single continuity, and because they are of a single nature and various natures.

In the phrase "in all things (sabba-dhammesu)," the word "sabba" (all) should be understood as standing in a partial "all," referring to the aforementioned consciousness or the object, by the power of the context (adhikāra). In the explanation of the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu-niddesa), it is said: "Immediately after the eye-consciousness element has arisen and ceased, the mind element arises; immediately after the mind element has arisen and ceased, consciousness (mind-consciousness element) arises." Just as the mind element arises immediately after the eye-consciousness element, all consciousnesses that arise until another mind element (pañcadvārāvajjana) arises are taken as one and so preached; this meaning can also be obtained. If this is so, the fault that the mind element arising immediately after the mind-consciousness element must become a mind-consciousness element no longer exists. The demonstration of the sequence of the five-fold sense-consciousness elements and the mind element is for the purpose of showing the state of the mind-consciousness element of the mind, which is delimited by its contrary nature and its place of arising, and not merely by its immediate arising. Therefore, it is appropriate to show them by bringing them into unity in that contrary nature. Even if not brought into unity, by showing one (santīraṇa) that has that contrary nature, it should be understood that all others of that nature are also shown by way of generality (sāmañña). When the mind-consciousness element is combined by the word "pi" (also), it follows: "Immediately after the mind-consciousness element also, consciousness arises... the consciousness element born from that..."
49:
If it is asked: "By the term 'mind-consciousness element' (manoviññāṇadhātu), when encompassing the mind-consciousness element, is the mind element (pañcadvārāvajjana) that arises immediately after the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) excluded?" The answer is: No, because it is not established that such a mind element is not a mind-consciousness element. Indeed, the very word that is questioned cannot serve to exclude that mind element from the name of mind-consciousness element.

By the mention of the two "minds" in the phrase "of the mind element also, of the mind-consciousness element also," the mutually contrary nature of these two is shown. By that very statement, it should be understood that the state of the mind-consciousness element for the adverting (āvajjana) which is the mind element is prohibited. The nature of that mind element, which is contrary to the mind-consciousness element, has been preached in such passages as: "In all things, the first attention (paṭhamasamannāhāra) arises." The phrase "all those also" is merely a primary illustration. For not only the consciousnesses ending with impulsion (javana) are the mind-consciousness element; registration (tadārammaṇa) and life-continuum (bhavaṅga), etc., are also the mind-consciousness element. Thus, having shown the entire mind-consciousness element by way of its distinct nature from the five-fold sense-consciousness elements and the mind element, and wishing to show again the mind-consciousness element of impulsion which is pre-eminent by way of the mind-door, he said: "Dependent on the mind," and so forth. If, in this context, only the consciousnesses ending with impulsion by way of the six doors were taken as the "mind-consciousness element," it would result in an incomplete teaching (sāvasesadesanā) because death (cuti), rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), and life-continuum (bhavaṅga) would not be included. Therefore, the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated. Alternatively, it should be understood that other consciousnesses (bhavaṅga, tadārammaṇa) which have characteristics similar to the consciousnesses occurring in the six doors are also shown as the "mind-consciousness element."

In the place where the word "paṭicca" (dependent on) appears—in such places as "the mind experiences the range and domain of these [five faculties]," it is appropriate to treat the adverting (āvajjana) separately. However, just as in the passages "dependent on the eye," etc., the adverting is also treated as being dependent on the eye, etc., by combining them with the word "ca" (and), so too in the place where "dependent on the mind" appears, it means that only the adverting dependent on the life-continuum, which is called the mind-door, should be taken.

## 4. Sacca-vibhaṅga
## 1. Suttanta-bhājanīya
## Uddesa-vaṇṇanā
"Sāsanakkama" refers to either the Noble Truths (Ariya-sacca) or the teaching of the Noble Truths. Indeed, the entire Dispensation (Sāsana), which is the word of the Blessed One, is never apart from the Four Noble Truths; therefore, it proceeds within the Four Noble Truths. Alternatively, the Dispensation consisting of virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā) proceeds within these four truths. Thus, it is called "kama" because it is the place where it proceeds. What proceeds? The Dispensation proceeds. Because it is the place where the Dispensation proceeds, the truths are called "Sāsanakkama," meaning the places where the Dispensation occurs and resides. The teaching that expounds these truths is also called "Sāsanakkama" by way of metaphorical usage.

"Tatha" (Real) means the state of having that very nature of suffering and so forth. "Avitatha" (Not unreal) means the absence of a false nature. "Anaññatha" (Not otherwise) means being devoid of any other mode. The state of being undesirable due to the nature of suffering and the cause of that suffering is the meaning of "pīḷana" (oppression). In both cases, burning or the association with the heat of defilements is the meaning of "santāpa" (torment). This is the distinction between these meanings. Alternatively, the harming of the person in whom it resides is called "pīḷana" (oppression). The intense burning, which is the sharp nature of the state itself, is called "santāpa" (torment). Among these four meanings, "pīḷana" (oppression) is the mode that is manifest by the very functional nature of suffering. The remaining meanings are modes that become manifest through the vision of the truths of origin (samudaya), the path (magga), and cessation (nirodha), respectively. This is the mutual distinction among the four meanings.

Spreading with great delight in various existences and sense objects, thereby creating a mass of suffering and producing suffering, is called "āyūhana" (accumulating). Alternatively, suffering is called "āya" because it comes from the origin (samudaya). Producing that suffering is "āyūhana." This is the mode manifest by its own nature. It is called "nidāna" (source) because it bestows suffering. It means it originates suffering as if making one accept it, saying, "This is that suffering." This meaning of "nidāna" becomes manifest through the vision of suffering. The meanings of "saṃyoga" (bond) and "palibodha" (obstacle) become manifest through the vision of the truths of cessation and the path. These should be understood as the mode of bonding to saṃsāra and the mode of obstructing the path.

In this Nibbāna, beings escape from saṃsāra. Or, because it is the state of relinquishing all acquisitions (upadhi), it is itself escaped and disconnected from all conditioned things (saṅkhata). Therefore, it is called "nissaraṇa" (escape). This is the mode of the truth of cessation manifest by its own nature. The meanings of "viveka" (seclusion), "asaṅkhata" (unconditioned), and "amata" (deathless) are modes that become manifest through the vision of the truths of origin, the path, and suffering. Alternatively, they are the natures of the exhaustion of origin, the absence of conditions, and indestructibility. Departing from saṃsāra is called "niyyāna" (leading out). This is the mode of the truth of the path manifest by its own function. The remaining meanings become manifest through the vision of the truths of origin, cessation, and suffering. Among those meanings, the very attainment of Nibbāna by cutting off the origin (samudaya) that obstructs the path is the meaning of "hetu" (cause).
51:
Taking Nibbāna as the cause is called the sense of cause (*hetvaṭṭha*). Because the Path is led by wisdom, seeing Nibbāna or seeing the Four Truths is called the sense of seeing (*dassanaṭṭha*). Because the factors of the Path exercise predominance over associated states in the seeing of the Four Truths and in the calming of the heat of the suffering of defilements, it is called the Path's sense of predominance (*adhipateyyaṭṭha*). Alternatively, the factors of the Path are predominant over the object; according to the expression 'states having the Path as predominant' (*maggādhipatino dhammā*), that mode of theirs is the sense of predominance. Thus and so forth, the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta) spoke. In that text, the sense of realization (*abhisamayaṭṭha*) means the sense that is to be fully realized. Or, the sense that is the object of the knowledge of realization is *abhisamayaṭṭha*. Or, the mode of occurrence of the knowledge of realization is *abhisamayaṭṭha*. That sense should be understood here as being shown through oppression (*pīḷana*) and so forth, which are to be fully realized.

That which is contemptible (*kucchita*) and empty (*kha*) is called suffering (*dukkha*). In words such as *samāgamo* and *sametaṃ*, the sense of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) cannot be obtained by using the words *āgama* or *eta* alone without the prefix *saṃ-*; it is obtained only when *saṃ-* is used, hence it is said to 'indicate conjunction.' The same applies to the terms *uppannaṃ* and *uditaṃ*. The word *aya* indicates a cause, just as the word *hetu* does; it is called *aya* because it occurs (*ayati*) by bringing about its own fruit. Or, it is *aya* because the fruit comes (*eti*) from this cause. The cause of the arising of suffering in conjunction with causes such as ignorance is called origin (*samudaya*). Here, the prefixes used separately, together with the root, indicate the sense of conjunction and the sense of arising. This is because they qualify the action.

It is called cessation (*nirodha*) because there is no obstruction (*rodha*)—meaning bond or suffering—in this Nibbāna. By this statement, the nature of Nibbāna as being secluded from suffering is shown. When that Nibbāna is fully attained, there is no longer any obstruction for the person who has attained it. This is because they have attained the cessation which is the opposite of the obstruction known as the constant occurrence [of the aggregates]. In this sense also, the compound should be formed as 'the absence of obstruction in this [Nibbāna] is *nirodha*.' However, the absence of suffering is for the person, not merely a quality of Nibbāna itself. Since only non-arising (*anuppāda*) is cessation, it is called 'cessation as non-arising' (*anuppāda-nirodha*). It refers to non-occurrence in future existences and so forth, not to dissolution (*bhaṅga*). Therefore, rejecting the word *nirodha* in the sense of dissolution, one takes the word *nirodha* in the sense of non-arising. In this sense, by attributing the name of the effect (non-arising cessation) to the cause (Nibbāna), it is said that 'the cause of cessation is cessation.'

There is also the practice (*paṭipadā*) for a person to reach the cessation of suffering. One might object: 'Is not that practice itself the reaching of the cessation of suffering? Therefore, it is inappropriate to say that the practice is the way to that reaching of the cessation of suffering.' No, it is appropriate. Because it is spoken of in terms of the person's attainment (*patti*) of realization, and in terms of the factors of the Path, which are the causal states for that person's realization, as the practice (*paṭipadā*). Although realization (*sacchikiriya*) and the states that perform realization (*sacchikaraṇa-dhamma*) are not different in essence, they are presented as distinct by distinguishing between the person's act of realization and the states that realize. Or, the culmination of reaching the cessation of suffering is the Fruit (*phala*). Therefore, it should be understood that the practice is the way to the Fruit, which is the reaching of the cessation of suffering.

In the Pali phrase 'The Noble Ones, such as the Buddha, fully realized [the truths],' just as in the statement 'The Bodhisatta went to Rājagaha,' the name 'Buddha'—which is acquired at the time of realizing the truths—is used metaphorically for the period prior to that realization. This is because those Noble Ones, beginning with the Buddha, fully realized them through the four Paths. In the phrase 'The truths that are to be fully realized by the Noble Ones are the Noble Truths,' it should be noted that in the preceding term *ariyapaṭivijjhitabba*, the subsequent word *paṭivijjhitabba* is elided. In the statement 'The Noble Ones [fully realize] this truth,' the Blessed One said 'this truth' (*imaṃ*) in the singular, bringing it into a single unity by way of the sense of what is to be fully realized. In the Commentary, however, it appears as 'these truths' (*imāni*). Because the Blessed One is called 'Noble' (*ariya*), the truths of that Blessed One are called 'Noble Truths' (*ariyasaccāni*). This is because they were realized by the Blessed One himself, and because the Blessed One himself [taught them].
52:
The detailed exposition (niddesa) has been made. Alternatively, the culmination of attaining the cessation of suffering is the fruit (phala), and the practice leading to that cessation of suffering should be understood as the cause (paṭipadā).

In the phrase "The Noble Ones (ariyas), beginning with the Buddha, penetrate [the truths]," the designation "Buddha and so forth," which arises at the time of penetration, is applied metaphorically even to the preceding period before becoming a Buddha, just as it is said, "The Buddha went to Rājagaha" [referring to the Bodhisatta]. This is because those individuals, beginning with the Buddha, penetrate the truths through the four paths. In the phrase "The truths to be penetrated by the Noble Ones are the Noble Truths (ariyasaccāni)," it should be understood that the latter part of the compound "paṭivijjhitabba" has been elided from the preceding term "ariyapaṭivijjhitabba." When the Blessed One says "this truth," He uses the word "imaṃ" (this) by bringing it into a state of unity in the sense of that which is to be penetrated.

Therefore, because the Tathāgata is a Noble One (ariya), His truths are called "Noble Truths" (ariyasaccāni). This is because He Himself attained them, He Himself proclaimed them, and only because of His proclamation can others also attain them; thus, they belong to Him. Also, in the phrase "Because they bring about the state of a Noble One," it should be understood that the latter part of the compound is elided as before, meaning "The truths that bring about the state of a Noble One are the Noble Truths." In the context of "True Truths," they are called "Noble" (ariya) because they are to be realized in an unerring manner. Alternatively, this term should be understood as the designation of the Noble Ones, which is unerring and non-deceptive.

In the phrase "the characteristic of oppressing," the state of being the cause of the suffering of suffering is "oppression" (bādhanā), or it is the oppression by arising and vanishing. The occurrence of various sufferings in existence, such as through birth and so forth, or through eye-disease and so forth, is itself the tormenting of a person; that tormenting is the function (rasa) of the Truth of Suffering. Between saṃsāra and nibbāna, because it is perceived by knowledge as the process of occurrence (pavatti), that occurrence is the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of the Truth of Suffering. From this craving (samudaya), suffering originates; it arises in rebirth; because it links and joins the previous life with the subsequent life, it is called the source (pabhava).

As it is said, "As long as the latent tendency of craving is not uprooted, this suffering arises again and again," thus, causing repeated arising and making it uninterrupted is the function [of the Truth of Origin]. Preventing the escape from existence is called the obstacle (palibodha). The subsiding of all suffering through the nature of the destruction of lust and so forth is called peace (santi). "The function of deathlessness" (accutirasa) means having the function of the attainment of deathlessness. Alternatively, the absence of passing away (falling) is metaphorically spoken of as a function, meaning it has the function of non-passing away. It should be understood as non-passing away, not abandoning its own nature, and being without change. Because it is void of the signs of the five aggregates and is thus perceived by knowledge as being without form, signlessness (animitta) is the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of the Truth of Cessation. Being the means of escape from the prison of saṃsāra by cutting off the latent tendencies is called the departure (niyyāna). Because it is perceived by knowledge as the mind's emergence from the signs of formations and the misery of the round of rebirth, emergence (vuṭṭhāna) is the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of the Truth of the Path.
53:
Illusion (māyā), which appears as gold though it is not gold, is said to be the perversion (viparītatā) of an object due to its actual nature. A mirage (marīci), which appears as water, is empty to those who approach it; because not even a trace of an object is found in it, it is called deceptive (visāṃvādikā). The nature that is contrary or opposite to the self-illusion of a mirage is the state of being true and non-perverted (tacchā-aviparīta-bhūta-bhāva).

Noble knowledge (ariya-ñāṇa) is knowledge that grasps without error. Through that noble knowledge, penetrative knowledge (paṭivedha-ñāṇa) and reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) should be taken. The nature that is the object of those knowledges should be understood as the state of being penetrated and the state of being an object. The characteristic of fire is heat. That heat, even if there are differences in fuel such as wood in certain places, never at any time becomes deceptive, perverted, or false by being anything other than hot.

The nature of birth (jāti) and so forth, as taught in the passage, 'Subject to illness, subject to old age, and also subject to death,' is the natural order of the world (loka-pakati). People say that the upward tallness of humans, the horizontal length of some animals, the cessation of growth upon reaching maturity, and so forth, are also the customs of the world. Among the terms 'true' (taccha), 'non-perverted' (aviparīta), and 'real' (bhūta), the last one, bhūta-bhāva, is called 'suchness' (tathatā). The first, taccha-bhāva, is called 'unfalseness' (avitathatā). The middle one, aviparīta-bhāva, is called 'not-otherness' (anaññathatā). This is the distinction between these terms.

Why is it said, 'There is no other oppressor besides suffering'? Is it not that craving (taṇhā) also oppresses because it is the cause of suffering, just as birth (jāti) is? No, because it is taken separately as the origin (pabhava) of the oppressing suffering. Or rather, like birth and so forth, only the basis of suffering and the state of 'suffering-as-suffering' (dukkha-dukkhatā) are called 'oppressing'; the state of being the origin of suffering is not called 'oppressing.' Therefore, there is no occasion for craving, which is taken as the origin, to be considered an oppressor. Thus it is said, 'There is no other oppressor besides suffering.'

The 'certainty of being an oppressor' (bādhakatta-niyāma) means the confirmation of the state of being an oppressor in two ways: 'Suffering is indeed an oppressor' and 'Only suffering is an oppressor.' The phrase 'It does not occur from anything else excluding that craving' means that although the remaining defilements, unwholesome states, and wholesome roots accompanied by taints (sāsava) are causes of suffering, they cannot be causes of suffering without craving. However, even without those other states, craving can be a cause of suffering—such as being unwholesome without being wholesome, or being of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara) without being of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), etc.—because craving is the producer of suffering.

The 'nature of true deliverance' (taccha-niyyāna-bhāva) means that this Path possesses the nature of true deliverance as confirmed in two ways. It is not false like the wrong path due to perversion, nor is it untrue like the mundane path which is uncertain in reaching a happy destination. Therefore, the Path is called the state having the nature of true deliverance. Because it has such a nature of true deliverance, it is called 'taccha-niyyānabhāvatta.' Since the nature of being true, non-perverted, and real has been stated as confirmed in two ways for all the Truths, it is said, 'Thus, truth and non-perversion,' and so forth.

The extraction of the appropriate meanings of the Truths is called 'atthuddhāra.' Alternatively, stating the meanings that have arisen and then extracting the desired meaning is called 'atthuddhāra.' The 'Truth of Abstinence' (virati-sacca) is evident only in abstinence from false speech; in other abstinences, the name 'Truth' is not prominent. The wrong view held as 'Only this view is true, any other is empty' is called the 'Truth of Views' (diṭṭhi-sacca). Nibbāna has the nature of not perishing; the Noble Ones know that Nibbāna as a reality. Because it has such an imperishable nature, Nibbāna is called the 'Ultimate Truth' (paramattha-sacca). Knowing Nibbāna and the Path leading to Nibbāna in detail is called 'Penetration' (paṭivedha), which is the cause of non-dispute. Therefore, regarding both Nibbāna and the Noble Path, it is said in this verse: 'The Truth is real, it is consistent, it is only one, there is no second; regarding that Truth, beings do not dispute.'

By the passage beginning 'This is not suffering,' the non-perversion of states such as birth in being the Noble Truth of Suffering is shown. By the passage 'There is no other suffering,' the state of the Noble Truth of Suffering in birth and so forth...
54:
The extraction of the appropriate meanings of the word 'Sacca' (Truth), or the extraction of the intended meaning after stating the possible meanings, is called 'Atthuddhāra' (Extraction of Meaning). 'Virati-sacca' (Truth of Abstinence) refers to abstinence from false speech (musāvāda). This is because the word 'Sacca' is not prominently established in other types of abstinence. The view held as 'This alone is the truth, any other is empty' is called 'Diṭṭhi-sacca' (Truth of Views). As it is said, 'Nibbāna is of an unfailing nature; the Noble Ones know that Nibbāna as the truth,' Nibbāna is called 'Paramattha-sacca' (Ultimate Truth) because of its unfailing nature. The penetrative knowledge of that Nibbāna and the Path (Magga) that leads to Nibbāna is the cause of non-dispute; therefore, in the verse:

'Indeed, the truth is one, there is no second,
Knowing which the people do not dispute,'

both Nibbāna and the Path are referred to as 'Sacca'.

By the statement that there is no possibility of the claim 'This Dhamma is not the Noble Truth of Suffering (Dukkha-ariya-sacca),' the non-perverted (aviparīta) nature of birth (jāti) and so forth as the Noble Truth of Suffering is shown. By the statement that there is no possibility of the claim 'Another Dhamma is the Noble Truth of Suffering,' the fixed nature (niyata) of the status of the Noble Truth of Suffering in birth and so forth is shown. Even if someone, for some reason, were to come with such a mind, the phrase 'There is no possibility that one would come saying, "I will point out this..."' is stated to show that there is no one capable of pointing it out either by way of reasoning or by way of pointing out their own doctrine. The non-existence of birth etc. in any other way than as suffering, and the non-existence of any other Dhamma that has such a nature of suffering apart from birth etc., is what is meant here by the 'absence of possibility' (ṭhānābhāva). If someone wishes to come and speak, let them come, but there is no ground (reason) to sustain their doctrine; this is the meaning of this Sutta. This method is the same in the second Sutta as well. In that second Sutta, the arrival at and the manifestation of the suffering of birth etc. is the first aspect; being the cause of that suffering is the second aspect (Dukkha-samudaya); being the peace of both that suffering and its origin is the third aspect; and being that which leads to Nibbāna is the fourth aspect.

For one who desires Nibbāna, there is no other duty to be performed apart from the functions such as full understanding (parijānanā); or, there is no other function of knowing the nature of things (dhamma-ñāṇa) apart from this; and the things to be fully understood (pariññeyya) etc. have only these four as their ultimate limit; thus, only four are taught. By virtue of those who habitually see the danger in craving, it is said, 'The five aggregates etc., which are the objects of craving, have only these four as their ultimate limit.' Likewise, by virtue of those who habitually see the fault in suffering—whether it be the five cords of sensual pleasure, all objects of sensuality, or the three realms of existence, which are the objects of attachment (ālaya)—it is said, 'Attachment (ālaya) etc. have only these four as their ultimate limit.'

By the phrase 'with suffering together with its cause,' the ground for a sense of urgency (saṃvega-vatthu) is shown by demonstrating the uninterrupted occurrence of suffering.
55:
It is called 'Anubodha' (Subsequent Knowledge) because it is not known all at once like the Knowledge of Penetration (Paṭivedha-ñāṇa/Magga-ñāṇa), but is known repeatedly and successively. Alternatively, the knowledge that follows oral tradition (anussava), reflection on reasons (ākārapariwitakka), and acceptance of views after pondering (diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti) is 'Anubodha'. This is because that Anubodha-ñāṇa cannot know through direct experience but takes hold by way of conceptualization through oral tradition and so forth. 'By way of function' (kiccato) means because of functions such as full understanding (parijānana). Through the performance of those functions, the Four Noble Truths become clear to that person. For one whose mind recoils from formations (saṅkhāra) through insight that repeatedly views the turning away from the round (vivaṭṭānupassanā), the Path Knowledge (Magga-ñāṇa) that arises takes the unconditioned Nibbāna, which is the escape from suffering, as its object and fully understands suffering; it abandons craving directed towards suffering; and it realizes Nibbāna just as the sun, with its light, dispels darkness and reveals light. That Path (Sammā-diṭṭhi), which arises together with the seven path factors such as Right Thought (Sammā-saṅkappa), also develops itself just as the sun makes itself manifest. Mundane knowledge occurring within the signs of formations cannot perform all these functions because it has not emerged from those formations. Therefore, that Path Knowledge, which performs these four functions, clarifies suffering and the rest by removing delusion regarding the Four Noble Truths; thus it is said, 'He sees all four truths.'

If it is asked whether the statement 'He also sees the origin of suffering' is said with reference to seeing at a different time after seeing suffering? The answer is no. This is because this Sutta was cited by the Elder Gavampati to establish the investigation that one who sees one truth also sees the other three, as in: 'Friends, he who sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering,' and so forth. This is because the seeing of the other three is joined whenever each truth is seen. Otherwise, in the case of gradual realization, the truth seen first would not be seen later, and thus it would not be appropriate to join them by saying that one who sees the origin also sees suffering and so forth. By seeing the mere heap of pure formations without a self, the obsession of personality belief (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) is prevented. According to the word, 'Kaccāna, for one who sees the origin of the world as it really is with right wisdom, the view of non-existence (uccheda-diṭṭhi) in the world does not occur,' seeing the origin removes the obsession of annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi) by way of seeing the uninterrupted connection of cause and effect. According to the word, 'For one who sees the cessation of the world... the view of existence (sassata-diṭṭhi) in the world does not occur,' seeing cessation prevents the obsession of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) by way of seeing the cessation of the effect due to the cessation of the cause. By seeing the Path, which is the direct vision of the cause of purification, one abandons the obsession of the view of the inefficacy of action (akiriya-diṭṭhi), such as 'There is no action of one's own, no action of another, no human effort.' The view of non-causality (ahetuka-diṭṭhi), such as 'There is no cause, no condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled without cause and condition... there is no cause... for purification; beings are purified without cause and condition,' should also be understood as included here by the mention of the view of the inefficacy of action. For that [ahetuka-diṭṭhi] is also abandoned by seeing the Path, which is the cause of purification.
56:
The knowledge of the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) can prevent wrong practices regarding the result, because it sees the nature of impermanence (adhuvādi) and such of the phenomena of suffering (mind and matter) which are the results of the origin (samudaya).

Those who hold the view of a Creator (Issara-vādī) say, "The Lord (Creator) causes the world to arise and to cease." Those who hold the view of Primal Matter (Padhāna-vādī) say, "The world becomes manifest from Padhāna (primal nature) and dissolves back into that same Padhāna." Those who hold the view of Time (Kāla-vādī) say, "The world arises and ceases only by the power of time." Those who hold the view of Nature (Sabhāva-vādī) say, "The world arises and perishes according to its own inherent nature (sabhāva)."

By the word 'ādi' (and so forth), one should understand the wrong grasp of non-causes as causes, such as "The world arises because of atoms (aṇu)," or "All results are due only to causes performed in the past (pubbekata-hetu)." This includes the assumption that liberation exists in the immaterial world (arūpa-loka), as held by Udaka the son of Rāma and Āḷāra the hermit, or that liberation (mokkha) exists at the summit of the world, as held by the Nigaṇṭhas.

By the word 'ādi', one should also understand such views as the non-arising of Padhāna, the self (atta) devoid of qualities remaining within itself, dwelling in a realm similar to Brahmā, and the view that Nirvana exists in the present life (diṭṭhadhammanibbāna-vāda). Here, "devoid of qualities" means being separated from the nine qualities of the self: intellect (buddhi), pleasure (sukha), pain (dukkha), desire (icchā), aversion (dosa), effort (payatta), merit (dhamma), demerit (adhamma), and mental formations (saṅkhāra); this is the doctrine of the teacher Kaṇāda. The practice of assuming that there is no liberation apart from gratifying the sense faculties or looking at the face of a son, and acting accordingly, is called the devotion to sensual pleasures (kāmasukhallikānuyoga).

In the twelve internal and external bases (āyatana), there are thirty-six diversifications of craving (taṇhā-vicarita) consisting of twelve groups of three, by way of craving for sensual pleasures (kāma-taṇhā), craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā), and craving for non-existence (vibhava-taṇhā). Alternatively, these are the cravings spoken of without considering the division of time, according to the method found in the Khuddakavatthu Vibhaṅga. Although the requisites of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) such as the basis of success through investigation (vīmaṃsiddhipāda) are taught separately due to their various functions, they are identical in ultimate sense and are thus included within the truth of the path (magga-sacca) headed by Right View.

The three factors such as the thought of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka) are distinct in the mundane moment because they are associated with non-greed, loving-kindness, and compassion. However, in the path moment, although they are called three, they are actually one (Right Intention) because they absolutely cut off greed, ill-will, and cruelty.

This same method applies to Right Speech and the others. When there is fewness of wishes (appicchatā) and contentment (santuṭṭhitā), Right Livelihood (sammā-ājīva) arises; therefore, it should be understood that they are included within that Right Livelihood. Whether in another life or for the sake of life itself, the virtues dear to the Noble Ones (ariyaka-kanta-sīla), such as Right Speech, are not to be transgressed by the Noble Ones; by undertaking them, they are grasped by the hand of faith (saddhā). Since that hand of faith is already taken, the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) and the power of faith (saddhā-bala), which are not different from that faith, are included in those virtues. Because of the presence of the faculty of faith, the power of faith, and the basis of success through desire (chandiddhipāda), virtue exists; thus, because those three are taken by the three types of virtue (Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood), they are included in the truth of the path. "Concentration of mind" (citta-samādhi) refers to the basis of success through mind (cittiddhipāda). For, in the passage "Develop the mind and wisdom," by heading with the mind...
57:
When it is said, "Concentration (samādhi) has been spoken of," the mind should also be mentioned by heading with concentration. Due to the development of the basis of success through mind (cittiddhipāda), concentration also becomes superlative; therefore, instead of directly saying 'cittiddhipāda' as in the case of 'vīmaṃsiddhipāda' and others, it is called "concentration of mind" (citta-samādhi) here. Because of the statement, "The body of one who has joy (pīti) becomes tranquil; one whose body is tranquil experiences happiness (sukha); the mind of one who has happiness becomes concentrated (samādhi)," joy and tranquility are factors that benefit concentration; thus, they are included by the taking of concentration. Equanimity (upekkhā) is also included by way of Right Concentration because it benefits concentration and has a function similar to concentration.

Suffering is like a burden because it is oppressive. It is like a famine because it is harrassing. Because Nirvana is the supreme happiness, it is like an abundance of food (subhikkha). Because it is undesirable and accompanied by doubt and fear, suffering has similes such as an enemy, a poison tree, a danger, and this shore.

"Tathattha" means by way of true nature, or by way of being fully understood (pariññeyya). By this statement, it is shown that the two Noble Truths (origin and path) might be suffering in some sense but not the Noble Truth of Suffering, or they might be the Noble Truth but not suffering. The words such as 'suffering' that follow the term 'Noble Truth' (ariya-sacca) denote the state of being fully understood and so forth. For this reason, referring to the word 'suffering' without regard to the term 'Noble Truth', the inclusion of factors associated with the path and the fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala) is mentioned in the first section; and with regard to it, the inclusion is mentioned in the fourth section.

Regarding the origin (samudaya) and others: defilements other than craving are only 'origin' but not the 'Noble Truth'. The cessation of formations and the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) are only 'cessation' but not the 'Noble Truth'. Path factors other than the Ariyan Path are only 'path' but not the 'Noble Truth'. This is how the connection should be made. Although suffering has the nature of being felt, there is no being or person who feels it; it is merely a conventional expression to say "one feels suffering" when it is occurring due to its own conditions. The same applies to the other truths.

By the phrase "Only the act exists," it refers to the origin (samudaya) itself, or the fact that the origin is the condition for suffering. Where it should be said "maggō atthi," it should be understood that the 'o' sound has been elided as "maggamatthi." "Gamaka" means the goer. Because they are associated with taints (āsava), they are unlovely; therefore, cessation (nirodha) and the path (magga) are indeed lovely (subha). Although the three truths such as suffering can figuratively be the origin and so forth, they cannot be cessation; nor can cessation be suffering and so forth; thus, there is no mutual identity, which is why it is said, "Or they are empty of cessation," and so forth.

"The absence of suffering in the origin" means the absence of the result of renewed existence in the craving that leads to rebirth. Or, unlike the views of the Naturalists (Pakativādī) where transformations remain latent before appearing and exist only as primal nature, the suffering associated with the origin does not exist in the form of the origin; thus it is said, "There is no suffering in the origin."
58:
In this way, because it is meant that suffering associated with the origin does not exist in the state of the origin, it is said: "Because of the absence of suffering in the origin." Just as in the view of the Pakativādins (Proponents of Nature), nature (pakati) exists as if pregnant with the effect, remaining in its natural state through unmanifested transformations such as the great superior faculties and specific elements; in this Dispensation, the cause is not "pregnant" with the effect. This is the meaning. To clarify the lack of inherence (samavāya) between suffering/origin and cessation/path, it is said: "The effect does not exist as inherent in the cause," and so forth.

In that statement, in this world, the connection of distinct and evident things that produces knowledge and designation—such as cloth in threads, a pot in pot-shards, a mat in biraṇa grass, or a dyad (dviaṇuka) in two atoms (aṇu)—is called inherence (samavāya). Through that inherence, the effect, the dyad, exists in the two causal atoms as if combined into one; and in three atoms, a triad (tiaṇuka), and so on up to the masses of the Great Earth, Great Water, Great Fire, and Great Air, the effect exists inherent in its own causes. This is what the Samavāyavādins (Proponents of Inherence) say. By saying this, it implies that one large-scale effect exists inherent in its immeasurable causes, and is not empty, as if pregnant with the causes contained within it. In this Dispensation, however, because there is no inherence, the cause does not exist in the effect; the effect is empty of the cause. This is the meaning.

"Because of the state of occurrence" means because of the state of the continuous occurrence of saṃsāra. By the phrase "by way of the four types of nutriment," it includes the four types of nutriment as well as the various phenomena resulting from those nutriments. The divisions such as delighting in form (rūpābhinandana) occur by way of the aggregates such as the form aggregate (rūpakkhandha), or by way of objects. Because it is clung to by the graspings (upādāna), it is called upādi, which is the group of the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha). Nibbāna is the escape from those aggregates of clinging, and because it is their subsiding and peace, it is designated in two ways: "Nibbāna element with residue remaining" (sa-upādisesa-nibbānadhātu) and "Nibbāna element without residue remaining" (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu), based on the existence of a residue until the final consciousness, and the absence of residue thereafter.

Some say: "Right View and Right Intention are insight (vipassanā), and the remaining six path factors are serenity (samatha)." Since virtue (sīla) is also a supporter of serenity, it is their intention that virtue is included in the taking of serenity. Alternatively, the path obtained by way of the two vehicles of serenity and insight is to be understood as being called "serenity and insight" by way of its origin. "Because of being partial" (sappadesattā) means because of being a portion of the virtue-aggregate (sīlakkhandha) and so forth. For the virtue-aggregate and others include all mundane and supramundane virtue, whereas the Noble Path is exclusively supramundane; thus, it is a portion of them.

Right Effort is like a companion who stoops down, because of the common function of uplifting. Mindfulness is like a companion who stands providing his shoulder, because of the common function of making the mind steady by not allowing the object to float away. "Because of being of the same class" (sajātito) means it is included by way of the same class of concentration (samādhijāta) among the various types of concentration, such as those with initial and sustained application.
59:
It means because of having the same nature of concentration (*samādhi-jāti*). *Kriyato* means they are grasped by a mode appropriate to concentration. Because of that very mode appropriate to concentration, it was said: 'The four foundations of mindfulness are the causes (*nimitta*) of concentration; the four right efforts are the requisites (*parikkhāra*) of concentration.' This states that right mindfulness and right effort are the causes and requisites for concentration.

'As if striking' (*ākoṭentena viya*) means that wisdom penetrates the object that is taken and reflected upon, as if striking from all sides with an action similar to wisdom, such as 'impermanent, impermanent,' or as if revolving [around it] with such thoughts as 'impermanent in the sense of passing away, suffering in the sense of fear.' Although right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*) and right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*) occur simultaneously, right intention is described as if it were in the preceding period because of its causal state (*paccaya-bhāva*). *Sajātito* means it is grasped by the same nature of wisdom as in 'knowledge of suffering,' etc. Here, *kriyato* refers to an action similar to wisdom. Previously, however, it referred to an action appropriate to and supportive of concentration. This is the distinction here. According to the statement, 'Monks, all things should be known with higher knowledge (*abhiññeyya*),' all four [truths] should be known directly and face-to-face, or they are called *abhiññeyya* because they should be known with exceptionally distinguished knowledge.

*Durabhisambhavataraṃ* means much more difficult to accomplish or achieve; it means difficult to attain through the exhaustion of power. Defining by individual characteristics (*salakkhaṇa-vavatthāna*) means defining by the characteristics of oppression, origin, peace, and escape. The truths of suffering and its origin are deep in the sense of being difficult to plunge into. Indeed, even in animals, suffering and the craving for food, etc., are obvious. However, they are deep because it is impossible to plunge into them as they really are, such as 'This is suffering, this is the cause of it,' by way of oppression, accumulation, and so on. The truths of cessation and the path are difficult to plunge into because they are subtle and refined phenomena, and because they are deep by their very nature. Therefore, when the path has arisen, there is no failure to plunge into cessation and the path as they really are. Since Nibbāna is to be attained through the path, it is designated as its fruit (*phala*); thus he said, 'by way of designating the fruit' (*phalāpadesato*). For has it not been said: 'Knowledge of the cessation of suffering is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*)'? Since the path is the cause that leads to cessation, it is designated as the cause (*hetu*); thus he said, 'by way of designating the cause' (*hetu-apadesato*). And it has also been said: 'Knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*)'. In the phrase *iti vijaññā*, the word *iti* shows the sequence of understanding. In the phrase *evaṃ pakārehi*, the word *evaṃ* shows the methods that are the causes of understanding.

## The Description of the Summary is finished.
60:
## 1. Exposition of the Noble Truth of Suffering

## Explanation of the Exposition of Birth

In that context (at the beginning of the *Niddesavāra*, the exposition of birth, etc.), the phrase "This is the matrix (*mātikā*)" means that this matrix of suffering, beginning with "suffering-suffering" (*dukkha-dukkha*), should be understood for the purpose of teaching the Noble Truth of Suffering by way of the detailed exposition of birth and so forth; or for the purpose of teaching the Noble Truth of Suffering by way of the detailed exposition of birth and so forth, in order to understand the meaning of suffering in those things such as birth. Alternatively, "therein" (*tattha*) refers to that *Niddesavāra*. The passage "Birth is also suffering... in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering" shows the status of the matrix for the exposition of birth, etc., as previously shown, for the purpose of teaching the Noble Truth of Suffering. Having shown its status as a matrix, and then intending to collect all suffering to extract the terms based on which the Noble Truth of Suffering should be taught—namely, figurative suffering (*pariyāyadukkha*) and non-figurative suffering (*nippariyāyadukkha*)—he said: "This, indeed, is called suffering," and so on.

"By nature" (*sabhāvato*) means by the nature of being felt as painful. "By name" (*nāmato*) means by the name acquired through that very nature. Therefore, this (physical and mental pain) is not called suffering by some other figurative sense, but is called suffering precisely because it is suffering; thus, the name is specified by its nature. Alternatively, "by name" means by the name acquired due to having arising and passing away. Just as other phenomena that have arising and passing away are not suffering by nature, this (physical and mental pain) is not like that; rather, it is suffering by nature, it is truly suffering—thus the first word "suffering" specifies the subsequent word "suffering." Because it has the nature of change, pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) is indeed undesirable and thus becomes known as suffering. For that very reason, he said: "Because of the cause of the arising of suffering." Although the oppression of suffering can be known through the moaning of one afflicted by earaches and so forth, the suffering of earaches, etc., can only be known after asking, "Where does it hurt you?" Therefore, that suffering is called "concealed suffering" (*paṭicchannadukkha*). By the words "due to the manifestation of the affliction," he shows the manifestation of specific suffering.

Suffering that is called suffering for some other reason, setting aside its actual nature, is called "figurative suffering" (*pariyāyadukkha*). For the purpose of showing the manner in which the Noble Truth, which is acknowledged as that which should be taught, should be taught in brief or in detail, he said: "This is called the Noble Truth," and so on. "Brief" (*saṅkhepa*) means general; and since the general exists by including the specific, it is appropriate to teach in both ways (briefly and in detail) therein. "Detailed" (*vitthāra*) means the specific, such as birth and so forth; and since the specific excludes other specifics, in the detailed exposition of birth, etc., it is not possible to condense aging and so forth; therefore, in that detailed exposition, it should be taught only in detail.
61:
"Aparassa aparassa" (to another, to another)—showing this to another being and to another being is called *aparatthadīpana*. This is because the word *aparattha* can also be established in the possessive sense (*sāmī*). Alternatively, wishing to state the meaning expressed by the possessive case "of those, of those" (*tesaṃ tesaṃ*) by way of the locative case, he said "*aparatthadīpanaṃ*," which means showing in another and in another. Or, *aparatthadīpana* means the elucidation of the meaning called "birth" of another and of another. [It is shown] by way of the five destinations (*gati*), and in each destination, by way of the species (*jāti*) such as khattiyas among humans, terrestrial deities among devas, and elephants among animals—thus it is shown by way of destination and species.

The distinct characteristic of grass is called the species of grass (*tiṇajāti*); and since that characteristic is a designation (*paññatti*) based on [the grass], he said "in designation" (*paññattiyaṃ*). "Depending on that" (*tadupādāya*) means this birth occurs starting from that first consciousness; it does not occur starting from that being's departure from any [previous] existence. Since it occurs starting from the first consciousness in this way, it means that the first consciousness itself is called that person's birth. Alternatively, because it is said that the being is born depending on that first consciousness, it means that the first consciousness itself is called that person's birth. Since all five aggregates are also taught by taking consciousness as the lead, he said "in rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhiyaṃ*). Because it brings about the state of a Noble One (*ariya*), the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint is called "Noble Virtue" (*ariyasīla*). Considering that characteristics such as birth are also modes and variations of phenomena, the aggregates that arise together [with them] are said to be aggregates that have variations. The words beginning with "in the sense of being born" (*jāyanatthena*) are spoken to show birth by encompassing all beings through pairs of terms: by way of sense bases (*āyatana*) and by way of modes of birth (*yoni*). In the previous method, however, birth was shown by encompassing all beings with only a single term; this is the distinction. Some teachers say, "In the previous method, the designation of the agent (*kattu*) was made; in the latter method, the designation of the state (*bhāva*) was made." However, since the possessive designation of the agent is made as "the birth of those and those beings" (*tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ jāti*), the designation of the state (*bhāvaniddesa*) is appropriate in both cases. Complete birth is called *sañjāti*. Manifest birth is called *abhinibbatti*. The passage "The birth... manifestation of those and those beings" is called conventional discourse (*sammutikathā*) because it proceeds by way of beings.

In the phrase "here and there" (*tatra tatra*), the inclusion should be understood by way of: two sense bases each in one-constituent and four-constituent existences; five sense bases arising at the moment of rebirth-linking in the remaining fine-material realm (*rūpadhātu*); and seven, nine, ten, again ten, and eleven sense bases in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*) by way of beings with deficient or non-deficient faculties. Because the aggregates of rebirth-linking are the first manifestations of the continuity of aggregates included in a single existence, he said "characterized by the first manifestation" (*paṭhamābhinibbatti-lakkhaṇā*). It has the function of handing over (*niyyātana*) because it proceeds as if delivering that continuity of aggregates, as if saying, "Here, take it," and making [the next existence] receive it. It is called the manifestation of emerging (*ummujjana-paccupaṭṭhānā*) because it is grasped by knowledge as the surfacing of the continuity. The variety of the mass of suffering is "variety of suffering" (*dukkhavicittatā*); or the parts of that mass of suffering, which are specific sufferings, are "variety of suffering." It is called the manifestation of the variety of suffering (*dukkhavicittatā-paccupaṭṭhānā*) because it causes that variety of the mass of suffering to be present, or because it bears fruit.
62:
Among indirect suffering (pariyāya-dukkha) and direct suffering (nippariyāya-dukkha), there exists that indirect suffering which is birth (jāti); the very nature of being the cause of that indirect suffering is the meaning of suffering in that birth. If it were possible to understand it through a complete exposition, the Blessed One would have taught it to the end. The Blessed One also said—

"Monks, what do you think? Which is greater: this small pebble I have taken up in my hand, or the Himalaya, the king of mountains?" When asked thus, they replied, "Venerable Sir, the pebble the Blessed One has taken up is very small; compared to the Himalaya, the king of mountains, it does not count, it does not even form a fraction, it does not even admit of comparison." "Monks, in the same way, the pain and grief experienced by that man being pierced by three hundred spears is, compared to the suffering in hell, not even a fraction... it does not even admit of comparison." Thus, he illustrated the suffering of the lower realms by way of a simile.

Because pure blue lotuses (uppala) and the like are causes for the arising of happiness, by prohibiting the arising in those lotuses, he showed the fact that birth is the basis of suffering with the words beginning with "Atha kho." In the cause of the arising of suffering, the suffering that is merely the arising in the mother's womb without the effort of carrying the pregnancy has its root in the descent into the womb (okkantimūlaka), because it is independent of other causes of suffering. However, the suffering produced by effort has its root in the carrying of the pregnancy (pariharaṇamūlaka), because it is independent of the mere descent into the womb. This is the distinction between these two.

Pulling towards oneself is called ākaḍḍhana; pulling from all sides is called parikaḍḍhana. Shaking downwards is called odhunana; shaking crosswise or from all sides is called nidhunana. Flaying the skin and pouring alkaline water is called khārāpaṭicchaka.

Bathing the entire body is called nhāpana; washing a part of the body is called dhovana; heating by facing the sun is called ātāpana; heating from all sides by the five fires is to be understood as paritāpana. (The practice of heating oneself by kindling four fires in the four directions and enduring the heat of the sun from above at noon is called pañcatāpana.) Alternatively, all forms of heating are taught by both terms, ātāpana and paritāpana.

In what place could one find a footing? The meaning is that without birth, there is no footing for that suffering. Or, the meaning is: without birth, where would that being stay and find that suffering? How could suffering occur in those animals without birth among those animals? "Na cassa" should be determined as "na ce assa" (if it were not). The connection should be made as "nanu nevatthi" (is it not that it does not exist?), or as "nanu āha" (did he not indeed say?). In the word "yadato," "ya" is explained as "yasmā" (because) and "ato" as "tasmā" (therefore), thus the meaning is "Because it does not exist, therefore he said so."
63:
(Is it suffering) excluding (birth)? Here, the phrase 'excluding birth' (*jātiṃ vinā*) after 'among those animals' (*tahiṃ tiracchānesu*) does not seem appropriate; 'excluding birth' should only be connected to the preceding 'would be' (*bhaveyya*). The word *na cassa* should be determined as *na ce assa*. The connection of words should be made as 'certainly there is not.' Or the connection should be made as 'he truly taught.' Because *nanu* and *nevatthi* are far apart, the connection is shown by adding words. In the word *yadato*, it means 'because' (*yasmā*) 'there is not' (*nevatthi*), 'therefore' (*tasmā*) 'he said' (*āha*).

## Description of the Explanation of Old Age
Decay itself is *jīraṇatā*. Or, the state of a decaying object is expressed by the suffix *-tā*. 'Not noticing as before' (*yathāpure asallakkhente*) means that for one who does not notice [the previous] respect, service, etc., unhappiness (*domanassa*) arises due to that cause of not noticing. 'Of mindfulness, etc.' (*satādīnaṃ*) means that the time of an old person becomes like the time of an ignorant child because of being separated from mindfulness, learning, energy, wisdom, etc.; because of being rebuked by one's own children and wife whom one used to rebuke; because of having limbs and organs that do not follow one's will; and because of lacking the ability to investigate what is pure or impure. With this in mind, he said, 'because of reaching a further state of childhood.'

## Description of the Explanation of Death
In the world, what is called 'the action of time that makes an end' is the falling away (*cuti*), which means death (*maraṇa*). Or, the time of falling away itself is called 'Time' (*kāla*) in a special sense because it cannot be transcended; the action of that time is the reaching of the breaking up of the aggregates together with the death-consciousness. In this phrase 'death is *maccu*' (*maccu maraṇaṃ*), it is not inappropriate to connect them separately without making a compound, as 'that breaking up which is called *maccu*' and 'that giving up of life which is called *maraṇa* is called death'; it is indeed suitable. Because that breaking up of aggregates occurs, the conventional expression 'Tissa is dead, Phussa is dead' arises; that breaking up of aggregates is called 'conventional death' (*sammuti-maraṇa*) because the continuity of aggregates has not yet been cut off. The absolute cutting off of the continuity of aggregates is called 'death by cutting off' (*samuccheda-maraṇa*). In this context of 'death is also suffering,' since the talk on the truth of suffering is a talk on the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), he said, 'conventional death is intended.' The phrase 'the name of that very thing' (*tasseva nāmaṃ*) is said for the purpose of non-confusion regarding the many uses of the word 'death,' because of its state as that [conventional death] or as a part of it. By the term 'characteristic of falling away' (*cuti-lakkhaṇaṃ*), he means the characteristic of falling away (*savana-lakkhaṇa*) shown as 'the state of falling away.' It is called 'the function of separation' (*viyoga-rasa*) because it causes separation from the aggregates in a successful existence. Or, it is called 'the function of separation' because it is the action of separating. It is 'manifestation as being away' (*vippavāsa-paccupaṭṭhānaṃ*) because it appears in knowledge as being away from the being's previous life.

'Ending in death' (*maraṇantikā*) refers to [feelings] that occur near death. If there were no death, the aforementioned bodily and mental suffering would not exist; therefore, he said, 'by way of being the basis for both kinds of suffering.' In the phrase 'the sign of evil karma, etc.' (*pāpakammādi-nimittaṃ*), it means an evil sign of karma and an evil sign of destiny (*gati-nimitta*). Or, here, karma is also called 'sign' (*nimitta*). This is because it appears as the cause of arising in a new existence. According to this, evil karma is also meant by 'sign.' It should be understood that when that evil karma appears as an object, much unhappiness (*domanassa*) arises, such as 'Alas, I did not do good.' 'Of the good' (*bhaddassa*) means of a good person who has good karma.
64:
Pāpakammādinimitta means an evil sign of kamma (kamma-nimitta) and an evil sign of destiny (gati-nimitta). Alternatively, in this context, kamma itself is called 'nimitta' because it appears as the cause of rebirth (upapatti). When it appears thus, much mental distress (domanassa) arises, such as 'Alas, I have not done good deeds,' and so on. Bhaddassa means one who has good kamma. The word 'avisesato' should be connected with the word 'sabbesaṃ.' 'Sabbesaṃ' refers to all those in whom bodily pain arises, because it is specified as 'those whose limbs are being pierced.' The suffering produced by the cutting of the ligaments that bind the joints is called 'sandhibandhanacchedana.' Alternatively, the word 'ādi' has the sense of cause, thus it means suffering rooted in the cutting of the ligaments.

Anayavyasanāpādanaṃ viya means as if reaching ruin and misfortune. The reaching of ruin and misfortune involved in the destruction caused by wild beasts and so on is the illustration here.

## Description of the Explanation of Sorrow (Soka-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)

The cause of happiness is called 'hita'; its fruit is 'sukha' (happiness). Ñātikkhaya refers to the loss and death of relatives through wealth and so on. But the phrase 'ayaṃ pana viseso' was said with reference to the specific meaning of terms like 'bhogavyasana' (loss of wealth) and the specific compound in 'rogavyasana' (loss through disease) and so on. With the meaning that relatives and wealth are merely concepts (paññatti), or that their destruction is merely a concept, he said 'anipphannāni' (non-produced states). With reference to this state of being non-produced (aparinipphanna), it is also stated in the Visuddhimagga that 'ten kinds of matter are non-produced (anipphanna-rūpa).' In the commentary on the Rūpakaṇḍa as well, these are called 'aparinipphanna.' In the Khandha-vibhaṅga, however, the produced nature (nipphannatā) of things to be produced, such as the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), is mentioned; thus, it should be understood as the produced nature of non-ultimate realities (asabhāva-dhamma) and the non-produced nature (anipphannatā) of Nibbāna alone.

Since the word 'dhamma' expresses the sense of cause (hetu), he said 'by the cause of the arising of suffering.' Jhāmaṃ means burnt. Since mental feeling (domanassa-vedanā) endowed with the characteristics previously mentioned is sorrow (soka), its characteristics and so on should not be stated again; nevertheless, because sorrow is a specific type of mental distress, he said 'kiñcāpi' and so on, intending to state its distinct characteristics. Thinking that is devoid of aspiration and is merely shrunken within, or an internal withering and burning, is called 'antonijjhāna.' Parinijjhāyana means burning. Sorrowing in accordance with the loss of relatives and so on is 'anusocana'; or, sorrowing and grieving by following after various qualities and faults is 'anusocana.'
65:
"Javanakkhaṇe" means occurring at the moment of mind-door impulsion (manodvāra-javana). To show that moment of mind-door impulsion, he said "so much of mine..." and so on. In fact, even in processes (vīthi) such as body-consciousness (kāyaviññāṇa), it is indeed a cause for mental distress (domanassa) at the moment of javana. Therefore, he said "and at the moment of javana." Otherwise, one might take it that it is only the cause of bodily and mental pain occurring in the mind-door based on the body-base. In that context, it is because of the occurrence of the sounds "bodily" and "mental" specifically.

"Tujjati" should be understood as being stated by way of grammatical substitution (vyattaya) when it should have been "tudati."

## Description of the Explanation of Lamentation (Parideva-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)
"Ādeva" is so called because one laments by means of this sound. Having made the sound of lamentation, for those who reach a distinct state such as the shedding of tears, that sound is spoken of as the instrument (karaṇa) for reaching that state. Empty speech without essence, like the chaff of paddy, is "palāpa." The sound that has the function of proclaiming or making known qualities and faults is "lālappa." Because the sound of lamentation appears as a state of confusion or agitation of a person who does not discriminate between what is beneficial and what is not, or before those who should be shamed, it is said to be "manifesting as confusion" (sambhama-paccupaṭṭhāna). Or, the confusion (sambhama) caused by the non-disappearance of the causes of sorrow, such as the loss of relatives, is not the kind of confusion caused by terror. Since that confusion is made manifest by the sound of lamentation, parideva is said to be "manifesting as confusion."

One overcome by sorrow performs acts such as beating with fists because of the cause of lamentation. Because of the cause of lamentation itself, one thinks about the passing away of relatives and so on. Therefore, lamentation is said to be the basis (vatthu) for pain and mental distress.

"Bhiyyo" (excessively) includes other bodily and mental pain, and pain rooted in that lamentation, which occur excessively beyond the mental distress (or pain) without which lamentation does not occur, or beyond the previously mentioned pain, or beyond the pain caused by the drying up of the throat, lips, and palate.

## Description of the Explanation of Pain and Grief (Dukkha-domanassa-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)
196-7. Because bodily pain (kāyika-dukkha) is a strong dependence condition (upanissaya-paccayo) for bodily pain, it is said "pain arises for one who is suffering." Being overcome and oppressed by this pain (dukkha), one thinks "I no longer have the opportunity to enjoy the nakshatra festival," and thus strong mental distress (domanassa) arises. Therefore, pain is the basis for mental distress. It is called "pīḷeti" (oppresses) because it oppresses at the moment when bodily pain itself arises. Or, it means it oppresses because it has that bodily pain as a strong dependence. "Āvဋ္ဋန္တိ" means they roll around. "Vivaṭṭanti" means they roll over and fall like a pillar thrown into a valley, or like a tree falling when its roots are cut, or like a person with severed legs falling. Having a mind that is burnt all around, they think of this and that by the power of the strong dependence of the previously arisen mental distress. It should be noted that when mental distress disappears, such thinking no longer exists.
66:
Thinking, "I can no longer enjoy myself at the festival," strong mental distress (domanassa) arises; therefore, that physical suffering is the basis for mental distress.

With reference to the moment of its occurrence, physical suffering (kāyika-dukkha) is said to "oppress," or it is said to oppress because it has that physical suffering as its strong decisive support (upanissaya).

"Āvaṭṭanti" means rolling around in one place. "Vivaṭṭanti" means tumbling down like a pillar thrown into a mountain cleft, or falling down like a tree whose roots have been severed. Those whose minds are completely consumed [by grief] think of this and that due to the strong decisive support of previous mental distress; when mental distress has vanished, such thinking no longer exists.

## Explanation of the Description of Despair (Upāyāsaniddesavaṇṇanā)
Sinking down all around by way of preventing the approach to all objects is "saṃsīdana." Sinking that is very strong or distorted, making one unable even to rise, is "visīdana." Distorted attachment to the destruction of relatives and so on, without going to other objects, and being bound only to that object is "byāsatti." It has the function of moaning because it causes moaning. Distorted sinking is "visāda."

Upāyāsa is not suffering in itself because its nature is hatred (dosa) or because it is a different state included in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha).
