If some were to say that mental distress (domanassa) itself is despair (upāyāsa), they should be refuted by this Dhātukathā Pali: "Despair is associated with three aggregates, one base, and one element; it is associated in some ways with one aggregate, one base, and one element" (Dhatuk. 249). For those who, having reached despondency, stand in misery without considering the causes of happiness or suffering, despair is the cause of physical suffering. For those who think of the destruction of relatives and so on by the power of despondency, it is the cause of mental distress. At the moment of its own occurrence, despair consumes the mind because it is associated with mental distress; it causes the body to sink by making it inactive. Because it performs both these functions, it subsequently generates excessive physical and mental suffering based on that cause; thus it is called "suffering" (dukkha).

## Explanation of the Description of Association with the Unloved (Appiyasampayoganiddesavaṇṇanā)
"Na appiyanti" means they are not approached, they are not entered. "Anattha" means destruction or suffering. "Ahita" means the cause of that destruction. In the second interpretation of the meaning, because one does not desire the growth of welfare, the term "anatthakāma" (desiring harm) and such improper compounds (asamatthasamāsa) should also be applied.
67:
In words such as "anatthakāma," an improper compound (asamatthasamāsa) with an unsuitable meaning is also applied. Just as in words like "asūriyapassāni mukhāni" (faces that do not see the sun), the "a-" prefix does not negate the word it is compounded with. In the sense of being free from any specific danger, the word "yogakkhema" is well-known because it is security (khema) due to being free from the yoke of suffering (dukkha-yoga).

In words like "saṅgati" (association), whatever meaning can be obtained by the power of formations (saṅkhāra) should be taken. Since formations do not have postures such as standing or sitting, nor do they act together in activities like eating, it cannot be said that the latter two terms (samodhāna and missībhāva) are obtained by the power of that meaning. "Yaṃ labbhati" means whatever meaning is obtained. Therefore, just as the meaning is obtained in words like "saṅgati," it should be applied in that manner. For a person, "saṅgati" is going and associating with formations, and associating with those formations that have come; it is the coexistence of a person with formations in his own postures like standing, and the mixing in all activities. "Anatthabhāva" is the state of being a calamity (upaddava).

The mere approach of undesirable beings and formations, and the mere grasping of that undesirable object, is called "association with the unloved" (appiyasampayoga). However, there is no single distinct state called "association with the unloved" like the states of earth (pathavī) or contact (phassa); thus it is said, "In terms of ultimate reality, it is not a single distinct state." Undesirable formations like thorns and so on, and enemies, produce suffering such as being pierced by arrows and so on.

The word "idha" (here) should be applied as "suffering occurs in this world," or "it is called suffering here in this description of the Truth of Suffering (dukkhasacca-niddesa)."

## Explanation of the Description of Separation from the Loved (Piyavippayoganiddesavaṇṇanā)
"Minanti" means they put inside, like putting grain into a measuring vessel; it means they do not put it outside. The word "amā" indicates coexistence. Or they are known as "insiders" (ajjhattika). Because it arises in the mind as the ruin of relatives (ñātibyasana) and so on, it is called "manifesting as ruin" (byasanapaccupaṭṭhāna). By causing sorrow, they dry up the body and make it thin; even if not thin, they make it wither by removing its vitality (ojā). Because of that withering, physical suffering arises; thus it is said that they are the producers of that physical suffering.

By the phrase "pierced by the arrow of sorrow" (sokasarasamappitā), mental suffering is shown; by the phrase "they are tormented" (vitujjanti), physical suffering is shown.
68:
## Explanation of the Description of Desire (Icchā-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)

Since the intended meaning is the non-coming of birth (*jāti*) that occurs in those who have attained *Parinibbāna*, the phrase "the non-coming of birth that occurs in those who have attained *Parinibbāna*" is stated by taking the time when rebirth (*jāti*) cannot come. The meaning of the word "*yampi*" is "*yena pi*" (because of which also). Alternatively, when the word "*yaṃ*" refers to the word "*icchā*" (desire), it expresses a desire characterized by non-attainment. However, when it refers to the word "*na labhati*" (does not get), it expresses a non-attainment characterized by desire. Although that non-attainment has no other ultimate reality (*dhamma*) than greed (*lobha*), it refers only to the craving (*taṇhā*) that desires what should not be obtained. Because it occurs in things that cannot be obtained, it is called "*appatti-paccupaṭṭhāna*" (manifesting as non-attainment). The reason is that such desire occurs in a certain object, and it is perceived (by knowledge) as being unable to reach that object.

"*Chinnabhinnagaṇena*" means either by a group of shameless rogues or by a group of wretched people wearing rags.

"*Vighātamayaṃ*" refers to mental distress (*domanassa*) consisting of mental exhaustion/vexation, and also to physical suffering (*dukkha*) such as hanging oneself, illness, dysentery, etc., which arise from that very mental exhaustion. By the word "*icchitālābhaṃ*", the desire for an unobtainable object is meant.

## Explanation of the Description of the Aggregates of Clinging (Upādānakkhandha-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)

Showing the vast suffering as "having this much extent" is the summarization of suffering; such summarization cannot be done [exhaustively] because the extension of suffering is infinite. However, setting aside the extension of the teaching (*desanā*) that has reached the vastness of suffering, the defining of the teaching at the point where all extensions of suffering converge is called summarization; such summarization can be done because the objects known as the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandhā*) clearly exist.

Just as a man who knows a region and shows the way is called a "*desaka*" (shower/pointer), the Blessed One is also a "*desaka*" who points out suffering. There is also a variant reading "*dukkhantadesakena*", which means one who teaches the end of suffering.

Just as fire and so on oppress fuel and so on, they [the aggregates] arise while oppressing. By this very obvious suffering called "the oppression of suffering occurring at the time of death," the Buddha shows the sufferings such as sorrow (*soka*) caused by the oppression of the suffering of birth (*jāti*) and the suffering of aging (*jarā*). "*Tato*" refers to the suffering of oppression (*ābādhana-dukkha*) that occurs after lamentation (*parideva*). The bodily suffering that severely oppresses the body due to the conjunction of the disturbance of elements (*dhātu*) which causes dryness of the throat, the breaking of joints and ligaments, etc., is called "*dukkha*" (bodily pain). "*Yesu kesuci*" means that all sufferings such as eye disease, etc., occurring in the aggregates of clinging of Tissa or Phussa, or in all beings, are only of this nature, categorized into the five aggregates of clinging; this is the meaning intended to be shown in summary.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Truth of Suffering is finished.
69:
## 2. Explanation of the Description of the Truth of the Origin (Samudayasacca-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)

By eliding the latter word '*karaṇa*', it is said: "*punabbhavakaraṇaṃ punobbhavo*" (it is called *punobbhava* because it makes for renewed existence). In the word "*manosamphasso*", the ending in 'o' of the preceding word should be understood as in the word '*mano*'. Alternatively, since it has the meaning known by the suffix '*ika*' which has the sense of habit (*sīla*), it should be understood that the word expressing the action is not shown. For example, one who has the habit of eating cake is called "*āpūpiko*". The formation of the word '*ponobbhavika*' should be understood in meanings such as "it gives renewed existence" (*punabbhavāṃ deti*) because of the plural designation "*taddhitā*", because of the diversity of *taddhita* suffixes, or because they have the characteristic of expressing the meaning of a sentence.

Among those cravings (*taṇhā*), the craving that co-arises with *kamma* gives renewed existence. The craving that is a companion to *kamma* but does not co-arise with that *kamma* leads to renewed existence. Both types cause birth in existence again and again. Therefore, it is said: "*punabbhavassa dāyikāpi*" (being a giver of renewed existence), and so on. Regarding the phrase "it receives the name *ponobbhavika*": both the craving that can give renewed existence and the craving that cannot give it receive the same name '*ponobbhavika*' as having the same result. This is because they have the same nature in terms of longing for existence and because they have the power to give that existence. The same should be understood for the remaining cravings. Among those cravings, the *kamma* that ripens in the individual existence (*attabhāva*) already produced by other *kamma* called '*upadhi*' belongs to this craving; therefore, it is called "*upadhivepakkā*". It is called '*nandī*' in the sense of delighting; it is called '*rāgo*' in the sense of lusting. Whatever delight-and-lust (*nandīrāga*) and whatever craving (*taṇhā*) there are, these two are the same in meaning and differ only in phrasing; thus craving is said to be "identical in meaning with delight-and-lust." Because of the connection with lust (*rāga*), it is said "*uppannassa*" (of the arisen). Since the lust for fine-material existence and immaterial existence will be mentioned separately, it should be understood that the arising of craving that longs for existence only in the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) is mentioned here.

It is said "*uppajjati*" (arises) by way of the first arising in various pleasant objects, and "*nivisati*" (settles/establishes) by way of repeated occurrence. Alternatively, the arising and settling should be applied by way of obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) and underlying tendency (*anusaya*). "*Sampattiyaṃ*" means it occurs in human prosperity and in the state of being a deity. "*Attano cakkhu*" refers to the eye-sensitivity (*cakkhu-pasāda*) together with its physical base, or the eyeball together with the sensitivity. "*Vippasannapañcapasādaṃ*" refers to the sensitivity having very pure colors of blue, yellow, red, black, and white. Because the interior is white, they perceive the ear-hole like a silver tube. They perceive it like a hanging thread tied to a pendulous earlobe. A nose that is both high and long is called '*tunganāsikā*'; [people cherish] their own nose which has gained such a designation. Alternatively, if the reading is "*laddhavohārā*", it means those who have a high nose are called '*tunganāsikā*'; beings who have gained such a designation [cherish] their own nose—this is how the meaning should be applied. They also perceive the tongue by way of color, shape, and function. They perceive the mind as a noble mind capable of investigating matters such as the past. "*Attanā paṭiladdhāni*" means those obtained within one's own internal continuity...
70:
Smells of the body and external scents such as perfumes and ointments [are connected to the fourfold-originated base of smell, etc.]. In the phrase 'it arises while it is arising,' when it is in the process of arising, it arises here in this eye; thus, the act of arising taken generally is stated as the characteristic (lakkhaṇa), and the act of arising distinguished by its locus is stated as the object to be characterized (lakkhitabba). It is not that there is no conventional usage distinguished by generality and specificity (it indeed exists). Alternatively, 'arising' (uppajjamānā) refers to the undecided act of arising stated as the cause. 'Arises' (uppajjati) refers to the decided act of arising stated as the result, as in 'if it is in the process of arising, it arises in this eye.' That act of arising is as if it were joined with the process of arising.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Truth of the Origin is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Description of the Truth of Cessation

'Anūhata' means not uprooted, not abandoned.

A lion acts against the shooter, not the arrow; a dog acts against the stone, not the thrower. [Craving] is dispassionate through the power of reaching exhaustion. It ceases through the power of reaching non-occurrence. It is abandoned through the power of giving up without regard and through the power of decrease. It is relinquished through the power of throwing far away so that it cannot occur again. It is released through the power of liberation from craving, which is a bond. It does not cling through the power of being without defilement. Accumulation is the origin (samudaya); non-accumulation through the power of its opposite is [cessation].

'Apaññatti' means reaching non-manifestation, or the absence of the conventional expression 'the bitter gourd exists.' The Path should be understood like a man who desires the non-occurrence of the bitter gourd vine. Just as that man, with a mind inclined toward the non-occurrence of that vine, cuts the root, so the Path, having Nibbāna as its object, abandons craving. Nibbāna should be understood as the non-occurrence of craving, like the non-occurrence of that vine. In the second simile, Nibbāna should be understood like the south gate (or the area near the south gate), and the Path like the executioners. Alternatively, the previous simile was stated to show that craving, which has ceased because of the Path, should be said to have ceased in pleasant and agreeable things. The latter simile was stated to show that it is also said to have ceased in pleasant and agreeable things even though it has ceased by taking Nibbāna as its object.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Truth of Cessation is finished.
71:
## 4. Explanation of the Description of the Truth of the Path

'Aññamagga-paṭikkhepanattha' means to reject the fact that the path devised by sectarians is not the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. Alternatively, rejecting the status of being a path for other practices is called 'rejecting other paths' (aññamagga-paṭikkhepa).

It is called 'Noble' (Ariya) because it makes a person reach the state of a Noble One. It is called 'Noble' because it causes the attainment of, or produces, the fruit of a Noble One. It should be understood that this refers only to obtaining the name 'Noble' through the power of its own function and through the power of the fruit. One should understand the formation of the word 'Aṭṭhaṅgika' (Eightfold) as 'the eight factors exist in this path,' without making it a compound where the meaning is external (aññapadattha-samāsa).

Speech endowed with four factors embraces the people. Right Speech (Sammā-vācā), which has the nature of abstinence from the opposite wrong speech, is said to have the 'characteristic of embracing' (pariggaha-lakkhaṇā) because, by abandoning wrong speech that causes division, it has the function of embracing those who hear it and the associated states. Just as work such as making robes brings about a task to be done, or the 'action' (kammanta) called volition (cetanā) which completes various actions brings about movements such as those of hands and feet, so Right Action (Sammā-kammanta), by abandoning wrong action that brings about blameworthy tasks, has the function of bringing about blameless deeds. It is said to have the 'characteristic of originating' (samuṭṭhāpana-lakkhaṇo) because it occurs only while originating the associated states. Right Livelihood (Sammā-ājīva) is said to have the 'characteristic of purifying' (vodāpana-lakkhaṇo) because it abandons wrong livelihood, which is a defilement of the body, speech, and the continuum of the aggregates.

Its own opposing defilements are ignorance (avijjā) and so on, which are abandoned along with [wrong] view. 'Passatīti' means 'pakāseti' (it manifests/clarifies). For by that factor (Right View), reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā) occurs therein. 'Tatheva' means 'together with its own opposing defilements.'

'Kiccato' (by way of function) is because the task to be performed by the knowledges of suffering, etc., which occur in the preliminary stage, is completed at this moment of the Path. Or, it is because of the function of this Right View knowledge itself in clarifying suffering, etc. It receives three names because of the completion of the function of abandoning sensual thought (kāma-saṅkappa) and so on. In the Vibhaṅga of the Precepts (Sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga), it is stated that 'abstinence-volitions and all associated states are precepts'; therefore, by the power of the abstinence-volitions which are primary among those three, it is said that 'there are both abstinences and volitions.' Abstinences should be applied at the time of abstaining from false speech, etc., and volitions should be applied at the time of speaking well-spoken words, etc. At the moment of the Path...
72:
Because they are not factors of the Path, volitions (cetanā) are not path factors; only abstinences (virati) are path factors. It should be understood that only abstinences are path factors because a single knowledge is like the state of knowing suffering etc., and a single abstinence is like the state of abstaining from false speech etc.; whereas a single volition does not have the nature of accomplishing the triad of functions such as Right Speech etc., and thus cannot attain the state of Right Speech etc.; and even if it were to attain the state of Right Speech etc., it could not attain the state of being the three factors.

Right Concentration (Sammā-samādhi) occurs both in the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga) and at the moment of the Path (maggakkhaṇa). Although Right Concentration is extensively analyzed by way of the four jhānas through the power of applied thought (vitakka), sustained thought (vicāra), rapture (pīti), happiness (sukha), and equanimity (upekkhā), which are aids to concentration, a single concentration cannot accomplish the concentration-function of all four jhānas, just as effort (vāyāma) accomplishes the fourfold function of effort such as preventing the arising of unarisen unwholesome states, and mindfulness (sati) accomplishes the fourfold function of mindfulness such as abandoning the perception of beauty in the body etc., which are unattractive (asubha), painful (dukkha), impermanent (anicca), and non-self (anatta). Therefore, just as the jhāna-concentration in the first jhāna concentration-consciousness in the preliminary stage is only the first jhāna concentration, so it is at the moment of the Path. Similarly, just as the jhāna-concentration in the fourth jhāna concentration-consciousness in the preliminary stage is only the fourth jhāna concentration, so it is at the moment of the Path.

Applied thought (vitakka), which assists vocal utterance, also assists Right Speech (Sammā-vācā) which prevents blameworthy vocal utterance and causes blameless vocal utterance to arise; therefore, he said "Svāyaṃ" etc. Speech that regulates vocal utterance assists Right Action (Sammā-kammanta) which regulates bodily action. "Idaṃ vīriyaṃ" refers to the four Right Exertions (Sammā-ppadhāna). "Gatiyo" means accomplishments or natures such as functions. "Samanvesitvā" means having investigated and reflected.

The connection should be made as: "having learned the two preceding truths, namely the Truth of Suffering (Dukkha-sacca) and the Truth of the Origin (Samudaya-sacca)." By the phrase "iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ" (desirable and lovely), he shows the inclination towards the Truth of Cessation (Nirodha-sacca) and the Truth of the Path (Magga-sacca), not delight (abhinandana). The very inclination towards those truths should be understood as the practice of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) in that context.

"Kiccato" (by way of function) means by way of functions such as full understanding (pariññā) etc. "Ārammaṇa-paṭivedha" (penetration of the object) refers to the penetration that is realization (sacchikiriyā). Why is it said that "all penetrative knowledge is supramundane"? Is it not true that penetration through learning (uggaha) etc. is also penetration, yet it is not supramundane? No, it is not so. This is because the word "penetration" (paṭivedha) alone is not intended to mean penetration through learning etc., or because the knowledge in the preliminary stage regarding suffering etc., which proceeds by way of learning etc., is called "penetration" because it is a cause for penetration, not because it is penetration itself. However, referring only to knowledge that is actual penetration, he said: "All penetrative knowledge is supramundane." Since knowledges arising from learning and questioning are included only in the knowledge of hearing (savana-ñāṇa), he mentioned only three types of knowledge: "The knowledge of hearing, remembering, and contemplating is mundane." Comprehending the truths through learning etc. is called "pariggaha" (comprehension).
73:
"Payoga" means action or effort (vāyāma). He shows the desirability and the extreme difficulty of that great effort through similes such as "bhavaggagahaṇatthaṃ" (for the sake of grasping the peak of existence) etc.

In this context of "padaghāta", the track or cause of occurrence is called "pada". The means or cause by which sensual thought (kāma-vitakka) arises is its track; the destruction of that is "padaghāta". "Ussukkāpetvā" means having made it endowed with successive higher distinctions of peace, i.e., having increased it.

Regarding "vibhattesu pāḷiyaṃ" (analyzed in the texts), in which texts? First, in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, 8 kasiṇas, 10 asubhas, 4 brahmavihāras, and 4 āruppas are analyzed. In the Agamas (Suttas), 10 recollections (anussati), the perception of repulsiveness in food (āhāre paṭikūlasaññā), and the analysis of the four elements (catudhātuvavatthāna) are analyzed in various places. "Imesu tīsu" (in these three) refers to the three instances such as sense-desire (kāma) etc.

By the phrase "known as wrong speech", he shows the unity of what is to be abandoned by a single volition. Here, "ariya-sāvaka" (noble disciple) includes the virtuous worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) and the trainee (sekkha). "Kāyadvāravītikkaṃā" (transgressions through the body-door) should be applied to the respective abstinences from killing etc., which are rooted in livelihood (ājīva).

"Ayaṃ panassā" refers to taking the fourfold path as a unity by way of being the Path; this is the distinction of this Path by way of jhāna, being entirely similar, entirely dissimilar, or partially similar. "Pādakajjhāna-niyāmena hoti" (it occurs by the rule of the basic jhāna): here, he speaks making the rule of the basic jhāna the primary focus. In the Atthasālinī, however, he speaks making the rule of insight (vipassanā-niyāma) the primary focus, because there it is not in conflict with all doctrines. But here, he mentions the rule of the basic jhāna to exclude the doctrines of the "contemplated jhāna" (sammasita-jjhāna) and the "disposition of the person" (puggalajjhāsaya). The rule of insight, being common to all, should be understood as not being rejected here either. Intending that other teachers' doctrines to be mentioned should also be analyzed, he said "pādakajjhāna-niyāmena tāva" (firstly, by the rule of the basic jhāna) and analyzed the rule of the basic jhāna in detail.

The statement "In the formless realm, the fourfold and fivefold jhāna... is mentioned in the Atthasālinī" is the intention of the commentator. Is it not said there that "In the formless realm, the threefold and fourfold jhāna arises," and not "the fourfold and fivefold jhāna"? True, but by showing the arising of those jhānas about which there is doubt, it is effectively said that the fourfold and fivefold jhāna arises. Thus it should be understood. Considering the group as a whole, he said: "And that is supramundane, not mundane." For only the fourth jhāna arises there as mundane, while the fourfold and fivefold group does not arise as mundane.
74:
In this context, "how" means: how should it be understood in the absence of the base jhana (pādakajjhāna)? It means that for those possessing jhana in that formless realm, the three higher paths arise by making the first fruit and so on the base for the development of the higher paths. When developing the path associated with the threefold or fourfold jhana, for a person born in that formless realm, other paths associated with different jhanas also arise by making the formless jhana and the fruit associated with that jhana the base for the development of the higher paths. Therefore, the preliminary attainment (pubbābhisaṅkhārasamāpatti) that determines the jhana factors and so on is the base; since it is said that the attainment to be contemplated is not the base, the status of the fruit as a base should also be understood.

Because the knowledge of suffering and so on has the six objects such as visible forms, and because thoughts of renunciation (nekkhammasaṅkappa) and so on have various wholesome objects such as kasinas, and because the factors such as right speech have various objects to be abstained from, it is said "according to suitability" (yathānurūpaṃ). "Suitability" means that since virtue (sīla) without remorse is a special cause for effort (vīriya), it refers to the suitability of virtue for effort and its associated states. Since it refers only to the associated states, it was not said "to a person who has stood on the ground of virtue," but "to a person who is standing." "Non-confusion of mind" means the state of the mind being guarded by mindfulness (sati), which is described here as "having a single guard." Therefore, it was said, "Thus... for a person who has a well-established guard of the mind."

The state of knowledge (vijjā) of the insight that exhausts taints (āsavakkhaya) has been mentioned. In the path known as the exhaustion of taints, which is comprised of the three aggregates, the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha) is called vijjā. The state of conduct (caraṇa) of virtue and the four jhanas has been mentioned. The remaining two aggregates (the aggregate of virtue and the aggregate of concentration) are called caraṇa. That by which they go to Nibbāna is called a vehicle (yāna). Since insight itself is the vehicle, it is called the vehicle of insight (vipassanāyāna). Virtue is a special cause for concentration, and concentration is a cause for insight. Because it is helpful to tranquility (samatha), the aggregate of virtue is also included in the vehicle of tranquility. While making clear the danger in sensual pleasures through the vehicle of insight, and not abandoning the unworldly bliss of jhana through the vehicle of tranquility, one avoids the wrong paths of the two extremes. Just as wisdom is the opposite of delusion, virtue and concentration are the direct opposites of hatred and greed, as they are to be accomplished through non-hatred and non-greed. Due to the union of virtue, concentration, and wisdom, there is goodness (kalyāṇa) in the beginning, middle, and end. This is because virtue and so on are the beginning, middle, and end of the Dispensation (Sāsana). The Dispensation, comprised of the three aggregates known as the Path and Fruit, in which a person standing in the Path or Fruit is called a Noble One (Ariya), is called the ground of the Noble Ones (ariyabhūmi).

## The Explanation of the Description of the Truth of the Path is finished.
## The Explanation of the Suttanta Classification is finished.
75:
## 2. Explanation of the Abhidhamma Classification

206-214. The term "Ariya-sacca" (Noble Truth), when occurring in the Truth of Origin (Samudaya-sacca), applies only to the origin known as craving (taṇhā), which is devoid of the state of being fully known (pariññeyya) and is to be abandoned (pahātabba) exclusively. It does not apply to the remaining defilements and unwholesome states that are both to be abandoned and fully known, nor to the three wholesome roots accompanied by taints (sāsava-kusalamūla) and the remaining wholesome states with taints which are not to be abandoned. Therefore, in that term "Ariya-sacca," the Origin is partial (sappadesa). In the term "Sacca" (Truth) alone, without the word "Ariya," it is without remainder (nippadesa). Therefore, [the commentator] said, "In order to show the Origin without remainder."

The Truth of Suffering and the Truth of Cessation are naturally without remainder (nippadesa) in the teaching of the Noble Truths. This is because there is no other state in the teaching of the Truths that should be called "Suffering" or "Cessation." The Truth of the Path also has no new states in the sections on the eight factors and five factors. Therefore, it is said only of the Origin, "In order to show it without remainder," because that [Origin] is shown as not being new in all three sections. For the purpose of showing the new Truth of Origin, the statement in the teaching of the Truths, "Therein, what is the origin of suffering? It is craving," has the purpose of showing the occurrence of the term "Truth" in craving alone, without involving the unwholesome roots and so on.

By the power of the teaching, the Truth of Suffering by setting aside various origins, the Truth of Cessation by the power of abandoning various origins, and the Truth of the Path by the power of all supramundane wholesome states consisting of eight factors or five factors, are not mentioned in the teaching of the Noble Truths. Therefore, suffering and so on are shown as being partial (with remainder) in that teaching of the Noble Truths. It should be said that the teaching of the Truths (Sacca-desanā) was taught in order to show those states of suffering and so on as being without remainder (nippadesa). "Paccaya-saṅkhātaṃ" means the root cause of suffering such as birth, due to the power of kamma and defilements.

"The Truth of Cessation... is described by five modes"—this shows the distinction of the teaching of the Truths from the teaching of the Noble Truths. Among those five modes, the statement "the abandoning of the three wholesome roots and the remaining wholesome states with taints" should be understood as being taught by the power of abandoning their causes, namely ignorance, craving, and clinging. Or, it should be understood as being taught by the power of their non-occurrence when ignorance and so on are abandoned. This is because wholesome states are not to be abandoned (na hi kusalā pahātabbā). By the word "abandoning" (pahāna), it shows the cessation to be attained by the power of the function of the path. Alternatively, the non-occurrence of craving and so on, which is the nature of cessation itself, should be understood as "abandoning."

Even if, for the purpose of showing the strong support (upanissaya) for the fulfillment of the Noble Eightfold Path at the moment of the supramundane path, [it is said:] "Even before that, his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood are very pure; when they are thus pure, this Noble Eightfold Path reaches fulfillment in development"...
76:
Although it is taught in this way, the phrase "Even before [the path]" shows the remote supporting condition (dūratarūpanissaya) resulting from the purity of bodily actions and so forth. It also shows the proximate supporting condition (āsannatarūpanissaya) of the five factors such as right view, which arise at the moment of insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā). This occurs for the practitioner who dwells frequently contemplating the disadvantages [of formations], being unattached, unjoined, and undeluded regarding the eye and so forth. This happens by way of turning away from all formations as the five aggregates of clinging diminish in the future, by the remoteness of defilements as craving that leads to rebirth is abandoned, and by way of tranquility of body and mind while experiencing physical and mental happiness as the distress, fever, and burning of body and mind are abandoned. This is in accordance with the teaching: "Whatever view such a person has, that is his right view" (M. iii. 431), etc. Thus, it illustrates the occurrence of the teaching on the fivefold path according to the inclination (ajjhāsaya) of individuals who easily understand the fivefold path by way of the proximate supporting condition. Therefore, it was said: "Because of the statement: 'Even before... is perfectly pure,'" and so forth.

In this way, the word "vacanato" (from the statement) in the ablative case is an indicator that makes known the means of the teaching. Alternatively, "vacanato" means that in accordance with His own words, the Blessed One taught that even the fivefold path is indeed the practice (paṭipadā). Where was it taught? In the city of the devas (Devapura). Therefore, to show that method of teaching, the Elders who compiled the Dhamma (dhamma-saṅgāhaka) also pointed out the section on the fivefold path (pañcaṅgika-vāra).

Alternatively, by the very statement "Even before [the path]," which indicates the cause for the specific inclination, it is taught that even the fivefold path is indeed the practice according to the individual's inclination. Therefore, it was said: "Because of the statement: 'Even before... because of the statement... it is taught.'" Thus, it means that the Blessed One also showed the section on the fivefold path in the city of the devas to demonstrate that method taught in the Suttanta.

The entry into the teaching or the entry into meditation (bhāvanā) by way of the jhanas is called "application of jhana" (jhānābhinivesa). It should be understood that the demonstration of four thousand methods in each portion is for the sake of ease in counting. However, according to the way the Pali text stands, it is understood that the flow of the Pali is made by combining five portions each in each practice and in [the sections on] emptiness (suññatā) and so forth. Among those sections, in the eightfold section (aṭṭhaṅgika-vāra), in the second jhana and so forth, the connection should be made as: "At that time, there is a sevenfold path." In the section on the comprehensive inclusion (sabba-saṅgāhika-vāra), the connection should be made according to the nature of the existing phenomena.

## The Explanation of the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya is finished.
77:
## 3. Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā

Why is it said, "As in the previous two [truths]"? Is it not the case that in the exposition of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering in the Suttanta-bhājanīya, the path is taught as a mixture of mundane and supramundane? Indeed, in the commentary on that Suttanta-bhājanīya, it is said: "With reference to the arising of knowledge in the preliminary stage by way of learning and so forth regarding the four truths, it is said: 'knowledge of suffering,' etc. However, at the moment of penetration (paṭivedha), there is only a single knowledge." Thus, the mixed mundane and supramundane nature of right view is shown. Likewise, is not the mixed mundane and supramundane nature of right intention and so forth also shown by such passages as: "This so-called right view has various moments and various objects in the preliminary stage; however, at the moment of the path, it has a single moment and a single object"?

This objection is true. Nevertheless, by way of its connection with insight as the cause for the arising of the path, even in that commentary, the Noble Eightfold Path, which is remote from defilements, is shown by taking the demonstration of the meditation on the four truths as the starting point. Because this was done, the nature of the single path-knowledge as "knowledge of suffering" and so forth was extracted by saying: "However, at the moment of penetration, there is only a single knowledge." Also, the nature of intention and so forth associated with the path as "right intention" and so forth was extracted by saying: "At the moment of the path... a single wholesome intention arises; this is called right intention," and so forth. In the Pali text as well, after briefly indicating the eightfold path, "knowledge of suffering" and so forth is stated in order to explain that very path in detail. Because the Noble Eightfold Path was briefly indicated in the Pali and that same path was then explained in detail, in the Suttanta-bhājanīya as well, by this passage "As in the previous two," the mundane nature of the two [truths] (the truth of suffering and the truth of the origin) and the supramundane nature of the [other] two (the truth of cessation and the truth of the path) are stated.

## Explanation of the Question Section is finished.

## Explanation of the Analysis of the Truths is finished.
78:
## 5. Indriyavibhaṅga
## 1. Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

Regarding the phrase "exercises the function of a faculty in the eye-door," it means that in the matter of taking a visible object, which is the cause and occasion of the eye-door, it causes the states occurring at that door to exercise its own supreme lordship or sovereignty as the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda). For that eye-sensitivity makes those door-states follow itself in the task of taking the visible object, and those states do follow that eye-sensitivity. This method should be applied to the remaining faculties as well. Because of the reason that either the person endowed with that faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya) or the states associated with that faculty are those who have known the Four Noble Truths, the state of being one who has known (aññātāvi) is the knowledge that knows the task has been completed.

In some Suttas, the Buddha taught two faculties, saying: "Bhikkhus, because two faculties have been developed and cultivated, a monk whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) declares final knowledge... because of noble wisdom and noble liberation. Bhikkhus, that which is his noble wisdom is his faculty of wisdom (paññindriya). That which is his noble liberation is his faculty of concentration (samādhindriya)" and so forth. In other places, He taught three, such as: "Bhikkhus, because three faculties have been developed and cultivated, the monk Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja has declared final knowledge... the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya), the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom"; and "Bhikkhus, there are these three faculties. Which three? The faculty of 'I shall know the unknown' (ananya-taññassāmītindriya), the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya), and the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya)"; and "These three faculties... the faculty of femininity (itthindriya), the faculty of masculinity (purisindriya), and the faculty of life (jīvitindriya)." In other passages, He taught five, such as: "Brahmin, these five faculties have different domains... the eye-faculty... the body-faculty"; and "These five faculties... the faculty of pleasure (sukhindriya)... the faculty of equanimity (upekkhindriya)"; and "These five faculties... the faculty of faith (saddhindriya)... the faculty of wisdom." The teaching of two faculties and so forth in those Suttas is due to their being the means of escape [from the round of rebirth] and so on. In reality, however, all faculties are to be fully understood (abhiññeyya), and since the teaching that explains states to be fully understood is the Abhidhamma, all faculties are taught together here in this Indriyavibhaṅga.

Because it arises as the nature of an Arahant, it is said: "Because it arises only in the Arahant."

It is called 'liṅga' because it makes known, or because it is known by this faculty. What does it make known, or what is known? It makes known or is known as the previous kamma called 'Inda'. The faculty which is the effect that makes known the previous kamma called 'Inda' is called 'indaliṅga'. The sense of the nature of 'indaliṅga' is 'indaliṅgaṭṭha'. 'Indaliṅga' itself—
79: —or rather, the meaning of the word 'indriya' is the sense of being the mark of the Lord (indaliṅgaṭṭha). That which is prepared or produced is called 'siṭṭha'; because it is prepared by the Lord (Inda - the master or kamma), it is called 'indasiṭṭha'. 'Juṭṭha' means that which is resorted to. In the sense of being the marks of the Lord called kamma, and being prepared by that kamma, only the karma-born (kammaja) faculties should be applied, not others. Those two meanings (indaliṅga and indasiṭṭha) should be applied only to kamma, while the remaining meanings should be applied only to the Blessed One; thus it is said "according to the application" (yathāyogaṃ). The word 'tena' is used because of the lordship (indatta) of the Blessed One and of kamma. 'Ettha' means "in these faculties." They are said to "manifest" (ulliṅgenti) because they enable the knowledge of the success or failure of the cause (kamma) through the success or failure of the fruit. In such passages as "He resorts to that sign (nimitta)," the act of taking an object is also called 'resorting' (āsevanā); therefore it is said, "some faculties are for the purpose of resorting to an object (gocarāsevanā)." In that context, although all faculties can take an object, the word "some" (kānici) is used because those faculties that should not be contemplated via insight are not to be resorted to by frequent attention. For in those faculties, there is only mere reflection. In such passages as "He cultivates that path," cultivation is called 'āsevanā'; therefore, referring to the faculties such as faith (saddhā) which are to be cultivated, it is said, "some faculties are for the purpose of cultivation (bhāvanāsevanā)." Overlordship (ādhipacca) is the state of being a faculty-condition (indriya-paccaya). Although the faculty-condition does not exist in the femininity and masculinity faculties, they possess the nature of lordship in being able to make the marks (features) and so on, which arise by their own causes, follow them without arising in any other way in the continuity associated with them. In this sense, they are called faculties (indriya) because they exercise supreme lordship. According to the method shown for the eye-faculty and others, the lordship over the states that follow them should be applied to other faculties as appropriate. "Below" refers to the Atthasālinī commentary. It is only non-delusion (amoha), not four separate states. Therefore, the meaning is that the characteristics and so forth of non-delusion explained under the term 'paññindriya' should be understood as the characteristics of those [four faculties related to wisdom]. The remaining faculties appear in the Atthasālinī with their own characteristics and so forth. If it is asked, "Are not the characteristics of the faculty of pleasure (sukhindriya) and the faculty of pain (dukkhindriya) not mentioned there?"—even if they are not explicitly mentioned, they are indeed mentioned by way of the characteristics already stated for the faculty of joy (somanassindriya) and the faculty of grief (domanassindriya), as they can be understood through them. How? The faculty of pleasure has the characteristic of experiencing a desirable tangible object, the function of enjoying the desirable aspect, the manifestation of bodily pleasure, and the eye-faculty [sic: body-faculty] as proximate cause. The faculty of pain has the characteristic of experiencing an undesirable tangible object, the function of enjoying the undesirable aspect, the manifestation of bodily affliction, and the body-faculty as proximate cause. Here, it should be understood that the function of enjoyment applies only to objects that are desirable or undesirable by nature, not to the enjoyment of a perverted aspect.
80:
The attainment of the Noble (Ariya) state by beings is a common and primary benefit in the teaching of the Blessed One; therefore, it was said: "Having fully understood the internal states (ajjhatta-dhammaṃ pariññāya)," and so forth. In the Commentary, the sequence of teaching the life faculty (jīvitindriya) after the female faculty (itthindriya) and the male faculty (purisindriya) is mentioned, and that sequence is consistent with the Indriya-yamaka teaching. However, in this Indriya-vibhaṅga, the life faculty is taught after the mind faculty (manindriya). It should be understood that it is taught in the middle because it protects the preceding and succeeding internal and external faculties. Every single feeling (vedanā) that is experienced is indeed suffering (dukkha). This is to make it known that as long as the life faculty, which protects the two types of individual existence (attabhāva), exists, these feelings which are suffering will continue to arise without ceasing. By making this known, it shows that the faculties such as the eye (cakkhu), being constantly accompanied by suffering, are truths to be fully understood (pariññeyya).

The phrase "because it is to be developed thereafter" refers to the faculty of one who knows (aññindriya) associated with the path of development (bhāvanā-magga), because development (the higher paths) arises after vision (the path of stream-entry). Although there are conditions such as the pre-nascence condition (purejāta-paccaya), the function that is accomplished solely by the power of the faculty condition (indriya-paccaya) is called "function" (kicca), because it is not common to other states and follows the sequence of the Indriya teaching. Because it is the precursor, the mind faculty can make the associated states follow its will; other faculties cannot do so. The faculties associated with that mind faculty also accomplish their respective faculty functions as they are completed by the mind faculty, because they are mental factors (cetasika). In explaining all functions, it should be noted that the phrase "is accomplished by the power of the faculty condition" applies throughout.

Although the female and male faculties do not directly produce or support the marks (nimitta) and so forth, the fact that the kamma and other causes of those marks are involved as causes in the arising of the female marks and so forth is called conformity (anuvidhāna). The pleasant and painful feelings that arise by covering and pervading the associated states become prominent by overwhelming the co-nascent states; and because the co-nascent states seem to reach the state of pleasure or pain by the power of those feelings, it is said: "bringing about their own gross and prominent characteristics." For the neutral feeling associated with unwholesome or unwholesome-resultant states which are not calm or sublime, the bringing about of the neutral (majjhatta) characteristic should be applied. Or, it can be applied to the bringing about of a calm and sublime characteristic compared to the same class of pleasure and pain. The bringing about of the characteristics of clarity, exertion, presence, concentration, and vision are the functions of the five faculties such as faith (saddhā) and so forth, respectively. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana) are included. Although only the function of the aññindriya associated with the path is shown, by that itself, the function of the aññindriya associated with the fruition (phala) in abandoning those respective fetters through their subsiding is also shown. The faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya), having completed all functions, is directed only towards the Deathless (Amata) because there is no other task to be done; it is also the condition for the associated states to be so directed, and unlike other faculties, it is not occupied with other tasks. Therefore, it is said: "And it is the condition for being directed towards the Deathless."
81:
Even though this is so, they are called "all-inclusive" (sabbasaṅgāhaka) only because they can include wholesome and unwholesome energy and so forth, which are to be included by the term energy faculty (vīriyindriya) and so forth, and because they can include the eye and so forth, which are differentiated by time, person, and condition, and are to be included by the term eye faculty (cakkhu-ndriya) and so forth. It means they are not all-inclusive because of including those faculties that do not exist in a particular plane (bhūmi). Thus, because it is stated generally without specification, it shows that the word "all-inclusive" does not indicate the inclusion of faculties that are not present in those respective planes, thereby preventing the assumption that all faculties exist in all planes.

## The Explanation of the Abhidhamma Classification is finished.

## 2. The Explanation of the Interrogation (Pañhapucchaka)

In this context, "anābhaṭṭha" (not brought forward) is stated regarding the fact that the life faculty is definitely not without an object (anārammaṇa). Why is it said: "Because of being mixed with matter (rūpa), it is included among the material states that are objectless"? Is it not that because of being mixed (with both mind and matter), the life faculty is not included among the objectless states? Indeed, it is not said that "the eight faculties are objectless." This objection is true. However, this is said with reference to the fact that the material life (rūpa-jīvita), which is a part of the life faculty, is included among the objectless material states. The meaning is that because it has the nature of having limited objects (parittārammaṇa) and so forth by way of the mental part (nāma-jīvita), it is included in the "siyā" (it may be) portion. Because it has the nature of having limited objects and so forth by way of the mental part, and it cannot be said to have limited objects and so forth by way of the material part, it should be understood that it is included in the "siyā" portion only by the power of the whole life faculty which is a mixture, and not by the power of a single part. Indeed, it is not that an objectless material state is not a state that cannot be said (navattabba) to have limited objects and so forth.

The statement such as "Matter and Nibbāna are objectless; the seven faculties are objectless" shows the state of being indeterminable (navattabba) due to being objectless, among the states that are indeterminable as to whether they have non-existent objects or are objectless, such as having limited objects and so forth. It does not show the state of being indeterminable for something that already has an object. Or, it does not show that an indeterminable state has an object. In fact, the word "navattabba" (indeterminable/not to be said) is not established as referring to states with objects. If it were so, the statement "The three feelings, matter, and Nibbāna—these states are indeterminable as being associated with pleasant feeling" and so forth would not have been said. However, if the word "navattabba" related to having limited objects and so forth were to apply only to states with objects, then instead of saying "The two bases (āyatana) may have limited objects," it should have been said: "The mind base (manāyatana) may have limited objects... may have immeasurable objects," and "The mind-object base (dhammāyatana) may have limited objects... may have immeasurable objects," and "It may also be objectless." This is because in the Interrogation (Pañhapucchaka) method, there is no teaching that is left incomplete.
82:
Regarding the word "atthi," in the statement "eight faculties may have internal objects," it should also be understood that at the time of the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), the mental life-faculty and the physical life-faculty are not to be spoken of (as having objects, etc.) because they lack an object.

## The Commentary on the Interrogation Section is finished.

## The Commentary on the Analysis of the Faculties is finished.
83:
## 6. Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga
## 1. Suttantabhājanīya
## Uddesavāravaṇṇanā

When King Dhammāsoka asked, "Venerable sir, what did the Fully Enlightened One usually teach?", the Elder Moggaliputtatissa replied, "Great King, the Fully Enlightened One was an Analyticist (Vibhajjavādī)." Because of this, it should be known that the disciples of the Fully Enlightened One are Analyticists (Vibhajjavādins). Indeed, they speak by analyzing the state of the disciplined (venayika) and so forth. They speak by analyzing whether things like robes and so forth should be used or not used, and they analyze the eternalist view (sassatavāda) and the annihilationist view (ucchedavāda). They are known as Vibhajjavādins because they leave aside unanswered questions such as "the self and the world are eternal," and because they teach Nibbāna, which is the eternal state where lust and so forth are exhausted, and the annihilation of lust and bodily misconduct. However, they do not reject the three types of questions, such as those to be answered categorically (ekaṃsabyākaraṇīya), to speak only of questions to be answered analytically (vibhajjabyākaraṇīya). The group of disciples who speak analytically is called the Vibhajjavādimandala. Alternatively, it is said that the assembly of the Blessed One who speaks analytically is the Vibhajjavādimandala. By demonstrating the undistorted and true meaning taught by the former teachers, one should be a speaker who does not misrepresent those teachers.

A person who says, "Ignorance is the causal condition for meritorious formations and imperturbable formations," etc., or who speaks of the doctrine of a person (puggalavāda) and so forth which are rejected in the Kathāvatthu, is called one who deviates from his own tradition (sakasamaya). One should be a speaker without such deviation. Some teachers say that one should be a speaker who remains free from the effort of blaming others' traditions (parasamaya) and who does not mix with others' traditions by saying, "This view is also suitable and should be accepted."

A person who says, "As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this very same consciousness that runs and wanders (from life to life) without being another," etc., is called one who obstructs the Suttanta. One should be a speaker without such obstruction. A person who says, "Although the Blessed One has taught that certain things are obstructive, I understand that they are not actually capable of being an obstacle for one who indulges in them," or who says, "A transgression committed in a dream constitutes an offense," etc., is called one who opposes the Vinaya. Instead of such opposition, one should be one who conforms to the Vinaya. Indeed, one who opposes the Vinaya destroys the distinction of actions (kamma) and opposes the nature of the Dhamma. One must be a person who observes the four Great Authorities (mahāpadesa) taught in the Suttanta Pali, and the four Great Authorities explained in the Commentary: Sutta, Suttānuloma, Ācariyavāda, and Attanomati. By such observation...
84:
...one stands firm in the Sutta and Vinaya and does not overstep them. "Dhamma" refers to the Paṭiccasamuppāda Pali text. "Attha" refers to the meaning of that Pali text. Here, the technical terms for cause and effect (hetu-phala) are not intended. Having changed the meaning stated as "Ignorance is non-knowledge regarding suffering, etc.," it is further pointed out through other methods (pariyāya) such as "non-knowledge regarding the past," etc. It is said that they point out, "By this method, formations (saṅkhāra) are called existence (bhava), and by this method, craving (taṇhā) is called clinging (upādāna)," and so forth.

Regarding "satta" (being), they say it is the emptiness of a being, or it is merely the conventional term "being" applied to formations that are empty of a being. In the phrase "paccayākāram-eva ca," the letter "m" is a euphonic junction (sandhi) connecting the words.

Because it is necessary to explain the meaning according to the aforementioned method, and because it is difficult, (this was said).

"I do not find a footing" means that if there were a method upon which one could stand to make the commentary easy, I do not find that method by the power of my own wisdom alone. Wishing to state the reliance (nissaya), he said, "This Sasana..." and so forth. Here, "Sasana" refers to the Pali Dhamma, or specifically to the Paṭiccasamuppāda itself. Indeed, because it is adorned with various methods of teaching such as forward and backward (anuloma-paṭiloma) and continues uninterrupted to this day, it is the reliance. The path of the former teachers, known as the Commentary (Atthakathā) on that Pali, is also the reliance.

To show the purpose of generating respect by saying, "Listen to that with a concentrated mind," he said, "Thus it was said," and so forth. "Having made it the bone (aṭṭhiṃ katvā)" means having made it the purpose (attha), or listening in such a way that it does not disappear, as if it had reached the bone. The distinction that occurs in the later period from the earlier period is called "sequence of before and after (pubbāpariya)." It means that from the first endeavor onwards, at every moment, one can obtain special knowledge and the special destruction of defilements.

Because it is the root cause of the rounds of kamma, result, and defilements, and because it is taught at the beginning, ignorance (avijjā) is the root of Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). In that context, one should not make a comparison like this: just as when the root of a creeper is seen, the creeper is taken from that root, so when the root of dependent origination is seen, the teaching of dependent origination follows. For the Blessed One, there is no such division as "only this is seen, the other is not seen," because everything is seen by Him. However, this commonality is intended: just as a creeper is taken starting from the root, the teaching of dependent origination is made starting from the root. Alternatively, the commonality of seeing the root and so forth should be applied according to the state of being taught through the inclination (ajjhāsaya) of those who are to be enlightened.
85:
One should not compare the simile and the thing signified by saying that the teaching of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) arises starting from that fundamental ignorance only after seeing ignorance. For there is no need to distinguish for the Blessed One that He saw only this Dhamma and not yet another; He had already seen the entirety of Dependent Origination. In this context, the similarity desired is only that He began the teaching of Dependent Origination from ignorance, which is the root, just as one takes a creeper starting from its root. Do not take the meaning as He taught starting from ignorance because He saw ignorance first like one seeing the root of a vine first; rather, take it as 'taking the vine from the root and teaching starting from the fundamental ignorance are similar.' Or, the similarity between seeing the beginning of the vine and seeing the beginning of Dependent Origination should be applied in connection with the disposition (ajjhāsaya) of those to be taught, or because of the need to make it known.

'Tassa' means—Monks, when that young boy grows up and his faculties mature, he is endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure... he delights. When that young man sees a form with the eye, he is lustfully attached to a pleasing form and is resentful toward an unpleasing form. He dwells without mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati) established, with a limited mind. He does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind (cetovimutti) and liberation by wisdom (paññāvimutti) wherein those evil unwholesome states that have arisen in him cease without remainder. Thus, having reached favor (taṇhā) and opposition (dosa), whatever feeling he feels—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he delights in that feeling, welcomes it, and remains attached to it (Majjhima Nikāya, 1, 408). This is the meaning of the words spoken.

The same method applies to the ear and other sense doors. 'Abhivadato' means speaking 'Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!' with strong craving that reaches the point of verbal expression as 'I' and 'mine'. 'Ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati' means remaining attached because of the inability to be freed from a craving stronger than that. Craving that is even stronger and becomes grasping (upādāna) is called 'nandī'. Here, craving is taught by words like 'abhinandana' and others. By the word 'nandī', it should be understood that the four types of grasping rooted in that craving are taught due to delighting, non-separation from it, and the states of delighting in craving and views. The passage 'With birth as condition, aging and death come to be' is also taught in that same Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta.

Referring to contact (phassa) and so on occurring at rebirth and during the course of existence as the result-round (vipākavaṭṭa), and the nutritive essence (ojā) produced by kamma, it is said: 'The four nutriments are rooted in craving.' Other nutriments that support the round (vaṭṭa) also cannot exist if craving is absent, so it is appropriate to say they are 'rooted in craving.'

'Tato tato' means from this or that teaching among the four types of teachings. In the phrase 'ñāyappaṭivedhāya saṃvattati', 'ñāya' means the Path or Dependent Origination itself, according to the words: 'The Noble Method (Ariyo Ñāyo) is well-seen by the noble disciple with wisdom.' Because Dependent Origination is good in every way (samantabhadra) and is to be penetrated in various ways, it leads to its own penetration through various teachings. Being good in every way and reaching the elegance of teaching (desanāvilāsa) are common reasons for all four types of teachings.
86:
## Special Cause
He said "visesato" (specifically/especially) because He wishes to state a special cause. It should be connected as "the teaching of that Blessed One" or "the teaching of this Dependent Origination." The specific cause of the process (pavatti) is ignorance and so on. (He also wishes to show) the non-causality of things like primordial nature (pakati) which are wrongly taken as causes, and the causality of ignorance and so on. Some who are confused about that special cause take what is not a cause as a "cause," while others do not know any cause at all. Therefore, the forward teaching (anuloma-desanā) proceeded to show them the arising of formations (saṅkhāra) and other effects through causes appropriate to them. Although this benefit might exist in the other three teachings, those teachings did not proceed solely for that benefit because other special benefits exist. This forward teaching, however, exists solely for that benefit; thus, its purpose is so stated. Ignorance, which conceals the danger of the process, is the beginning; from that, formations arise; from that, consciousness—thus (the forward teaching) also proceeds to show the sequence of the arising of the process.

The reverse teaching (paṭiloma-desanā) proceeded to show the cause, such as birth (jāti), for the effect, such as aging and death (jarāmaraṇa), which was attained according to the penetration of various effects that occurred in the preliminary stage before the enlightenment of the Bodhisatta who was repeatedly contemplating. Or, it is connected as: the reverse teaching proceeded for the Blessed One who was contemplating. Even while teaching, the Blessed One, having contemplated the world fallen into distress, teaches to show the cause He Himself had realized for various sufferings which are effects like aging and death, according to the sequence He realized in the preliminary stage. "Having transcended until the past time" is said with the intention that nutriments, craving, etc., are the present time, while formations and ignorance are the past time. Or, nutriments to be produced by craving are the future time, craving etc. are the present, and formations and ignorance are the past. Since it is appropriate to show the sequence of cause and effect by showing the manifest effect and then its cause: nutriments produced by craving in a previous life are the present time, craving etc. are the past, and formations and ignorance are the even more remote past. To show the beginningless nature of Saṃsāra, the meaning "until the even more remote past time" for "until the past time" is appropriate.

There are also the four nutriments that bring about the production of renewed existence in the future—

"I do not say 'one consumes'. If I were to say 'one consumes', then the question 'Venerable Sir, who consumes?' would be appropriate. But I do not say so. If someone were to ask me, who does not say so, 'Venerable Sir, for what purpose is the consciousness-nutriment?', that question would be appropriate. This is (the answer):"
87:
That question is appropriate; in that regard, the answer 'Consciousness-nutriment is for the sake of the production of renewed existence in the future' is appropriate. This is because of the statement spoken [in the Nidānavagga of the Saṃyutta Nikāya], and because contact-nutriment and mental-volition-nutriment are associated with that consciousness-nutriment, and because physical-nutriment is the cause for the arising of that consciousness-nutriment and so forth (those nutriments cause future rebirth). Indeed, for a person whose physical body is supported by that physical nutriment, and for one who desires that nutriment, there is the accumulation of kamma-consciousness. It has been stated that the food which is physical nutriment is a strong decisive support (upanissaya) for faith and so forth, as well as for lust and so forth. Therefore, in this teaching, 'Those nutriments included in the round of kamma belong to the present time,' only the previously mentioned meaning is appropriate. Starting from the past, by the method beginning with 'Monks, thus with ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be,' the meaning is that this teaching has arisen to show the sequence of cause and effect to those veneyya (beings to be tamed) who do not understand without returning after ascending by way of seeing the origin of the nutriments manifest in the past and thereafter. 'For the sake of showing the future' means that for persons who cannot penetrate or see the things occurring in the future, it is for the sake of showing that future through the succession of cause and effect by demonstrating the manifest present cause.

With reference to the word 'mūlakāraṇa' (root cause), the indication is made in the neuter gender as 'na akāraṇaṃ' (not without a cause). If [ignorance] were a root cause without a cause for itself, it would contradict the Sutta which says, 'With the arising of taints (āsava), ignorance arises'; desiring to show this, he cites the Sutta. In the discourse concerning the round (vaṭṭa), being the head or foremost also means being the cause of kamma, which is the cause of the round. Among those, ignorance is also the cause of craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā), because craving arises in existence where the faults are concealed by that ignorance. Therefore, because ignorance is especially the head or foremost, it is called the 'root cause' (mūlakāraṇa). Since the first beginning is not evident, it might be taken as permanent (nicca) because of being devoid of arising; therefore, he said, 'Monks, thus this word is spoken,' etc. By that statement, he shows this meaning: that because the state of having arisen before this time is not evident, the non-evidence of the first beginning is spoken of.

When the effects are spoken of according to the sequence of causes, namely ignorance and craving, the expression 'leading to a happy destination or a miserable destination' is for the sake of not contradicting the characteristics of grammar. The reason is that in a dvanda compound, the word with the more venerable meaning must be placed first. It is said that the Savaras (hunters) repeatedly heat and beat the meat to prevent it from sticking to the bone, make the cow drink hot water to cause diarrhea, and then kill the cow whose meat is swollen and loosened from the bone. Therefore, he said, 'heating with fire,' and so forth. In that simile, just as the cow to be slaughtered, being overcome by ignorance, starts drinking the hot water as mentioned, so too the worldling performs the kamma that leads to a miserable destination as mentioned. Just as that cow [does not see] the danger in drinking hot water...
88:
...seeing [the danger in drinking hot water], she strives to drink cold water through the power of craving; so too this worldling (puthujjana), because ignorance is weak, sees the danger in kamma leading to an unhappy destination and strives to perform kamma leading to a happy destination through the power of craving. Indeed, it should be noted that in suffering, craving follows after ignorance, and in happiness, ignorance follows after craving.

'Evaṃ' (thus) means because of being obstructed by ignorance and being joined with craving. 'Ayaṃ kāyo' (this body) refers to the five aggregates which are the body together with consciousness. Alternatively, because it is stated, 'With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises,' and this group of dhammas is called the cause of contact, it refers to the group of the six sense bases. 'Samudāgato' means arisen (uppanna). 'Bahiddhā ca nāmarūpaṃ' (and external mentality-materiality) refers to the five aggregates which are the body together with consciousness externally, or the six sense bases.

'Itthetaṃ' means this group of two dhammas. It means that one's own and others' five aggregates, as well as the twelve bases defined as doors and objects, are named 'dvaya' (the pair). In other Suttas, it is stated, 'Dependent on a pair, contact arises,' referring to pairs such as the eye and forms, etc., giving rise to eye-contact and so on. In this Bālapaṇḍita Sutta, however, the internal and external bases are spoken of. This pair of internal and external bases is called the 'Mahādvaya' (the Great Pair).

The meaning here is: In other Suttas, it is stated, 'Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact,' and so on, where contact is spoken of dependent on pairs such as eye and forms... mind and mental objects. In this Sutta, however, by saying 'this body alone,' the remaining dhammas which are the support for the eye, etc., are treated as being dependent on the eye, etc. Taking the group of the eye, etc., as a unity called 'internal bases' (ajjhattikāyatana), and taking the objects such as forms, etc., spoken of as 'external mentality-materiality' as a unity called 'external bases' (bāhirāyatana), contact is spoken of dependent on those internal and external bases. Therefore, this pair is called the 'Mahādvaya.'

By doing so, it is stated, 'This meaning should be illustrated by the five aggregates and six bases of oneself and others.' Indeed, the eye, etc., together with their supports, spoken of as 'this body,' are one's own five aggregates. The forms, etc., spoken of as 'external mentality-materiality,' are the five aggregates of others. Likewise, 'this body' is one's own internal bases, and 'external mentality-materiality' are the external bases of others. Otherwise, if only the internal bases were called 'this body,' it would not be possible to illustrate with the five aggregates of oneself and others, because the internal bases alone are not one's own five aggregates.

'Saḷāyatana' (six sense bases) refers to the six bases that are the causes of contact. The fool, being touched by the contact arisen through those bases which are the causes, experiences pleasure and pain.
89:
With the word 'ādi' (etc.), the passage 'Monks, for the wise man hindered by the hindrance of ignorance and fettered by craving, one of these...' and so forth should be connected. For in that Bālapaṇḍita Sutta, the Blessed One, having treated formations as dependent on ignorance and craving, and having taken consciousness, mind-and-matter, and the six sense bases by the term 'body' (kāya), and having treated the contact of the six sense bases in this body as dependent on those sense bases, showed the specific conditionality of feeling. Thus, He showed to the fool and the wise the dependent origination ending in feeling, rooted in ignorance and craving in the past. Furthermore, wishing to show the distinction between the fool and the wise, He said: 'Monks, for the fool hindered by that ignorance and fettered by that craving, this body has been produced. That ignorance has not been abandoned by the fool, and that craving is not yet exhausted. Why is that? Monks, because the fool has not lived the holy life rightly for the complete destruction of suffering. Therefore, with the breaking up of the body, the fool goes to another body. Being one who has gone to another body, he is not released from birth... and from suffering, I say' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.19). Having shown craving accompanied by ignorance arising from feeling, and having treated clinging and existence as dependent on that craving, He showed birth and so forth with the words 'he goes to another body' (kāyūpago hoti). Thus, He taught the dependent origination with two roots, starting from the arising of present causes. Conversely, for the wise man, it should be understood that He showed the reverse dependent origination (paṭiloma-paṭiccasamuppāda) with two roots, starting from the exhaustion of present causes.

Because it is the specific cause of actions leading to woeful states, ignorance is said to 'know what should not be known' (avindiyaṃ vindati). Likewise, because it is not the specific cause of the good conduct that should be known, it is said to 'not know what should be known' (vindiyaṃ na vindati). The producing or arising of eye-consciousness and so forth, which depend on it, is called 'āyatana'. Because it cannot be penetrated due to its nature of intense delusion, it makes the unknown 'unknown' (aññāta). It is also said to cause one to run in the endless cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra). By means of the fivefold linguistic characteristics (nirutti-lakkhaṇa)—namely, addition, reversal, modification, elision, and the specific meaning of the root—taking the letters 'a', 'vi', and 'ja' from the three words (anta, virahita, a), eliding other letters, and adding a second 'ja', it is called 'avijjā'. After showing the literal meaning of the syllables, He said 'apica' (furthermore) and so forth to show the natural meaning. When ignorance exists, the base and object of eye-consciousness and so forth, such as 'this is the base, this is the object'...
90:
...cannot be known; thus, ignorance is said to be the concealer of those bases and objects. Because it conceals the nature of the bases and objects, and because it conceals the state of being dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) of causes like ignorance, and the state of being dependently arisen (paṭiccasamuppanna) of effects like aging and death, it should be understood as the concealer of dependent origination and the dependently arisen.

Formations included by taking the word 'saṅkhāra' are called 'formations arrived at by the word saṅkhāra'. Although formations caused by ignorance are also included by the word 'saṅkhāra', they are mentioned separately because they are principal in this teaching. Therefore, in the phrase 'there are two kinds', referring to the volitional formations (abhisaṅkharaṇaka-saṅkhāra) arrived at by the word 'saṅkhāra', and excluding those already mentioned therein, the formations arrived at by the word 'saṅkhāra' should be connected. Or, the term 'formations arrived at by the word saṅkhāra' refers to the whole, and a part of that whole, the volitional formations, is described here as 'with ignorance as condition, formations arise' (avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā). Thus, it should be understood that the twofold nature is stated by way of including everything that should be described. By the passage 'First, verbal formations (vaci-saṅkhāra) cease' and so forth, verbal formations such as initial application, sustained application, inhalation, exhalation, perception, and feeling are mentioned; bodily volitions (kāya-sañcetanā) and so forth mentioned under 'formations dependent on ignorance' are not meant here.

'Paritassati' means thirsting (desiring to drink). 'Bhavati' is said with reference to the rebirth-process (upapatti-bhava). 'Bhāvayati' refers to the kamma-process (kamma-bhava). The shifting of the aggregates is called death (maraṇa), as it is said, 'by this, they die'. Because of the statement, 'Painful feeling has the suffering of arising and the suffering of presence' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.465), it undermines in two moments. 'Āyāsa' means fatigue or despair. The word 'kevala' means 'unmixed' in the phrase 'unmixed rice' (kevalā sālayo), and it means 'entire' or 'without remainder' in the phrase 'the entire Anga and Magadha' (kevalā aṅgamagadhā). Therefore, it expresses both meanings. Among those two, the 'unmixed' meaning refers to being devoid of happiness (sukha). Indeed, in this dependent origination, there is nothing that is devoid of arising and passing away.

Because it causes the states associated with that delusion or the person to be intensely deluded, it has the function (rasa) of deluding (sammohana). Because it is apprehended by the mind as concealing the nature of the object, it has the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of concealing (chādana). Because of the statement 'with the arising of taints, there is the arising of ignorance' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.103), it has taints (āsava) as its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). Because they strive to produce rebirth, they [formations] have the function (rasa) of striving (āyūhana); or, striving means accumulating. Because it occurs as the precursor of mind-and-matter, it has the function of being the precursor (pubbaṅgama). Because it is apprehended by the mind as connecting with the previous life, it has the manifestation of rebirth (paṭisandhi). Because it associates with consciousness, it has the function of association (sampayoga). Because it disperses matter due to the absence of mutual association, it has the function of dispersing (vikiraṇa). In this way, it is like rice grains being crushed and dispersed into powder. Since the mind (nāma) sometimes possesses the state of being wholesome and so forth...
91:
Then, to distinguish [matter from wholesome and unwholesome states], it was said: "it has the manifestation of being indeterminate (*abyākata*)." Just as in this Pali passage, "States without volition are indeterminate," the state of being without an object should also be understood as the state of being indeterminate. The characteristic of a base (*āyatana*) is the characteristic of exertion, or the characteristic of expanding the consciousness and mental factors that arise according to causes. The state of being the cause for seeing and so forth is the function (*rasa*) of seeing and so forth. Since equanimity (*upekkhā*) which is an unwholesome resultant is an undesirable object, it is included under painful feeling (*dukkha-vedanā*); and since the other [wholesome resultant equanimity] is a desirable object, it is included under pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*). Thus it was said: "it has the manifestation of pleasure and pain."
