Craving (*taṇhā*) has the characteristic of a cause because it is the origin of suffering. It has the function of delighting because it is taught: "it delights here and there." It has the manifestation of being insatiable (*atittabhāva-paccupaṭṭhāna*) because it appears as the state of being insatiable for the mind or the person regarding forms and so forth. Sense-desire clinging (*kāmupādāna*) appears as the firmness of craving; the remaining clingings appear as views (*diṭṭhi*). Therefore, they have the manifestation of the firmness of craving and the state of views (*taṇhādaḷhatta-diṭṭhi-paccupaṭṭhāna*). The characteristics and so forth of existence (*bhava*) should be applied by way of kamma-existence (*kammabhava*) and rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*).

In [the section on delusion, etc.], by the word "beginning" (*ādi*), the state of not understanding accordingly and so forth is taken. Ignorance (*aññāṇa*) regarding the Truth of Suffering and so forth is non-practice (*appaṭipatti*). Perversion (*vipallāsa*) as beautiful in what is foul and so forth is wrong practice (*micchā-paṭipatti*). Alternatively, delusion not associated with views is non-practice; delusion associated with views is wrong practice. Having six doors and six objects is not only for ignorance (*avijjā*); rather, it exists for mental states in other factors of dependent origination as well. Thus it was said: "in all of them too." In saying "that which is not the range of both," the mind-base (*manāyatana*) is meant. This is because mental states have no shape, and thus there is no nearness or farness in terms of location. Therefore, the object of the mind-base cannot be said to have reached or not reached the location of the mind-base.

Regarding the danger that the factors of dependent origination might exceed twelve due to the presence of sorrow (*soka*) and so forth, the delimitation of the factors as "only twelve" should be understood. Sorrow and so forth are not taught as actual factors (*aṅga*) of dependent origination; rather, they are taught to show the root factor, ignorance (*avijjā*), which is the cause, by way of its effects. It is said that sorrow and so forth arise for the fool who is oppressed by aging and death (*jarā-maraṇa*); thus, the state of sorrow and so forth having aging and death as their cause has been stated. In the Sutta, "He is touched by painful bodily feeling," suffering caused by aging and death is included; thus, that Sutta is stated as evidence for sorrow and so forth being the cause of that suffering. However, since sorrow and so forth are summarized together with aging and death, it is appropriate that they have birth (*jāti*) as their cause. If aging and death were the cause, they should be summarized together with ignorance. But because of birth, aging and death as well as sorrow and so forth arise. Among them, aging and death are taken as an absolute factor.
92:
Sorrow and so forth, however, are not absolute because they do not exist in the fine-material realm (*rūpabhava*) and so forth. They are taken merely to point out ignorance (*avijjā*) through its evident effects. By thus pointing out ignorance, when birth (*jāti*) exists in the future, ignorance—which is the cause of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) that are the cause of rebirth—is shown. Thus, the non-interruption of the wheel of existence is shown. The Sutta should be understood as evidence for this very meaning: that ignorance is the cause of sorrow and so forth. It is not merely that sorrow and so forth have aging and death as their cause in the fool. By the words "the uninstructed worldling," it is shown that ignorance is the cause of sorrow and so forth. And it is not that only suffering caused by aging and death is suffering; [suffering caused by ignorance is also suffering].

## The Explanation of the Summary Section is Finished.
## The Explanation of the Word-Definition of Ignorance

By the passage "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," the reason why volitional formations should be pointed out in detail is shown, because ignorance is stated as the qualifier and volitional formations as the principal. It is like saying of a father: "Mitta is tall and dark; Datta is short and fair."

The nature that should be penetrated is called function (*rasa*). One's own function is *sarasa*. The true *sarasa* is *yāthāva-sarasa*. That very true nature is called characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) because it is to be noted. Therefore, it is called "the characteristic of the true nature and function" (*yāthāva-sarasa-lakkhaṇa*). Because only four are taught in the Sutta: "Bhikkhus, what is ignorance? It is non-knowledge regarding suffering," and so forth, it is said: "by way of the Suttanta method." In the *Nikkhepakaṇḍa* (Summary Section), however, the very same ignorance taught in four places in this Vibhaṅga Pali is explained by way of its occurrence in eight places, and by its characteristics through twenty-five terms. Thus, it is clarified by way of explaining those meanings. Teaching by analyzing without diminishing the meaning is called the Abhidhamma method (*abhidhamma-pariyāya*).

It is called *jāti* (birth/source) because it arises there; it is the place of arising. Although ignorance does not take the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-sacca*) and the Truth of the Path (*magga-sacca*) as objects, it is said to arise there because it occurs by way of concealing them for one who wishes to know those truths, and by way of being the cause for taking what is not the Path of Cessation as the Path of Cessation. Therefore, those [Cessation and Path] are also the places of arising for ignorance. For the others [the Truths of Suffering and Origin], [they are places of arising by being objects].
93:
By way of being an object as well (it should be understood as the locus of ignorance). Just as marks such as a robe or a plow-shaped horn on the oxen belonging to the Saṅgha or Baladeva can distinguish and exclude them from other white oxen, so too, the nature of non-knowledge (aññāṇa), which can exclude states like greed (lobha) that cause blindness and have the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca) and so forth as their objects, should be known as the characteristic of ignorance (avijjā).

'Atthattha' means the benefit of a benefit (successive results). The repetitive expression 'atthattha' serves the purpose of making each and every benefit distinct and clear. Alternatively, it means the benefit that is truly a benefit; thus, the word 'attha' is qualified by the word 'attha' itself to show the unerring and true nature of the benefit. This is because wisdom (ñāṇa) does not take what is not a benefit as a benefit. In this same way, the term 'kāraṇakāraṇa' (cause of a cause) should also be understood. 'Taṃ ākāraṃ' means the aspect of being the benefit of a benefit and so forth. 'Gahetvā' means having introduced it into the mind, or having made it something grasped by the mind (by the person). The re-examination of a truth already penetrated is called 'paccavekkhaṇā' (reviewing). The state of a fool characterized by wrong thinking and so forth is called 'bālya' (foolishness). 'Pajānāti' means knowing through various modes such as impermanence (anicca). Intense delusion is called 'pamoha'. Delusion that is all-encompassing is called 'sammoha'.

'Dukkhārammaṇatā' means (ignorance occurs) because of having the Truth of Suffering as its object. Alternatively, when a certain ignorance covers the truth, the mental states associated with that ignorance take the Truth of Suffering as their object; because that ignorance is the cause or locus of those states, it is called 'dukkhārammaṇatā'. Or again, the object itself is called 'ārammaṇatā'; since this ignorance has the Truth of Suffering as its object, it is called 'dukkhārammaṇatā'.

Suffering (dukkha) and the Origin (samudaya) are profound because they are difficult to see, not because they are profound by nature (sabhāvato). Therefore, ignorance arises by way of having that suffering and origin as its object. The meaning is that ignorance cannot arise with the other two (Cessation and the Path) as its objects because they are profound by nature. Furthermore, by the phrase 'api ca kho pana', it is shown that the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca) is even more profound than the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca), because the Path has a conditioned nature (saṅkhata-sabhāva).

## The Explanation of the Section on Ignorance is Finished.
## The Explanation of the Section on Volitional Formations

'Punāti' means it purifies or cleanses from the suffering of result (vipāka-dukkha) which is the fruit of demerit, and from the suffering of defilements (kilesa-dukkha). It is called 'puñña' (merit) because one performs good deeds with an inclination (āsaya) toward welfare and happiness, and because by producing that welfare and happiness, it fulfills the desire of the doer. According to the rules of etymology (nirutti), it should be known as 'puñña' in the sense of 'pūraka' (one who fulfills) and 'pujjanibbattaka' (one who produces honor). The meaning is that it does not shake or waver because it is very far from the states opposing concentration (samādhi). In the word 'kāyassa' (of the body), the description is made by way of the body being the master of the door (sense-door).
94:
'Puññūpaga' means reaching the attainments of existence (bhava-sampatti). That meaning is found in the Vibhaṅga Sutta (Saṃ. Ni. 2.2). The author of the summary primarily took it from that sutta. However, in the Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta (Ma. Ni. 1.102), it is stated: "Friends, there are these three volitional formations."

This Abhidhamma was indeed spoken by the Omniscient Buddha (Sabbaññu), not by a Paccekabuddha. To clarify this meaning, those volitional formations are taken by the power of those suttas. How is this meaning clarified by such a taking? To show this, it is said: "In both the Abhidhamma and the Suttas, these states are described as having the same form." The meaning is that because it is similar to the well-known Suttanta, this Abhidhamma should also be known as spoken by the Omniscient Buddha.

When it is said "there are also thirteen," among those thirteen, the nature of being 'made of mental development' (bhāvanāmaya) for volitions dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇa-vippayutta) is not obvious; therefore, the phrase "for example" and so forth is stated. Practices such as meditating on "earth, earth" and the preliminary work for kasiṇas (kasiṇa-parikamma) and the preparation of the kasiṇa-disk are included within 'mental development' (bhāvanā).

States of mind and mental factors arising by way of giving are called 'dāna' (giving). Among those, the volition (cetanā) which is the exertion or activity (vyāpāra) that arises based on and starting with the act of giving is called 'dāna'. The same applies to the remaining virtues like morality (sīla) and so forth. The phrase "with a joyful mind" should be understood merely as an illustration of how rejoicing (anumodanā) occurs. This is because one can also recollect with a mind accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā).

It (the fourth jhāna result) produces kamma-born matter (kaṭattā-rūpa) that is dissimilar to itself along with the fourth jhāna resultant (vipāka) which is similar to itself in the fine-material realms such as Vehapphala; and it produces it even without the fourth jhāna resultant in the realm of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta). Matter (rūpa) is called 'with shaking' (saiñjana) because it possesses vibration. This is either because it cannot suppress the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and so forth which cause shaking, or because it is the cause of the shaking known as craving for fine-material existence (rūpa-taṇhā). For that very reason, the entire fourth jhāna which has a material object or a material sign (nimitta) as its object is not called 'unshakable' (aniñjana) in the primary sense.

A person weighing with a large scale or measuring with a measure (nāḷi) weighs or measures only the collective heap, not each individual red-bead (guñjā) or each individual grain of rice. Similarly, the Blessed One takes the immeasurable first wholesome volitions only by way of a collective group, and because they are of the same class (ekajātika), He shows them as one. The same applies to the second volition and so forth.

Instead of saying "occurring in the body-door," saying "arising while leading to pulling, grasping, and moving" is merely to show a distinction in terminology. This is because occurring in the body-door is itself the act of leading to pulling and so forth. Alternatively, the former expression states the door's status as a distinguishing mark, while the latter states the volition's ability to produce the form of intimation (viññatti-rūpa). In that latter expression, taking by pulling is 'ādāna', easy grasping is 'gahaṇa', and movement is 'copana'.
95:
In this context, in taking bodily formations and verbal formations, or in taking bodily volitions and verbal volitions, the volition of supernormal knowledge (abhiññā-cetanā) should not be taken as a condition for consciousness (viññāṇa) in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). This is because it is not a condition that assists consciousness. Why is it not so? One might ask: "Is not that volition of supernormal knowledge also wholesome and of the nature to produce a resultant?" True, however, in the continuity of worldlings (puthujjanas) and trainees (sekhas) whose craving, ignorance, and conceit are not yet severed, its wholesomeness and its nature of producing a resultant are mentioned because of its occurrence with activity (byāpāra), not because it actually produces a resultant (vipāka). If that volition of supernormal knowledge were to produce a resultant, it would only produce a fine-material sphere resultant (rūpāvacara-vipāka). This is because kamma belonging to one plane does not produce a resultant belonging to another plane. It would produce that resultant which has an object similar to itself and occurs in the three stages (ṭhāna). This is because in the Cittuppāda-kaṇḍa, it is stated that the fine-material sphere resultant has an object similar to the kamma. In the fine-material sphere resultant, there is no limited (paritta) object, whereas the volition of supernormal knowledge has only a limited object. Therefore, it is understood that it does not produce a resultant. Supernormal knowledge is the benefit (ānisaṃsa) of the fourth jhāna concentration produced in the kasiṇas. As it is said: "When the mind is thus concentrated..." and so on. Therefore, it is similar to the fruit of concentration, but it does not give a resultant. Just as the acquisition of requisites in this life is a benefit of giving and virtue, so too this volition of supernormal knowledge does not produce a resultant. Like the volition of supernormal knowledge, the volition associated with restlessness (uddhacca-cetanā) also does not become [a condition for consciousness]. This point should be examined because, having separately extracted the states associated with restlessness, it is stated: "Knowledge of the result of those states is the discrimination of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā)."

The decision here in accordance with the Amataggapatha is as follows: Even in the absence of the Path-knowledges, for those worldlings and trainees who are to attain the Path-knowledges, the unwholesome states that can be abandoned by those Paths at the time of their arising are called "states to be abandoned by vision" (dassana-pahātabba) and "states to be abandoned by cultivation" (bhāvanā-pahātabba). For worldlings, however, since the higher Path (bhāvanā) is absent, there is no consideration of states to be abandoned by cultivation. Therefore, although those unwholesome states occurring in them cannot be abandoned by vision, they are not called "states to be abandoned by cultivation." If they were so called, unwholesome states to be abandoned by vision would condition some states to be abandoned by cultivation through the conditions of object (ārammaṇa), object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati), and strong-dependence (upanissaya). However, it is not stated in the Paṭṭhāna that "a state to be abandoned by vision conditions some states to be abandoned by cultivation by any condition." For trainees, however, the states to be abandoned by cultivation that are present are indeed states to be abandoned by cultivation. For this very reason, for trainees, the states to be abandoned by vision—having been relinquished, vomited, released, abandoned, renounced, detached, and well-detached—which are to be enjoyed...
96:
Those unwholesome states to be abandoned by vision (dassane-na-pahātabba) are not to be relished, nor are they to be greatly delighted in. Because they have been abandoned, even though they become causes for joy and non-distraction, they do not give rise to grief (domanassa) and restlessness (uddhacca). Therefore, those states do not reach the status of object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), object-predominance-condition (ārammaṇādhipati-paccaya), or natural-decisive-support-condition (pakatūpanissaya-paccaya) for those unwholesome states to be abandoned by development (bhāvanāya-pahātabba). Indeed, a Noble One (ariya) does not give rise to defilements such as lust (rāga) by depending on defilements that have been abandoned.

It is also stated: 'Whatever defilements have been abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), one does not return to those defilements, does not approach them, does not come back to them... by the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga)... one does not come back to them.' It cannot be said that the unwholesome states to be abandoned by vision in the continuity of worldlings (puthujjana) do not assist other unwholesome states by any condition (i.e., they do assist). This is because it is stated that wrong view (diṭṭhi) and doubt (vicikicchā) act as object-conditions for restlessness: 'One relishes and delights in wrong view; taking that wrong view as an object, lust arises, wrong view, doubt, and restlessness arise. Taking doubt as an object, doubt, wrong view, and restlessness arise.' Here, 'restlessness' refers to the arising of consciousness associated with restlessness (uddhacca-sahagata cittuppāda). With this intention, in the description of the predominance-condition (adhipati-paccaya), it is stated only this much: 'Having made wrong view a priority, one relishes and delights in it; having made that a priority, lust arises, wrong view arises,' but it is not stated that 'restlessness arises.'

Therefore, although unwholesome states to be abandoned by vision and development are not to be spoken of as past, etc., those Paths bring about the nature of non-arising for such unwholesome states. Among those unwholesome states, those occurring in worldlings are called 'to be abandoned by vision' because they can be abandoned by vision (the Path of Stream-entry). Those occurring in trainees (sekha) are called 'to be abandoned by development' because they can be abandoned by development (the three higher Paths). Among them, unwholesome states to be abandoned by development do not produce results (vipāka) because they are devoid of companions. Therefore, the status of asynchronous kamma condition (nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya) for the volition to be abandoned by development is not mentioned. However, for worldlings who are devoid of the vision and development to be expected, the production of results cannot be denied for the attachment to one's own property (chandarāga), etc., for the arising of consciousness associated with restlessness, and for the defilements that are co-resident (tad-ekaṭṭha) with the three fetters, because they have not been cut off and thus have companions that are not yet exhausted. Therefore, the result of states associated with restlessness is mentioned in the Vibhaṅga.

If so, do unwholesome states devoid of vision and development not fall into the category of 'to be abandoned neither by vision nor by development' (neva-dassane-na-na-bhāvanāya-pahātabba)? They do not. This is because only states that are not to be abandoned (appahātabba) are called 'to be abandoned neither by vision nor by development,' and because unwholesome states are of a nature contrary to those not to be abandoned. Even so, will those unwholesome states not fall into the 'not-to-be-declared' (navattabba) category in this triad? They do not. This is because the twelve types of unwholesome consciousness-arising shown in the Cittuppāda-kaṇḍa are included within the first two factors.

For example, just as in the Triad of the Arisen (Uppanna Tika), past states that are not included by way of time are not called 'not-to-be-declared' because all conditioned (saṅkhata) states are included by way of their nature (dhamma). In this Triad of Vision (Dassana Tika) as well, since there are no states not-to-be-declared among those already taken as consciousness-arisings, it should be understood that the status of 'not-to-be-declared' is not mentioned. Indeed, if in any triad there were any consciousness-arising that was always not-to-be-declared, there would be a fourth portion (catuttha-koṭṭhāsa) for those consciousness-arisings in that triad. Therefore, just as in the three factors taught, one would include them in that fourth portion by distinguishing them, saying 'there are states with limited objects that are not-to-be-declared,' and so on. Because that fourth portion does not exist, the status of 'not-to-be-declared' is not mentioned in the Uppanna Tika or in this Dassana Tika. Alternatively, it is like the three Great Elements (mahābhūta) in the Realm of Form (rūpadhātu) being taught as 'with impact' (sappaṭigha) because they have a nature similar to states with impact. How is it taught? It is taught that: 'Depending on one Great Element that is non-manifesting and with impact, the remaining Great Elements arise for beings born in the realm of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta).'
97:
Because it is said that all conditioned phenomena are included, in the Triad of the Arisen (Uppanna-tika), past phenomena that are not included by the power of time are not stated as 'indescribable' (navattabba). Just as there is no 'indescribable' among the phenomena taken as consciousness, mental factors, and matter, it should be understood that in this Triad of Vision (Dassana-tika), 'indescribability' (navattabbatā) is not mentioned because there is no 'indescribable' among the phenomena taken as the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda). If in any triad there were some 'indescribable' arising of consciousness by necessity, then, as in the aforementioned passages where there is a fourth category for them, the arisings of consciousness that should be classified and included in that fourth category are classified and included by such methods as 'There are indescribable phenomena with limited objects,' etc. Because that fourth category does not exist, it is not so stated in the Triad of the Arisen nor in this Triad of Vision.

Alternatively, it is like the three Great Elements (mahābhūta) in the fine-material element (rūpadhātu) being called 'impinging' (sappaṭigha) because they have a nature similar to impinging matter. As it was said: 'Depending on one non-manifesting impinging Great Element of the beings in the realm of non-percipient beings, the other Great Elements arise; depending on two Great Elements, one Great Element arises.' In this way, the unwholesome states existing in the continuity of worldlings (puthujjana) which have a nature similar to those to be abandoned by development (bhāvanāya pahātabba) might be called 'to be abandoned by development'; if so stated, there is no fault of falling into 'indescribability'. If this is so, although they occur in the continuity of worldlings, the lust and greed (chandarāga), etc., regarding one's own property which are to be abandoned by development, assist the lust and greed, etc., regarding others' property by way of decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya); and lust (rāga) assists lust and wrong view (diṭṭhi) by way of predominance condition (adhipati-paccaya)—this meaning is obtained. However, just as the three Great Elements in the fine-material realm are not impinging in the ultimate sense (paramattha) because they are not the base of touch (aphoṭṭhabbattā), so the lust and greed, etc., regarding one's own property occurring in worldlings, being devoid of the development that should be considered, are not 'to be abandoned by development' in the ultimate sense. Therefore, the state of being a multi-moment kamma condition (nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya) of phenomena to be abandoned by development is not stated, nor is it stated that 'phenomena to be abandoned by vision assist phenomena to be abandoned by development by any condition.' For the defilements that have 'to be abandoned by vision' as their cause do not occur above the Path of Stream-entry. However, the Path of Stream-entry only brings about the deficiency of associates for the arising of consciousness associated with restlessness (uddhacca-sahagata) which has 'to be abandoned by vision' as its cause. Since the Path of Stream-entry does not cause the essential nature of that restlessness to reach the state of non-arising in the future, its state of being 'definitely to be abandoned by development' (ekanta-bhāvanāya pahātabba) is stated. Therefore, regarding such restlessness, the statement that it can produce a result when associates are present, and the statement that it cannot produce a result when associates are absent, are not contradictory.

If that volition of restlessness is also to be removed from being a cause of consciousness, why is it said 'twenty volitions'? To show the reason for that, he said: 'With ignorance as condition...' (avijjāpaccayā...)
98:
"...indeed, all these come to be." If so, should it not be said 'twenty-one' along with the volition of super-knowledge (abhiññā-cetanā)? No, because the non-mention of the volition of super-knowledge has the stated reason (not assisting subsequent consciousness). That same reason is also the reason for not mentioning the other volition, restlessness. By the statement of the reason for not mentioning the similar volition, it shows that with regard to the reason (being caused by ignorance), one volition of restlessness is mentioned; by that same reason, the other volition of super-knowledge should also be mentioned. And with regard to the reason (not being able to assist rebirth-linking consciousness), the other volition of super-knowledge is not mentioned; by that same reason, the state of the already mentioned volition of restlessness as 'not to be mentioned' is also shown. The imperturbable formation (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra) is just a type of mental formation (cittasaṅkhāra) and is very clear because there is no distinction; therefore, its association with bodily formations, etc., is not shown.

By the words "taking it with the perception of pleasure (sukha-saññā)", the occurrence of craving (taṇhā) is shown. "Requisites of craving" (taṇhā-parikkhāra) means the retinues of craving, or the formations (saṅkhāra) prepared and adorned by craving with such thoughts as "it is pleasant, it is beautiful," etc. A being who does not know that craving is the origin of suffering, longing thus: "Oh, would that I, after the breaking up of the body, after death, might reach the company of the Khattiya Great Halls," prepares and manages formations. The practice of difficult austerities (dukkara-cariyā) undertaken for the sake of not dying is called 'deathless penance' (amara-tapa). Or, the practice performed for the sake of becoming a deva or brahma is called 'deathless penance'. Or, the penance that kills oneself because it is extremely painful is 'deathless penance' (amara-tapa). Just as the word 'unseen' is used for a seen object, the word 'deathless' (amara) should be understood for things that are subject to death (mara).

Because it produces suffering such as birth (jāti), which is like the suffering caused by falling into a precipice, the meritorious formation (puññābhisaṅkhāra) is said to be like jumping down from the summit of the deva or brahma realms. The fruit of merit (puññaphala) taken as something delightful and enjoyable is like a blade smeared with honey over a flame. The meritorious formation which has that fruit is like falling into that flame or licking that blade.

With the perception of pleasure, such as "Pleasant is the touch of the arm of this young, soft, and hairy female wanderer," etc., a fool performs demeritorious formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra) which are loathsome suffering in both the moment of performance and the moment of result, just as one plays with excrement, or as one overcome by defilements and anger, unable to follow one's own will and wishing to die, eats poison. Alternatively, the mind associated with greed should be compared to playing with excrement, and the mind associated with hatred to eating poison. Just as the city of spirits (pisācanagara), though abundant in sensual pleasures, is accompanied by danger and is a cause for the perversion of pleasure, so the immaterial results (arūpa-vipāka), because there are no dissimilar phenomena in between, the arising and passing away cannot be noted; because the continuity is long, the nature of change (vipariṇāma) cannot be grasped; thus, though they are suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha) and suffering due to change (vipariṇāma-dukkha), they are the cause of the perversion (vipallāsa) of permanence, etc. Therefore, those immaterial results should be compared to the city of spirits, and the imperturbable formation (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra) should be compared to going towards that city.
99:
The word 'tāva' is a particle that anticipates another meaning to be mentioned. Therefore, the meaning 'ignorance is the condition for volitional formations' is established first. However, it means that another problem should still be stated. By the statement 'Because of ignorance, all these formations arise,' the state of being a condition for the intentions of direct knowledge (abhiññā-cetanā) is shown. It should be applied [as an object condition] at the time of knowing the deluded mind of others or oneself through the knowledge of mind-reading (cetopariya-ñāṇa), the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa), and the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa).

'Avijjāsammūḷhattā' means due to the state of being greatly deluded by ignorance which covers the faults of existence (bhava). 'Rāgādīnaṃ' means that when one enjoys lust etc. associated with ignorance—namely lust, views (diṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), restlessness (uddhacca), and displeasure (domanassa)—the arising [of those states] should be understood by taking ignorance as the object. Enjoyment with high regard should be associated only with ignorance that is associated with lust and views. Since enjoyment is lust, and the factor inseparable from it is views, it should be understood that by the word 'enjoyment' itself, views that regard ignorance with high regard are also mentioned. By the mention of lust etc. in their own form in the Pali, it shows the state of having ignorance as an object for the formations associated with them. The phrase 'yaṃ kiñci' is said for the purpose of including all first impulsions (javana) that do not have ignorance as an object. 'Vuttanayena' means by the method already mentioned, by way of overcoming [ignorance] and longing for existence.

In saying 'it arrives at the single-cause theory (ekakāraṇavāda)', the fault of such an attachment is meant. A single-cause theory is undesirable. This is because it would lead to the consequence that all effects would arise at all times, or they would all arrive at an identical nature. Since there is a purpose in showing the fourth method—one cause and one effect—while the three [other] varieties are absent, it [the single-cause theory in this specific context] is not inappropriate.

'Because of the determination of feeling according to contact' means: 'Bhikkhus, dependent on a contact to be experienced as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises,' and so on; and 'Dependent on the eye... the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, feeling,' and so on. This is because of the separate existence of feelings born of eye-contact, such as pleasant feeling, in accordance with the eye-contacts to be experienced as pleasant. It is also because, even when the eye and forms etc. are the same, there is no reversal of pleasure etc. due to the power of contact; and because, even when forms and attention (manasikāra) etc. are the same, there is no reversal of feelings born of eye-contact due to the power of impingement (saṅghaṭṭana) upon the eye etc.; and because, even when other conditions are common, there is no confusion of coarse or subtle [feelings] among feelings such as pleasure due to the power of contact. The non-perverted [nature] of the aforementioned contact for pleasure etc...
100:
Thus, in the separate determination of contact according to feeling, [it is so] because there is no confusion of coarse or subtle [feelings] among feelings such as pleasure and feelings born of eye-contact due to the power of contact even when other conditions are the same; or, because the distinction of effect and cause is decided by the distinction of cause and effect, the decision regarding both cause and effect is called 'vavatthāna' (determination). 'Kammādayo' refers to causes such as kamma, nutriment (āhāra), and temperature (utu). These are not evident. [They are like the case where] a disease is cured by treating phlegm, [so only phlegm is evident].

'For one who contemplates gratification, craving increases'—according to this statement: 'Bhikkhus, for one dwelling contemplating gratification in things that lead to fetters, craving increases; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence,' it means that by this sutta, craving is taught as the cause of formations. Again, to show that ignorance is also the cause of that [craving], it says: 'With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of taints (āsava).' Or, it is evident that craving, or the taints of sensual desire, existence, and views which constitute the fourfold clinging, are the causes of formations; thus, by both suttas, only the state of ignorance being the cause of formations is shown. Indeed, by the word 'for one who contemplates gratification' (assādānupassino), ignorance, which has the function of covering faults, is shown to be the cause of craving.

Because one does not know (is ignorant), therefore one performs and exerts in meritorious formations (puṇṇābhisankhāra) and so on. Thus, because the state of ignorance being the cause of formations is evident, the state of not knowing (ignorance) is taught as the cause of formations. This is also because an Arahant (khīṇāsava) has no formations, and because [ignorance] is an uncommon (asādhāraṇa) cause. Alternatively, for meritorious formations etc., the bases (vatthu) and objects (ārammaṇa) etc. are common (sādhāraṇa) causes. Therefore, the meaning should be understood that ignorance, which covers the faults of meritorious existence etc., is the uncommon cause of meritorious formations and so on.

'Ṭhānaviruddha' means a condition that is opposed by way of presence (atthitā). Some teachers, however, say: 'Rebirth (paṭisandhi) and so on are the locations (ṭhāna).' If that were so, the preceding mind would be a condition opposed by location for the succeeding mind; this would not be absolute. For bhavaṅga is the proximity condition for bhavaṅga, and javana for javana. Moreover, since arts and sciences etc. do not have locations like rebirth, that [meaning] is not intended here.

Kamma is a condition opposed by nature (sabhāvaviruddha) to matter (rūpa) because of the opposition between the characteristic of bending (namana) and the characteristic of being deformed (ruppana), and because of the opposition between having an object (sārammaṇa) and having no object (anārammaṇa). Milk etc. [are opposed] to curd etc. due to the opposition of natures such as sweet and sour tastes. Light, which has the function of non-knowing, [is opposed] to consciousness, which has the function of knowing; and molasses etc., which do not have the function of intoxicating, [are opposed] to liquor (āsava), which has the function of intoxicating.

Cow hair and goat hair are the conditions for devāda grass. Curd etc. are the conditions for bhūtiṇaka grass. Here, 'avi' refers to red goats. Those [effects] are not only resultants (vipāka). Therefore, the state of being a condition...
101:
The point that ignorance (avijjā), which has painful results, is the cause of meritorious volitional formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) and imperturbable volitional formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra), which are not the results of that ignorance, is not incorrect; it is indeed correct. Even though they are not the results of that ignorance, because they are associated with faults, it might be assumed that ignorance is only the cause of demeritorious volitional formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra) which are similar to and not opposed to it, and not the cause of others (meritorious and imperturbable formations). To prevent such an assumption, it was said: "Whether opposed or unopposed, and likewise whether similar or dissimilar, the causality of states is established." Therefore, desiring to make this meaning clear, the concluding words beginning with "Thus, this ignorance..." were spoken.

There is a fixed nature (niyati), like the determination of the sequence of unblemished gems threaded on an unbroken string. The coming together in that fixed manner is called 'niyati-saṅgati' (coincidence of destiny). Those who have reached the states of humans, devas, birds, etc., and are inclined toward those respective states due to that fixed coincidence, are called 'niyati-saṅgati-bhāva-pariṇata' (developed through the coincidence of destiny). Others also interpret 'niyati-saṅgati-bhāva-pariṇata' as those who have reached various diversities by being inclined through fixity, through coincidence, and through those respective states. Desiring to show that through these various conceptualizations, ignorance makes the mind unwholesome and occurs in any one of the meritorious formations and so on, the words beginning with "He, thus through ignorance..." were spoken.

"Apariṇāyako bālo" means a fool who is devoid of a noble friend (kalyāṇamitta) who brings about the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga). Alternatively, the knowledge ending with the Path of Arahantship is called "pariṇāyaka" (leader/guide) because it shows what is even and uneven and leads to Nibbāna; one who is devoid of that knowledge that leads to Nibbāna is called "apariṇāyaka". "Having known the Dhamma" means having known the Dhamma such as the Suttas that reveal the Four Noble Truths through the support of a virtuous person; or it means having known Nibbāna, which is the most excellent of all states, through the Path Knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). Although the penetration of the remaining three truths occurs simultaneously with the knowledge of Nibbāna, it is spoken of as if the knowledge of Nibbāna occurred in a prior moment because the other penetrations are dependent on it.

## The Explanation of the Section on Volitional Formations is Finished.

## Explanation of the Section on Consciousness

Since the consciousness arising due to the aforementioned cause of formations (saṅkhāra) should only be the resultant consciousness produced by that kamma, it was said: "The thirty-two mundane resultant consciousnesses (lokiya vipāka viññāṇa) are included." However, in the Dhātukathā Pāḷi, in the section on 'Inclusion and Non-inclusion by way of Association' (vippayuttena saṅgahitāsaṅgahita-padas), it was taught as "By the consciousness conditioned by formations, those states which...", thereby including all consciousness, contact (phassa), and feeling (vedanā). If in this Dhātukathā, consciousness, contact, and feeling were only partial, the answer would be like that for the term "resultant states" (vipākā dhammā). Therefore, it should be understood that in that Dhātukathā, consciousness and so on, which are caused by formations, are taken according to the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya method.

Furthermore, in the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya, formations caused by ignorance are taught as wholesome formations and unwholesome formations belonging to the four planes. It should be noted that the formations mentioned in that Abhidhamma-bhājanīya are the ones taken in the Dhātukathā. As for 'existence' (bhava), it is not taken according to the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya method in the Dhātukathā for the purpose of showing the distinction between kamma-existence (kamma-bhava) and rebirth-existence (upapatti-bhava). For this reason, in that Dhātukathā, instead of extracting it as "existence conditioned by clinging" (upādāna-paccayā bhavo), existence is extracted only by the method of "kamma-existence" and so on.
102:
According to the words of the (Dhātukathā) Pāḷi: "By the consciousness conditioned by formations, those states which... are not included," the inclusion of all consciousness, contact, and feeling was made. If indeed consciousness, contact, and feeling were partial in this Dhātukathā, the answer would be like that for "resultant states" (vipākā dhammā); therefore, it should be understood that in that context, consciousness and so on conditioned by formations are taken by way of the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya. And the formations conditioned by ignorance are stated in the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya as wholesome formations and unwholesome formations of the four planes; it should be seen that those same ones are taken in the Dhātukathā. However, existence (bhava) is not taken by way of the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya in the Dhātukathā, for the purpose of showing the distinction between kamma-existence and rebirth-existence. Having done so, in that context, existence is extracted not as "existence conditioned by clinging," but only by the method of "kamma-existence" and so on. 

By the phrase "for this is a resultant" (vipākañhetaṃ), the fact of having formations as a condition is established because consciousness is a resultant. To establish that it has formations as a condition, it was said: "Because there is no resultant in the absence of accumulated kamma." Desiring to explain that meaning, the words beginning with "And the resultant..." (vipākañca) were spoken.

Regarding the phrase "mostly at the end of impulsion (javana) associated with greed," it should be understood that this refers only to registration (tadārammaṇa) accompanied by joy (somanassa), because in determining registration by way of impulsion, registration accompanied by joy is taught immediately after impulsion accompanied by joy. Because at the end of triple-rooted impulsion, rootless registration sometimes occurs, it was said "mostly." The phrase "or once" (sakiṃ vā) should be understood as in the phrases "two nights or three nights" and so on. In fact, some say that (registration) occurs only twice. In the phrase "two nights or three nights," since the word "vā" (or) is absent, taking "two nights" is appropriate merely for the sake of euphony; or it is appropriate for the sake of showing three consecutive nights. But here, the word "vā" is used in the sense of an alternative (vikappana). Therefore, it should be noted that "or once" was said with reference to it sometimes occurring only once. Desiring to show that such a single occurrence of registration should be investigated, the words beginning with "But in the counting of the occurrence of consciousness..." were spoken. In that context, "in the counting of the occurrence of consciousness" refers to the counting of the occurrence of consciousness stated in the Vipākakathā regarding powerful objects such as visible forms. Indeed, in that Vipākakathā, only the cases where registration occurs twice appear. For registration, which experiences the object of impulsion...
103: The intention of the commentator is that tadārammaṇa (registration), which experiences the object, should not arise in an object that is nearing its end and has only about one mind-moment of life remaining. The woeful rebirth-linking of unwholesome resultants, and the happy rebirth-linking in the sense-sphere, fine-material sphere, and immaterial sphere of wholesome resultants such as those of the sense-sphere, are appropriate according to karma. Considering that the discourse on rebirth-linking is a vast subject, he first said "In the course of existence, however" (pavattiyaṃ pana), etc., wishing to show only the occurrence during the course of existence. Because the two ahetuka (rootless) rebirth-linkings, etc., are themselves doors, and because those consciousnesses which are death and rebirth-linking do not arise through another door called bhavaṅga, it is impossible to say whether they have a fixed or unfixed door; therefore, the fixedness or unfixedness of the door is not mentioned. The fine-material resultant occurring in the continuity of a single being arises in whichever object among the objects such as the earth kasiṇa; since it does not occur in any other object, the fine-material resultants are said to have a fixed object. "Therein, for him" (tatrassa) means for the thirty-two types of consciousness during the course of existence. Due to the power of the occurrence of the faculties, there should be distinctions such as the eye-door and ear-door; and because that distinction of doors depends on the distinction of the cognitive series of consciousness, there should also be a distinction of the cognitive series. In that case, there should be a fixed order of consciousness (citta-niyama) such as "seeing or hearing immediately after adverting, and receiving immediately after that." When there is such a fixed order of consciousness, the occurrence of receiving and investigating is also established. It is not that only seeing and hearing are accomplished by the power of the occurrence of the faculties, nor is it that the function of seeing and hearing belongs only to the faculties; wishing to show this meaning, he said, "due to the distinction of doors and cognitive series, and due to the fixed order of consciousness." If tadārammaṇa arises because of the first great wholesome consciousness, when it arises immediately after the first great wholesome javana, it is said to follow its progenitor (janaka). Tadārammaṇa arising immediately after the second great wholesome consciousness, etc., is said to follow what is similar to the progenitor. Tadārammaṇa arising immediately after an unwholesome consciousness is also said to follow what is similar to the progenitor, because it belongs to the sense-sphere. Although the eleven tadārammaṇa consciousnesses are named "tadārammaṇa" because they are the cause for the occurrence of registration, the meaning is that they do not take the state of registration, or they do not occur by way of the state of registration. Alternatively, when javana occurs having made a name or lineage the object, tadārammaṇa does not take the object of that javana; it does not objectify it. Fine-material and immaterial states (rūpārūpa-dhamma) refer to the states of the fine-material and immaterial spheres. Having said this, the specific mention "having made the supernormal knowledge (abhiññā) the object" is for the purpose of showing the non-arising of tadārammaṇa even in states similar to the sense-sphere, because supernormal knowledge takes the limited (paritta), etc., as objects. Wrongly fixed states (micchātta-niyata dhamma), like the Path, are accomplished through meditation and are of great power. Therefore, when javana occurs in those states, it should not be accompanied by a following tadārammaṇa; thus, tadārammaṇa is rejected in those states.
104: Even though it is established by the phrase "having made the supramundane states the object," the separate mention "in the rightly fixed states (sammatta-niyata dhamma)" is for the purpose of showing that when those states are made the object, they are not the basis for tadārammaṇa, because the rightly fixed and wrongly fixed states are mutually opposed and very powerful. Having thus shown the occurrence of consciousness during the course of existence, he said "But that which was said" (yaṃ pana vuttaṃ), etc., to show it at the time of rebirth-linking. "By what [consciousness], where" means by what consciousness and in what existence does rebirth-linking occur. The nineteen rebirth-linkings occur at the moment of rebirth-linking together with their respective consciousnesses, and material and immaterial states arise; therefore, it is said that rebirth-linking occurs in various planes of existence through those respective consciousnesses. "Of that" (tassa) refers to the meaning of that consciousness. "Having come" (āgantvā) means as if it has come. "Gopaka Sīvali" refers to a person named Sīvali born in a herdsman (gopaka) family who protected the king's wealth. Because it is devoid of the activity of recollecting karma, etc., it is called "death while confused" (sammūḷha-kālakiriyā). Indeed, without any activity of recollection, one of the objects such as karma appears at that time of nearing death. Some teachers give the reason: "A small fly being crushed first does not cause the body-door adverting to turn in the bhavaṅga because there is some object being thought of by itself." However, that reason is not appropriate. This is because there is no other object being thought of besides the object of the bhavaṅga, and because it is impossible for the bhavaṅga to turn while another consciousness is occurring. In fact, the reason here is this: according to the teaching, "At that time, those [objects] hang, hang down, or hang forward for him," one of the objects such as karma must appear even before the three types of javana processes occur. Due to the occurrence of many javana processes, the objects appear as if hanging down or hanging forward. Therefore, without causing the body-door adverting to turn, the mind-door adverting alone takes one of the objects such as karma and first causes the bhavaṅga to turn. After that, because of the strength of the tangible object (phoṭṭhabbārammaṇa) caused by being struck with a stick, the body-consciousness cognitive series occurs in the second turn regarding the present tangible object. After that, having experienced the mind-door javana in sequence regarding the objects such as karma already taken by the previous javana process, it descends into the bhavaṅga which is registration, called either the original bhavaṅga or the adventitious bhavaṅga. If there is no registration, it descends into the bhavaṅga itself. "He passes away in this place" means he passes away with the death-consciousness (cuti-citta) immediately following registration, or if there is no registration, with the death-consciousness which is called the bhavaṅga itself. Since the bhavaṅga itself occurs as the death-consciousness, the death-consciousness is here called "bhavaṅga." "The object of the mind-door is light" means "the immaterial states... are light," referring to their appearing quickly. The object of the mind-door, which is an immaterial state, tends to appear quickly. By showing how the mind first arises in the object of the mind-door such as karma before the mind arises in the object of the body-door which is a powerful material state, the lightness of the objects of immaterial states is shown. Alternatively, although objects such as the visible form of the eye, etc., are clearly present, the phrase "of immaterial states" is used because he primarily wishes to show the immaterial states that possess objects. Therefore, the ability to take the object quickly due to the arising of consciousness in quick objects such as karma is called "lahuka" (light/quick).
105:
By showing that the mind first arises in one of the objects such as kamma, which is the object of the mind-door (manodvāra), even before the mind arises in a strong tangible object (phoṭṭhabbārammaṇa) such as that caused by being struck with a mallet—which is the object of the body-door (kāyadvāra)—it should be understood that the lightness (lahukatā) of the manifestation of the objects of mental phenomena (nāmadhamma) is demonstrated. Alternatively, although the objects of the eye and other physical senses, such as visible forms, are clearly present, the mention of "mental phenomena" is to be understood as being solely for the purpose of showing those mental phenomena which primarily possess an object. Therefore, the state of being quickly grasped as an object due to the arising of the mind in swift objects such as kamma is called lahukatā (the state of being quick).

Because the objects such as kamma have infinite divisions in detail by way of planes (bhūmi), the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda), and so on, he said, "in brief" (saṅkhepato).

Only while defilements such as ignorance (avijjā) and craving (taṇhā) have not yet been severed do objects such as kamma tend to appear. Because the stream of consciousness (cittasantāna), taking that object as its basis, tends to incline, lean, and tend towards another existence, he said, "inclined by the force of unsevered defilements." Indeed, when the stream of consciousness is inclined, the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta), which is a part of that stream, is also inclined; for there can be no inclination of the entire stream without the inclination of its parts. In all cases, they conclude: "The impulsions (javanas) occurring before the death-consciousness (cuti) that inclines towards an unhappy destination (duggati) are unwholesome; those occurring before the other (which inclines towards a happy destination) are wholesome."

It was taught: "Monks, if consciousness stands relishing the sign (nimitta) or relishing the detail (anubyañjana), and if one should pass away at that time, it is possible that one would reach one of two destinations: hell or the animal realm." Therefore, unwholesome states occurring near death become the sufficing condition (upanissaya) for rebirth-linking in an unhappy destination, and wholesome states for rebirth-linking in a happy destination.

An inferior object (hīna-ārammaṇa), which is the cause of lust (rāga) and so on, refers to an unpleasant object (aniṭṭhārammaṇa) that is suitable to be the object of an unwholesome resultant (akusalavipāka). Indeed, even that unpleasant object can become a cause for lust by the power of wrong thinking (sankappa). Alternatively, the state of being the cause of lust and so on, which arise together with the kamma that produces unwholesome resultants, or which arise together with the death-proximate impulsion (maraṇāsannajavana) volition similar to that kamma, is itself called hīnatā (inferiority). That object, being the object of kammas that produce subsequent remorse, would become the object of an unwholesome resultant that is undesirable by the power of kamma; otherwise, the result of an unwholesome kamma occurring in a pleasant object (iṭṭhārammaṇa) could not have a sign of kamma (kammanimitta) as its object. For an unwholesome resultant cannot have a pleasant object. A present sign of kamma that comes into focus at the five doors should be understood as an object occurring in the continuity of the kamma-object performed near death, or as an object similar to that sign of kamma. Otherwise, that very death-proximate impulsion would both cause the rebirth-linking object to appear and produce the rebirth-linking itself, like the access (upacāra) of rebirth-linking, saying, "In this object..."
106:
"...you must arise," as if entrusting the object of rebirth-linking, the death-proximate impulsions (maraṇāsannajavana) occurring near the time of death would produce rebirth-linking. Is it not taught (in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī): "Because of being performed, because of being accumulated" (katattā upacitattā)? At that time, how could those impulsions, occurring as if in a cognitive process (vīthi) similar to that rebirth-linking, be kammas that are performed and accumulated? At that time, the object is not relished either. Nor can mundane kammas produce results in the same cognitive process like supramundane (magga) states.

"Either previously that evil kamma to be experienced as suffering was performed by him, or subsequently that evil kamma to be experienced as suffering was performed by him, or at the time of death wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) was fully undertaken and adopted by him; because of that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he reaches the plane of misery, the unhappy destination, the nether world, hell"—thus it was taught (in the Majjhima Nikāya).

In this and other Suttas, the giving of rebirth-linking by the volition (cetanā) associated with wrong view or right view fully adopted at the time of death is taught. However, wrong view or right view cannot be fully adopted by weak five-door impulsions (pañcadvārikajavana).

(In the Vibhaṅga Commentary) it will also be said: "This entire function, from the discerning of wholesome and unwholesome states up to the end of death (cuti), occurs only by way of mind-door consciousness, not by five-door consciousness; thus, in the performance of this entire function, cognitive-process consciousnesses (vīthicitta) occurring with five-door impulsions are excluded."

For in that commentary, it is also said: "He does not discern any state; 'states have mind as their forerunner'—thus it was taught; he does not discern even a single wholesome or unwholesome state." That discerning of wholesome and unwholesome states, which is followed by happiness or suffering, is excluded from the five doors. The undertaking of wholesome and unwholesome kamma should be understood as being excluded in the same way.

However, the death-consciousness (cuti) immediately following the registration (tadārammaṇa), and the rebirth (upapatti) immediately following that death-consciousness, occur only in the mind-door; they are not included in the cognitive-process consciousness occurring with five-door impulsions. With this intention, it should be understood that the death-consciousness immediately following the registration occurring in the five doors, and the rebirth-linking immediately following that death-consciousness, are mentioned here.

In showing the rebirth-linking object in that way, referring only to the rebirth-linking occurring in a visible form or other object that has a remaining lifespan of five thought-moments (cittakkhana), it is said: "The rebirth-linking consciousness having a present object is a condition by way of proximity condition (anantara-paccaya) for the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) having a present object." And referring to the rebirth-linking occurring in a visible form that has a remaining lifespan of one thought-moment...
107:
It should be understood that it is stated (in the Paṭṭhāna): "The rebirth-linking consciousness (upapatti-citta) having a present object supports the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) having a past object by way of proximity condition (anantara-paccaya)."

"Or by the pure" (suddhāya vā) means [immediately after] an impulsion process (javana-vīthi) that has a sublime (mahaggata) sign of karma (kamma-nimitta) as its object and is devoid of registration (tadārammaṇa). That impulsion process should be regarded as a proximity (upacāra) to the sublime resultant. Some teachers, however, say that this process ends with the sublime. There are eleven types of rebirth-linking with a past object, and seven types with a concept (paññatti) object.

Why is it said, "In this same way, the rebirth-linking occurring immediately after death from the formless sphere (arūpa-cuti) should also be understood"? Is this rebirth-linking not already included in the method beginning with, "For one situated in a sublime happy destination attained by way of earth-kasina jhāna, etc."? No, because in that context, only the rebirth-linking occurring immediately after death from the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara-cuti) was mentioned. For there, it is understood that only rebirth-linking immediately after fine-material death is spoken of by the words, "Either a sign such as the earth-kasina or a sublime mind appears at the mind-door, or at the eye or ear..." and so on.

Nevertheless, if one connects them according to possibility, although this rebirth-linking could be included there, this separate extraction is made to show this distinction: that there is no fine-material rebirth-linking immediately after formless death; and in the formless sphere, there is no lower rebirth-linking immediately after a higher death; thus, there is no rebirth-linking with a concept object immediately after death from the fourth formless realm. Therefore, from that fourth formless death, one should connect: rebirth-linking with a past object in that same realm; rebirth-linking with past and present objects in the sense sphere; and from the remaining formless deaths, as possible, formless rebirth-linking with past and concept objects, and sense-sphere rebirth-linking with past and present objects.

Thus, by way of objects, the following have been shown: two types of woeful rebirth-linking immediately after a single type of sense-sphere happy death; two types of happy rebirth-linking immediately after a woeful death; five types of happy rebirth-linking by way of the sense, fine-material, and formless spheres immediately after a sense-sphere happy death; likewise five types after a fine-material death; and eight types of rebirth-linking by way of the sense and formless spheres after each of the two types of formless death. However, the two types of woeful rebirth-linking after a single type of woeful death have not yet been shown; to show that, the text beginning with "But for one situated in a woeful destination..." (duggatiyaṃ ṭhitassa panā) is stated. The aforementioned rebirth-linkings are:

Two, two, and five varieties,
Five, eight, and two as well,
All those rebirth-linkings,
Amount to twenty-four.
108:
By the passage beginning with "Because of having performed wholesome karma of the sense sphere," the state of being an asynchronous karma condition (nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya) is shown as described; then, wishing to show only the state of being a strong dependence condition (upanissaya-paccaya), the author says "For this has been said" (vuttañhetaṃ) and so on.

By the word "beginning with" (ādi), it means occurring together with consciousness conjoined with matter. The statement "at the minimum, two or three decads (dasaka) arise" is said with reference to womb-born beings (gabbhaseyyaka). In other modes of birth, many groups (kalāpa) arise simultaneously. Even in the individual existence (attabhāva) of a Brahma, which is many gāvutas in size, many groups arise simultaneously. Therefore, there are more than thirty types of matter, because although odor, flavor, and nutritive essence are excluded in the fine-material realm, the eye-heptad, ear-heptad, base-heptad, and life-hexad are numerous.

In the Commentary, however, it is said that in that Brahma existence, the eye-decad, ear-decad, base-decad, and life-nonad also arise. In the Pali, it is stated: "At the moment of rebirth-linking in the fine-material element (rūpa-dhātu), excluding the non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), five bases (āyatana) appear, five elements (dhātu) appear." Likewise, it is said, "In the fine-material element, there are six bases and nine elements," to show the bases and elements existing there by way of a general summary.

In the Kathāvatthu, the existence of the odor-base (gandhāyatana) and so on in that fine-material realm is rejected, just like the nose-base (ghānāyatana) and so on, in the passage: "Is there the nose-base there? Yes. Is there the odor-base there? One should not say so." Just as one can speak of the existence of the earth element (pathavī-dhātu) etc., which are of a nature free from being tangible (phoṭṭhabbāyatana) because they cannot be touched, one cannot speak of the existence of odor and flavor that are not the odor-base or flavor-base, because there is no nature of odor or flavor that is distinct from the essence of odor or flavor.

If it is argued that odor and flavor should not be called bases (āyatana) because they do not serve as causes for nose-contact (ghāna-samphassa) etc., there is no reason not to call them odor-element (gandha-dhātu) and flavor-element (rasa-dhātu), since the word 'element' (dhātu) denotes that which is soulless and soulless. Their status as mental objects (dhamma) must certainly be accepted, as there is no other characteristic than the characteristic of bearing their own nature. The status of mental objects as bases is certainly stated in the Yamaka: "Is a mental object (dhamma) a base (āyatana)? Yes." Therefore, even if they lack the status of odor-base or flavor-base, some kind of base-nature must be stated for them. If there were some nature of theirs other than the nature of odor and flavor, like the nature of the earth element etc. is other than the nature of tangibility, they would be included in the mental-object base (dhammāyatana). But if the nature of odor and flavor and the nature of a base both exist, then because it is both odor and a base, it is simply called the odor-base (gandhāyatana).
109:
Since taste is both a sense-object and a base, it simply arrives at the name 'taste-base' (*rasāyatana*); thus, the existence of the smell-base (*gandhāyatana*) and taste-base cannot be denied. According to the teaching 'three nutriments' (*tayo āhārā*), it should be understood that physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*) does not exist in that Rūpa realm. Therefore, the counting of material phenomena (*rūpa*) should be done in a way that does not contradict the Pāḷi. By counting in this way, the nature of things (*dhammatā*) remains consistent.

*Jāti-uṇṇā* is also said to be wool taken by cutting open the womb. *Sambhava-bheda* refers to the variety of existence. It is said that *Nijjhamataṇhikā* petas, because they are constantly oppressed by suffering, do not conceive even if they indulge in sensual pleasure.

By the phrase *rūpībrahmesu tāva opapātikayonikesu*, the Rūpī Brahmās are distinguished from other beings of spontaneous birth (*opapātika-yoni*). In explaining the statement 'among the moisture-born and those of spontaneous birth, there are at minimum 30 material phenomena,' it is said starting with *avakaṃsato panā* etc. That statement does not agree with the Pāḷi. In the Pāḷi, the rebirth of *aghānaka* (those without the nose-organ) beings among the moisture-born and spontaneously-born of the sensual sphere is not taught. In the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*, however, it is taught:

'At the moment of rebirth in the sensual element (*kāmadhātu*), for some beings eleven bases (*āyatanas*) appear; for some, ten bases; for some, another ten bases; for some, nine bases; for some, seven bases.'

It is not taught that 'eight bases appear.' Likewise, if there were *aghānaka* (noseless) rebirths, it should have been stated three times that 'ten bases appear,' and three times that 'nine bases appear.' But it is not so stated. Thus, in the problems concerning the appearance of elements and in the *Yamaka*, the co-occurrence of the nose, tongue, and body is taught.

The similarity between death (*cuti*) and rebirth (*paṭisandhi*) in terms of aggregates (*khandha*) etc., is called *abheda* (non-difference), and their dissimilarity is called *bheda* (difference). Having shown only a mere outline of the method, and encompassing all mentioned and unmentioned death and rebirth, it is said: 'This is the method in the immaterial planes (*arūpa-bhūmi*) only.' Because of the strength of the access concentration of the Fine-material and Immaterial spheres, there is no rebirth in the states of loss (*duggati*) after passing away from those planes. Therefore, it is said *ekaccasugaticutiyā* (from some happy deaths). In this context of *ekaccaduggatipaṭisandhi* (some unhappy rebirths), the purpose of using the word 'some' (*ekacca*) should be sought. The intention here would be: among the beings with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions (*nānattakāya nānattasaññī*), some *vinipātika* asuras are mentioned who have triple-rooted rebirth (*tihetuka-paṭisandhi*) etc. Taking their rebirth as an unhappy rebirth (*duggati-paṭisandhi*) due to its fallen state (*vinipāta*), [it is said that] after all happy deaths...
110:
In this passage *ekaccaduggatipaṭisandhi*, the purpose of including the word 'some' (*ekacca*) should be sought. Among the beings with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, some *vinipātika* asuras are mentioned who have triple-rooted rebirth etc. Because their rebirth is a fallen state, it is taken as an unhappy rebirth (*duggati-paṭisandhi*). This rebirth does not occur after all happy deaths, nor does it occur only after some happy deaths; thus, the word 'some' is included to exclude that *vinipātika* rebirth. Indeed, rebirth in the states of loss (*apāya-paṭisandhi*) occurs only after some happy deaths; it does not occur after all sensual, fine-material, and immaterial deaths. Alternatively, unhappy rebirth is of two kinds: that which occurs immediately after some happy deaths and that which occurs after an unhappy death. Between these two, the word *ekaccaduggatipaṭisandhi* is spoken to exclude the latter and take only the former, which occurs after some happy deaths. In the passage *ahetukacutiyā sahetukapaṭisandhi*, the rooted rebirths—both double-rooted and triple-rooted—should be associated. Indeed, as in the case of the frog deity (*Maṇḍūka-devaputta*) and others, even a triple-rooted rebirth can occur immediately after a rootless death.

By reversing those respective meanings, they should be associated as appropriate. In the various distinctions such as 'after some happy deaths, some unhappy rebirth occurs,' the meaning should be associated as 'after some unhappy deaths, some happy rebirth occurs,' and so on, wherever it is fitting. The neuter gender *yojetabbaṃ* is used in consideration of the mere fitting meaning, or it should be understood as an abstract sense (*bhāva-attha*). However, in phrases such as 'after a death with a non-sublime external object, a rebirth with a sublime internal object occurs,' a reverse association should not be made. This is because after a death having a sublime internal object, there is no rebirth in the immaterial planes having a non-sublime external object. The reversal of 'after an immaterial death with four aggregates, a sensual-sphere rebirth with five aggregates occurs' has already been associated by itself. And there is no reversal for 'after a death with a past object, a rebirth with a present object occurs.'

Thus, only the specific differences (*bheda-visesa*) have been shown in detail. As for the specific non-differences (*abheda-visesa*), they should be associated within each specific difference in those respective existences by way of death and rebirth associations, such as: 'after a sensual-sphere death with five aggregates, a sensual-sphere rebirth with five aggregates occurs... after a death without initial and sustained application, a rebirth without initial and sustained application occurs.' The association of a four-aggregate rebirth after a four-aggregate death has already been made by itself. Since it can be known by this very method, the specific non-differences in death and rebirth of five aggregates etc., are not shown. The phrase *tato hetuṃ vinā* means that it does not occur without excluding causes such as ignorance (*avijjā*) and formations (*saṅkhāra*) in that old existence.

*Aṅgapaccaṅgasandhibandhanāni* refers to the ligaments that bind the joints of the major and minor limbs; *chedakānaṃ* means those [pains] which cut them (the death-proximate feelings). The statement 'when the eye etc. have ceased' should be understood as referring to them reaching a state of extreme weakness. This is because death has been shown previously to occur even immediately after the five-door consciousness. And in the *Yamaka*... (the momentary cessation of the eye-base etc., along with the death-consciousness, has been taught).
111:
If it is asked, "For whom the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) ceases, does the mind-base (manāyatana) also cease for that person?" the answer is given as "Yes" (āmantā). Again, if it is asked, "For whom the mind-base ceases, does the eye-base also cease for that person?" the answer is: For those who are dying with mind but without eyes, the mind-base ceases, but the eye-base does not cease for them. For those who are dying with eyes, both the mind-base and the eye-base cease. In this manner, the momentary cessation of the eye-base and others along with the death-consciousness (cuticitta) is stated.

By this principle, because the conditions for consciousness such as ignorance (avijjā), which remain apart from kamma, are obtained, it is called "volitional formation with remaining conditions obtained" (laddhāvisesapaccayosaṅkhāra). When the object of kamma and so forth, whose faults are concealed by ignorance, becomes the place of arising as an object for rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa), because craving (taṇhā) has not yet been abandoned and because the preceding stream of consciousness has matured, the consciousness facing the place of rebirth arises inclining, leaning, and sloping toward that object. Thus it is said, "Craving causes [it] to incline." Co-nascent formations (sahajāta-saṅkhāra) refer to the volitions (cetanā) arising together with the impulsion consciousness (javana) near death, or otherwise, all factors such as contact (phassa). These act as the cause for the establishment of consciousness through the power of rebirth in that object of kamma and so forth, as if throwing the consciousness into that place of rebirth.

"Taṃ" refers to that consciousness. Through the power of the continuity (santati) of the death-consciousness, rebirth-linking consciousness, and the consciousness proximate to them, it is brought into a single unity as "consciousness." It is shown that the acts of inclining, being thrown, abandoning the previous support, obtaining the subsequent support, and proceeding without a support occur only for that single consciousness by way of the stream of continuity, and not for another. By saying "by way of the stream of continuity," the following wrong view is also refuted: "It is this very same consciousness that runs and wanders [through rebirths], not another." For when there is the method of diversity, there is also the method of unity by way of continuity.

The object of kamma and so forth, which is bound to the previous existence (attabhāva), should be understood like a rope tied to a tree on this bank. Consciousness should be understood like the man. Craving should be understood like the man's desire to cross the ditch. The "throwing" formations should be understood like the effort and exertion to cross. Just as that man, when standing on the other bank, whether he reaches and obtains something tied to a tree on the other bank or not, stands solely on the ground by his own strength and effort; likewise, this consciousness, whether it obtains the support of the heart-base (hadayavatthu) bound to another existence in the five-constituent realm (pañcavokāra-bhava) or does not obtain it in the four-constituent realm (catuvokāra-bhava), arises solely due to kamma associated with the object. In that context, "assādayamānaṃ" means reaching or obtaining.
112:
The term 'bhavantarādipatisandhānato' means because of the initial connection of a new existence other than the previous one. Alternatively, 'bhavantarādi' refers to a new existence, a new mode of birth (yoni), a new destination (gati), a new station of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), and a new abode of beings (sattāvāsa) other than the previous ones; it means because of the connection of these existences, modes of birth, destinations, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings. 'Kamma' refers to the kamma that produces rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). 'Saṅkhāra' refers to the volitional formations that occur along with the impulsion consciousness (javana-viññāṇa) near death (cuti), which cast the consciousness into the object.

In the phrase 'saddādihetukā' (having sound, etc., as cause), an echo has sound as its cause. A lamp [lit from another] has the original lamp as its cause. An impression has a seal as its cause. A shadow has the face, etc., situated in a mirror, etc., as its cause. 'They arise without going elsewhere' means they have sound, etc., as their cause without moving to the location of the cause (sound, etc.), because the echo did not exist prior to the occurrence of that sound, etc. Similarly, this rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa) does not move to the location of the kamma which is its cause and then become caused by it, because the rebirth-linking consciousness did not exist prior to the occurrence of that kamma, etc. Therefore, this rebirth-linking consciousness does not come from the previous existence, which is the location of the cause, just as echoes, etc., do not come from the location of the sound, etc. Nor does it arise there without a cause, just as echoes, etc., do not arise without sound, etc.

Alternatively, 'they arise without going elsewhere' means they do not first exist in the location of the cause and then move to another location of the effect to become caused by that [cause], because they did not exist prior to their arising. Nor is it that they do not have sound, etc., as their cause; they indeed have them. This rebirth-linking consciousness should also be applied to the analogy in the manner stated. The phrase 'this is the method' (esa nayo) indicates that the application should be made as appropriate to all effects produced by causes, such as seeds and sprouts.

Indeed, in the arising of the effect, rebirth-linking consciousness, from causes in this previous existence, if there were absolute identity (ekatta) of the consciousnesses produced by causes such as kamma, a person in a human destination (gati) would not become one in a deva destination. If there were absolute difference (nānatta), the result would not occur in the continuity of the one who possesses the kamma. Therefore, there would be the loss of conventional expressions such as 'the seed of the red [plant], the fruit of the red [plant]' and 'Venerable Sir, in the past, I was the hermit named Rohitassa.' Therefore, while there is a connection of continuity (santāna) in the arising of rebirth-linking consciousness from causes in this previous existence, one should not, through wisdom, arrive at either absolute identity or absolute difference in the effects produced by causes.

Here, by refuting absolute identity, the wrong view 'pleasure and pain are self-created' (sayaṅkataṃ sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ) is prevented. By refuting absolute difference, the view 'pleasure and pain are created by another' (paraṅkataṃ sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ) is prevented. By stating the nature of being produced by a cause, the view 'it arises by chance' (adhiccasamuppanna) is prevented. 'Ettha' (here) means in a single continuity (ekasantāna).

The infusion (bhāvanā) with the four sweets (catumadhura), lac-juice (alattaka-rasa), etc., is the preparation (abhisaṅkhāra) of seeds such as mango and citron. Here, the being who possesses kamma should be understood like the seed. Kamma should be understood like the preparation.
