The continuity of the being's rebirth-linking consciousness, etc., should be understood like the continuity of the seed's sprout, etc. The occurrence of a fruit that is sweet or has red filaments, which arises through that sprout, etc., is due to that very seed and due to that preparation; similarly, the occurrence of the result for the being who is the doer of kamma is due to that kamma. Education, training in arts, or medical treatment performed on a child's body do not move to the adult body. Nevertheless, the proficiency in arts, the mastery of knowledge, and the freedom from disease, which are caused by that education, etc., arise in the adult body. This result does not occur in the continuity of another, but only in the body included within that same continuity. The great continuity...
113:
In this way, the occurrence of the result should be understood. The learning of arts, the practicing of arts, and the application of medicine performed in the body of a child do not move (transfer) to the body of an adult. However, based on those (learning, etc.), proficiency in arts, knowledge of arts, and freedom from disease occur in the adult body. Moreover, that result does not occur in another person; it arises only in the adult body that is included within that same continuity. Furthermore, it does not arise from any other cause apart from the specific application of learning arts and so forth; for if that learning and so forth are absent, proficiency and so forth are also absent. Similarly, in this case (where consciousness arises due to kamma), whatever result exists in the continuity should be applied thus: this result does not occur to another, nor does it arise from kamma performed by another. By the phrase "not from another," it only shows that if volitional formations (saṅkhāra) are absent, the result (consciousness) is absent; it does not exclude other conditions.

Regarding the statement that has been made, there is an ellipsis: "we shall say [this] in that regard." Alternatively, it is connected as: "even though there is no enjoyer, the conventional designation 'eater' is established." The conventional designation "it bears fruit" is called phalatisammuti.

Even though there is manifestation without transmigration from the previous life, the meaning is that the avoidance of the aforementioned fault is accomplished in such a case. (It cannot bring about the result) before the moment of accumulating kamma, nor after the time of its ripening. Kamma that has not yet yielded its fruit acts as a cause because it has been performed. To prevent the doubt that kamma which has already yielded its fruit might also bring about a result—since the fact of having been performed is the same—it is said, "it does not always bring about a result." By the passage "not because of existence nor because of non-existence," it only removes the aforementioned faults based on existence and non-existence.

The mere act of giving a guarantee, the mere act of purchasing goods, or the mere act of taking a loan, etc., becomes the cause for the subsequent returning of that benefit, the providing of replacement goods, and the repayment of the debt. The meaning is that there is a result such as returning [the loan] even before the [final] result has manifested.

"Without distinction" means generally (by way of a collective), without making distinctions such as "a triple-rooted [cause] for a triple-rooted [result]," etc. In all cases, the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya) should be applied by the power of strong kamma. For it will be stated in the Paṭṭhāna Commentary that weak kamma is not a decisive support condition. By the words "without distinction," all meritorious volitional formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) are included together with that (strong kamma). In this context of "the twelve types of unwholesome volition," it should be investigated why the volition associated with restlessness (uddhacca-sahagata) is included. The statement that it is a cause for a single consciousness in rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) in that way, but not in the course of existence (pavatti), is a restriction of the conditionality to rebirth-linking only, and not to the course of existence. For in the course of existence, it is the cause for all seven [resultant consciousnesses]. Similarly, it is said that in the sense-sphere deva realms, there are no undesirable visible objects and so forth. However, when the portents (pubbanimitta) for the devas appear, why should the undesirability of withered flowers and so forth not occur? (They indeed occur). In the passage "should be cultivated," specifically regarding the mental formation (cittasaṅkhāra) which has twenty-nine types of volition...
114:
It is said that in the sense-sphere deva realms, there are no undesirable visible objects and so forth. However, when the portents (pubbanimitta) for the devas appear, why should the undesirability (aniṭṭha) of withered flowers and so forth not occur? (It certainly does).

In the passage "that very mental formation in the two planes of existence," the mental formation (cittasaṅkhāra) consisting of twenty-nine types of volition is unified under the aspect of being a mental formation and is thus called "that very mental formation." It should be noted that only the sense-sphere mental formation, which is a part of that mental formation, is the condition that assists the thirteen types of consciousness and the nine types of consciousness. This is because the whole (the collective mental formation) is spoken of by way of its part acting as a condition.

Since the detailed explanation has already been given for a certain life, and wishing to show only a brief outline from that life onwards, he said "starting from the beginning." Therefore, the words "in the two planes of existence" and so forth were spoken. By the passage "by way of the third jhāna plane," it should be understood that the fourth jhāna plane is also included—excluding the non-percipient (asaññasatta) and the formless (āruppa) planes—due to the similarity of having "unity of body and unity of perception" (ekattakāya ekattasaññī). "According to possibility" means that among the twenty-one sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere wholesome resultants, [the condition] assists fourteen at the time of rebirth-linking and in the course of existence, and seven only in the course of existence. This is the meaning of "according to possibility."

The passage "of the four types of consciousness" is spoken with reference to the planes of existence and so forth. In fact, the conditionality for the three types of consciousness included within the four should also be applied to the three stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti). Even though there is no consciousness arising from volitional formations in the non-percipient plane where consciousness is absent, the words "furthermore" and so forth were spoken to show that this abode of beings (sattāvāsa) still has volitional formations as its cause. In this brief exposition, it should be understood that the conditionality of meritorious volitional formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) and so forth for wholesome resultant consciousnesses and so forth during the course of existence in woeful states (duggati) and so forth is not mentioned because it can be understood by the method already stated regarding the planes of existence.

## The Explanation of the Section on Consciousness is finished.

## The Explanation of the Section on Name-and-Form

The distinction in the teaching of name-and-form in the Suttanta and Abhidhamma texts is called the "distinction of teaching" (desanābheda). Although the phrase "the three aggregates" is not in the Pali text, it should be understood that it was spoken with the consideration that it is indeed taught by way of meaning.

It should be applied thus: "and of egg-born beings who lack the sex-materiality (bhāvarūpa)." "Heads of continuity" (santatisiīsa) refers to the primary origins of the clusters of materiality. Although the alterable materiality (vikārarūpa) does not exist at the moment of rebirth-linking...
115:
Characteristic matter (lakkhaṇa-rūpa) and delimiting matter (pariccheda-rūpa) do exist; however, because these are non-concretely produced matter (aparinipphanna-rūpa), the Teacher said "from the standpoint of matter as matter" (rūparūpato), wishing to exclude them from the ultimate sense.

In the sense-sphere (kāmabhava), regarding the phrase "of the remaining spontaneously born beings" (sesa-opapātikānaṃ), it should be understood that even if there are no beings specifically called "spontaneously born" in the sense-sphere that would make the word "remaining" (sesa) meaningful, the term "remaining" is used because there are spontaneously born and moisture-born (saṃsedaja) beings who remain apart from the egg-born (aṇḍaja) and womb-born (gabbhaseyyaka) beings. Alternatively, he said "of the remaining spontaneously born beings" referring to those spontaneously born beings other than the Brahmakāyika and others already mentioned. Since those remaining spontaneously born beings also include formless beings, he said "in the sense-sphere" (kāmabhava). It should be understood that the name-and-form of beings with incomplete sense-bases (āyatana) can be known by the number of phenomena according to the method already stated in the Rūpamissaka-viññāṇa-niddesa as they arise, and thus they are not mentioned again.

At the minimum, only two octads (aṭṭhaka) produced by temperature (utu) and consciousness (citta) arise; referring to the time when sound is present, he said "at the maximum, two nonads (navaka)." Regarding the word "previously" (pubbe), some say it refers to the Khandha-vibhaṅga. For in that Khandha-vibhaṅga, it is said, "arising three times in each mind-moment (cittakkhana)." Or else, referring to the statement in this very text starting from the two types of continuity (santati) up to the heptads (sattaka), he said, "the kamma-produced matter mentioned previously is of seventy kinds." That kamma-produced matter, when arising, arises three times in each mind-moment; with this intention, he said, "arising three times in each mind-moment."

"Established in the four directions" means having their tops intertwined with each other and being established in the four directions by their bases, standing like different boats that have embraced one another.

He said the words "in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava) and during the course of existence (pavaṭti)" referring to the time of the occurrence of the fivefold consciousness produced by kamma that does not generate matter, and to the name (nāma) which has conascent consciousness (sahajāta-viññāṇa) as its condition. For at that time, only name arises due to that fivefold consciousness. However, it can be said that due to the condition of kamma-consciousness (kamma-viññāṇa) from a previous life, both name and form arise at all times. Due to the condition of post-nascent consciousness (pacchājāta-viññāṇa), it should be noted that matter is merely supported. The words starting with "among the unconscious beings" (asaññesu) were said referring to the condition of kamma-consciousness. It is appropriate to say that the words "in the five-constituent existence and during the course of existence" refer to the time of the arising of matter due to kamma other than the previous kamma that produces the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and so on, to the time of the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), and to times other than the arising of the life-continuum and so on. For at the time of the arising of the life-continuum and so on, matter arises precisely because of the kamma that produces that life-continuum, and that resultant (vipāka) can be said to have kamma-consciousness as its condition. Even without depending on the condition of conascent consciousness, the matter and name proceeding by kamma during the course of existence cannot occur without depending on kamma-consciousness. "In all places" means both at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and during the course of existence. Name-and-form caused by conascent consciousness and name-and-form caused by kamma-consciousness should be applied as appropriate.
116:
In this phrase "nāmañca rūpañca nāmarūpañca nāmarūpaṃ," the fourth term "nāmarūpa" is identical in form to the first "nāma" through its own part "nāma," and identical in form to the second "rūpa" through its part "rūpa." Therefore, by the rule "Sarūpānaṃ ekaseso," it should be understood that only the one term "nāmarūpa" remains, while the other terms "nāma," "rūpa," and "nāmarūpa" are not seen (they are elided).

Consciousness other than resultant (vipāka) is called non-resultant (avipāka). Since it is known in two ways, it should be construed that this statement is indeed appropriate. In the term "at the moment of wholesome consciousness and so on" (kusalādi-cittakkhane), by the word "and so on" (ādi), it should be understood that matter produced by kamma that does not generate resultants is included in the moment of resultant consciousness, just as it is in the moments of unwholesome and functional consciousness. However, in the moment of resultant consciousness, both name and form are obtained by the method previously stated, due to the condition of the volitional consciousness (abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa) performed in a previous life. To exclude such moments of resultant consciousness, he said "at the moment of wholesome consciousness and so on."

He said "according to the Suttanta method" (suttantika-pariyāyena) because the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya) of matter is not taught in the Paṭṭhāna. In the Suttas, however, considering that "when this exists, that comes to be; with the non-existence of this, that does not come to be; this is the decisive support, the source, the cause, the origin of that," he taught the fact that matter has consciousness as its decisive support in the phrase "name-and-form has consciousness as its decisive support" (viññāṇūpanisaṃ nāmarūpaṃ). Also, in the Vanapattha discourse, he taught the dwelling in postures having the forest, village, market town, city, district, or person as a decisive support. And because of that dwelling in postures, the arrival of the requisites of life such as robes and so on occurs either with difficulty or without difficulty. Forests and so on do not reach the state of being an object-decisive-support (ārammaṇūpanissaya) and so on for the postures or for the arrival of robes and so on. Therefore, only the non-existence without the cause is to be understood as the state of decisive support according to the Suttanta method. The fact that the volitional consciousness of name is only an object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) at the time of rebirth-linking with kamma as object and so on is so obvious that it need not be specifically mentioned. Therefore, he taught the state of being a condition in only one way for matter according to the Suttanta method. For when it is said that the volitional consciousness is the condition for matter which is subject to doubt, it goes without saying that it is the condition for name (which is not subject to doubt).

Since name-and-form in the course of existence is obvious, he asks about the non-obvious rebirth-linking with the words "How then is this?" and so on. It should be understood that name is due to consciousness according to the Sutta, and matter is due to consciousness according to logic (yutti). Having established it by logic, and wishing to make that point firm by the Sutta, he said the words starting with "For even of the kamma-produced..." (kammasamuṭṭhānassapi hi). "Just like that produced by consciousness" (cittasamuṭṭhānasseva) means in the same way as matter produced by consciousness. Since only name-and-form is seen occurring, the Blessed One, by teaching only that name-and-form, set in motion the peerless Wheel of Dhamma. The meaning is that setting in motion the Wheel of Dhamma is the manifestation of emptiness (suññatā), which is void of a self. Or, by the mere statement of name-and-form, the nature of the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) in the course of existence is already stated. By manifesting the truth of suffering, its cause, the truth of origin (samudaya-sacca); the cessation of that origin, the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca); and the truth of the path (magga-sacca) leading to cessation are also clearly manifested. Because there is no suffering without a cause, because there is no effect that does not cease when the cause ceases, and because cessation cannot be attained without the path which is the cause, this should be connected with the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, which thus manifests the Four Noble Truths.

The explanation of the section on the term Name-and-Form is finished.
117:
The Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca), which is the cessation of that Origination, and the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca), which is the way leading to Cessation, have also been clearly manifested. Because there is no Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca) without a cause, because there is no Suffering that does not cease when its cause, the Truth of Origination (samudaya-sacca), ceases, and because the Cessation that is the goal cannot be attained without the Path which is the means—thus, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, which clearly manifests the Four Noble Truths, should be applied.

## The Explanation of the Section on Name-and-Form is finished.

## The Explanation of the Section on the Six Sense Bases

The word "niyamato" (by rule/certainly) is also spoken with reference to the causal state that assists the six sense bases (saḷāyatana) which definitely arise through conditions such as conascence (sahajāta), dependence (nissaya), prenascence (purejāta), faculty (indriya), and so on, according to the circumstances of the four great elements (bhūta-rūpa), the six physical bases (vatthu-rūpa), and the life-materiality (jīvita-rūpa). However, regarding the sense-object base (rūpāyatana) and so on, it should be understood that they are not included [among the physical bases, etc.] because they do not have the nature of life that protects by way of conascence-dependence. The causal state of those objects such as rūpāyatana as object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), object-prenascence-condition (ārammaṇa-purejāta-paccaya), and so on, does not occur only in the visible forms included within one's own continuity; nor is the causal state of assisting in only one way like the eye-base (cakkhu-vatthu) and so on. Therefore, they have a causal state that assists in an uncertain way (aniyamato). In this text, "niyamato... jīvitindriyanti evaṃ," it should be understood that by the word "evaṃ," rūpāyatana and so on are also included.

In the passage "chaṭṭhāyatanañca saḷāyatanañca saḷāyatanaṃ," although the words chaṭṭhāyatana and saḷāyatana do not have the same form (saddato), since the sixth base (manāyatana) is only a part of the six sense bases in meaning (atthato), it should be understood that a "retention of one of similar parts" (ekadesa-sarūpekasesa) has been made, which is said to have a similar form in terms of being a part. Just as in the example "vaṅko ca kuṭilo ca kuṭilā" (the crescent and the plow-head are both curved), where terms with similar meanings are desired to have a "retention of one of similar parts," so too, in terms that have a similar form as a part in meaning, there should be an ekasesa.

Alternatively, an ekasesa is made of chaṭṭhāyatana and manāyatana as "chaṭṭhāyatanaṃ" or "manāyatanaṃ," or of chaṭṭhāyatana and chaṭṭhāyatana as "chaṭṭhāyatanaṃ," or of manāyatana and manāyatana as "manāyatanaṃ," and then it is spoken as "saḷāyatanaṃ" together with the bases such as the eye. Wishing to show the meaning of that very ekasesa made by way of the manāyatana which has only name as its condition and the manāyatana which has name-and-form as its condition, the commentator said: "chaṭṭhāyatanañca saḷāyatanañca saḷāyatananti evaṃ katekasesassa." For the aforementioned ekasesa is indeed what is made in meaning as "chaṭṭhāyatanañca saḷāyatanañca." And in all cases of making an ekasesa...
118:
...when it is made, the indication by the singular number should be understood as being made by the power of the commonality of the meaning to be expressed by the words such as saḷāyatana which have undergone the ekasesa. Although it is said "nāmapaccayā chaṭṭhāyatanaṃ" in the unwholesome section (akusala-vāra) and the wholesome section (kusala-vāra) as will be mentioned in the indeterminate section (abyākata-vāra), since in the Suttanta-bhājanīya method only the resultant (vipāka) sixth base is taken, it should be understood that only the Abyākata-vāra is cited as evidence with that intention. However, in the method showing the way of conditioning, by the passage "chaṭṭhā hoti taṃ avakaṃsato" and so on, the conditioning for non-resultant wholesome and unwholesome states is also extracted; it should be known that such extraction is done with the desire to speak without remainder. "Included here" means included here in this Suttanta-bhājanīya by the ekasesa method; the intention is that it should be known that the resultant which is included is analyzed in the analysis of the mundane resultant of the Abyākata-vāra in that Abhidhamma-bhājanīya method.

"Neyya" means that which should be known. In the passage "ukkaṃsa avakaṃsa," the ability to assist by 8 ways more than the 7 ways of assisting is called ukkaṃsa; beyond that, the ability to assist by 9 ways or 10 ways is also called ukkaṃsa. Avakaṃsa, however, should be understood as the ability to assist by 9 ways less than the 10 ways, then 8 ways, then 7 ways. One should not apply both ukkaṃsa and avakamsa starting from the 7 ways of assisting, because there is no avakamsa below those 7 ways.

By the phrase "being an associate of the heart-base," it shows only this much: that name does not occur without an associate as in the formless realm (arūpa-bhūmi), and that the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu), together with name, is a condition for the sixth base. It is not intended to mean that name assists in the same way as the heart-base assists. For the [heart] base is a dissociated-condition (vippayutta-paccaya), but name is not a dissociated-condition. Name is a resultant-condition (vipāka-paccaya), root-condition (hetu-paccaya), and so on, whereas the base is not. In the course of existence (pavatti), mental states (nāma-dhamma) assist only the karma-born materiality (kammaja-rūpa) that has reached the stage of presence (ṭhiti); they do not assist it while it is arising (uppāda). Therefore, regarding the eye and so on, one should apply the dissociated (vippayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata) conditions, or only the post-nascent-dissociated (pacchājāta-vippayutta) conditions and so on.

In the phrase "to the remaining mind-base," because of the following of the phrase "pañcakkhandhabhave pana" (but in the five-constituent existence), it should be understood that the mind-base remaining from the five-fold consciousness (pañcavijñāṇa) that occurs only in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava) is spoken of. The state of being a common condition such as conascence (sahajāta) of name-and-form, and the state of being an uncommon condition such as association (sampayutta), should be applied according to the circumstances.

## The Explanation of the Section on the Six Sense Bases is finished.
119:
## Commentary on the Explanation of the Factor of Contact

The Abhidhamma-bhājanīya-pāḷi text, "saṭṭhāyatanapaccayā phasso" (contact conditioned by the sixth base), is stated in accordance with the sequence of the Pāḷi because it refers to the sixth base (manāyatana) arising in the formless realm (arūpabhūmi). By the term "ajjhatta" (internal), only the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) and so forth, which are included within one's own continuity, are taken. Indeed, that sixfold base (saḷāyatana) produced by kamma and included within one's own continuity is the condition for such contact. On the other hand, external objects such as visible forms (rūpārammaṇa) and so forth, which are not-grasped (anupādinnā), are also objects of contact. Those external forms and so forth are not taken in the view of the first teacher (pathama-ācariya-vāda) because they are not conditions for contact in the sense of being produced by the causes of kamma and defilements (kilesa) included within one's own continuity, unlike the eye-base and so forth. However, in the view of the second teacher (dutiya-ācariya-vāda), it is noted that if there is a state of being a condition in any way, they cannot be excluded (thus, external bases like visible forms are also taken).

If a single contact could arise from all bases, then the statement of a single contact as "saḷāyatanapaccayā phasso" (contact conditioned by the sixfold base) would be appropriate. Alternatively, if all contacts could arise from a single base, then since all contacts arise from all bases, there would be no distinction of contact by the distinction of bases; thus, the statement in the singular would be appropriate due to that lack of distinction. However, since that is not possible, an objection is raised with the words "na sabbāyatananehi" (not from all bases) and so forth. In another way, the phrase "nāpi ekamhā āyatanā sabbe phassā" (nor do all contacts arise from a single base) is stated only for the purpose of making known another impossible arrangement. In fact, it should be understood that this statement, "na sabbāyatananehi eko phasso sambhoti" (a single contact does not arise from all bases), is the reason showing the inappropriateness of stating contact in the singular. Or, this is stated by way of illustration: just as all contacts do not arise from a single base, so too a single contact does not arise from all bases; therefore, the statement in the singular is inappropriate.

As for the answer, wishing to show that a single contact can arise from many bases, the text says "tatridaṃ vissajjanaṃ" (herein is the answer) and so forth. The term "ekopi anekāyatanappabhavo" is actually "eko panekāyatanappabhavo" (but one [contact] originates from many bases). In the state of being a condition in six ways, the five bases such as the eye-base should be clearly demonstrated; in this way, the meaning should be applied to the remaining terms as well. The phrase "tathā ca" (and likewise) is stated referring to present visible forms and so forth, as well as to the material form (rūpa-rūpa) included within the present mental-object base (dhammāyatana). The phrase "ārammaṇapaccayamattena" (merely by way of object-condition) is stated referring to all those non-present bases and to the mental-object base other than material form.

## The Commentary on the Explanation of the Factor of Contact Ends.
120:
## Commentary on the Explanation of the Factor of Feeling

In this phrase "sesānaṃ" (to the remaining), although the five contacts such as eye-contact (cakkhu-samphassa) are conditions for the receiving consciousness (sampaṭicchana-citta) by way of proximity (anantara) and other conditions, it is stated as "in one way" (ekadhā) because the proximity and other conditions are included within the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya), and by the power of that decisive support which is common to the investigating (santīraṇa) and registering (tadārammaṇa) consciousness.

It should be applied that for the resultant feelings (vipāka-vedanā) occurring in the three planes (tebhūmaka), that contact known as co-nascent mind-contact (sahajata-manosamphassa) is a condition in eight ways. Because some teachers desire even the non-grasped (anupādinnā) contact as a condition, the state of being a condition of the mind-door adverting contact (manodvārāvajjanaphassa) is stated with the words "yā pana" and so forth; that statement should be seen as being for the purpose of showing a mere summary. By this method, the decisive support nature (upanissayatā) of all proximate and non-proximate contacts for their respective resultant feelings should be applied.

## The Commentary on the Explanation of the Factor of Feeling Ends.

## Commentary on the Explanation of the Factor of Craving

By "mamattena" (with possessiveness), it means with craving that is characterized by being very dear and very delightful. In this context, feeling (vedanā) should be regarded as a son; the objects such as visible forms which are the causes of feeling should be regarded as milk and so forth; and the six such as the artist (cittakāra) who provide the six objects such as visible forms should be regarded as wet-nurses (dhāti). Among those six, the physician (vejja) should be regarded as the provider of the mental object (dhammārammaṇa) by way of the nutritive essence (rasāyana-ojā) and by way of the life supported by that essence. The object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) is merely an object for the state that is arising; it is not a producer like the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya). Therefore, it is stated as "only in one way" (ekadhāva) by the power of the producing decisive support. Alternatively, the object-decisive support condition (ārammaṇūpanissaya-paccaya) is included within the decisive support condition; and by that object-decisive support, other objects of the same nature are also shown. Thus, it should be understood that the state of being a condition is stated only by way of decisive support.

By the words "yasmā vā" (or because) and so forth, it is shown that not only resultant pleasant feeling (vipāka-sukha-vedanā) is a decisive support condition for craving, but all three resultant feelings are specifically decisive support conditions for craving, and other feelings are also conditions without distinction. Neutral feeling (upekkhā), because it is peaceful, is spoken of as "pleasant" (sukha); therefore, that neutral feeling is also a decisive support for craving by way of excessive desire. This is the view of the Commentator. In another way, neutral feeling is included in painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) because it is an unwholesome resultant (akusala-vipāka) and an undesirable feeling (aniṭṭha-vedanā); neutral feeling associated with wholesome states and so forth, other than unwholesome resultant neutral feeling, is included in pleasant feeling because it is a desirable feeling (iṭṭha-vedanā). Therefore, it should be noted that neutral feeling is a decisive support like painful feeling and like pleasant feeling.

By the statement "vedanāpaccayā taṇhā" (craving conditioned by feeling), since the cause which is feeling exists in the continuity of all beings who have feeling, there is a cause for craving to arise. In such a case, for the purpose of preventing the arising of craving, the words "vedanāpaccayā cāpi" and so forth are spoken. If one objects, "Is it not impossible to prevent the extreme attachment of craving whenever feeling arises, because there is no statement that 'feeling accompanied by latent craving (anusaya-taṇhā) is the cause of craving'?", it is not impossible; it is indeed possible, because this is a discourse concerning the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). If, because it does not exist in the Arahant who is free from the latent tendencies (anusaya) of the round, that which arises with the latent tendencies...
121:
The meaning is: equanimity feeling (upekkhā-vedanā) which is an unwholesome resultant (akusala-vipāka) is classified under suffering (dukkha) because it is undesirable (aniṭṭha). Other [wholesome or resultant] equanimity feelings are classified under happiness (sukha) because they are desirable (iṭṭha). Therefore, it can be said that such equanimity feeling is a strong decisive support (upanissaya) for craving (taṇhā), just like suffering or happiness. To prevent the excessive implication (atippasaṅga) that craving must arise in everyone who has feeling, based on the statement "with feeling as condition, craving arises," [the teacher] said "with feeling also..." and so on.

It should not be said that this excessive implication cannot be prevented because the phrase "only feeling accompanied by latent tendencies (anusaya) is the condition for craving" is absent. This is because this is a discourse on the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa-kathā). Since the round of rebirth cannot exist without latent tendencies, it is implied by meaning that only feeling accompanied by latent tendencies is the condition. Alternatively, since the phrase "with ignorance as condition..." follows in sequence, it is understood that only feeling accompanied by latent tendencies is the condition. Also, in the phrase "with feeling as condition, craving arises," only the rule (niyama) that craving arises only due to the condition of feeling, and cannot arise without feeling, is understood. It does not mean that craving must arise whenever there is feeling. Therefore, there is no possibility of excessive implication for the Arahants (vusīmanta).

"Vusīmato" means one who has lived the holy life of the path (magga-brahmacariya) [an Arahant]. Alternatively, the Path is called "vusī" because it is lived (vussati); one who has practiced that Path is a "vusīmā." Or, the fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphala) is called "vusī" because it is the completion of the living; one who possesses that fruition of Arahantship is a "vusīmā."

## The Explanation of the Exposition of the Factor of Craving is finished.
## The Explanation of the Exposition of the Factor of Clinging

The phrase "eternal self" is stated to indicate a subsequent view by clinging to a preceding view. Just as this subsequent view clings to the preceding one for the sake of reinforcement, so too do views such as "there is no result of giving," etc. It should be understood that the grasping as "self" is only clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna), and thus this is not a demonstration of clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna). By the phrase "and the world," it should be understood that the grasping which is free from the grasping as self, and which constitutes clinging to views, is spoken of here by the terms "preceding view" and "subsequent view." In the "Brief and Detailed Account of States" (dhamma-saṅkhepa-vitthāra), the firm state of craving is shown briefly, and it is shown briefly as mere view, while in detail... and so on, the brief and detailed aspects are distinguished. In the term "dhamma-saṅkhepa-vitthāre," the locative case (sattamī-vibhatti) should be understood in the sense of distinction (niddhāraṇa).
122:
The grasping of self as being some eternal or destructible master of the views preceded by the grasp of "eternal" regarding primordial atoms (pakaṭi-aṇu), etc., and the views preceded by the grasp of "annihilation" regarding the body, occurs occasionally; therefore, it is said "mostly" (yebhuyyena). Or else, it should be connected with the sentence "Mostly, clinging to the doctrine of self occurs first," and so on.

Even if the bhavarāga-javana-vīthi (impulsion process of lust for existence) occurs at the very beginning of all processes for a person who has taken rebirth, due to the necessity of the occurrence of craving that finds delight in existence (bhavanikanti-taṇhā), the first occurrence of clinging to sense pleasures (kāmupādāna) was not mentioned, considering that such lust for existence has not yet reached the firm state of craving. If no distinction is made between craving (taṇhā) and clinging to sense pleasures (kāmupādāna), then all craving is indeed clinging to sense pleasures. If a distinction is made, craving other than lust for sense pleasures is called clinging to sense pleasures when it reaches a firm state; it is stated that such clinging to sense pleasures is to be abandoned by the path of Arahantship (arahattamagga).

The arisings of consciousness (cittuppāda) which are the place of origin for clinging are called the "sphere" (visaya). The five aggregates of clinging (pañcupādānakkhandhā) are called the "abode" (ālaya); because they delight in those five aggregates, the multitude of beings is called "delighting in the abode" (ālayarāma). For that very reason, that state of delighting in the abode is evident in one's own continuity and in the continuity of others. By the word "decisive support" (upanissaya), the object-decisive support (ārammaṇūpanissaya), proximity-decisive support (anantarūpanissaya), and natural-decisive support (pakatူpanissaya) are spoken of; thus, proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya), etc., are also included.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of the Factor of Clinging is finished.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of the Factor of Becoming

Since kammabhava (kamma-becoming) is called "becoming" (bhava) by the name of its fruit, [the teacher], speaking by making the derivation of upapattibhava (rebirth-becoming) common to both, said: "It is called becoming because it becomes (bhavatīti bhavo)." "It goes to becoming" means that by the power of producing the fruit, it occurs facing towards becoming at the time of its own occurrence; or else, "going" here is intended as "bringing about."

The becoming of beings who have perception (saññā) is called "perceptive becoming" (saññābhava); here, the elision of the word vantu should be noted. Or, by applying the suffix a in the sense of that vantu word, there is also a reading as "saññabhava." It is called vokāra because it is scattered, spread, or expanded; or else, the scattering or expanding is vokāra. That vokāra, because it occurs in a single [aggregate], is called "one-constituent becoming" (eka-vokāra); it means an aggregate that has an occurrence by being spread in one part.
123:
By the passage "Associated with volition... etc... are included," it shows the state known as 'kamma' because it leads to rebirth, destination, and death which are flowed into by defilements, and it speaks figuratively of its inclusion in Kammabhava (Action-process of existence). In the ultimate sense, however, only volition (cetanā) is Kammabhava. Regarding this, it is stated in the Dhātukathā: "Kammabhava is associated with three aggregates (feeling, perception, and consciousness), one base (mental-object base), and one element (mental-object element); it is associated with some mental factors (other than volition) among the one aggregate (formations aggregate), one base, and one element."

Upapattibhava (Rebirth-process of existence) refers only to the aggregates of rebirth as taught by the three triads. Regarding this, it is stated: "Upapattibhava, Kāmabhava (Sense-sphere existence), Saññābhava (Percipient existence), and Pañcavokārabhava (Five-constituent existence) are included within five aggregates, eleven bases, and seventeen elements," and so forth. If things that are not karma-born (such as wholesome, unwholesome, functional consciousness, and mind-produced matter) were also included, it should have been stated as "within twelve bases and eighteen elements."

If one objects: "Since Saṅkhāra (formations) and Bhava (existence) are different in nature, it is not that Saṅkhāra is being taught again. Therefore, the statement 'this repetition is meaningful' is inappropriate." This is not so (it is indeed appropriate). This is because Saṅkhāra is taught again as "Bhava" in the sense of being a part of existence, specifically Kammabhava. Alternatively, because another objector questioned the repetition without considering the specific distinction of the Dhamma, it is stated as "this repetition is meaningful" according to the wish of that objector.

The name of the existence, such as Kāmabhava, is applied to the kamma that produces Kāmabhava, etc., in the Commentaries by way of the name of the result (metonymy of the effect). Without counting the internal existences separately, but by considering those within and multiplying Kāmabhava, etc., by the two divisions of Kammabhava and Upapattibhava, it is stated as "six kinds of existence."

"Avisesena" means without making a distinction between the four types of clinging (upādāna). Because the twelve divisions are included by the power of inclusion without making a distinction between the types of clinging, it is stated as "six kinds of existence."

It is taught that by perfectly undertaking the cow-practice and the dog-practice, one attains companionship with cows and dogs. Therefore, thinking that the attainment of jhāna is impossible for a person who has Sīlabbatupādāna (clinging to rules and rituals), some teachers say that Rūpabhava and Arūpabhava cannot occur because of that Sīlabbatupādāna. However, because it can be a supporting condition in the manner to be described later, it is stated, "that statement should not be accepted." Sīlabbatupādāna is the wrong adherence to practices that are not the path to purity as being the path to purity. (Although some say) it is inappropriate to produce Rūpāvacara and Arūpāvacara jhānas through such wrong adherence to the path of purity, (it is actually appropriate).

Hearing the Puranas, the Bharata stories, the Sītāharaṇa (the abduction of Queen Sītā), and the procedures for binding animals in sacrifices, etc., is called Asaddhammasavana (hearing false teachings). By the word "ādi" (etc.), it includes associating with bad people, not having performed merit in the past, and setting oneself in the wrong direction.
124:
It also includes the lack of merit performed in previous lives (akatapuññatā) and wrong self-aspiration (attamicchāpaṇidhi). "Included in that (Kāmabhava) alone" means they are included only in that Kāmabhava which is produced by bad conduct or good conduct.

The phrase "they are included" is said because they are included as a part of Saññābhava and Pañcavokārabhava. Indeed, those (Saññābhava and Pañcavokārabhava) are not entirely included within Kāmabhava. "With its divisions" refers to Kāmabhava which has divisions such as the happy destinations, miserable destinations, and the human realm. The reason for stating the state of being a condition for existence at the end of Sīlabbatupādāna, without following the regular order, is because it does not occur constantly like Attavādūpādāna (clinging to the doctrine of self), and because it has Attavādūpādāna as its cause.

In the phrase "by the divisions of root-conditions (hetu-paccaya)," the path-condition (magga-paccaya) should also be mentioned. This is because Diṭṭhupādāna (clinging to views) and others are path-conditions.

## The Description of the Exposition of Existence is finished.

## Description of the Exposition of Birth, Aging, Death, etc.

Stating that "Upapattibhava is not (the cause of birth)," it is said that the arising of Upapattibhava is itself Jāti (birth). However, the birth of a being who is being born is called Jāti; since Jāti cannot exist if there is no Upapattibhava, it can be said that Upapattibhava is also a condition for Jāti. In describing the birth of matter (rūpa), the state of having the presently-arising matter as the proximate cause is stated: "Upacaya (accumulation) has accumulated matter as its proximate cause; Santati (continuity) has continuous matter as its proximate cause."

The inferior and superior states of the aggregates that have arisen are called Hīna (inferior) and Paṇīta (superior). By the word "ādi" (etc.), it includes distinctions such as beautiful and ugly complexions. It is stated as "in the internal continuity" because there is no other cause that creates the distinction other than what exists within one's own continuity.

"By this or that cause" means by a painful state other than aging and death, such as the ruin of relatives (ñātibyasanādi). "By the aspect of decisive support (upanissaya-koṭiyā)" means by way of a portion of decisive support, or a trace of decisive support. That which is not directly mentioned in the Paṭṭhāna, but is a condition in the sense that "when this exists, that exists; when this does not exist, that does not exist" according to the Suttanta method, is called "Upanissaya-koṭi."

## The Description of the Exposition of Birth, Aging, Death, etc. is finished.
125:
## Explanation of the Wheel of Existence

'Samitaṃ' means connected or uninterrupted. 'Kāmayānassa' means for one who desires the objects of sensual pleasure, or for one whose vehicle is the desire of defilements. 'Ruppati' means being affected or deformed by grief.

One who habitually remains in the arising of wrong view (diṭṭhi), which is the cause of pervasive agitation, is called 'pariyuṭṭhānaṭṭhāyī'. Alternatively, there is the reading 'pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyino'; in that case, it should be understood as 'pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyī' because one stands by the pervasive arising of wrong view. 'Pañca pubbanimittāni' refers to the five premonitory signs of death for deities as taught: "Divine flowers wither, divine garments become soiled, sweat exudes from the armpits, the body loses its luster, and the deity no longer finds delight in the celestial seat." Seeing these signs, intense grief arises in deities due to the power of desire for existence (bhavachanda) in the resultant existence (upapattibhava), which consists of the aggregates produced by kamma. 'Bālo' means an ignorant person. By this word, the nature of ignorance (avijjā) as a cause is shown. 'Tividhaṃ' refers to the three types of suffering, such as grief, which have as their root causes: hearing words of blame suitable for one's misdeeds, witnessing torture, or the appearance of unwholesome kamma at the time of death. 'Āsave sādhenti' means they make known or cause the understanding of the taints (āsavas).

Since the beginning is unknown, it is without a beginning. 'Ādimattakathanaṃ' means the teaching of the state of the Wheel of Existence as having a beginning. Alternatively, the word 'matta' has the sense of excluding a distinction; if there is no beginning, ignorance could exist at the beginning, middle, and end—in all places. Therefore, it means: would it not be contradictory to teach ignorance as merely the beginning? 'Avijjāggahaṇena' means by the production or mention of ignorance, or by the act of firmly embedding it within one's own continuity because it cannot be abandoned by the Path. 'Kammādīni' refers to the round of kamma (kammavaṭṭa) and the round of result (vipākavaṭṭa). Ignorance is called the 'principal state' (padhānadhamma) because it is the primary cause of the round. 'Vado' is so called because it explains what is beneficial or not. 'Vedeyyo' is so called because it experiences pleasure and so on, or because it knows all objects; it is known or understood by oneself and others as "I am happy," etc. In the phrase "by Brahma or by oneself," the word 'vā' (or) has the sense of 'ca' (and). Thus, it is stated as a compound with the sense of 'and': "void of an agent (kattar) and an experiencer (vedaka)."

'Dvādasavidhasuññatāsuññaṃ' means empty through the emptiness of the twelve factors such as ignorance, etc., from permanence, beauty, happiness, and self. Or, taking the four types of emptiness as one, it means empty by that twelvefold emptiness because there are twelve factors.
126:
'Pubbantāharaṇato' (by way of bringing from the past) means that because it brings the present result such as consciousness and mentality-materiality from the past causes of ignorance and formations, this Wheel of Existence is said to end with the delimited feeling (vedanā). Indeed, even a part of the Wheel of Existence is called the Wheel of Existence.

Alternatively, feeling is a condition for ignorance which is associated with craving. Thus, from feeling comes ignorance, and from that, formations. Because of this connection, it is appropriate to say the Wheel of Existence ends with feeling. In the same way, this should be applied to the Wheel of Existence rooted in craving. Both types of the Wheel of Existence can enter into each other.

Ignorance is called the 'Conductor of Saṃsāra' (saṃsāranāyikā) because it conceals the true nature of things, produces perverted attention, and leads those of wrong-view temperament into saṃsāra, or because it causes the occurrence of saṃsāra, which is the arising of formations and so on.

The term 'phaluppattiyā' indicates the agent. In this first Wheel of Existence, the arising of present fruits such as consciousness is directly seen. It also clearly shows that the causes from the previous life—ignorance and formations—which are not directly seen, do not cease without producing their fruit. Alternatively, the previous Wheel of Existence is taught as connected to the second one, showing the non-interruption of causes like craving through the arising of the fruit called feeling. Therefore, it is said: 'phaluppattiyā hetūnaṃ anupacchedappakāsanato' (by way of showing the non-interruption of the causes through the arising of the fruit). Or, the first Wheel of Existence shows the non-interruption of causes like ignorance through the arising of fruits like formations without failing to produce fruit, or it shows the sequence of formations, etc., which are the causes of consciousness, etc. Unlike the second one, it does not show the end; hence it is said: 'phaluppattiyā hetūnaṃ anupacchedappakāsanato'.

In the phrase 'with consciousness as condition, mentality-materiality', it refers to the embryonic matter (kalala-rūpa) before the sense bases are complete. Following that, 'with mentality-materiality as condition, the sixfold sense base' describes the occurrence of the six sense bases. Thus, it is said: 'anupubbapavattidīpanato' (by way of illustrating the sequential occurrence). In the phrase 'with existence as condition, birth', the sequential arising of the sense bases is not taught; thus it is said: 'sahuppattidīpanato' (by way of illustrating the simultaneous arising).

Because it has three connections preceded by the cause and so on, this Wheel of Existence is called 'hetuphalhetupubbakatisandhi'. Because it has a grouping of the factors into four parts by way of cause, fruit, cause, and fruit, it is called 'catubhedasaṅgaha'. Although not explicitly mentioned by their own nature, they are called 'ākāra' (aspects) because they are made manifest in those respective groupings by the inclusion of ignorance, formations, and so on. Or, the varieties of past causes and so on are called 'ākāra'. Defilements, kamma, and results revolve repeatedly, being connected as result-defilement-kamma. Therefore, the name 'round' (vaṭṭa) is metaphorically applied to them, and they are called the 'three rounds' (tivaṭṭa). They are also called 'rounds' (vaṭṭāni) because they are parts of the round.

'Sandhīnaṃ ādipariyosānavavatthitā' means the delimitation by the preceding and succeeding parts of the connections.
127:
"Whatever volition is becoming, and the states associated with volition are striving-formations." This statement is made according to the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pāḷi taught in this Dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇabhājanīya. This is because in this Paṭisambhidāmagga Pāḷi, it is stated that "volition is becoming." However, in the Bhava-niddesa, regarding the phrase "according to the meaning," it is shown according to the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi that "volition alone is formation, while becoming also includes the states associated with volition." This is because in the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi, the nature of formations as volition is taught as: "Therein, what is the meritorious formation (puññābhisaṅkhāra)? It is the wholesome volition of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara-kusala-cetanā)," and so on.

Between these two Pāḷi texts, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pāḷi, the states associated with volition are called "formations" (saṅkhāra) because they have the nature of producing results, and through the function of constructing and conditioning the conditioned states known as "striving" (āyūhana) together with the resulting vipāka to be given. In the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi, it is stated that "all kamma leading to becoming is kamma-becoming (kamma-bhava)." It is called "becoming" (bhava) because it causes rebirth-becoming (upapatti-bhava), being the cause of becoming, the means of reaching becoming, and being of the nature of kamma as an associate mixed with kamma. Since the function of producing rebirth-becoming is predominant in volition, volition is called "becoming" in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pāḷi. Since the function of constructing and conditioning becoming is predominant in volition, volition is called "formation" in the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi with phrases such as "wholesome volition." Therefore, it is appropriate to state both in both places according to those respective methods (pariyāya); thus, there is no contradiction here.

By the word "gahaṇa" (grasping), the function of taking up by clinging to sense-pleasures (kāmupādāna) is meant. By the word "parāmasana" (misapprehension), the remaining types of clinging (upādāna) are meant. "Āyūhanāvasāna" means at the end of the striving (āyūhana) mentioned in the three types of meanings. The striving-formations mentioned in the first two meanings are called "its preceding part," and the striving-formations mentioned in the third meaning are called "states associated with it."

The mental process of a young person is mostly composed of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and thus is generally incapable of striving for kamma that generates a new existence. Therefore, it is said, "because the faculties (āyatana) are mature here." By the phrase "delusion at the time of performing kamma," the delusion (moha) which is the cause of kamma is shown. It does not only show the delusion associated with kamma.

Kamma itself is called "kamma-sambhāra" (accumulations of kamma) because it accumulates and increases the results (vipāka). Alternatively, formations (saṅkhāra) and becoming (bhava) are kamma, and ignorance (avijjā), craving (taṇhā), and clinging (upādāna) which support them are called kamma-sambhāra. Or, becoming that gives rebirth is kamma, and the striving-formations, ignorance, etc., which support it are kamma-sambhāra. Thus, kamma and the requisites of kamma are collectively called "kamma-sambhāra" by a single term. In the phrase "ten states are kamma," ignorance and so on are also called "kamma" because they are associates of kamma, resemble kamma, and support that kamma.
128: In this kamma and result, the causes such as ignorance (avijjā) and the effects such as consciousness (viññāṇa) are summarized; because they are thus summarized, it is called saṅkhepa (summary/group). Alternatively, because it is summarized as "kamma" and "result," it is called saṅkhepa; these are ignorance etc., and consciousness etc. It should be understood that the singular form "saṅkhepo" is used due to the commonality of being a summary. Alternatively, the word saṅkhepa is a synonym for "portion" (bhāga); thus, the portion of kamma is called kamma-saṅkhepa. "Evaṃ samuppannaṃ" means the arising of result from kamma. In that arising, formations arise due to ignorance. It means this wheel of existence (bhava-cakka) which has arisen well in this way, or has arisen well by way of the three connections (tisandhi), etc. "Ittaraṃ" means having the nature of moving towards destruction, having the nature of perishing. By that word "ittaraṃ," it indicates the rejection of staying for another time, which is not shown by the word "anicca" (impermanent) indicating the possession of arising and falling, and the word "cala" (unstable) indicating the occurrence of change. By the word "adhūvaṃ" (non-permanent), the absence of essence which rejects stability is shown. Only the causes are called hetu-sambhāra (collection of causes) because they increase the effects. The "station" (ṭhāna - supporting cause) mentioned here in the phrase "by way of station, by way of cause," as well as other common causes connected with those respective effects, are called sambhāra. The uncommon cause is called hetu. "Evaṃ" means when there is only the occurrence of states due to causes in this way, or when there is the cessation of the round (vaṭṭa) due to the cessation of causes, and when the Dhamma is taught for the sake of that cessation. The two words brahmacariyaṃ and idha form the compound brahmacariyidha. In the phrase "satte ca," the word "ca" has the sense of conjunction (samuccaya), meaning "thus the holy life exists, and the views of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) and annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi) do not occur." Thus, when there is only the occurrence of states dependent on causes, a "being" (satta) or "self" (atta) is not found. If that being were found, there would be either eternalism or annihilationism. Since that being is not found, it means there is neither annihilationism nor eternalism. "Saccappabhavato" means by way of truth, or because of arising from the causal truth of the result-truths. "Kusalākusalaṃ kammaṃ" is understood as mundane wholesome and unwholesome kamma associated with taints (sāsava) because it is spoken within the context of the round of existence (vaṭṭa). "Avisesena" means that all that wholesome and unwholesome kamma is called "the truth of the origin" (samudaya-sacca) without making a distinction between volition and states associated with volition. It is taught as "craving and... the remaining wholesome states associated with taints" without making a distinction between volition and states associated with volition. Alternatively, it means it is called "the truth of the origin" without making a distinction between the Noble Truths (ariya-sacca). "Vatthūsu" means in the objects, or in the bases such as the eye which are to be covered. "Sokādīnaṃ adhiṭṭhānattā" means because of being the cause of those states such as grief (soka). The meaning is that when ignorance is accomplished through those states such as grief, it becomes a condition for the manifestation in another existence through the formations associated with ignorance. Alternatively, the death-consciousness (cuti-citta) is the proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya) for the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa); thus it is said, "it becomes a condition for the manifestation in another existence."
129:
There is the aforementioned statement. Since that death-consciousness (cuticitta), when devoid of ignorance (avijjā) and formations (saṅkhāra), cannot be a cause for another existence, it is said, 'Because it is the basis for sorrow and so forth,' in order to show its companions, ignorance and formations. 'In two ways' means both by its own nature and by being a causal condition for other states.

By the statement 'With ignorance as condition, formations arise,' showing the conditioned nature of formations, it demonstrates that the question 'Who performs the formation?' is improper. By showing this, it prevents the view that there is a doer (creator). By the phrase 'preventing such views,' it refers to preventing views such as 'he sorrows, he laments, he suffers.' Since sorrow and so forth are dependent on conditions and are not under one's control, it is taught by the statement 'With birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow... arise.'

'Like small boils breaking out from an old wound' means like small boils appearing on top of a ripening boil about to burst, or like boils when a large wound breaks in many ways. Swelling, redness, and suppuration are the corruptions of a wound.

Just as a person with eyes covered by a cataract cannot see forms, or if they see something, they see it wrongly, so one overcome by ignorance does not know or see the truth of suffering and so forth, or they see it wrongly. Therefore, ignorance is like a cataract. Just as a silkworm makes its own cocoon, and because they are the cause of one's own wandering in saṃsāra, formations are like parts of a cocoon. Consciousness (viññāṇa), which finds no footing without being grasped by formations, is like a prince who finds no footing without being grasped by a guiding minister. In this analogy, the common point is the lack of a footing without being grasped.

By the word 'uppattinimitta' (sign of rebirth), it refers to objects such as kamma. 'Because of thinking' means because of making an object or because of thinking with the associated initial thought (vitakka). Because of its various forms such as devas, humans, animals, and birds, mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa) is like a magic trick. Because it reaches a specific growth due to a specific footing, the sixfold sense base (saḷāyatana) is like a forest or a thicket of trees. Because the sense bases, as subjects and objects, face each other, there is the impingement of the sense bases. Here too, since formations and so forth are similar to the cocoon, the guiding minister, and so forth in two ways each, it should be understood that two analogies are given for each.

Because it is deep and yet appears, is manifest, and is seen, it is called 'deep in appearance.' 'The sense of arising and following continuously due to the condition of birth' means the sense of arising well due to the condition of birth and appearing continuously upwards in accordance with its cause. Or, the sense of arising well and the sense of following continuously is 'sambhūtasamudāgataṭṭha.' 'It is not that aging and death do not occur because of birth, nor [without] birth...'
130:
By the statement 'it arises without other causes,' the sense of arising well due to the condition of birth is expressed. Thus, because it arises in continuous connection from birth, it is called the sense of continuous arising due to a condition. Whatever birth assists by whatever causal power, the manifestation of aging and death in accordance with that birth and causal power is the meaning.

In the phrase 'anulomapaṭilomatō' (in forward and reverse order), in this teaching of dependent origination, it does not mean the forward order called the arising of the conditioned due to the arising of the condition, nor the reverse order called the cessation of the conditioned due to the cessation of the condition. Rather, going from the beginning, ignorance, to the end is called forward order (anuloma), and going from the end to the beginning is called reverse order (paṭiloma). By the reverse teaching starting from the middle, craving, such as 'What is the source of these four nutriments?', and by the forward teaching such as 'Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, feeling arises,' it is taught as two junctions and three groups. In passages such as 'Monks, in one who dwells contemplating the gratification in things that can be fettered, craving increases; with craving as condition, clinging arises,' it is taught as one junction and two groups.

Because the nature of ignorance and so forth is penetrated and known, it is called penetration (paṭivedha). It has been said: 'The non-perverted nature, known as the individual characteristic (salakkhaṇa), of those various taught states that is to be penetrated, is penetration.' The formation associated with greed, which is a part of demeritorious formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra), is called 'with lust' (sarāga); other demeritorious formations are called 'without lust' (virāga). Alternatively, all demeritorious formations that increase lust because they are not the opposite of lust are called 'with lust'; the others, meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) and imperturbable formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra), are called 'without lust' because they are the opposite. 'Monks, this consciousness has been entered into, cherished, and misapprehended by the uninstructed worldling for a long time thus: "This is mine, this I am, this is my self."' Thus it was taught. Because consciousness is taught as the special basis for the misapprehension of a self, the sense of consciousness being empty of a self is deep. Because of the strong preoccupation with activity and transmigration, thinking 'the self knows, the self wanders,' the senses of being without activity, without transmigration, and appearing in rebirth are also deep. Because mind (nāma) is not conjoined with matter (rūpa), and matter is not conjoined with mind, their distinctness should be applied; and the non-distinctness of mind from mind should be applied. If non-distinctness is intended by way of simultaneous arising and simultaneous cessation, then the non-distinctness of matter from matter is also obtained. Alternatively, in the one-constituent and four-constituent planes of existence, because mind and matter cannot exist together, their mutual distinctness should be known; in the five-constituent plane of existence, because they can exist together, their non-distinctness should be known.
131:
The meaning of predominance (adhipatiyaṭṭha) is the state of the faculty condition (indriya-paccaya). The meanings such as 'world,' 'door,' and 'field' should be applied to the five bases (āyatana) starting with the eye (cakkhu). Since the mind-base (manāyatana) is also subject to disintegration and acts as a door and a field for mind-contact (manosamphassa), etc., these meanings are also appropriate for it. Illumination (obhāsana), characterized by the suitability to manifest visible forms (rūpa), etc., that have come into range, is the objective state (visayibhāva) of the eye, etc. The cognizing of the mind-base is also the objective state.

The meaning of impact (saṅghaṭṭanaṭṭha) specifically applies to the five such as eye-contact (cakkhusamphassa), but it should also be applied to all six. Touching (phusana) is the nature of contact (phassa), while impact (saṅghaṭṭana) is its function (rasa). The others (saṅgati, sannipāta) are the modes of manifestation (upaṭṭhānākāra) appearing in knowledge.

The meaning of experiencing the flavor of the object (ārammaṇarasānubhavanaṭṭha) is stated by way of function (rasa). The meaning of feeling (vedayitaṭṭha) is stated by way of characteristic (lakkhaṇa). Because of the strong insistence (abhinivesa) that 'the self feels,' the meaning of soullessness (nijjīvaṭṭha) in feeling is very profound. The feeling of a soulless feeling is called 'soulless feeling' (nijjīvavedayita). Since that soulless feeling itself is the meaning, it is called the meaning of soulless feeling (nijjīvavedayitaṭṭha).

The meaning of taking (ādānaṭṭha) is common to all four types of clinging (upādāna). The meaning of grasping (gahanaṭṭha) is the meaning of clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādāna). The meanings of the other three types of clinging are insistence (abhinivesa), etc. Because it is preached as 'the jungle of views,' there is also the meaning of being difficult to transcend (duratikkamanaṭṭha) for the three types of views. Alternatively, because of firm grasping, the meaning of being difficult to transcend should be applied to all four types of clinging. In the term 'yonigatithitinivāsesu khipanti,' the non-elision (alopa) of the locative case in the compound should be understood. Therefore, that term forms a compound with the words 'āyūhana' and 'abhisaṅkharaṇa.'

The factor of aging and death (jarā-maraṇa) emphasizes death. Therefore, exhaustion (khaya), etc., which are meanings of death, are shown as profound meanings. Aging (jarā) is the occurrence of maturity such as broken teeth due to the exhaustion of ever-new phenomena. Alternatively, the meaning of aging should be understood as exhaustion (khaya), as it is appropriate to call the departure from a new state 'exhaustion.' The meaning of change (vipariṇāmaṭṭha) pertains to both aging and death. Alternatively, the nature of exhaustion and fall of aging should be applied by way of continuity (santati), and the nature of destruction and change of death should be applied by way of conventional (sammuti) and momentary (khaṇika) death.

## The Method of Meanings (Atthanaya)
Atthanaya means the methods of the meanings. Because they are led (known) to their own nature such as oneness (ekatta) by the meanings of ignorance (avijjā), etc., oneness, etc., are called the methods (naya) of those meanings. They are called 'naya' because they are known. Alternatively, the meanings themselves, being known by way of oneness, etc., are called 'atthanaya.' Alternatively, they are called 'naya' because meanings are known through them; and since meanings are known as 'one,' etc., through oneness, etc., therefore oneness, etc., are the methods of the meanings (atthanaya). Just as a seed reaches the state of a tree and continues as a tree through the non-interruption of the continuity (santānānupaccheda), which is called oneness (ekatta), so too in this wheel of existence, the non-interruption of ignorance, etc., is shown as oneness.
132:
Bhinnasantanasseva means that because of grasping at separate occurrences without connection, one thinks 'a being other than the one who died has ceased, a being other than the one who died has arisen,' and thus clings to the view of annihilation (uccheda-diṭṭhi).

Yato kutoci means that if an effect could arise from any cause whatsoever, why would oil not arise from sand or milk from sugarcane? Therefore, one clings to the view of non-causality (ahetuka-diṭṭhi) thinking 'there is no cause for any effect,' or to the doctrine of fatalism (niyati-vāda) thinking that even without a cause, oil, milk, and the body arise from sesame, cows, and semen/blood respectively due to fixed necessity, as appropriate.

Why? Because without breaking this wheel of existence, there is no one who has transcended the danger of saṃsāra, even in a dream. Durabhiyānaṃ (or duratiyānaṃ) means that which is difficult to cross. Asanivicakkhamiva means like a thunderbolt-disk. Just as that thunderbolt-disk only exists in the act of crushing and destroying and does not exist without crushing, so too this wheel of existence is called 'that which constantly crushes' because it certainly produces suffering.

To provide evidence that no one transcends the danger of saṃsāra without cutting it with the sword of knowledge, it is said 'Vuttampi cetaṃ,' etc. Tantākulakajātā means being extremely entangled with defilements (kilesa), kamma, and results (vipāka), like a tangled ball of thread. Guṇāguṇḍikajātā means being like the nest of the bird called Guṇā (a weaver bird's nest). They do not transcend the fourfold states of deprivation: the state of deprivation (apāya) because of the absence of progress, the unhappy destination (duggati) because of going to suffering, and the perdition (vinipāta) because of falling away from happiness; nor do they transcend saṃsāra, which is described as 'the succession of aggregates (khandha),' etc. Alternatively, the entire round of saṃsāra is here called by names such as 'apāya' because of meanings such as the absence of progress, and simply because it is a mass of suffering.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Wheel of Existence is finished.

## The Explanation of the Suttanta Classification is finished.

## 2. The Explanation of the Abhidhamma Classification

Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) is spoken of by way of meanings as vast as the earth and the sky. Just as one might spread out and expand the earth and the sky which are not already spread out or expanded, the Blessed One, through the method of the Suttanta Classification, has expanded and widened that which is contained within a single mind-moment by relating it to all beings and all minds.
133:
The Blessed One, without restricting it (to a single mind), made it extensively pervasive in connection with all beings and all minds, and showed it by way of the Suttanta-bhājanīya (Suttanta classification). In showing it thus, the phrase "by way of various minds" is said with reference to the state of being produced in various minds by causes (paccaya) and resultants (paccayuppanna) that are non-co-nascent (asahajāta) and co-nascent (sahajāta). Because there are nine root terms (mūlapada) such as ignorance (avijjā) in these methods, they are the "nine root terms" methods. Where it is said, "because of being included in four cycles (vāra) by each method," it should be stated here as "by each tetrad (catukka)." This is because in this Abhidhamma-bhājanīya method, the cycles of the tetrads are defined within the methods, due to the nature of the tetrads already shown.

## 1. Paccaya-catukka-vaṇṇanā
(Description of the Tetrad of Conditions)

Without taking ignorance (avijjā) as a factor (aṅga), the resultants that occur together with their causes, such as "with ignorance as condition, formations arise," are spoken of as factors; with this intention, it is said, "because that ignorance is not a factor." Having done so, in the Niddesa, after answering the question "Therein, what is ignorance?" by explaining ignorance separately from formations, the resultants such as formations which have those respective causes are answered by way of "Therein, what are formations caused by ignorance?" and so on. Among the three types, the first cycle (paṭhama vāra) can enter into the second cycle and others, and because it is common to all distinctions such as specific conditions, it can encompass those specific cycles; therefore, it is called "all-inclusive" (sabba-saṅgāhaka). It is only the first cycle that shows that not only the sixth sense-base (chaṭṭhāyatana) alone is the condition for contact (phassa), but indeed name (nāma) is also a condition for contact. Or, name is not only the condition for the sixth sense-base alone, but indeed it is also a condition for contact. For the purpose of showing such specific conditions, and for the purpose of showing the specific meaning for which the Mahānidāna Sutta teaching arose, the first cycle is spoken of by excluding the factor of the sixth sense-base; thus its entry into the second cycle is mentioned, not because of the inclusion of all factors.

"Yattha" (wherein) refers to the group of four cycles as well as to each individual cycle. "Aññathā" (otherwise) means being taught as "formations" (saṅkhāra) in a manner other than the Suttanta-bhājanīya method. "Avuttaṃ" (not mentioned) means that "matter" (rūpa) and "sixfold sense-base" (saḷāyatana) are not mentioned. In all those four cycles, sorrow and so on, which are not mentioned here, were mentioned in the Suttanta-bhājanīya methods. It should be understood that the very sixfold sense-base mentioned in those Suttanta-bhājanīya methods is mentioned here in this Abhidhamma-bhājanīya method in another way as "sixth sense-base" (chaṭṭhāyatana).

"Sabbaṭṭhāna-sādhāraṇato" (by being common to all places) means by being common to all cycles in the manner already stated, or by being common to the state of existence (bhava) which is the place of occurrence for all consciousness. Because they cannot exist without consciousness, the group of three mental aggregates is also an equal result and a cause; with this intention, it is said "without distinction" (avisesena). However, because of the statement "the meeting of the three is contact," consciousness is... for contact.
134:
...a specific condition; therefore, contact, which is the result of that consciousness, is a specific result. Although the state of being a nutriment condition exists among the associated states in the nutriment condition (āhāra-paccaya), mental volition (manosañcetanā) has the specific function of bringing about rebirth-consciousness; therefore, formations (saṅkhāra) are also a specific condition for that consciousness.

"Acittakkhaṇamattāni" refers to states that are devoid of the duration of a single thought-moment. The meaning of those taught states such as ignorance and so on should be understood in the same manner as stated in the commentary on the Suttanta-bhājanīya.

In this context of "hetukādīni" (rooted and so on), it should be understood that in whichever tetrad the word "hetuka" is spoken, that tetrad is called "hetuka" because it is associated with the word "hetuka." The word "hetu" indicates a destination (gati). Since the state of non-disappearance (avigata) is indeed a destination by way of preventing the state of disappearance (vigata), it is said that the Hetuka-catukka is spoken of by way of the non-disappearance condition (avigata-paccaya).

In the phrase "threefold, fourfold, or fivefold," the word "or" (vā) should be understood as also distinguishing "sixfold." This is because concentration (samādhi) acts as a condition through the three common conditions, as well as through the Jhana condition, Faculty condition, and Path condition. The statement "sevenfold," meaning clinging (upādāna) also conditions existence (bhava) through the Path condition, is said by way of clingings excluding sense-clinging (kāmupādāna). As for the manner in which sense-clinging conditions existence, that has already been stated in the section on craving (taṇhā), so it is not mentioned again.

In this tetrad, the phrase "they are conditions by way of the co-nascent condition (sahajāta-paccaya)" (starting from the first tetrad) is the view of the teachers who say so (vadanti). In truth, it is not that the nature of conditional states does not act as a condition for their own resultants through their respective conditional forces in any cycle (it does indeed act). However, because this first tetrad is taught only by way of the co-nascent condition, they say that only the co-nascent condition exists here. In the place of "paṭhama vāra" (first cycle), it should be stated as "paṭhama catukka" (first tetrad).

Regarding the absence of such (co-nascent) nature in existence (bhava) and so on—if the first tetrad were taught only by way of the co-nascent condition, then existence cannot be a co-nascent condition for birth (jāti), nor birth for death (maraṇa). Just as in the Avigata-catukka and others, "existence as condition, birth; existence-rooted" etc., are not mentioned because existence and so on do not have the conditional force of non-disappearance and so on (in that specific way), so too here, "existence as condition, birth" etc., should not be mentioned. The word "condition" (paccaya) itself would imply co-nascence here, as in the Avigata-catukka, because there is no other word to indicate a specific condition; yet, it is not that those (existence as condition for birth, etc.) are not mentioned (they are indeed mentioned), and existence and so on are not co-nascent conditions. Therefore, this tetrad is not taught solely by way of the co-nascent condition.

This phrase "the possibility of the remaining conditions" is said with reference to the possibility of other conditional forces remaining besides the co-nascent condition in ignorance and so on, in general, without connecting it to the phrase "of existence and so on" (bhavādīnaṃ). The meaning here is: if it were said that other conditional forces besides co-nascence are not possible in ignorance and so on because there is no other word indicating a specific condition, then it should be said that this tetrad begins only by way of the co-nascent condition. However, it is not that those other conditional forces are not possible (they are indeed possible). Therefore, this tetrad does not begin as those teachers (vadanti) say.
135:
This first tetrad should be said to be undertaken only in connection with the conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya). However, it is not that other conditional forces do not arise from that conascence condition (they do arise). Therefore, it should be understood that this tetrad is not undertaken in that way (solely as conascence).

It is said, "In the Mahānidāna Sutta, the Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) is taught with eleven factors." In that Sutta, when "With name-and-form as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, contact," etc., occur, if name-and-form is taken as one, nine factors are taught; if taken as two, ten factors are taught.
