In other Suttas, when ignorance (avijjā) and volitional formations (saṅkhāra) are taught and connected to show the three periods, it becomes eleven factors; thus it should be understood as stated. To encompass the teaching of the Mahānidāna Sutta means: in that Sutta, by including the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) etc. in form (rūpa) and the sixth base (chaṭṭhāyatana) in name (nāma), it was taught as "With name-and-form as condition, contact" to show the contact's dependence on form without remainder and on name without remainder. Similarly, in this second section, by showing the distinction presented in that Sutta, for the purpose of encompassing that teaching, in the single-thought-moment Dependent Origination, the sixth base is included in name and taught as "With name as condition, contact."

Because it is taught with reference to the place of the arising of form, the remaining words "of this person" should be added. This is not the case in the preceding sentences. For this reason, it says, "This Dependent Origination, however," and so on.

Regarding "among those of spontaneous birth (opapātika)" by way of the mode of birth (yoni), it should be understood that those of moisture-born birth (saṃsedaja) are also included in the spontaneous birth category because they have complete sense-bases. Alternatively, "opapātika" is mentioned to show the mode of birth with entirely complete sense-bases as the primary mode. By way of showing such inclusion, in the Dhammahadaya-vibhaṅga as well, only "opapātika" is taken, as in "of spontaneously born hungry ghosts (petas)" etc., and "saṃsedaja" is not taken. In a single thought-moment, the arising of contact through the six bases does not exist. There is no base other than the sixth base existing at the same moment as a condition for a single unwholesome contact. Here, the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) is not taken as the producer of contact. Therefore, to show that it cannot be said "With the sixfold base as condition, contact," it says "But because this," and so on.

Although the sixfold base can occur in the first two modes of birth (egg-born and womb-born), it is said "because of not always occurring" because it does not always occur for some beings at times such as the stage of the embryonic kalala drop. In the latter two modes of birth (moisture-born and spontaneous), however...
136:
...for those in whom it occurs, it should be understood that it always occurs. "From this" (ito) means from this tetrad, or from this method, a distinction is intended.

## The Explanation of the Tetrad of Conditions is finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Tetrad of Causes

"Because of non-existence at the mere moment of birth" (jātikkhṇamatte eva abhāvato) means because of existence in the subsequent period above that moment of birth (which is called aging and death). Because of the lack of necessity of the non-disappearance condition (avigata-paccaya), the term "caused by clinging" (upādāna-hetuka) is not used in "becoming" (bhava). Because of the total absence of the non-disappearance condition, the term "caused by becoming" (bhava-hetuka) etc. is not used in birth (jāti) etc.; this should be construed accordingly. Just as the heart-base (hadayavatthu) occurring after consciousness is the non-disappearance condition for the consciousness that cannot be obtained as long as the heart-base exists, so too clinging (upādāna) would be the non-disappearance condition for birth etc. included in becoming, and becoming (bhava) would be the non-disappearance condition for birth. If it were not so, because birth etc. are included in the aggregate of volitional formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), consciousness would not be the non-disappearance condition for name, and name (though not existing at that moment) would not be the non-disappearance condition for the sixth base. If that were the case, as in this instance, the word "caused by" (hetuka) should not be used where name arises because of consciousness. Therefore, it is not appropriate to give as reasons the inability to obtain birth etc. as long as clinging lasts, and the non-existence of becoming only at the moment of birth.

Because birth etc., which are conditioned characteristics (saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa) and not ultimate realities (asabhāva-dhamma), are included in becoming, and because there is no other kind of becoming in the ultimate sense for what is not an ultimate reality, the conditions such as cause (hetu) do not exist. Therefore, clinging is not necessarily the non-disappearance condition for becoming. Becoming is not the non-disappearance condition for birth, and birth is not the non-disappearance condition for aging and death. Thus, because of the lack of necessity and the total absence of the non-disappearance condition, it is proper that the word "caused by" (hetuka) is not used in becoming etc.

If so, should it not be said that "Name has consciousness as its cause; the sixth base has name as its cause"? For the state of being a non-disappearance condition for birth etc. included in name, and the state of being a non-disappearance condition for other resultant states, do not exist because they are not ultimate realities. That is not so, because those factors like birth are not included in "name". Name is defined by the function of "bending" (namana) towards an object, and that function belongs only to ultimate realities (sabhāva-dhamma). Therefore, only the three mental aggregates which are ultimate realities are called "name". Thus, the use of the word "caused by" (hetuka) there is appropriate. Here, however, it is called "becoming" (bhava) in the sense of "it becomes". It is not that birth etc. do not become; they do indeed become. It should be construed as "With becoming as condition, birth arises; with birth as condition, aging and death arise." Therefore, just as birth etc. are included in the aggregate of volitional formations in the sense of "performing/arranging" (saṅkhāra), so they are included in becoming in the sense of "becoming" (or appearing). Thus, because of the lack of necessity and the total absence of the non-disappearance condition, the word "caused by" (hetuka) is not used. Furthermore, in this Abhidhamma method, because name is included in becoming...
137:
Because of the absence of a fixed rule or total absence, such as 'birth and so forth are included in existence (bhava) because they are produced by it, just as they are included in formations (saṅkhāra) because they are arranged by them,' the term 'hetuka' is not employed.

With the words "Keci pana" (But some), the view of Elder Revata is stated. Here, the mental aggregates are intended as 'existence' (bhava). For it is said: "Therein, what is existence conditioned by clinging? Excluding clinging, it is the feeling aggregate... the consciousness aggregate" (Vibhaṅga 249).

Although it is said "because of the absence of a part to be spoken," even if there were a part to be spoken, birth and so forth are not ultimate realities (sabhāva-dhamma) like clinging. Therefore, it is appropriate to say that exclusion should not be made simply because there is no other ultimate reality to be excluded. Since birth belongs to those being born, and aging and death belong to those already born, it is said: "Conditioned by existence is birth; conditioned by birth are aging and death" (Vibhaṅga 225).

Just as it is shown in the part to be spoken of name-and-form, which is the condition for contact and the sixfold sense base, in such passages as: "Conditioned by name is contact. Therein, what is name? Excluding contact, it is the feeling aggregate... the consciousness aggregate. This is called name" (Vibhaṅga 259); and "Conditioned by name-and-form is the sixfold sense base. There is name and there is form. Therein, what is name? The feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, the formations aggregate. This is called name. Therein, what is form? The four great elements and the form derived from them on which the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element turn. This is called form" (Vibhaṅga 261); so too, in existence which is the condition for birth, although there is a distinction between what should be excluded (birth, aging, and death) and what should be taken (the four mental aggregates), it cannot be said that there is no part to be spoken.

## The Explanation of the Fourfold Cause is finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Fourfold Mutuality

To show that it cannot be said "clinging is also conditioned by existence" because clinging is already included in existence due to the absence of a separate part, and because there is no clinging existing separately as a result of existence, he said "Yasmā pana bhavo nippadeso" (But because existence has no separate part), etc. If this were so, it would follow that "consciousness is also conditioned by name" should not be said. However, the intention is that 'name' is taken only along with its parts as both result and condition. In such Pali passages as "conditioned by name is the sixth sense base, conditioned by name is contact" (Vibhaṅga 150-154), excluding the result...
138:
...name is taken. Similarly, here too, it is not impossible to take existence by excluding clinging, which is the result, in the phrase "clinging is also conditioned by existence." Therefore, just as the fixed rule of the 'un-disappeared condition' (avigata-paccaya) for clinging does not always exist, so too the fixed rule of the 'mutuality condition' (aññamañña-paccaya) in existence does not always exist according to the method previously stated. Thus, it should be understood that "clinging is also conditioned by existence" is not taught.

In this context, 'mutuality condition' (aññamañña-paccaya) should be understood as including the associated condition (sampayutta-paccaya), dissociated condition (vippayutta-paccaya), and presence condition (atthi-paccaya). It is taught: "consciousness is also conditioned by name-and-form." The physical base (vatthu-rūpa) is not a mutuality condition for unwholesome consciousness, but it is a pre-nascence dissociated condition (purejāta-vippayutta-paccaya). Likewise, it is taught: "name-and-form is also conditioned by the sixth sense base." The sixth sense base (manāyatana) is not a mutuality condition for the eye-base, growth (upacaya), etc., nor for mind-produced form (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa), but it is a post-nascence dissociated condition (pacchājāta-vippayutta-paccaya).

## The Explanation of the Fourfold Mutuality is finished.

## Explanation of the Matrix of the Methods Starting with Formations, etc.

It is said: "The method starting with existence as the root is not taught because there is no other new thing to be spoken of as a condition for ignorance." If this were so, the methods starting with the sixth sense base, etc., such as "ignorance is conditioned by the sixth sense base," should also not be taught. For in the phrase "ignorance is conditioned by name," all four aggregates that are conditions for ignorance are taught as 'name.' Here, the intention should be: because the conditionality of specific types of name, such as the sixth sense base, for ignorance must be stated, the methods starting with the sixth sense base, etc., are taught. Whatever name is the condition for ignorance, that same name would be spoken of here in "ignorance is conditioned by existence"; there would be no specific distinction to be stated. Therefore, it should be understood that it is not taught because there is nothing new. By taking 'existence' (bhava), only the ultimate realities (sabhāva-dhamma, i.e., mental aggregates) that are conditions for ignorance should be taken here, not birth and so forth. Thus, it should be noted that it is not taught because there is nothing new.

It is said: "It might also be said that ignorance is conditioned by ignorance." However, just as when it is said "contact is conditioned by name," it does not mean "contact is conditioned by contact" because the condition is taken by excluding the result, so too it would not be the case here. Therefore, the word 'existence' (bhava), which occurs generally among ultimate and non-ultimate realities by way of 'becoming,' can be said not to be the condition for ignorance. Thus, it should be understood that the method starting with existence as the root is not taught.
139:
In this context, such as in the phrase "With clinging as condition, existence [comes to be]" (upādānapaccayā bhavo), although a part of existence was not previously taken separately, the word 'existence' (bhava), being stated at the beginning for the purpose of clarifying the cause, signifies the whole without remainder; however, the word 'name' (nāma) does not do so. It should be understood that because these linguistic expressions have such a nature, it was said, "It might also be said that with ignorance as condition, ignorance [comes to be]" (avijjāpaccayā avijjātipi vuttaṃ siyā) with this intention. It should also be understood that with this same intention, because there is no part of existence [left out], the meaning that "With existence as condition, clinging [comes to be]" is not stated in the Section on Mutuality Condition (aññamaññapaccayavāra).

In that [commentary], by the phrase "because of being cut off," it is as if the fact of birth, aging, and death being conditions for ignorance is permitted. However, for those things being born, there is only birth (jāti); there is no such thing as a 'being born' of birth. There are only aging (jarā) and death (maraṇa) which are growing old and dying; there is no such thing as a 'growing old and dying' of aging and death. Therefore, states such as birth do not become conditions for ignorance in a single mind-moment. Thus, because it is impossible, the methods rooted in those [birth, etc.] are not taken. Nevertheless, because there is a cutting off, it should be understood that it is said, "because of being cut off therein." For that very reason of impossibility, he said "Furthermore" (apica) and so on.

## The Explanation of the Table of Contents is finished.

## Explanation of the Exposition on the Unwholesome

248-249. In saying, "Clinging would arrive at the state of being a condition for clinging," is this not a fault? For clinging to sense-pleasures (kāmupādāna) is a condition for clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna), and that [clinging to views] is a condition for the other [clinging to sense-pleasures], is it not? True. However, because clinging to sense-pleasures is already included by the term 'craving' (taṇhā), and because it does not have the status of a distinct condition as in the case of 'name' (nāma), by taking 'clinging' (upādāna), only 'view' (diṭṭhi)—which is the condition for existence that has craving as its cause—is taken. Therefore, it should be understood that this fault was stated. Furthermore, because in the place of clinging, the result and the cause are one and the same, the cause is not separately analyzed in the exposition of "With clinging as condition, existence [comes to be]," as it is in the expositions of "With name as condition, contact" and "With name-and-form as condition, the sixfold base." Alternatively, even if clinging to sense-pleasures is taken as a condition for existence, if it were not stated as "excluding clinging," then clinging to sense-pleasures would be the condition for clinging to sense-pleasures, and view would be the condition for view; thus, he shows that "excluding clinging" is stated to prevent the cause and the result from being of the same kind.
140:
Consciousness, which produces mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa) that supports the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) and so on, is said to be a condition for the integration (upacaya) of the eye-base and so on, even though it does not directly produce them; it is in this sense that he said "of whatever mind-produced matter" (yassa cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpassa) and so on. The phrase "for those also" (tāsampi hi) means that consciousness is indeed a condition for the continuity of temperature-produced matter (utuja-rūpa) and nutriment-produced matter (āhāraja-rūpa) by way of supporting, originating, and post-nascence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya).

"Accordingly" (yathānurūpaṃ) means: matter called the great elements (mahābhūta) assists the five [bases] by way of conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya) and so on; matter called the physical base (vatthu) assists the sixth [the mind-base] by way of pre-nascence condition (purejāta-paccaya) and so on; the mental (nāma) assists the five bases by way of post-nascence condition and so on; and it assists the sixth by way of conascence condition and so on—this is the state of being "accordingly."

"Of which" (yassa) should be connected as: for which resultant name (nāma), consciousness becomes a condition by way of association condition (sampayutta-paccaya).

Regarding "With contact as condition, name also" (phassapaccayāpi nāmaṃ), the occurrence of the name, which ought to be spoken of as having contact as its condition, by its own resultant contact has been shown. Therefore, showing that there is no special purpose in stating "excluding contact" (ṭhapetvā phassaṃ) again, and thus it is not stated, he said "Even so" (tathāpi) and so on.

Because decision (adhimokkha) also does not exist, therefore the ground for clinging (upādānaṭṭhāna) is merely deficient; thus it is connected. However, the reason for filling the term by means of powerful defilement—the absence of craving—has already been stated in the section on consciousness accompanied by displeasure (domanassa). Therefore, that term [of doubt] should be connected with that absence of craving. "Everywhere" (sabbatha) means that in the third consciousness and so on, the Pali text is abbreviated after showing the specific distinction in the answer such as "With craving as condition, decision."
"Below" (heṭṭhā) refers to the Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness (Cittuppādakaṇḍa) and so on.

## The Explanation of the Exposition on the Unwholesome is finished.

## Explanation of the Exposition on the Wholesome and Indeterminate

'Clarity' (pasāda) means faith (saddhā).

According to the words, "Non-greed is a cause (nidāna) for the arising of kammas" and so on, the wholesome roots together with activity (sabyāpāra) are the causes (nidāna) of volitional formations (saṅkhāra), not...
141:
In resultant consciousnesses cast by the momentum of kamma, non-greed and so forth, which arise like the shadow of the kamma associated with non-greed and so forth, are not the root causes of formations. Therefore, just as in the fivefold sense-consciousness, the absence of a root cause (nidāna) should be understood as falling into the stream of the teaching. Functional states (kiriya-dhamma), because they are merely functional and are devoid of the roots that are the causes of kamma, also fall into the stream of the teaching. Thus, they should be understood as states where the station of ignorance has ceased.

Why is it said, "Because the third and fourth cycles (vāra) are impossible"? Do eye-consciousness and so forth not assist the growth (upacaya) of the eye-base and so forth by way of post-nascence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya)? They do assist. However, it should be understood that this was said as "impossible" with reference to the inability to produce mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa) which supports that growth of the eye-base and so forth. Yet, by the power of conascent consciousness and post-nascent consciousness, the arising of mentality-materiality due to consciousness is obtained even then. By the power of post-nascent mentality, conascent mentality, and conascent or pre-nascent matter such as the eye-base, the arising of the six sense bases due to mentality-materiality is also obtained. Therefore, it is not that the third and fourth cycles are impossible; they are indeed possible.

## The Explanation of the Exposition on the Wholesome and Indeterminate is finished.

## The Explanation of the Wholesome Exposition Rooted in Ignorance

"By the power of delusion" (sammohavasena) means by the power of not seeing the danger in the results of wholesome deeds—which are accompanied by fear because they are impermanent and so forth, and are like the seeds of a poisonous tree with sweet fruit—and in the wholesome deeds that produce those results. Meditation for the sake of transcending is called "transcending meditation" (samatikkama-bhāvanā). Alternatively, meditation that has become a means of transcending by the power of abandoning by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna) and abandoning by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna) is called transcending meditation.

Similarly, the phrase "are not obtained here" is said with reference to the fact that ignorance alone does not assist formations by way of the non-disappearance condition (avigata-paccaya) and so forth. However, formations and so forth do assist consciousness and so forth by way of the non-disappearance condition and so forth. Therefore, it is not that the connection cannot be made as "with ignorance as condition, formations arise; with formations as condition, consciousness arises; it has formations as its cause," and so forth; it can be made. Thus, it is not that the tetrad of non-disappearance (avigata-catukka) and so forth cannot be obtained in this wholesome exposition rooted in ignorance; they can be obtained. This is because the meaning is shown through the method of "application according to what is obtained" (yathālābha-yojanā), such as "with consciousness as condition, mentality-materiality arises; mentality is associated with consciousness," and so forth.

## The Explanation of the Wholesome Exposition Rooted in Ignorance is finished.
142:
## The Explanation Showing the Resultant Rooted in the Wholesome

Regarding the statement, "There is nothing more to be said about the asynchronous kamma condition (nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya)," one might ask: Can wholesome roots and unwholesome roots be the kamma condition? Directly, they cannot. However, because they are mixed with volition (cetanā), which is the kamma condition, they are conditions that assist just like that volition-kamma. It should be noted that this was said because they have reached a state of unity, as it were, with that volition. Just as kamma cannot produce a resultant (vipāka) without wholesome and unwholesome roots, and thus those roots are called the natural strong dependence condition (pakatūpanissaya-paccaya) for the resultant figuratively (pariyāyena), so too, because they are mixed and unified with kamma and act as conditions for the states born of kamma, their status as kamma condition is stated figuratively. The word "esā" should be applied as "this wholesome root-condition and this unwholesome root-condition."

Ignorance, wholesome roots, and unwholesome roots, which produce wholesome and unwholesome resultants, do not exist as producers of functional (kiriya) consciousness. Therefore, it is said, "They do not obtain the status of strong dependence (upanissaya)." Attention (manasikāra) also, being merely a provider for the impulsion process (javana-vīthi), does not act as a strong dependence for ignorance in the way wholesome and unwholesome states do. It merely serves as the advertence of the life-continuum (bhavaṅgāvaṭṭana) for the sake of the occurrence of those states that have ignorance as a strong dependence. For the functional consciousnesses of those who have abandoned ignorance (Arahants), ignorance is not a productive condition but merely an object (ārammaṇa). For this reason, in the Paṭṭhāna texts such as "Wholesome state is a condition for indeterminate state by way of strong dependence condition" and "State that has the nature of resultant is a condition for state that is neither resultant nor has the nature of resultant by way of strong dependence condition," unwholesome states are not excluded from being the strong dependence condition for functional consciousnesses. Alternatively, the wholesome method rooted in ignorance is taught by the power of "with ignorance as condition, formations arise." The resultant method rooted in wholesome and unwholesome is taught by the power of "with formations as condition, consciousness arises." As for functional consciousnesses, they are not included under the term "formations" nor under the term "consciousness" [in the context of the links]; therefore, it should be understood that the functional method rooted in those is not obtained and thus not taught.

"By many divisions" (aneka-bhedato) means that in the first method ending in functional consciousness, the single-mind-moment (ekacittak္khaṇika) root-terms like ignorance and so forth are taken as many conditions such as conascence (sahajāta) and so forth; thus it refers to the power of those conditions, or the power of the methods having nine or more root-terms, or the power of the four tetrads (catukka) which have many varieties. In the passage "of the wholesome and unwholesome, and in the resultant," it should be stated as "in the wholesome and unwholesome, and in the resultants of the wholesome and unwholesome." Just as the mode of conditions is taught in the preceding and following methods...
143:
To show that distinction, it is said: "In many ways, but in one way only." In the subsequent method, Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) in the wholesome (kusala) is not taught in many ways; rather, it is taught as "in one way." "In one way" means either by virtue of the single causal condition of the root term, or by virtue of a single method in one way. Alternatively, it means by virtue of the first tetrad only.

"In the distinction of phenomena and conditions" refers to the distinction of the causal efficacy of phenomena such as ignorance (avijjā), or the distinction of causes such as birth (jāti) for phenomena such as aging and death (jarāmaraṇa), or the distinction of momentary causes such as ignorance for phenomena such as contact (phassa) delimited by the time of the arising of various consciousnesses. The sequence of learning and so on is called the sequence of learning (pariyatti) ... the sequence of practice (paṭipatti). Indeed, in Dependent Origination, the term "sequence" (kama) is used because the practice of meditation (bhāvanā-paṭipatti) must be performed in order, starting with learning the Pali text, hearing its meaning, and reflecting on its meaning, such as "Aging and death are impermanent, conditioned ... of the nature to cease." Beyond that, there is no other special task to be done. This is because the ending of suffering depends on the effort made according to that sequence.

## The Description of the Resultant Section Rooted in the Wholesome is finished.

## The Description of the Abhidhamma Classification is finished.

## The Description of the Analysis of Dependent Origination is finished.
144:
## 7. Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga
## 1. Suttantabhājanīya
## Uddesavāravaṇṇanā
With the passage "Tayo satipaṭṭhāna" (Three foundations of mindfulness), the summary of the meaning of the term "satipaṭṭhāna" is extracted. However, the meaning of the term "satipaṭṭhāna" as taught in this Satipaṭṭhāna Vibhaṅga Pali is not shown. This is because, in the passage "Ādīsu hi satigocaro," the word "ādi" (etc.) includes the parts of the Sutta that show the objective domains of mindfulness called "foundations of mindfulness," as taught in: "With the arising of contact, there is the arising of feeling; with the arising of name-and-form, there is the arising of consciousness; with the arising of attention (manasikāra), there is the arising of phenomena." Similarly, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali, the word "ādi" should be understood as having the meaning of showing the remaining portions of the Pali. For one performing acts of giving and so on, visible forms and so on, as well as kasinas and so on, become the station of mindfulness. To exclude those visible forms, kasinas, and so on, it is said "padhānaṃ ṭhānaṃ" (the principal station). The meaning is that the prefix "pa-" indicates the sense of "principal" (padhāna).

The word "Ariyo" refers to the Noble, Excellent, Perfectly Enlightened Buddha. In the word "ettha" (herein), the meaning should be understood as "in this Saḷāyatana-vibhaṅga Sutta." A part of the Sutta is used to represent the whole Sutta. In that Sutta:

"There are three foundations of mindfulness which the Noble One, having cultivated, is worthy of instructing a group." Thus have I spoken. In reference to what was this said? Here, monks, a Teacher is compassionate, seeking the welfare of his disciples, and out of compassion, he teaches the Dhamma to the disciples: "This is for your welfare, this is for your happiness." His disciples do not wish to listen, do not lend an ear, do not apply their minds to knowledge, and they proceed by deviating from the Teacher's instruction. Therein, monks, the Tathāgata is not displeased, nor does he experience displeasure; he dwells unattached (anavassuto), mindful and clearly comprehending. This, monks, is the first foundation of mindfulness, which the Noble One, having cultivated, is worthy of instructing a group.

Furthermore, monks, the Teacher... (as above) ... "is for your happiness." Some disciples of that Teacher do not wish to listen... (as above) ... they proceed. Some disciples...
145:
The disciples listen attentively... they do not practice by departing from the Teacher's instruction. In that case, monks, the Tathāgata is neither displeased nor does he experience displeasure. He is neither pleased nor does he experience pleasure. Avoiding both pleasure and displeasure, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. Monks, this is the second [Satipaṭṭhāna].

Furthermore... it is for the sake of happiness (so he teaches). The disciples of that Teacher listen attentively... they do not practice by departing from the Teacher's instruction. In that case, monks, the Tathāgata is pleased and experiences pleasure; he dwells unsullied, mindful, and clearly comprehending. Monks, this is the third [Satipaṭṭhāna] (Majjhima Nikāya, 3, 311).

Thus, being unsullied by aversion and affection, having mindfulness constantly established, and transcending both of these is called Satipaṭṭhāna. It is said that only Buddhas possess mindfulness that is constantly established, not Paccekabuddhas and others.

The syllable 'pa-' indicates the beginning of exertion; considering that the beginning of exertion is 'occurrence' (pavatti), it is said to mean 'because it should be made to occur' (pavattayitabbato). Satipaṭṭhāna is the state that should be established (paṭṭhāpetabba) by means of mindfulness acting as the instrument (karaṇabhūta). Grammarians desire the suffix '-ana' in the sense of the object (kamma) by the rule of 'bahulaṃ'; likewise, they also desire it in the sense of the agent (kattu). Therefore, in the third method, it is said, 'it is paṭṭhāna because it stands firmly' (patiṭṭhātīti paṭṭhānaṃ). In that method, since the syllable 'pa-' indicates exceeding or plunging into, it is said, 'it occurs by entering and plunging into' (okkantitvā pakkhanditvā vattati). Again, wishing to explain the words 'sati' and 'paṭṭhāna' in the sense of state (bhāva), he says 'atha vā' (or else), etc. By explaining the sense of state, it is understood that in the previous sense, the words 'sati' and 'paṭṭhāna' have the sense of the agent.

Specifically, the body (kāya) and feelings (vedanā), which are the group of form, are the causes of gratification (assāda); therefore, for the sake of abandoning that craving, the contemplations of foulness (asubha) and suffering (dukkha) in those coarse and subtle bodies and feelings—which are the bases of craving—are easy for those of craving temperament with dull or sharp wisdom. Thus, those contemplations are called their path of purification (visuddhimagga). Similarly, the contemplations of impermanence (anicca) and non-self (anatta) in the mental factors (citta-dhamma), which are specifically the causes of wrong view, are easy for those of view temperament with dull or sharp wisdom for the sake of abandoning that view in those mental factors, whether they have reached extreme diversity or not. Therefore, those contemplations are called their path of purification. One who has tranquility as their vehicle (samathayānika) and has sharp wisdom, when discerning a coarse object, does not stop at that object but enters into meditative absorption (jhāna), and after emerging from jhāna, discerns feeling. Therefore, it is said, 'because of not stopping at a coarse object' (oḷārikārammaṇe asanthahanato).
146:
For one who has insight as their vehicle (vipassanāyānika), the mind plunges into the subtle mental objects and mental factors (dhamma). Therefore, for those who possess the contemplations of mind and mental factors, it is said that their cause of purification is the contemplation of impermanence and non-self.

In the phrase 'tesaṃ tattha', the word 'tattha' should be connected with the word 'pahānatthaṃ' (for the purpose of abandoning). The five cords of sensual pleasure are obtained specifically in the physical body. Therefore, distinct from feelings and so on, the physical body is the basis for the flood of sensual desire (kāmogha). Lust that finds gratification in existence arises by way of perceiving happiness in existence. Therefore, feeling is the basis for the flood of existence (bhavogha). The dogmatic adherence to the notion of self arises in the mind by way of perceiving it as a compact continuity. Therefore, the mind is the basis for the flood of views (diṭṭhiogha). Intense delusion arises because of the difficulty in penetrating the nature of mental factors (saññā and saṅkhāra) as mere phenomena and because of the lack of analytical discernment of these phenomena. Therefore, the mental factors are the basis for the flood of ignorance (avijjāogha). Thus, only these four were taught for the sake of abandoning the floods of sensual desire, existence, views, and ignorance in the body, feelings, mind, and mental factors respectively. The underlying tendency of aversion (paṭighānusaya) lies latent in painful feeling. Therefore, feelings which consist of the suffering of pain, the suffering of change, and the suffering of formations are specifically the basis for the bodily tie of ill-will (byāpādakāyagantha). The wrong grasp of 'purification through rites' of an eternal self arises by way of perceiving the mind as permanent. Therefore, the mind is the basis for the adherence to rites and rituals (sīlabbataparāmāsa). For one who does not see the true nature of mind and matter as they really are through the discernment of mind and matter, there arises the dogmatic insistence that 'this is the truth' (idaṃsaccābhinivesa), known as the view of existence and non-existence. Therefore, the basis for that bodily tie of dogmatic insistence is the mental factors... By way of gratification in pleasant feelings, without regard for the next world, one produces wrong graspings such as 'there is no result of giving'. Therefore, feeling is the basis for the clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna). Intense delusion arises in the mind accompanied by lust, etc., by way of grasping at the compactness of continuity. Therefore, the mind is the basis for the wrong course of delusion (mohāgati). Fear arises due to the lack of penetration into the nature of phenomena. Therefore, the mental factors are the basis for the wrong course of fear (bhayāgati)... The status as a basis for the remaining factors not yet explained should be connected in the same manner as described.

Because of the words, 'With the arising of nutriment, the body arises; with the arising of contact, feeling arises; with formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, mind-and-matter arises,' the four nutriments—edible food, contact, mental volition, and consciousness—which are the causes of the body and so on, become fully understood through the full understanding of the body and so on. Therefore, it is said, 'for the sake of the full understanding of the four kinds of nutriment'. The 'Pakaraṇanaya' is the method of explanation in the Sinhalese language. They also say it is the method of connection used by Dhamma-preachers in the Netti-peṭaka treatise.

'Saraṇavasena' means by way of the power of 'dhāraṇatā' (bearing/retaining), which performs and remembers objects like the body and phenomena like the wholesome. By this factor, they go to Nirvana; therefore, it is called 'sati' (mindfulness). In this sense, the convergence into Nirvana, which has a single nature, is called 'ekattasamosaraṇa' (convergence into oneness). To show this meaning of convergence into oneness, he said 'yathā hi', etc. Alternatively, it is 'one' (a single way) because it is the cause for entering the single Nirvana, or because of its uniformity of nature.
147:
The nature of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) is called unity (ekatta). The convergence into that nature of satipaṭṭhāna, being of a similar nature, is called convergence into unity (ekattasamosaraṇa). To show the state of being the cause for entering the singular Nibbāna, he said "Yathā hi" and so forth. In this second alternative interpretation, the meaning of refuge (saraṇa) and the meaning of convergence into unity (ekattasamosaraṇa) should be understood as being stated together as the cause for the singular state of satipaṭṭhāna. In the first interpretation, however, they are distinct. Alternatively, when the meaning of refuge (saraṇa) is taken in the sense of going (gamana) and so forth, that very going is called convergence (samosaraṇa). Or, if in the sense of convergence, it is not stated as the meaning of the word 'sati', then the state of bearing or remembering (dhāraṇatā) alone is called 'sati'. Since there is no other meaning, the preceding word 'saraṇa' is the cause for the state of mindfulness, and the subsequent word is the cause for the singular state. Therefore, even in the sense of convergence in Nibbāna, those meanings of 'saraṇa' and 'ekattasamosaraṇa' are indeed the causes for the singular state of satipaṭṭhāna.

"By way of fourteen modes" means by way of the sections such as the section on breathing (ānāpānapabba) taught in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta. Likewise, it should be understood here also as "contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanā) in five ways." In this context, the power of the development of each foundation of mindfulness should be understood as being like goods appearing in their respective places. Indeed, these four foundations of mindfulness are the resorts of monks. For it was said: "O monks, roam in your own resort, the domain of your father (the Buddha)."

He shows the monk by saying "he dwells contemplating the body" and so forth, implying that one becomes a monk through the practice of contemplation of the body and so forth. This is because that practice is constant in such a monk. Therefore, he said: "Because of showing the state of being a monk through practice."

"Should walk evenly" means that having abandoned uneven conduct of the body and so forth, one should walk evenly with the body and so forth. He is peaceful (santa) due to the subsiding of lust and so forth; tamed (danta) due to the restraint of the faculties; assured (niyata) by the certainty of the four paths; and a holy-liver (brahmacārī) because of his habit of noble conduct. By the laying down of the rod of the body and so forth, it is said "having laid down the rod." Such a person is to be known by names such as 'Brahmin' because of having excluded evil, having calmed evil, and having broken the defilements.

## Explanation of the Summary of Contemplation of the Body

"By way of non-mixture" means that although feelings and so forth also depend on and are connected to this body, and thus the occasion for contemplating feelings and so forth in the body might arise, it means without mixing with those feelings and so forth. For the purpose of prohibiting the obsession of taking the whole body as a composite of parts, the tendency to run after conventional names, and the grasping of it as a core essence, he describes the body by way of its major and minor limbs, those limbs by way of hair and so forth, and hair and so forth by way of the primary elements and derived matter...
148:
One who contemplates by distinguishing (the limbs and parts) says, "In the same way, one does not contemplate the body (as something separate from the limbs)" and so forth. Even those who usually speak of a whole (an entity) in the collection of parts of a city such as a palace do not cling to it as a whole entity. Since some people might have the tendency to run after the name (samanya-atidhāvana), thinking "the name 'city' has some independent meaning," the city is given as an illustration for the tendency to run after names such as 'woman' or 'man'.

Whatever object one sees, whether a woman or a man—is it not true that there is no seeing of a woman or a man with the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda)? It is true; there is none. However, by the power of the perception (saññā) that has arisen as "I see a woman, I see a man," it is said "whatever object one sees." Or, in wrong seeing (micchā-dassana), whatever one sees through wrong view is not the thing actually seen; that (woman or man) is not the form-base (rūpāyatana), or the form-base is not that (woman or man). Alternatively, that (woman or man) is not the seen object which is called the collection of primary and derived matter such as hair; or the seen (collection of hair, etc.) is not the aforementioned (woman or man). "Does not see what is seen" means that whatever form-base, or whatever is called the collection of primary and derived matter such as hair, is seen—one does not see that thing as it really is with the eye of wisdom.

"Not contemplating other things" means not contemplating other natures; it means one does not contemplate an aspect other than the aspect of foulness (asubha) and so forth. "The body of earth" (paṭhavīkāya) refers to the earth element with its associated materials such as hair, which he calls "body" (kāya) because it is a collection of physical phenomena. Or, he calls it "body" by taking the characteristic earth element itself, which exists in many variations throughout the whole body and occurs in a continuous sequence, as a collective. The same method applies to other elements (such as the body of water, etc.).

"Internal and external" (ajjhatta-bahiddhā) means that there is no single object of consciousness that combines both internal and external phenomena as a joined object. Or, it means that internal and external phenomena are not this kind of joined object. "Of the defilements in the three planes of existence" means the defilements that have the three planes of existence as their object.

"Universally beneficial" (sabbatthika) means occurring in all instances. It is so called because it is desired at all times, whether the mind is sluggish or restless. Or, it is called "sabbatthika" because all the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) that should be developed when the mind is sluggish or restless are beneficial because of this mindfulness. "Contraction within" means the sinking of the mind within, which is laziness (kosajja).

Considering that the abandonment of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) by way of both (greed and distress) has been stated without distinction, he said "specifically" to show the specific mode of abandonment stated for each one. Or, instead of saying "having removed the hindrances," he said "specifically" and so forth to show the benefit of removing greed (abhijjhā) and distress (domanassa). For the benefit of this (removal of greed and distress) is to show the abandonment of attraction (anurodha) and opposition (virodha), which are the direct opposites of the development of contemplation of the body.
149:
By the term "development of the body" (kāyabhāvanā), the development of mindfulness of the body (kāyānupassanābhāvanā) is intended. By the word "tena" (by that), it refers to the abandonment of attachment (anurodha) and so forth (the power of yoga and the equanimity of yoga occur).

Recollection of the Buddha, loving-kindness, recollection of death, and the meditation on foulness (asubha-bhāvanā) are called universally beneficial meditation subjects (sabbattheka-kammaṭṭhāna). This yogi constantly carries out that meditation subject with mindfulness and clear comprehension; it is called a universally beneficial meditation subject. Because that meditation subject, which is uninterrupted by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension, should be carried out, or because calm (samatha) is taught by way of mindfulness since mindfulness is included in the aggregate of concentration (it is called sabbattheka-kammaṭṭhāna).

## The Explanation of the Summary of Mindfulness of the Body is finished.

## The Explanation of the Summary of Mindfulness of Feelings, etc.

By the phrase beginning with "Kevalaṃ panidha," the limit of what should be known in this summary is shown. The two words "adda" and "adakkhi" have the same meaning. "Sammaddaso" means one who sees correctly and truly.

Regarding the phrase "sukhadukkhatopi ca," because it is taught as the happiness of stability, the happiness of change, and the happiness of knowledge of feelings such as pleasant feeling, and as the suffering of change, the suffering of stability, and the suffering of ignorance, all three feelings should be repeatedly contemplated as happiness and as suffering.

One should contemplate by combining the power of the diversity of objects such as visible forms, the diversity of predominating factors (adhipati) such as desire (chanda), the diversity of conascent factors (sahajāta) such as those associated with wisdom, the diversity of planes (bhūmi) such as the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), the diversity of wholesome (kusala), unwholesome (akusala), their results (vipāka), and functional (kiriya) states, and by the word "ādi," the diversity of prompted (sasaṅkhārika), unprompted (asaṅkhārika), with basis (savatthuka), without basis (avatthuka), and so forth.

"Suññatādhammassa" means by the power of the nature of emptiness (suññata), which is void of a being, as it appears in the section on emptiness (Suññatavāra) in such Pali passages as "states arise, aggregates arise."

By the Pali beginning with "Kāmañcettha," an objection is shown: "Since it was already abandoned earlier (in mindfulness of the body), should its abandonment not be mentioned again?" Or, "At the moment of the path-consciousness, when greed and distress (abhijjhā-domanassa) are abandoned in one state, they are abandoned in all states; therefore, should they not be mentioned separately?"

Of these two objections, the answer to the first is the diversity of persons, and the answer to the second is that it occurs in various thought-moments.

Indeed, greed and distress abandoned in the material body by mundane development are not suppressed in feelings and so forth. Even if they do not arise, because it is not the case that greed and distress do not arise in that material body through the opposing development, their abandonment must certainly be mentioned again.

Or, it should be applied as both answers being appropriate for both objections. In one...
150:
The statement "it is abandoned in the remaining foundations of mindfulness as well" is taught either with reference to the development of the supramundane (magga) foundations of mindfulness, or with reference to the mere non-occurrence in all (body, etc.) through mundane development. Indeed, it is also taught in the four foundations of mindfulness that "the five aggregates are the world."

## The Explanation of the Summary of Mindfulness of Feelings, etc., is finished.

## The Explanation of the Section of the Summary is finished.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of Mindfulness of the Body

By the word "sabbappakāra" (in all ways), the types of contemplation such as internal (ajjhatta) shown in the summary are also included. The fourteen types included therein, the types of the four jhānas having the kasina of colors such as hair as objects taught in the Kāyagatāsati Sutta, and the types such as mundane are also included. In the exposition (niddesa), by explaining one type in detail, it is done merely as an illustration. The inclusion of all types is done because they can also occur partially in external (others/outsiders).

In this phrase "transversely bounded by the skin," is it not the case that hair, body hair, and nails are not bounded by the skin, and the skin itself is not bounded by the skin? Even if that is so, because the parts bounded by the skin are the majority, it is not that the body is not bounded by the skin (it is indeed so); thus it is taught. By the statement "the skin is its limit," the skin which is a part of the body is also included. Hair and so forth, which are connected to that skin and have roots entering that skin, also have the skin as their limit. Therefore, the whole body, which is a collection of the thirty-two parts, is known to be taught as "having the skin as its limit."

It is taught "full of various types." What are those types? To show this meaning—that the impure thing having various types is taught as hair, body hair, and so forth—he said, "These hair and so forth are the aspects (ākāra)." Indeed, "ākāra" and "pakāra" (types/aspects) have the same meaning.

The suffering rooted in sitting without moving that arises for a sitting person, or the time until one stands up, that much time is called one session of sitting (nisajjāvāra). The method by which one becomes skilled in learning (the meditation subject) is called the sevenfold method of "skill in learning" (uggahakosalla), or the knowledge arising from that method.

Because the brain is predominant in the earth element (pathavī-dhātu), he mentioned its inclusion in the Pali text at the end of "feces" (karīsa), which is also predominant in the earth element. Here, however, (the method of recitation in forward and reverse order is mentioned as) "flesh ... kidney ... hair."
151:
In the five-fold group starting with the kidney (vakkapañcaka), after stating the method of recitation in forward order (anuloma) as 'vakkaṃ' (kidney), the method of recitation in backward order (paṭiloma) is stated in connection with the previous groups of five and six. This method of recitation should be understood as being stated by way of showing the beginning and the end among the thirty days of recitation, which will be described later as three periods of five days (15 days) separately, and three periods of five days (15 days) together with the previous groups of five. Also, in the forward and backward recitation methods, the backward recitation is the final one. Alternatively, this should be known as another variety of recitation method. 'Hatthasaṅkhalikā' refers to the sequence of fingers. 'Lakkhaṇapaṭivedhassa' means either the penetration of the characteristic of foulness (asubha) or the penetration of the characteristic of the elements (dhātu).

One's own part is called 'sabhāga' (similar part). Delimitation by one's own part is called 'sabhāgapariccheda'. It means delimitation by the lower, upper, and transverse parts, as well as by one's own constituent parts such as the ends of the hair, etc.

'Dhātuvibhaṅga' refers to the Pukkusāti Sutta. Although the meaning is complete with just the phrase 'sādhāraṇavasena' (by way of commonality), the inclusion of the word 'sabba' (all) is for the purpose of showing the commonality with the serenity (samatha) associated with the fourth jhāna by way of the color kasina.

'Okkamanavissajjana' refers to the path that should be followed and the path that should be avoided. In this context of 'bahiddhā puthuttārammaṇe', it should be understood that hair and so on, which are taken by way of beauty (subha) etc., after abandoning the mindfulness of the body (kāyānupassanā), are also merely external manifold objects. 'Ukkhuṭṭhukkaṭṭhiṭṭhāneyeve uṭṭhahitvā' means that, while performing the act of shouting and scaring in one place as before, jumping down onto all the palm trees in sequence and then getting up, without going to the furthest palm tree or the very first palm tree, but getting up after shouting and scaring only at those respective palm trees where the shouting was done.

'Adhicitta' refers to the mind of serenity and insight (samatha-vipassanā). 'Anuyuttena' means one who is devoted or one who develops [the mind] within oneself. 'Samādhinimitta' is concentration itself, which has the characteristic of marking the object. 'Manasi kātabba' means that which should be performed or produced in the mind. Alternatively, it means the sign of concentration (samādhinimitta), which is the object that is the cause of concentration, should be adverted to. There is a remainder of the sentence: 'ṭhānaṃ atthi' (there is a possibility). It means there is a cause for that mind to lead to laziness. Alternatively, it means that the act of attention leads the mind to laziness; this is the cause for such an occurrence. 'Na ca pabhaṅgū' means that because it has reached the state of being fit for work (kammaniya) in the practice of the meditation subject, it does not have the nature of breaking or perishing.

'Ālimpeti' means to make it burn or to kindle. 'Tañca' refers to that benefit or purpose known as a particular ornament. 'Assa' is for the goldsmith. 'Anubhoti' means to cause to happen well or to accomplish.
152:
It accomplishes. Or, the goldsmith experiences or attains that benefit of the gold.

For the purpose of realizing through direct knowledge (abhiññā) such as the knowledge of supernormal powers (iddhividha); for realizing through direct knowledge such as personally experiencing supernormal powers. One who has personal experience is called a witness (sakkhī). The state of being one who is capable of being a witness is 'sakkhibhabbatā' or 'sakkhibhavanatā'. Or, because he is both a witness and capable, he is called 'sakkhibhabba'. This person is capable of supernormal powers and so forth, and since he is a witness in that regard, he is called 'sakkhibhabba'. His state is 'sakkhibhabbatā', and he attains that state. 'Āyataneti' means when there is a cause such as a preceding cause.

'Sītibhāva' means Nibbāna or the subsiding of the fever of defilements. 'Sampahaṃseti' means he gladdens or invigorates the balanced mind with wisdom that functions in such a balanced way. Or, when the mind without delight does not leap into the meditation, he gladdens or well invigorates it by reflecting on the grounds for urgency (saṃvegavatthu) such as birth (jāti) and so forth.

They are delimited from each other transversely. How? It means 'two hairs do not exist together.' 'Āsaya' means support (nissaya) or condition (paccaya).

The statement 'nails are delimited from each other transversely' is said with reference to their existing separately. To show that very meaning, it was said, 'two nails do not exist together.'

'Sukhuma' (subtle) refers to the subtle inner skin of the mouth and so forth, rather than the coarse skin mentioned before. Or, among the body parts, that which is difficult to distinguish because it is delimited by the skin is called 'sukhuma'. That becomes clear to one who opens the skin and looks in the manner described.

'Tālaguḷapaṭala' is the layer obtained by spreading the pulp of a ripe palm fruit on a palm-leaf mat, drying it, and then peeling it off.

In the phrase 'evaṃ timattāni', it should be understood that the words 'evaṃ' and 'matta' also indicate bones not directly mentioned, such as the ankle bones. 'Kīḷāgoဠက' (Kīḷāgoḷaka) refers to playing balls that are tied with string and made to strike each other in play.

Among those bones, the 'place where the shin bone is established' means the place where it enters and stays within the knee bone. The place on the hip bone where that shin bone is established is like a large Punnaga fruit with its tip cut off. 'Sīsakapaṭṭaka' is a flat piece made of black cloth that is wrapped around.
153:
Rollers pierced by bamboo splints for the entry of thread are called vaṭṭanā; a row of these rollers is called vaṭṭanāvali. Avalechanasatthaka refers to a small knife used for peeling sugarcane.

'Defined by the kidney portion' (vakkabhāgena paricchinnam) means defined by the boundary of the kidney.

'The color of gravel-plaster' (sakkharasudhāvaṇṇa) means having the appearance of plaster made from limestone. Some also recite the text as 'the color of white gravel-plaster' (setasakkharasudhāvaṇṇa), which means it has the color of white gravel and plaster.

A connection should be made between the words 'where food and drink fall and remain' (yattha annapānaṃ nipatitvā tiṭṭhati) and the word sīyanti.

Just as a bundle of lotus stalks cut unevenly leaks water unevenly, so too the body leaks unevenly from the pores of the hair and other openings—upwards, downwards, and across. To show this meaning, the author of the Saṅgaha uses the term 'unevenly cut' (visamacchinna).

Food that is extremely pungent, extremely hot, etc., is called 'incompatible food' (visabhāga-āhāra). This is because it is inconsistent with the elements (dhātus) prevailing during hot weather.

'Or by the power of a single-natured object' (ekattārammaṇabaleneva vā) means by the power of an object that has a single nature, due to the absence of wavering among various objects for one whose mind is well-concentrated and whose hindrances have been suppressed. Indeed, when that single-natured object appears, it produces great delight in itself, an extraordinary pervading rapture (pharaṇāpīti), and joy (somanassa) that experiences the desirable aspect. For without delight and joy, there is no manifestation of the single nature in the meditative mind which possesses rapture and pleasure that have not yet been transcended.

'But generally, by way of commonality' (avisesato pana sādhāraṇavasena) means by way of what is common to both tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), without making a distinction between the repulsive, the elements, or the colors. 'In three ways' (tividhena) refers to the methods such as the 'forward order' (anuloma) which will be mentioned. The phrase 'six months' (cha māse) should be understood as designating six months in the delimitation of recitation by months, even if it is fifteen days short. This is because the mention of 'six months' is to prevent the delimited recitation from exceeding six months, not for the purpose of constant recitation throughout the entire six months. 'Teachers' (ācariyā) refers to the teachers of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā).

'Characteristic' (lakkhaṇaṃ) refers to the characteristic of the elements and the characteristic of repulsiveness. They are called 'unworthy' (ajaññā) because they are not fit for people; it means they are disgusting and unsuitable to be brought among people.

'Bones in order' (paṭipāṭiya aṭṭhīni) means the bones are situated with their ends touching in sequence. In this collection of bones, there is no such thing as a 'self' (atta); this assembly is merely bones, just a heap of bones.
154:
It shows. 'Bound by many joints' (anekasandhiyamito) shows that this heap of bones is guarded and connected by many joints. By the words 'not by anyone' (na kehici), he negates a 'self' (atta) that guards or connects. 'Impelled' (codito) means urged and prompted by old age through the movement towards death.

The great elements (mahābhūta) are delimited by derived matter (upādārūpa) such as 'blue, yellow, good smell, bad smell,' etc. Derived matter is also delimited by the great elements, because that derived matter which depends on the great elements does not exist outside of them. The nature of shadow and sunlight is a state of mutual delimitation, where the presence of sunlight is the cause for the production of shadow. Because the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) is grasped and defined, the immaterial aggregates (arūpino khandhā) occurring at various doors become manifest by the power of the sense bases and doors (āyatanadvāra) such as the eye, which are included within that aggregate of form. Alternatively, it means the sense bases are the doors, thus 'sense-base doors' (āyatanadvāra). Therefore, it means 'by the power of the visible-data base (rūpāyatana), etc.'

'With causes' (sappaccayā) means they arise in dependence on causes due to the state of having causes. Or, a similar or appropriate cause is called sappaccaya; thus, they are 'with causes' because they have such causes.

'This much' (ettako) refers to the portion that has been thoroughly mastered in the manner described. The learning of the meditation subject itself is called the 'link of learning' (uggahasandhi). Because the manifestation of the meditation subject, starting with color, etc., is connected here with attention (manasikāra), it is called a 'link' (sandhi).

'Manifests' (upaṭṭhāti) means it appears by way of color, etc. In the phrase 'endowed with five factors' (pañcaṅgasamannāgate): being endowed with a path for coming and going that is neither too far nor too near is one factor; being uncrowded by people during the day and having little noise or sound of shouting at night is one factor; having little contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things is one factor; the ease with which a monk living in that lodging obtains robes and other requisites is one factor; and the fact that learned elder monks reside in that lodging is one factor (Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.11). 'Endowed with five factors' (pañcaṅgasamannāgate) [in another context] means being endowed with the factors of striving (padhāniyaṅga), namely: freedom from illness, absence of deceit, faith, wisdom, and energy.

'The yield of the fields' (uṭṭhānakadāyaṃ) means the grain that arises from those fields or is to be given from those fields. In this analogy, the task of washing the face should be seen like a field that yields eight kumbhas, and the task of eating and consuming should be seen like a field that yields sixteen kumbhas, in terms of being light or heavy. Because the suffering that arises from those tasks like washing the face, as well as other sufferings, subsides through the attention to the thirty-two parts of the body, he says, 'In this very place, the work of meditation should be performed.' 'By this much' (ettāvatā) means by establishing the attention thirty times a day.
155:
"Sahassuddhāraṃ sādhetvā" means connecting a debt that has increased to a thousand. Indeed, because it is to be extracted, the increase (interest) is called "uddhāra." "Suddhacittena" means with a mind free from defilements such as distraction (one should attend to it). Among hair and so forth, others who are lustful take the skin with a good complexion to be "skin" and are lustful, thinking, "My skin has a color like that of gold," and so on.

The meaning of the sentence "Tesu dve ekamaggaṃ paṭipajjamānā nāma na honti" is that they flee in whatever way they can. In that metaphorical statement, because they are the basis for defilements like lust, the thirty-two parts (koṭṭhāsa) should be understood as being like forest bandits and as bringing about harm.

Because the attention to a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) itself is the basis for attaining special distinction, the development (bhāvanā) is called "kammaṭṭhāna." Therefore, (the author of the Saṅgaha) says, "For one who attends to it, he reaches absorption (appanā)." Alternatively, the object which is the basis for the development known as the practice of meditation reaches absorption by way of arriving at the state of an absorption-object.

By this word "mānajātiko," it shows the state of being devoid of tranquility because of being associated with the ability to leap. Indeed, the mind also, like that (monkey), is increased in various objects and should be shown to be devoid of tranquility.

The statement "The matter of the problem held in the hand is indeed evident" is said with reference to what is stated in the Visuddhimagga. What is stated in that Visuddhimagga is: It is said that Elder Mālaka held the hand of Elder Abhaya, the reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya, and said, "Friend Abhaya, please learn this problem (meaning) first," and then said, "Elder Mālaka is an attainer of the thirty-two first jhanas in the thirty-two parts. If he enters one during the night and one during the day, it is completed in over fifteen days. But if he enters only one daily, it is completed again in over a month."

This matter of the problem held in the hand should be understood as being brought forward as an illustrative example to establish the statement that for one who attends to them individually, one by one, there are thirty-two.

By the words "They stand on the side of the unacquired (anupādinnaka)," it should be understood that for a meditator who is able to take the living body as being on the side of the unacquired—like Elder Mahātissa who lived on Cetiyapabbata, or like the novice attendant of Elder Saṅgharakkhita—when it appears by way of the ten kinds of foulness (asubha), the arrival at access concentration (upacāra) is shown. When hair and so forth are taken as a "being" (satta) in the sense of "It exists in this body"...
156:
"Imasmiṃ kāye" means the manifestation (of mindfulness) in one's own body, which is evident, always present nearby, where the I-conceit is destroyed in the basis of the I-conceit that is free from the grasping of a "being." It is not like that in another's body. Therefore, only the contemplation of disadvantages (ādīnavānupassanā), which is the fault of not reaching absorption, occurs in another's body; with this intention, it is said, "It should be understood that it is the development of insight (vipassanā-bhāvanā) known as the contemplation of foulness (asubhānupassanā)."

Cultivation at the beginning is āsevanā. Increasing is bhāvanā. Doing it again and again is bahulīkamma. This is the distinction between these (three).

"Vatthupariññāyā" means by fully understanding the (material) body which is the basis for greed and distress. "Appitā" means they have gone (gamitā). That going is also the state of being destroyed; thus he says, "vināsitā" (they are destroyed). Because of the meaning that they are placed in non-occurrence, they are also called "appitā." This meaning should be understood as being stated by way of etymological derivation (nirutti). "Vigatantā katā" means they are called vigatantā because there is no longer an end (limit) to be made for these (greed and distress) at this time. The meaning is that they are made such that there is no end to be made. Because the work of development itself is the cause (basis) for attaining special distinction, it is called kammaṭṭhāna. Or, standing in the work of development (undertaking development) is kammaṭṭhāna. And that work of development which is the cause for attaining distinction is indeed contemplation (anupassanā). Therefore, he says, "the kammaṭṭhāna called contemplation." The intention is that it is stated by way of contemplation.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Contemplation of the Body is finished.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Contemplation of Feeling

The feeling of one who clearly comprehends is called sampajānavediyana. By the word "vatthu," the object of feelings such as pleasure is meant. Therefore, because it has an object which is the basis for this feeling, it is called "vatthu-ārammaṇa"; it should be understood as a bahubbīhi compound. By the words "It is merely conventional usage," he shows that the statement "I feel a pleasant feeling" is said merely by way of worldly convention.

"Having associated energy and concentration" means, because of the excessiveness of the energy of endurance, in order to balance that energy and concentration, having associated both together so that they neither exceed nor fall short of each other. "Together with the analytical knowledges" means together with the supramundane analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Or, it should be understood that it is said "together with the analytical knowledges" with reference to the capability in those analytical knowledges even when the mundane ones arise. "Samasīsī" means being one with equal heads in terms of turns (vāra-samasīsī), in the turn immediately following the turn of the knowledge of reviewing...
157:
It means "attained Parinibbāna." By way of brief attention in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, and by way of detailed attention in the Rāhulovāda Sutta, Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, and so on, [He taught the discernment of the four elements].

In the phrase "phassapañcamakeyeva," by the word "eva," He shows the similarity of the grasping knowledge in the three methods mentioned (the method of color, the method of loathsomeness, and the method of emptiness). Because the definition of mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa) is desired, to show the grasping of materiality without remainder, He said, "The basis (vatthu) is the body (karajakāya)," and did not refer to the six bases such as the eye-base. To prove the status of the body as a basis, the sutta passage "This consciousness of mine is supported here, bound up here" (D. i. 235; M. ii. 252) is brought forward.

The manifestation of contact (phassa) and consciousness (viññāṇa) occurs for some individuals; referring to those for whom it does not manifest, He said, "By way of contact... it is not manifest." For those individuals [for whom it manifests] as well as for all other veneyyas (those to be tamed), feeling (vedanā) is manifest; thus He said, "But by way of feeling, it is manifest." "Satadhoutasappi" is ghee that has been melted a hundred times, placed in water, and then taken out.

"Vinivattetvā" means having extracted separately from the collection of the four mental aggregates. In the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta and others, in some places, He first taught the meditation on materiality (rūpakammaṭṭhāna) and later showed the meditation on immateriality (arūpakammaṭṭhāna) by extracting it by way of feeling. In some places, He showed only the meditation on immateriality by extracting it by way of feeling from the mental group, or from the states discerned by full understanding of the known (ñātapariññā), or from the group of mentality-materiality. Even in showing only the meditation on immateriality, in those suttas where full understanding of the known was taught first, the meditation on materiality is included within that full understanding. If full understanding of the known was not taught, it should be understood that He taught the meditation on materiality first, referring to the meditation on materiality which is merely the object of feeling, summarized, and not directly included in the Pali text.

The six types of household-based joy (gehassitasomanassa) taught by the method of "states cognizable by the mind that are desirable and lovely," etc., occur only for a person who repeatedly contemplates the gratification in the five cords of sensual pleasure; thus He said, "The six household-based feelings of joy dependent on the flesh of the five cords of sensual pleasure."

## The Explanation of the Section on Contemplation of Feeling is finished.
158:
## Explanation of the Section on Contemplation of the Mind
Unwholesome states associated with defilements (kilesa), even if not associated with certain defilements, are not pure from other defilements because they are similar in their nature of being defiled by the defilements they are associated with. Therefore, it is said, "They do not resort to the latter term." The separate word "two kinds" is for the purpose of taking the consciousness rooted in delusion (mohamūlacitta) as distinct from the consciousness with lust (sarāgacitta) and the consciousness with hate (sadosacitta). Because it does not reach the stage of insight (vipassanā), it is said, "There is no opportunity here."

## The Explanation of the Section on Contemplation of the Mind is finished.

## The Section on Contemplation of Mental Objects

## A. Explanation of the Section on the Hindrances
When one knows that there is no yoking together (yuganaddha) of dark unwholesome states and bright wholesome states, because there is no [sensual desire], it is said, "By way of frequent awareness."

"The beautiful object (subha)" is sensual desire (kāmacchanda) itself. For it is called "subha" by way of its own mode of grasping; and because it is the cause (nimitta) for another sensual desire arising in that same mode, it is also called "nimitta." Attention that is not a means to the desired welfare and happiness is called unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra). It occurs in both kinds of beautiful signs: in the sensual desire to be produced and in the beautiful sign which is the object.

"The unbeautiful object (asubha)" is the meditation on foulness (asubhajjhāna) itself. That meditation on foulness should be understood as occurring in the ten foul objects and in the parts of the body such as hair. The perception in hair, etc., is called "perception of foulness" (asubhasaññā) in the Girimānanda Sutta. Here, the showing of the four kinds of unwise attention and wise attention is done for the purpose of showing them without remainder. Among those four, attention as "beautiful" or "unbeautiful" in an unbeautiful object is intended here; or, because they are conducive to that, other types of attention are also intended.

It is said that one who is moderate in eating, because of the absence of being overwhelmed by sloth and torpor (thīnamiddha), abandons sensual lust (kāmarāga) which finds no entry. Also the perception of repulsiveness in food (āhārepaṭikūlasaññā) dependent on food, and the contemplation of the foulness, etc., of the change of that food and of the body which is its support, and the contemplation of the foulness, etc., of that food which is the strong support (upanissaya) for sensual lust, and the contemplation of the body's persistence due to food, etc...
159:
A person who knows the measure in food develops the knowledge of the foulness (asubha) of the stomach or the whole body. Because of such development, sensual desire (kāmacchanda) is indeed abandoned for that person. With the intention that, according to the Abhidhamma method, all greed is the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa), it is said, "by the path of Arahantship."

Regarding specified (odissaka), unspecified (anodissaka), and directional pervasion (disāpharaṇa) of loving-kindness (mettā): Pervading by way of those who should be respected, very dear friends, and neutral persons is called specified loving-kindness. Pervading by breaking down boundaries is called unspecified loving-kindness. Pervading towards a single direction is called directional loving-kindness; this should be understood in the learning of the meditation on loving-kindness. Alternatively, pervading by specifying monasteries, roads, villages, etc., is called specified directional pervasion. Pervading by way of directions such as the East, without referring to monasteries and so on, is called unspecified directional pervasion. With reference to these two types of learning, it is said, "specified, unspecified, and directional pervasion."

Learning (uggaha) should be understood as lasting until access concentration (upacāra). The repeated cultivation of the meditation that has been learned is called development (bhāvanā).

In that development, there are five types by way of the terms: all beings (satta), all breathing things (pāṇa), all creatures (bhūta), all persons (puggala), and all those embodied (attabhāvapariyāpanna). Since each of these is practiced in four ways—"May they be free from enmity, free from ill-will, free from suffering, and may they maintain themselves in happiness"—unspecified pervasion (anodhiso-pharaṇa) of loving-kindness has 20 modes. Specified pervasion (odhiso-pharaṇa) of loving-kindness, occurring by way of the seven bases—"all women, men, noble ones, non-noble ones, deities, humans, and those in states of deprivation (vinipātika)"—has 7 or 28 modes. Directional pervasion (disāpharaṇa) of loving-kindness, occurring by way of the ten directions, has 10 modes. Alternatively, in each direction, by combining beings etc., women etc., and freedom from enmity etc., the 528 modes of unspecified and specified pervasion of loving-kindness should be understood.

Kāyavināmanā means the bending or moving of the body in various ways.

Atibhojane nimittaggāha means taking up the cause of sloth and torpor (thīna-middha) in overeating. It means perceiving the cause and non-cause of sloth and torpor as, "If I eat this much food, it becomes a cause for sloth and torpor; if I eat this much, it does not." Since the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) depend on energy, it is said, "also by suitable talk depending on the ascetic practices."

Remorse (kukkucca) also occurs by way of regretting bad deeds committed and good deeds omitted. Since it has the same characteristic as restlessness (uddhacca), being of an unpeaceful nature, the lack of peace in the mind is called "restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca) alone."

For a person of great learning (bahussuta), who reflects on the meanings and so on according to the texts and their significance, distraction of mind (uddhacca) does not occur. Because of practicing according to the rules and because of appropriate remedial action, regret (kukkucca) over what was done or not done also does not occur. Therefore, it is said, "By great learning (bāhusacca) also, restlessness and remorse are abandoned." Associating with elders brings about the habit of one with mature virtue; thus, by making the mind peaceful, it abandons restlessness and remorse.
160:
The state of being one who abandons restlessness and remorse has been stated. However, regardless of seniority in years (vassa), those experts in the Vinaya (vinayadhara) who dispel remorse should be regarded as noble friends (kalyāṇamitta).

It stands in these (previous states of doubt); therefore, it is called a ground (ṭhānīya). Because it is a ground for doubt, it is called a ground for doubt (vicikicchā-ṭhānīya). Or, because they should be stood upon, they are called grounds; doubt stands in these things, thus they are grounds for doubt.

Indeed, by great learning and frequent questioning, doubt regarding the eight bases can be abandoned. Nevertheless, considering that the remaining doubts are rooted in doubt regarding the Triple Gem, it is said, "referring to the three jewels (Triple Gem)." Being knowledgeable of the nature of the Vinaya can perform the abandoning of the doubt stated as "he doubts concerning the training (sikkhā)." Therefore, it is said, "also for one who has mastery through practice in the Vinaya." "For one who has much determination (adhimokkha) known as convincing faith" means one who has an abundance of superior decision through determination known as faith that enters into the qualities of the Triple Gem. It should be understood that deciding (adhimuccana) is the same as producing determination (adhimokkha). Alternatively, the inclination through faith is called adhimutti.

## The Explanation of the Section on Hindrances is finished.

## B. Commentary on the Section on the Factors of Enlightenment

Considering that the meaning of the Pali text showing the aggregates (khandha) etc., is the meaning of the aggregates etc., it is said, "the abundance of questioning based on the meaning of the aggregates... p... insight (vipassanā)."
