## 10. Dasakaniddesa
## Paṭhamabalaniddesavaṇṇanā
A cause that is not evident is called "aṭṭhāna" (impossible/non-cause), or it is called "aṭṭhāna" because there is no cause. This method is the same for the term "anavakāsa" (no opportunity). The statement "netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati" (this case does not exist) is merely a conclusion of the aforementioned meaning. Perceiving pleasure (sukha) in conditioned things (saṅkhāra) that are not pleasure is only due to the perversion of view (diṭṭhi-vipallāsa). Here, desiring to show the cause of approaching it as pleasure, he spoke of the primary view as "ekanta... by the power of the view of self (attadiṭṭhi)." Making known words that are conducive to a schism in the Saṅgha is called "anussāvana"; or, informing by means of words conducive to a schism in the Saṅgha is "anussāvana."

Even if the gender (linga - female or male) changes, it is only that same continuity of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) produced by a single kamma, and not another; to show this, he said "api parivattalingaṃ." The phrase "ayaṃ pañho" (this is a question) is a statement arising from the desire to know.

The fourfold battle (saṅgāmacatukka) should be applied by way of the enemy soldier. In all cases, the initial intention to kill (abhisandhicitta) is not the criterion for whether it is an ānantariya kamma or not; only the murderous consciousness (vadhakacitta) and the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) which is its object are the criteria for being an ānantariya kamma or not. That gift is given only to a worldling (puthujjana). Why? Just as the murderous consciousness, though having a present object, occurs by taking the interruption of the life-faculty as its object, the volition of generosity (cāga-cetanā) does not occur in that way. That volition of generosity is merely the act of relinquishing, taking the object to be relinquished as its focus; relinquishing it is making it the property of another. Therefore, it is given only to the person for whom it was made their own property.

The statement "saṇṭha... he is released only at the destruction of the aeon (kappa)" does not agree with the Kappa Commentary. In that commentary, it is said: "This sutta 'āpāyiko' is spoken with reference to the life-span aeon (āykappa) where that person, having divided one aeon into eighty parts, would remain for just one part of that time." In the phrase "only at the destruction of the aeon," if the meaning is "only at the destruction of the life-span aeon," there is no contradiction. Here, the word "saṇṭhahante" (remaining/persisting) is spoken by way of imagining what is not there, like saying "it will be destroyed tomorrow." He is cooked in hell for only one day; after that, since there is no aeon, there is also no life-span aeon. Thus, the connection of meaning should be understood as non-contradictory.

"Pakatatta" means a monk who has not been expelled (from the Saṅgha). "Samānasaṃvāsaka" means a monk who has not committed a Pārājika offense.
208:
The meaning is: what dhamma makes that person, who is called 'fixed' (niyata), fixed? The state of being a fixed person as questioned does not exist by its own nature, like the states of fixed wrongness (micchatta-niyata) or fixed rightness (sammatta-niyata). Rejecting the cause of being fixed as questioned, [the teacher] said, 'By the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha...' and so on, to show the intended cause by which one is called 'fixed' or 'one with seven lives at most' (sattakkhattuparama) due to the insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) for the three higher paths.

Just as a name is given to a newborn boy, for a Sotāpanna born into the Noble birth (ariya-jāti), terms like 'niyata' and 'sattakkhattuparama' are merely names. It means it is a name distinguished by being fixed or not fixed.

If a prior cause (pubba-hetu) were the fixing factor, the Sotāpanna would be a fixed person. Because of the state of being a decisive support (upanissaya) for the three higher paths from the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), there is the function of the prior cause. However, before that Path of Stream-entry, there is no function of a prior cause, and thus it would lead to the fault that there is no decisive support for the Path of Stream-entry. If there were a prior cause as a decisive support for that Path of Stream-entry as well, and if that were the fixing factor, one would be fixed even before the arising of the Path of Stream-entry. That is undesirable. Therefore, regarding the meaning that it would lead to being without cause through the prior cause of this Path of Stream-entry, it was said: 'Thus, this person reaches an arising that is without cause and without condition.'

The path obtained is the Path of Stream-entry. When there is the fixing of 'seven lives at most' and so on because of that Path of Stream-entry, the defilements (kilesa) which are the root of suffering that would occur beyond the seventh birth are exhausted by that very path. Therefore, it means the three higher paths are without further function (needless). If the three higher paths were to fix the 'seven lives at most' and so on, then there would be no other Sotāpanna besides that, leading to the meaning that the Path of Stream-entry is without function or purpose. Alternatively, the function of seeing is the abandoning of self-identity view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) and so on. Due to the abandoning of those, the state of 'seven lives at most' and so on should occur. And that occurs only through the higher paths. Therefore, because of the continuous occurrence of results beyond the seventh birth, if there is insight that emerges from the formations (saṅkhāra) without that Path of Stream-entry, the abandoning of self-identity view and so on would occur without that Path of Stream-entry. Therefore, it was said: 'The defilements should be exhausted without having arisen through the first path.' The phrase 'no one else fixes it' means there is no other fixing factor besides insight (vipassanā), which is the cause for giving the name. The statement that 'only insight fixes it' is also said with reference only to the cause for giving the name. Therefore, it was said: 'Thus, it is merely a name given by the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha.'

There is the meaning 'they do not arise'. The Blessed One, standing in this world-system and saying, 'I have no teacher, no one like me exists,' and so on...
209:
"Friend Sāriputta, if I were asked whether there are other ascetics or brahmins who realize the Four Noble Truths equally with the Blessed One at this time, I would say, 'No, venerable sir.'" Having said this, to show the reason for being able to answer thus, the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, showed this sutta: "It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Worthy Ones, Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas, should arise simultaneously in a single world-system." This means that, excluding this world-system which is the Buddha-field (buddha-khetta), another Buddha cannot arise elsewhere [within it].

The training rules (sikkhāpada) taught with the words "Whichever monk..." and so on are called the Mātikā. When that Mātikā disappears, the Dispensation (Sāsana) stands in the Pātimokkha, known as the recitation of the introduction (nidānuddesa), and in the acts of novice ordination (pabbajjā) and higher ordination (upasampadā). Alternatively, novice ordination and higher ordination are included within the Pātimokkha; since there can be no Pātimokkha without both of them, it is said that the Dispensation stands in the Pātimokkha and in those [ordinations]. "Receded" (osakkita) means taking the two—the final penetration of the Four Noble Truths and the final breaking of virtue—together, after which the Dispensation is said to be destroyed. "Tā" refers to the rays of light. "Kāruñña" refers to the pitiable state of lamentation.

"Because there is no wonder" means because of the fault of lacking the quality of being a wonder if two Buddhas were to arise. "So that there is no dispute" means two Buddhas do not arise simultaneously in order to prevent disputes.

Because it bears only one Buddha, it is called "Eka-buddha-dhāraṇီ" (the one-Buddha-bearer). By this, it is shown that the qualities of the Buddhas are of such a nature that this world-system is unable to bear the qualities of a second Buddha. For it is not possible to bear the special nature of dhammas produced by special causes [perfections]. Because it can move evenly on the surface of the water, it is called "Samupādikā", meaning one who moves evenly on the water. "Of both" means both Buddhas, or the weight of the bodies of both Buddhas. "Covering" means making it pleasing. "With just one meal" means one would die after swallowing just one morsel of food.

"By the excessive weight of the Dhamma" means: since the earth stands because of the Dhamma, why does it shake because of that very Dhamma? Again, the Elder Nāgasena said: "In the world, a treasure that supports a household and is highly desired by people is seen to be an excessive weight that causes a cart to break because of its own heavy nature. Similarly, although the Dhamma is highly desired by the wise because it supports those possessed of it with special benefits and happiness, it becomes an excessive weight and the cause of the earth shaking because of its heavy nature due to its profound and immeasurable state."

Venerable Nāgasena spoke the words "a cart" and so on. It means it is brought in and carried from another cart. "Natural" means it is not a nature caused by shouting (not an artificial nature). Because the qualities of a Buddha arise due to many causes of perfections, it is said that "only one Buddha arises in the world." Just as things like the earth are great and exist as only one in their own sphere, similarly, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha is great and is the only one in His own sphere. What is the sphere of that Blessed One? Whatever knowable things (ñeyya-dhamma) exist to whatever extent, that is the sphere of the Buddha. Thus, it is said that the Blessed One, whose sphere is infinite like the sky, is the only one.
210:
To show the meaning that the wise consider [the Dhamma] to be very heavy because of its profound and incomparable nature, and its weightiness, which causes the earth to shake, the Elder Nāgasena said: "Great King, in this world, there are two carts..." and so on. "Ekassa" means from one cart, or taking the treasure of one cart from that cart. "Osāritaṃ" means brought in, conveyed, or spoken.

"Sabhāvapakatikā" means not having a nature produced by proclamation (or not having an artificial nature). "Kāraṇamahantattā" means that the qualities of the Buddha arise because of the greatness of the causes, namely the perfections (pāramīs). Just as the earth and other great elements are unique each in their own domain, so too the Sammāsambuddha is unique in His own domain. What is the domain of that Blessed One? As far as the extent of the knowable (ñeyya) reaches, so far is His domain. Thus, the Blessed One, who has an infinite domain like the sky, is unique; by saying this, the Elder Nāgasena shows that there is no second Buddha even in other world systems.

In the preliminary stage before the action, the "endowment of striving" (āyūhana-samangitā) should be understood through the power of exertion, and the "endowment of volition" (cetanā-samangitā) through the power of the decisive volition. Or, it should be understood in connection with the moment of the mental continuum performing the action. The word "vipākārahaṃ" (worthy of result) is spoken with reference to the nature of ripening in the second life and so forth. "Calati" means it changes (parivattati). A hunter who habitually travels with dogs is called "sunakhavājika".

## The Explanation of the First Description of Powers (Pathama-bala-niddesa) is finished.

## The Explanation of the Second Description of Powers (Dutiya-bala-niddesa)

To show that there is no other achievement of destination (gati-sampatti) apart from the state of existence reached, he said: "The destination is achieved" (sampannā gati). The time of good kings such as Mahāsudassana, and the time of good humans such as the first inhabitants of the world-cycle, is called achievement of time (kāla-sampatti).

Regarding the statement "Indeed, there is only an opportunity for the wholesome," if some enemy should oppress a person established in the achievement of effort (payoga-sampatti) such as good bodily conduct, such oppression occurs only because of the distorted view born of causes like the enemy's envy. That achievement of effort is, by its nature, only a cause for a pleasant result and not a cause for a painful result; this is the intended meaning. Just as a monkey does not know how to untie and eat a bundle of rice at the place where it is tied, but breaks and destroys it anywhere, so too one who is unskilled in means destroys wealth. By the words "discarding in a cemetery" and so on, he shows that just as a corpse killed and discarded cannot rise again, there is no rising up from the states of deprivation (apāya).
211:
"Paccari" is also the name of a raft; because it was compiled on that raft, this commentary is called "Mahāpaccari". Why is it said that "death in the water and death on land are the same," when Sakka, the King of Devas, had said, "I will protect the Elder Samuddarakkhita"? It is true that he said so, but the Elders said this to clearly show the nature of life as being quickly changeable (easily subject to death). The meaning is: "Because it is quickly changeable, I will not go for the sake of life." Alternatively, "in the water" refers to Nagadīpa, and "on land" refers to Jambudīpa.

"The Elder does not give" means he did not give because he thought, "How does this lay devotee know me? Could someone have told him something?" That is why he said, "We also do not know." "Of another monk" should be connected as: "Taking the bowl of another monk... he placed it in the hand of the Elder." "Anāyatanē" means in a place of destruction that is without cause or improper. The meaning is: "You should protect yourself; as for us, we are old and infirm, what could we do even if we protected ourselves? Being old and infirm, we will not be able to protect ourselves." Or, because the Elder was an Anāgāmi (Non-returner), he knew what he should say and gave the exhortation.

"Sammāpayogassa gatamaggo" means the cause for knowing that practice, because it was accomplished through right effort (sammā-payoga).

It means that he will state an unreal simile by making use of a real meaning. "Manussā" (Humans) refers to people appointed to jobs such as treasurers; they were unable to receive it because of its greatness.

## The Explanation of the Second Description of Powers (Dutiya-bala-niddesa) is finished.

## The Explanation of the Third Description of Powers (Tatiya-bala-niddesa)

"Añcitā" means gone or arisen. "Peccā" means again, or after death. "Ussannattā" is said to be due to an excess of thought (vitakka) or due to an abundance of courage and so on. "Dibbanti" means they sport and play.

There are eight Great Hells: Sañjီva, Kālasutta, Saṅghāta, Roruva, Mahāroruva, Tapana, Mahātapana, and Avīci. In each one, there are four gates, and at each gate, there are four Ussada hells such as the Hell of Filth (Gūtha-niraya); thus, they describe sixteen Ussada hells.
212:
The chief celestial king, like Sakka, Suyama, and others, as well as the attendant who performs the second and subsequent ranks of office, like Pajāpati, Varuṇa, Īsāna, and others, will arise.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Third Power is finished.

## The Description of the Fourth Power
'Kappa' means having a twofold end (having two different ends). In this description of the fourth power, the diversity of the aggregates (khandha) and other elements should be understood through the power of the diversity of elements such as seeds and so forth.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Fourth Power is finished.

## The Description of the Fifth Power
'Ajjhāsayadhātu' (the element of disposition) refers to the nature of disposition (ajjhāsaya). Just as the elemental nature of things like excrement (gūtha) and so forth associates only with excrement and so forth, so too the nature of the disposition of persons means that those who are immoral (dussīla) and so forth associate only with those who are immoral and so forth. The monks also said to one another, "Friends, these people, saying 'Enjoy according to your own nature,' know our similarity or dissimilarity, distinguish between those of low disposition and those of noble disposition, and then, wishing to see the application of that disposition, they lead us into actions connected with that element." Thus, because of the discernment of the element of disposition only by the power of similarity, it is meant that it is determined according to the similarity of the element of disposition.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Fifth Power is finished.

## The Description of the Sixth Power
In this (Ñāṇavibhaṅga Pāḷi), 'carita' (conduct) refers to misconduct and good conduct. Because those beings have the eye of wisdom with little dust (of lust, hatred, and delusion), the meaning is clarified as 'apparajakkha' (those with little dust in their eyes). The meaning of the word can also be 'apparajakkha' because there is little dust in the eye of wisdom of those beings. In this (description of the sixth power), by knowing the disposition and so forth...
213:
It should be understood that it clarifies the knowledge of those faculties, whether superior or inferior, by which beings have good or bad dispositions and so forth. By doing so, the distinctness and uniqueness of the 'Knowledge of the Higher and Lower Faculties' (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa) and the 'Knowledge of Dispositions and Latent Tendencies' (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa) are established, as well as the distinctness of the 'Knowledge of the Higher and Lower Faculties' and the 'Knowledge of Diverse Inclinations' (nānādhimuttika-ñāṇa) as powers (bala).

'Yadariyā' means those who are Noble Ones (ariya). 'Āvasiṃsu' means they lived depending on [certain abodes]. Who are those Noble Ones? "Monks, in this Dispensation, a monk is one who has abandoned five factors, is endowed with six factors, has a single guard, has four supports, has discarded individual truths, has well-relinquished searches, has pure thoughts, has calmed bodily formations, has a well-liberated mind, and has well-liberated wisdom." Thus it was spoken. Among those ten, the abandoning of the five factors, the discarding of individual truths, and the well-relinquishing of searches, as well as the 'dispelling' among the four supports spoken of as "reflecting with wisdom, he uses some, endures some, avoids some, and dispels some," are only the functions of the Path (magga); the remaining abodes of the Noble Ones (ariyāvāsa) are also accomplished only by the Path. Therefore, it was said, "This sutta... shows."

Between the latent tendency in the object and the latent tendency in the continuity, one lies latent in a pleasant object (iṭṭhārammaṇa) by way of the latent tendency in the object. By the phrase 'āciṇṇasamāciṇṇā,' it shows the state of lying latent by way of being established as if wrapped around from all sides. Because existence (bhava) is also an object of craving (vatthukāma), or because it is similar by the power of lust (rāga), it was said, "The latent tendency of lust for existence... is included."

"Those with noble inclinations (adhimutti) are those with sharp faculties; the others are those with dull faculties." Thus, the taking of 'inclination' is only for the purpose of showing the distinction of the faculties. Therefore, it was said, "For the purpose of showing the state of sharp faculties and dull faculties."

In the phrase 'by the power of the order of abandonment,' the order of abandonment should be understood as the order of the things to be abandoned and the person who abandons. Alternatively, whichever dhamma is to be abandoned, that dhamma is spoken of first by that abandonment; after that, the dhamma not to be abandoned is spoken of. This is the order of abandonment.

The faculties that are the strong dependence (upanissaya) for the Path are called 'upanissaya-indriya.'

Because of the lack of desire for peace (Nibbāna), they have entered the 'state of lack of desire' (acchandikaṭṭhāna). When a certain life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is occurring, the supramundane (lokuttara) arises in that continuity; that life-continuum is the basis for that supramundane [mind].

## The Explanation of the Description of the Sixth Power is finished.
214:
## Commentary on the Exposition of the Seventh Power

'Niddāyitvā' means that while attending to the meditation subject, one falls asleep, and upon waking, thinks, 'I have properly entered the meditative attainment.' The mental continuum that is particularly purified from hindrances and so forth is called the 'casket of the mind' (cittamañjūsā); alternatively, it refers to concentration or the meditation subject itself. 'Cittaṃ ṭhapetuṃ' means to restrain the mind of meditative attainment. The absence of perception and feeling is called 'liberation by departure' (apagamavimokkha).

The rushing of perception and attention towards sense desires and so forth, or towards the second jhāna and so forth, has been shown as 'states partaking in decline' (hānabhāgiya-dhamma) and 'states partaking in distinction' (visesabhāgiya-dhamma). However, the nature of the jhānas as being subject to decline or distinction due to those perceptions and attentions is expressed by the word 'dhamma'. The purity that comes from thorough mastery is called 'paguṇavodāna'. That same 'paguṇavodāna' is called 'emergence' (vuṭṭhāna) because it is the cause for attaining the second jhāna and so forth after emerging from the first jhāna and so forth. Because it is not included in the Vuṭṭhāna Pali passage which states, 'Purity is also emergence; emergence from various concentrations is also emergence,' the emergence from the attainment of cessation is called 'emergence not explicitly mentioned in the Pali' (pāḷimuttakavuṭṭhāna). If some should say, 'There is no Pali evidence for the statement that one emerges from the attainment of cessation by means of the attainment of fruition,' they should be refuted by this Paṭṭhāna Pali: 'For one emerging from cessation, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is a condition for the attainment of fruition by way of proximity-condition.'

## The Commentary on the Exposition of the Seventh Power is finished.

## Commentary on the Exposition of the Tenth Power

Concentration that is the means of the mind's liberation from lust and so forth is called 'liberation of mind' (cetovimutti). Wisdom itself is the means of liberation and is called 'liberation by wisdom' (paññāvimutti). 'Kammantaravipākantarameva' means only the specific result of a specific kamma. Taking volition and the states associated with volition, which are the practices leading to destinations such as hell or to Nibbāna, as 'kamma', it is called 'the delimitation of kamma' (kammapariccheda). It is not capable of reaching absorption (appanā) like the eighth and ninth power-knowledges, nor is it capable of creating various psychic powers like the knowledge of the modes of psychic power (iddhividha-ñāṇa) which is similar to those power-knowledges. By this, its similarity to the ten power-knowledges is denied; or rather, it is not capable of reaching absorption or creating [powers] like the knowledges of jhāna and so forth. Even though the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa) that reflects on jhāna and so forth is the seventh power, and its nature of being accompanied by initial and sustained thought (savitakka-savicāra) is taught...
215:
Since there is no reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā) apart from jhāna and so forth, it should be understood that the knowledge occurring together with jhāna and so forth is included within that (the seventh power, which is the reviewing knowledge of jhāna, etc.), and thus it is so stated.

Alternatively, in another way, to show that the Omniscient Knowledge cannot perform all the functions of the power-knowledges just as it does not perform the functions of jhāna and so forth, it is said: "That Omniscient Knowledge is not capable of becoming jhāna to reach absorption, nor of becoming psychic power to create [miracles]." It should be noted that this is not said because some power-knowledges have the nature of jhāna or psychic power.

## The Commentary on the Exposition of the Tenth Power is finished.

## The Commentary on the Analysis of Knowledge (Ñāṇavibhaṅga) is finished.
216:
## 17. Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga
## 1. Ekakamātikādivaṇṇanā
Although it is said, "Thirty-three triads" (tettimsati tikā), those triads are actually thirty-five. Similarly, although it is said, "Eight nonads starting with male stains" (purisamalādayo aṭṭha navakā), those nonads are nine, starting with the bases of resentment (āghātavatthu). The eighteen-folds (aṭṭhārasaka) mentioned in the Pali starting with "Two eighteen-folds" are made into three thirty-sixes (six eighteen-folds) by the method starting with "Thus the past thirty-six," and so it is said, "Six eighteen-folds." As for the sixty-two types of wrong views, since they are mentioned in other texts, they are laid down here as the Matika but should be understood as not being included (in the Niddesa).

## The explanation of the Ekakamātikā and so forth is finished.

## 1. Ekakaniddesavaṇṇanā
843-844. Regarding "Atthi paṭiccaṃ nāma": just as in the Pali passages like "Cakkhuñca paṭicca" (dependent on the eye), it is called "paṭicca" (dependent) by way of being a condition such as support (nissaya); it is not called so here in that way. This is because for castes (jāti) such as Khattiya, which do not exist in the ultimate sense, there is no state of being a condition such as support.

When those aggregates (khandhas) exist, the conventional designation (sammuti) of Khattiya and so forth occurs; the very continuity of those aggregates is the manifestation of the existence of the Khattiya caste and so forth. This meaning is expressed here by the word "paṭicca." "Ekissā seṇiyā" means of a single group/guild that is not mixed with others.

In activities such as answering questions, placing (something) in front (prioritizing) is called "purekkhāra." "Nikkheparāsi" means a hoard of stored wealth. "Patthaṭākittino" means having widespread fame. "Rattaññumado" is said to be the pride based on being one who knows the past. It is the intoxication of knowing what should be known by one of many nights (seniority), whether by birth or by ordination; or it is the intoxication of knowing the nights themselves. "Upaṭṭhāpakamāno" is the pride based on giving orders. For the ability to manage, which is the giving of orders, is called "yasa" (fame/glory) here. Pride based on a well-proportioned body is called "pariṇāhamado." Intoxication due to the perfection of the limbs of the body is called "pāripūrimado."

845. It is called "avatthukaṃ" (without basis) because it can be spoken of even without a basis (such as birth, etc., as a cause for pride), not because of the total absence of a basis.

846. The mind's release from mindfulness, or its rushing into bodily misconduct and so forth, is called "cittassa vossajjanaṃ" (vossagga). "Paṭiṭṭhābhāvo" means the lack of stability (lack of exertion) in performing wholesome deeds.
217:
Anuṭṭhāna means the lack of exertion or activity. There are limitless methods (pariyāya) of the meaning of negligence (pamāda), such as letting the mind loose in bodily misconduct, in killing, in wrong view, in anger, and in malice. The verbal methods (byañjana-pariyāya) such as vossagga (relinquishment) and nissagga (abandonment), which express the meaning of that negligence, are also limitless. Therefore, to summarize all those methods, because it is impossible to state every method, the term "of such a nature" was used to indicate this manner, and it was said "because it is limitless." By the word vissaṭṭhākāra (scattered state), the four aggregates which are the opposite of mindfulness (sati) are shown.

Stiffness of mind (thaddhatā) is said to be the mind itself arising in such a stiff manner; or it should be understood as a specific type of conceit (māna). Because one must pay respect when approaching elders, [one who is stiff with conceit] wanders only around the periphery [to avoid paying respect].

When told, "You have committed an offense," replying, "Friend, you are the one who committed it," and so on, by way of throwing back the fault mentioned by that person onto him, is called "retorting" (paṭippharaṇa). In this context, retorting in this way: "If even that poor person or that unskilled person can do this deed, why should I not be able to do it?" is appropriate. Doing more than what another has done is karanuttariya. This competitive action to surpass others is an unwholesome side, and thus it means sārambha (presumption/aggressive rivalry).

One is called aticchiccho because one desires beyond (aticca) what one has received. Regarding the state of such a person, which should be called aticchicchatā, the syllable "cci" is dropped and it is spoken as "aticchatā." That same aticchatā is also called "atricchatā." In that word atricchatā as well, the formation of the word should be understood according to the rules of grammar (neruttika). Alternatively, desiring this and that beyond what has already been received is atricchatā. In that same atricchatā, the letter "ra" is changed to "ta" and it is called "aticchatā."

Atricchan means aticchan (one who desires excessively) or one who desires this or that object. By what does one desire? One desires through excessive greed (atilobha), through the intoxication of excessive greed known as excessive greed and wrong [desire]. One's own benefit is called atta. That benefit tends to decrease and perish. Alternatively, the benefit that is taken or the benefit that is attained is called atta. That benefit decays and is lost. It is like the king who, by longing for a Candakinnarī (a mythical half-human half-bird), was separated from and lost Queen Asitābhū.

Icchāhatassa means to one who is afflicted by desire or one who is stamped [by it].

Atihīḷayāno means despising or regarding as inferior. Malaka refers to a district of that name or an open space. Kodaṇḍakena means with a loathsome short stick or a short stick. They also say it means with a "thong" (gaddula). Ruhiramakkhitaṅgo means having a body smeared with blood.
218:
(50) Even while knowing, one has the desire to be praised as if being urged excessively. "Requisite" (paccaya) means requisites such as fuel, etc.

(51) Those who deceive with counterfeits are gaṇṭhika (swindlers). Or they are those who have become "knots" through bad conduct. Those called gaṇṭhikaputtā are the sons of swindlers, and they themselves are indeed swindlers. Therefore, the co-residents (disciples) of such a teacher, due to their deceptive nature, say, "The Elder... is walking in the cloister," [when he is not].

"It is allowable, Bhante" is also one variety [of deception]; it means one hints at one's own attainment of meditative absorptions (samāpatti) with the intention that "only one who has attained [absorptions] can know this." The Pañcattaya Sutta is the second sutta in the Uparipaṇṇāsa [of the Majjhima Nikāya]. Because of the depth of that sutta, it is said, "to one who is looking at and contemplating the Pañcattaya Sutta."

(52) Singa means singāra (passion/lust). Because that passion pierces wholesome states, because it is frequently indulged, it is like a horn (visāṇa) that is well-fixed and well-embedded on the head; and because of its firmness, it is like a horn, thus it is called singa. In terms of meaning, it is passion (rāga).

(753) The word tintiṇa should be seen in the sense of moistening. "Reviling" (khīyana) refers to the greed by which one reviles another who says "This is mine." Reviling is also said to be "quarreling" (bhaṇḍana). Alternatively, tintiṇa means extreme greed (loluppa). For this word saññā is a synonym for extreme greed.

(754) By the words "even if it is the size of a thigh," it shows that it does not rot because of its great and solid nature. Alternatively, by the words "the adornment of this foul body or of external requisites," etc., it shows the qualifiers such as "adornment of robes" (cīvara-maṇډanā). Adornment with a robe or the adornment of a robe is called cīvara-maṇډanā. In this same way, "adornment of the bowl" (patta-maṇډanā) and "adornment of the dwelling" (senāsana-maṇډanā) should be understood. Filling in deficient places and making the skin and complexion beautiful should be applied as appropriate to the robes, etc., and to the body. "He becomes like a child born on that day" means he cannot give up the frivolity of a child.

(755) Similar and suitable attendance is called sabhāga (compatible). An incompatible portion is asabhāga; it is the stiffness of conceit or opposition. Conduct towards one's mother and others in that [incompatible] way is asabhāgavuttitā (incompatible conduct). This is a name for unwholesome states dominated by conceit.
219: Paritassitā means agitation due to laziness, or the craving of a lazy person for various objects. The lack of expansion or the shrinking of the body when performing wholesome deeds is natural laziness. Physical illness caused by disease, adverse climate, or bad food is not called tandī (laziness); rather, only natural laziness is meant by tandī. Kāyālasiya means the laziness of the mental body (nāmakāya), and it should be understood that this same laziness also occurs in the physical body (rūpakāya). Laziness that has its cause in the disturbance of the elements due to overeating and so forth is called vijambhitā (stretching). Laziness caused by the reason of food is called bhattasammada (food-drowsiness). 'By these things' means by the unwellness of the mind and so forth. In all instances, 'by the power of defilements' should be understood as by the power of defilements such as lust (rāga), which are the causes of sloth and torpor (thīna-middha). One is called apakata because they have been removed from right livelihood (sammā-ājīva). Because that person is oppressed by dangers related to livelihood, it is said, 'the meaning of one who is oppressed.' The meaning should be understood thus: to demonstrate the three types of deception (kuhana-vatthu) mentioned in the Mahāniddesa by means of this Vibhaṅga Pali, which is the basis of that Mahāniddesa. Pāpaṇika refers to things discarded from the market. Nantaka refers to clothes without borders or worn-out rags. Gilānappaccaya-bhesajja-parikkhāra refers to the supports of life called medicine, which are aids for the sick. The name pūtimutta (stale cow urine) is the name for all cow urine, whether old or not old. Some teachers also say it is medicine discarded because it has become putrid. It is said that a long hall or monastery with no inner rooms and only one door is called uddaṇḍa. Koraja is the restraint of useless bodily and vocal movements due to evil desire, which is like loathsome dust. One who has that koraja is called korajika. One who is excessively korajika is called korajika-korajika. Some say korajika-korajika refers to one who is extremely shriveled. Mukhasambhāvita is one who receives praise from others only by word of mouth through terms such as korajika-korajika. Such a person, because of that state, treats himself as if he were another and speaks saying, 'This monk...' and so forth. Paṇidhāya means setting the mind or aspiring, saying, 'Let them know me as an Arahant.' Āpāthakajjhāyī is one who meditates in the sight of people, sitting as if entering concentration in a place where people can see him.
220: Speaking nearby as if to another person is called sāmantajappita. By making the 'ā' sound short, it is preached as 'aṭṭhapanā'. Causing wonder is kuha; the occurrence of that causing wonder is kuhāyanā. Alternatively, the behavior or movement of a person who causes wonder is kuhāyanā. 862. 'Puṭṭhassa' means to the person who is asked, 'Who is the venerable one named Tissa? Who is the venerable one honored by the king?' 'Nahana' means binding or wrapping around. 863. One who wanders and lives by signs and omens, or one who makes signs, is called nemittika; the state of that person is nemittikatā. Making one's desire clear is obhāsa (hinting). What is that obhāsa? It is talk related to requisites, such as 'Today, requisites are difficult for monks to obtain.' Speaking near the desired object is called sāmantajappa. Casting out is called ukkhepanā. One who has the habit of eating the flesh of another's back (backbiting) is called parapiṭṭhimaṃsika; the state of that person is parapiṭṭhimaṃsikatā. Being crooked and desiring to take much by deceiving with a small gain is called nijigīsanā; the state of that desiring is nijigīsanatā. The manner of occurrence of that same desiring, or the act of seeking that arises together with it, is also called nijigīsanatā. In calling a body endowed with beauty 'vaṇṇapokkhara', it should be noted that the latter part of the preceding word is elided. Alternatively, the perfection of complexion is vaṇṇapokkharatā. As in the word 'atthajāpikā', the word japa expresses the meaning of 'arising' or 'producing,' thus it is said 'pavatteti'. Since the pride of being superior (seyyamāna) and the pride of being equal (sadisamāna) occur by way of loftiness, it is preached in both cases as 'mānaṃ jappeti'. However, since the pride of being inferior (hīnamāna) occurs by way of lowliness, it is not worthy of being described by the word māna alone; therefore, in the description of that hīnamāna, it is preached as 'omānaṃ jappeti'. One who is dependent on the king and enjoys the country in the manner of the king's enjoyment is called raṭṭhiya. 'Without referring to the person' means—just as in the descriptions of the pride of being superior and so forth, it says 'He regards himself as superior to others,' the person who is superior and so forth...
221:
Just as a person who gives rise to conceit is considered, so too in this state of conceit as 'superiority conceit' (seyyamāna), it is said that the intended meaning is simply 'he despises others,' without considering the specific individual who gives rise to conceit. Thinking of oneself as surpassing others is the excessive conceit (atimāna) of any person whatsoever.

The conceit that arises above a previous conceit is called mānātimāna. It should be noted that the word 'ati' expresses the meaning of the word 'upari' (above). Alternatively, conceit that surpasses a previous conceit is mānātimāna.

Among bird species, the crow is considered the lowest; thus, it is said, 'like the crow species.'

That Elder was said to be of an angry temperament (dosacarita); therefore, it is said that at the very beginning, instead of saying 'you are those whose taints are not yet destroyed,' he spoke by a certain means. Alternatively, because he was of an angry temperament, it means he quickly caused dispassion (virāga, i.e., the Fruit of Arhatship) to arise at the turn of the third phrase.

'Mānaṃ anugatacchando' means desire (chanda) associated with conceit, or it is the desire for conceit (mānacchanda) that follows the nature of conceit.

'Vilambana' (dallying/wit) should be noted as the action to be performed associated with the gestures of honoring women and men, etc. Therein, the wit (paṭibhāna) that is endowed with appropriateness, freedom, and smoothness is called vilambana-paṭibhāna.

Thought associated with the doctrine of immortality (amaravāda), or thought for the sake of one's own immortality or for the sake of becoming a deity, is called amara-vitakka.

Performing repeated protection over others by the power of lust (rāga) is called parānuddaya. Its state is parānuddayatā. Alternatively, the state of one who repeatedly protects others, such as by rejoicing together, is parānuddayatā. Such a state is indeed lust. Therein, the meaning 'in the state of parānuddayatā shown by living in association' is appropriate.

A person who desires not to be despised also desires sensual pleasures only for the sake of being one who is not despised. Therefore, it is said, 'relying on the five strands of sensual pleasure...'

## The Explanation of the Section of the Ones is finished.
222:
## 2. Dukaniddesavaṇṇanā

'Upanayhati' means he binds (harbors a grudge). The letter 'a' expresses the meaning of 'immediate' (anantara). Alternatively, because it is said as 'aṭṭhapanā' by shortening the letter 'ā' which expresses the meaning of 'limit' (mariyādā), it is spoken of as 'anantaraṭṭhapanā' and so forth. Among those, the mode of occurrence that first arises is called the limit (mariyādā). Establishing that very first state firmly without transgressing that limit is called mariyādaṭṭhapanā. It means it is merely the natural establishing (pakatiṭṭhapanā) devoid of qualifiers (such as ā, saṃ, anu, etc.).

'Niṭṭhuriya' is the spitting of saliva (letting saliva fall). It is called niṭṭhuriya because it is like spitting. 'Dassetvā' means by biting with the teeth (destroying another's virtues). Showing by such biting is described as domineering/rivalry (palāsa). The arising (āyanā) of palāsa is the occurrence of rivalry like taking up the yoke (yugaggāha) in pairs. Establishing the state of being equal is victory (jaya). Because it brings about that state of equality, it is called āhāra. 'Does not give the burden (dhura)' means he does not give the position of leadership.

One performs duties at the courtyard of a shrine (cetiya) and so forth with the body so that others may know, 'How could such a faithful person, endowed with duties, commit bodily misconduct and the like?' 'Aticca' means having committed an offense (transgressing). 'Āsaranti' means they return; the meaning is they proceed in concealing again. Concealing by means of cutting off, thinking 'Who would do such a thing?', is called vocchādanā.

By the Pali 'not well-spoken,' it is shown that whoever does not speak well is a deceitful person (saṭha). 'Neither the belly nor the back can be known' means that because of the absence of actions corresponding to the mind by making non-existent virtues manifest, it is meant that one cannot know, 'He has such a mind, he has such an action.'

A goat itself is called ajāmiga (a type of wild animal). 'Nelaka' refers to a young calf. Just as that yakkha, having shown such a form, eats whoever comes with the perception of 'a goat,' so too this person deceives various people by making manifest virtues similar to those of various people. Therefore, this treachery (sāṭheyya) should be understood as a deception more powerful than mere deceit (māyā). For that very reason, it is called 'parikkhattatā' (the state of being like a post dug in and planted all around).

Even when personality belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) and so forth are absent, that fetter (saṃyojana) which occurs, such as lust for form (rūparāga), is called bahiddhā-saṃyojana, being a qualifier of the person who has external fetters, because it binds beings to external existences (rūpabhava, arūpabhava).

## The Explanation of the Section of the Twos is finished.
223:
## 3. Commentary on the Explanation of the Triads (Tikaniddesa-vaṇṇanā)

Because it is stated that only the unwholesome roots are the roots of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa), the habitual practice of the roots of the round is explained by those unwholesome roots; thus it is said, "By the three... etc... it is explained" (tīhi...pe... kathi-to).

The view such as "The world is eternal" is considered by those with wrong views as the noble practice (brahmacariya) that leads to liberation (mokkha); therefore, it is said, "accepted by those with wrong views" (diṭṭhigatika-sammatassa). The phrase "to the Great Brahmas" (mahābrahmānaṃ) is said with reference to the excessive lust for existence (bhavarāga) in the resultants of the fine-material and immaterial spheres (rūpa-arūpāvacara-vipāka).

Since "kathaṃvidhaṃ" means "in what manner does it exist?", it is said to be "the form and shape" (ākārasaṇṭhānaṃ). "Establishing by pride" (māna-ṭhapanā) means establishing oneself through pride in terms of "better" (seyya) etc., or it is the establishment known as pride.

Terror of the mind (cetaso utrāso) refers to displeasure (domanassa), or anger (dosa), or mental factors such as volition (cetanā) associated with that anger.

Because it is easy to teach, the explanation of doubt (vicikicchā) in terms of the three periods of time is easy, as in "he doubts, he is perplexed" (kaṅkhati vicikicchati); however, it is implied that it is not so easy to teach delusion (moha) in that way. Regarding "having heard the distinctions of color etc.", some say: "The life-principle (jīva) of the Khattiyas is of a pale color. Why? Because they delight in the morning, and the shadow in the morning is pale." They say the life-principles of Brahmins, Vessas, and Suddas are white, yellow, and black respectively, because they delight in the midday, evening, and night when the shadows are white, yellow, and black. Having heard such distinctions of color and distinctions of shape described as "the self (attā) is all-pervading and circular" etc., (doubt arises).

This conventional expression (sammuti-kathā) arises for those who understand the two words "purisa-puggala" as a single term. Or, to show that this is a specific term denoting a person (puggala), it says "this, however" (ayaṃ pana) etc. Alternatively, it should be understood that "purisa-puggala" is said to show that although "purisa" is used, it refers only to a person (puggala) and not just to one endowed with the male faculty (purisindriya). The eight kinds of diseases are those originating from bile, phlegm, wind, change of season, personal or others' effort, improper care, the conjunction of the three humors, and the result of kamma. Regarding "kamma done in the past", they (the heretics) desire only ancient kamma and reject kamma to be experienced in the next life (upapajja-vedanīya-kamma). Regarding "having authority as the root cause", even if a ruler causes suffering such as torture or imprisonment by command, it is the view (of the heretics) that such suffering is not rooted in that ruler but is solely due to the creation of a supreme lord (issara-nimmāna) such as Brahmā.
224:
The continuous burning of delusion (moha) is mentioned because it is the cause of burning (by the ten fires such as lust and the fires of hell). In reality, the non-penetration (asampativedha) of the nature of delusion is a kind of suffering that is the opposite of the happiness of penetration; thus, it should be understood as having the nature of continuous burning. With this in mind, it is said: "The neutral feeling (upekkhā-vedanā) is pleasant when there is knowledge (ñāṇa) and painful when there is lack of knowledge (aññāṇa)" (Majjhima Nikāya).

"In many signs and objects" (puthu-nimittārammaṇesu) means in objects that have the nature of being various causes for defilements etc., by way of beautiful signs (subha-nimitta) etc., or in objects such as beautiful signs that have a manifold nature. Although the explanations of sloth (kosajja) and negligence (pamāda) are similar, the sluggish behavior known as lack of expansion is sloth, while the negligence known as the relinquishing of mindfulness is negligence; this is the distinction between the two.

By the term "living with respect" (sagaru-vāsa), living with moral dread (ottappa) is meant. By the term "living with elders" (sajeṭṭhaka-vāsa), living with moral shame (hiri) is meant. Not taking advice is "anādiyana", which means not accepting or not attending to (acittīkāra) the advice. The lack of moisture (anallatā) like dry wood or lack of softness (amudutā) is "anadda". "Asīlya" means the absence of good habits (asukkhasīlatā) or simply lack of softness.

"Upārambha" (fault-finding) would be the arising of consciousness associated with anger (dosa).

Since the word "karoti" (he makes) is also used in the sense of "placing" (ṭhapana), as in "he makes (places) a stone here", it is said: "karoti means he places (ṭhapeti)". Here, it should be understood that this advertence (āvajjana) is mentioned in the Minor Bases (khuddaka-vatthu) because it is the proximate cause of unwholesome states or because it has a function conducive to them.

## End of the Commentary on the Explanation of the Triads.

## 4. Commentary on the Explanation of the Tetrads (Catukka-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)

"Iti" is a particle indicating illustration and shows the same meaning as the word "evaṃ" (thus). In the term "bhavābhava-hetu", "bhava" refers to medicine such as ghee because health etc. arise (bhavanti) because of it. A more excellent and greatly increased "bhava" (good medicine) is called "abhava". Alternatively, because they are to be abandoned by the noble lineage (ariya-vaṃsa) which delights in meditation (bhāvanā), all cravings, excluding the three cravings mentioned earlier, are said to "arise due to the cause of existence and non-existence" (bhavābhava-hetu).
225:
“Etāya” means by way of prejudice (agati) such as desire (chanda), etc. “Na gacchanti” means they do not occur, or they do not perform those various actions. “Iminā” means by this cause of falling into prejudice such as desire, etc. Among desire and so on, if one is inclined toward a certain factor (regarding the person to be judged), acting by that factor is called “yathāninnagamana” (going according to inclination).

By the word “Rājā” (king) and so on, just as there is mental alarm caused by a king, etc., mental alarm caused by waves and so on is called “ūmiādibhaya” (fear of waves, etc.). According to the word of the Buddha, “Monks, ‘fear of waves’ (ūmibhaya) is a designation for anger (kodha) and despair (upāyāsa),” anger, despair, gluttony, the five cords of sensual pleasure, or women are called “fears.” In that context, by taking the five cords of sensual pleasure and women, it should be understood that the desire and lust (chandarāga) dependent on them are taken. Gluttony (odarikatta) is indeed greed (lobha). Legal acts such as the act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma) are disciplinary punishments of the Vinaya.

“Then the wanderer Timbaruka approached the Blessed One... and said: ‘Venerable Gotama, is pleasure and pain created by oneself?’ The Blessed One said: ‘Do not say so, Timbaruka...’” Since this appears in the Nidānavagga of the Saṃyutta Nikāya, it is called “Timbaruka-diṭṭhi” (the view of Timbaruka).

## The Explanation of the Section of the Fours is finished.

## 5. The Explanation of the Section of the Fives

“Āgantuṃ pana na denti” (But they do not allow coming) means they do not become the causes for coming (to the Fine-material and Immaterial realms).

“Avadehanato” (Due to filling up) means due to the increase caused by the fullness of the stomach and being the cause for the accumulation of flesh. For one who sleeps after eating in the summer, happiness often arises; that happiness caused by the season is called “seyyasukkha” (the happiness of sleeping), meaning the happiness occurring in the posture of lying down.

“Vata” refers to the ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas). “Tapa” refers to the major and minor duties in the Khandhakas or energy (viriya). If it is asked: “Since the practice of the Khandhaka duties and abstinence from sexual intercourse are already included by taking virtue (sīla), is it not unnecessary to take austerity (tapa) and the holy life (brahmacariya) separately?”—No, it is not so. This is because [the teacher] wishes to show that austerity and the holy life are specifically the causes for becoming a deity, distinguishing them from other types of virtue, or because he wishes to show the occurrence of the bonds of those outside the Dispensation.

The non-harming, etc., the cow-vow (go-vata), etc., the performance of difficult practices, and abstinence from sexual intercourse of those outside the Dispensation are, respectively, virtue (sīla), vows (vata), austerity (tapa), and the holy life (brahmacariya). They practice those virtues, etc., aiming for rebirth in the heavenly host. Alternatively, through faith (saddhā), preference (ruci), etc., they think in various ways: “O sirs, this self has form, is composed of the four great elements, is born of parents, and is annihilated at the breaking up of the body,” etc. (showing how the view of annihilationism arises).
226:
Among the ruins (byasana), by taking the ruin of relatives (ñāti-byasana), the ruin of wealth (bhoga-byasana), and the ruin of health (roga-byasana), it should be understood that the Blessed One has included sorrow and so on caused by those ruins. Repulsiveness in seeing and hearing is called "dassana-savana-paṭikūlatā." In this explanation of the dangers of impatience (akkhanti-ādīnava-niddesa), it should be understood that by way of the five faults, impatience (akkhanti) itself, which is the root cause of those faults, is explained by dividing it into five. Or, the faults such as wrong actions (dukkaṭa) and wrong speech (dubbhāsita), which have impatience as their root and are the causes of being unloved and so on, are explained.

The fear that arises at the time of death due to the cause of wrong livelihood (micchā-ājīva) is called "ājīvaka-bhaya." However, in the reading "ājīvika-bhaya," it should be understood as the mental agitation caused by the means of livelihood of one who sees the non-attainment of requisites. Fame (kitti) is called "siloka." The opposite of that "siloka" is "asiloka," which is indeed the blame (akitti) that is the opposite of fame. Therefore, it is called "garaha-bhaya" (fear of blame).

"Uppilāvita" is the state of non-calmness known as elation of the mind. Or, it is a mode of rapture (pīti) that is the cause of non-calmness.

## The Explanation of the Group of Fives is finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Group of Sixes

By the passage "He is angry and malicious (upanāhī)" and so on, malice (upanāha) and so on, which have anger (kodha) and so on as their cause, are stated in the Sutta texts as the accompanying causes of anger and so on. Therefore, anger and so on are indeed the roots of disputes (vivāda-mūla). For that reason, in this explanation of the roots of disputes (vivāda-mūla-niddesa), only those factors are stated. "Sandiṭṭhi-parāmāsitā" means being firmly attached to one's own view.

"Appatissayo" means being devoid of respectful persons who are one's refuge. The characteristic of diligence (appamāda-lakkhaṇa) means not being without mindfulness, or the constant application in wholesome states.

"Yutta-payuttatā" means being well-engaged through inclination toward that [work]. "Gaṇa-saṅgaṇikā" means mingling with a group that occurs by the power of defilements. Delight in hearing talk related to women and in hearing the voice of a woman is called "savana-saṃsagga" (association through hearing). Delight in giving or receiving anything from a woman is called "paribhoga-saṃsagga" (association through use).

In the passage "They wander together with joy (somanassa)," "somanassupavicāra" (mental explorations with joy) should be understood here as the explorations of forms (rūpa-vicāra) and so on, which are accompanied by unwholesome joy. Likewise, the explorations with equanimity (upekkhupavicāra) [should be understood]. By taking this "vicāra" (exploration), it should be understood that "vitakka" (thought) is also taken.
227:
By taking sustained thought (vicāra), it is shown that initial thought (vitakka) is also taken; by the occurrence of initial thought, this word "upavitakketi" (he ponders) is also intended.

Regarding "associated with ignorance" (aññāṇasampayutta), the equanimity (upekkhā) associated with consciousness accompanied by skeptical doubt (vicikicchā) and restlessness (uddhacca) is called delusion (moha). Furthermore, the equanimity associated with greed is not not dependent on the household (i.e., it is indeed dependent on the household of sensual pleasures).

Regarding "fortuitous originationist" (adhiccasamuppannika), it refers to one who holds the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi), grasping that "the self has arisen without a cause and will arise in the future." To show that it is like the view of such a person, it is said "adhiccasamuppannikasseva." In the phrase "na so jāto," the vowel 'u' of the particle "jātu" is changed to 'o' to say "jāto," or it should be understood as another particle with the same meaning as "jātu." "Sabbāsavadiṭṭhi" refers to the view that comes by way of the Sabbāsava discourse (Sabbāsavapariyāya).

## The Explanation of the Section of Sixes is finished.

## 7. Sattakaniddesavaṇṇanā (Explanation of the Section of Sevens)

Since there is no other group of seven among the sixty-two views, the seven doctrines of annihilationism (ucchedavāda) themselves are called "seven views" (satta diṭṭhi) here, without being directly called annihilationism.

## The Explanation of the Section of Sevens is finished.

## 8. Aṭṭhakaniddesavaṇṇanā (Explanation of the Section of Eights)

The arisings of consciousness occurring in a regressive manner, such as "I will have to do work," are the causes of laziness (kosajja). Alternatively, laziness itself should be understood as the cause of laziness because it is the cause for further laziness. In the phrase "māsācitaṃ maññe," the word "ācita" expresses the meaning of "wet," and the word "maññe" expresses the meaning of "like"; with this intention, the meaning is clarified as "like wet beans." Alternatively, it means "resembles a heap of beans."

"Pharati" means it touches or strikes. "By another reason" means when one is told, "Today you have eaten at the wrong time (after noon), therefore you have committed an offense (āpatti)"...
228:
...it means one conceals the other valid reason with another invalid reason, such as "Yesterday I ate at the proper time, therefore I am free from offense." Removing or throwing away the talk so that the fault does not stick to the outside of the questioned meaning is called "diverting [the talk] outwards" (bahiddhā apanāmanā).

By the term "asaññīvādā" (proponents of non-perception), the views of individuals are shown. Or, those fixed mental applications by which they say the self is non-percipient are "asaññīvādā." "Arūpasamāpattinimittaṃ" refers to objects such as the concept of space (ākāsapaññatti) and so on.

## The Explanation of the Section of Eights is finished.

## 9. Navakaniddesavaṇṇanā (Explanation of the Section of Nines)

Because the tenth (base of malice) was not preached, it is said, "They are preached only by way of arising in beings."

"Sukhavinicchayaṃ" means the decision between pleasure to be pursued and pleasure not to be pursued. "Ajjhattaṃ sukhaṃ" is the bliss of renunciation (nekkhammasukha) which is to be pursued (i.e., the bliss of jhāna). "Vinicchayā" refers to two kinds of decisions; this is said in the commentary on this verse:

"What they call the pleasant and the unpleasant in the world,
dependent on that, desire arises.
Having seen the dissolution and the becoming in forms,
a person makes a decision in the world."
(Sutta Nipāta 873, Mahāniddesa 102)

In this Vibhaṅga Pali, that initial thought (vitakka) which is called by the word "vinicchaya" (decision) by way of being a condition, is the same vitakka that appears in the Sakkapañha Sutta by the word "vitakka" because it is the cause of desire (chanda). Thus, it shows both the nature of vitakka as a decision and the fact that this very vitakka is taken here (in the Taṇhāmulakaniddesa). "Balavasanniṭṭhānaṃ" means the grasping of an object after finalizing it with strong craving.

Even though there is the conditioned nature (saṅkhatabhāva) of other states (such as contact), conceit (māna) is called "conditioned" (saṅkhata) with reference to the conditioned nature of conceit which is excessive, thinking "I am" and "I exist."
229:
The conditioning of oneself as "I am" by way of superiority and so on, or that which is conditioned, is called "saṅkhata." Here, since the occurrence such as "will be" is particularly the arising of craving and views, the state of vacillation (iñjita) and so on of those cravings and views is also mentioned.

## The Explanation of the Section of Nines is finished.

## 10. Dasakaniddesavaṇṇanā (Explanation of the Section of Tens)

The planning of skills such as arranging nets and so on is called "upāyacintā" (thinking of means). Delusion (moha) which occurs in the form of covering the wrongness and faultiness of that upāyacintā should be understood as arising by the power of thinking of means. The perception (saññā) or thought (saṅkappa) or reflection (paccavekkhaṇā) that occurs by way of seeing no danger in a committed evil deed is called "paccavekkhaṇā." The nature that covers the wrongness and faultiness of that reflection, or the delusion that arises in the form of reflection as seeing no danger, should be understood as such.

"Vimuttasaññitā" means being associated with overestimation (adhimāna, thinking one has attained what one has not). Or it is the heretics' perception of being liberated from defilements through their own views. Some teachers say that the arising of unwholesome consciousness occurring as "I am liberated" is wrong liberation (micchāvimutti). However, in the consciousness associated with views that is taken as being liberated from defilements like the Fruition (phala), it is appropriate to say that the view is wrong knowledge (micchāñāṇa) and the concentration is wrong liberation (micchāvimutti).

## The Explanation of the Section of Tens is finished.

## Taṇhāvicariṭaniddesavaṇṇanā (Explanation of the Ramblings of Craving)

"Samūhagāhato" is said by some to mean taking by way of the common grasping of craving, conceit, and views. However, taking without making a distinction such as "thus, in this way, or otherwise" should be understood as collective grasping (samūhagāha). "Aññāṃ ākāraṃ" means an aspect occurring in the continuity of another person. In the word "atthi," it means it always exists. "Sīdati" means it perishes. "Saṃsayaparivitakkavasena" means by the power of reflecting such as "Would I be? Would I not be?" "Patthanākappanavasena" means by the power of making a wish such as "If only I were..."

"Suddhasīsā" (pure headings) is said because the common headings of craving, conceit, and views do not depend on distinctions such as "thus, in this way, or otherwise." Among them, when views are taken by the headings of views, the craving that is not inseparable from views is also shown.
230:
He said, "These manifoldings of craving (taṇhāvicariṭadhamma) are thus to be understood," through conceit and views which are primary and have the primary as their root, as well as through craving itself. It should be understood that the term 'manifoldings of craving' is used even for views and conceit because they are constantly associated with craving without separation, and because they have craving as their root and craving is predominant.

The particle 'avakkari' is used in the sense of diversity or separation; therefore, not making separate is called 'anavakkari'. Intending to show this as either 'having made no separation' or 'having made no separation instead of making separate,' he said, 'having made no distinction (avinibbhoga)'. Alternatively, there is the reading 'anavakāriṃ karitvā'. In that context, 'avakiraṇa' means scattering, dispersing, or separating parts of a group; this is called 'avakāri'. Without making that separation (vinibbhoga), taking all five aggregates as a single group and not distinguishing them from the self, one acquires desire, conceit, and views as 'I am'. This is the meaning. 'Asitabyābhaṅgitāya' means either by means of these requisites, namely the sickle and the carrying pole, or 'asitabyābhaṅgī' refers to the act of reaping and carrying with the sickle and carrying pole.

'Avakāriṃ karitvā' means distinguishing form and so on from the self and acquiring desire as 'I am by means of this form... I am by means of this consciousness.' In all such places, the phrase 'by means of this' should be understood as 'by means of form and so on which are distinguished from the self.' Indeed, craving that arises by taking as an object form and so on, which are not distinguished from the self, not made external, and are grasped only as 'I', is called 'clinging to the internal (ajjhattika)'. Craving that arises by taking as an object things that are distinguished from the self and made external is called 'clinging to the external (bāhira)'. The meaning is that one thinks 'there is no destruction for me' because of things like a sword or an umbrella, which are regarded as highly auspicious, thinking 'I am permanent' by means of the sword or umbrella. The phrase 'of each person' is said for the purpose of showing the possibility of the thirty-six manifoldings of craving in the past and future for each individual in the beginningless and endless cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra). Alternatively, saying 'according to what each person obtains' is for the purpose of showing the possibility of some manifoldings of craving in the present for a worldling (puthujjana).

## The Explanation of the Description of the Manifoldings of Craving is finished.

## The Explanation of the Minor Points of the Vibhaṅga is finished.
231:
## 18. Dhammahadayavibhaṅga

## 1. Sabbasaṅgāhikavāravaṇṇanā

By the passage beginning with 'five aggregates,' the first cycle is called the Universal Summary Cycle (Sabbasaṅgāhikavāra) because it includes without remainder things such as the aggregates, which are distinguished by their suitability to arise in the three elements (realms) like the sense element, their inclusion therein, their manifestation, their distinction by way of different planes, the variety of results of wholesome and unwholesome kamma like giving that cause rebirth in the three destinations (gati), their distinction by way of things to be fully known (abhiññeyya), the two pairs of object-dyads, their distinction by way of things like the seen (diṭṭha), the five groups of wholesome triads, and the two pairs of material and mundane dyads; and because the second cycle and others are also appropriately included in this first cycle. The second cycle is called the Cycle of the Demonstration of Arising and Non-arising (Uppattānuppattidassanavāra).

In that second cycle, however, he only taught the existence of those aggregates and so on, by way of 'How many aggregates and how many sense bases are there in the sense element?' and so forth. Specific verbs are not used because they can be understood through general verbs like 'exists' (atthi), 'is' (bhavati), and 'is found' (saṃvijjati). Therefore, it is fitting to call this second cycle the Cycle of the Demonstration of Possibility and Impossibility (Sambhavāsambhavadassanavāra). The fourth cycle should also be called the Cycle of the Demonstration of Arising and Non-arising because it shows arising and non-arising at the moment of rebirth-linking, and because it mentions manifestation and non-manifestation in that fourth cycle.

Answering correctly and unerringly according to the question asked, even if done by others, is called the Omniscient One's Explanation (Sabbaññubyākaraṇa) because it is done by knowing the words of the Omniscient Buddha. What need is there to say more if it is answered by the Omniscient One himself? This is the meaning.

## 2. Uppattānuppattivāravaṇṇanā

'Kāmadhātusambhūtānañca' means they also arise in the continuity of sense-sphere beings who have reached the form element (rūpadhātu) through psychic power. In the passage 'due to the absence of the nose-base and so on' (ghānāyatanādīnaṃ abhāvena), if the smell-base and so on do not perform the function of a sense base because of the absence of the nose-base and so on, then the form-base would also not perform the function of a sense base in non-percipient beings (asaññasatta) due to the absence of the eye-base. If that were the case, the statement 'At the moment of rebirth-linking of non-percipient devas, two sense bases manifest' and so on should not have been taught. Sense-sphere planes and so on are called 'elements' (dhātu) because they are the locus for beings arising there or for the states included therein. Likewise, the groups of beings in which sense-sphere beings and so on arise are also called 'elements' because they are the place of arising for those beings, which is called the 'arising of beings' (sattuppatti).
232:
These groups of beings are also called elements (dhātu). However, in these elements such as the sense-sphere element (kāmadhātu), there is no unincluded (apariyāpanna) space (okāsa) nor an unincluded group of beings (sattanikāya) that could be called an 'element'. To show this meaning, it is said: "There is no such thing as an unincluded element by way of space or by way of the arising of beings." By the phrase "by way of the arising of beings", it takes both the world of space (okāsaloka) and the world of beings (sattaloka) together to show the non-existence of such an unincluded element. Alternatively, "the arising of beings" (sattuppatti) means arising in the state of a being. The clinging aggregates (upādinnakakkhandhā) that arise according to various existences (bhava) by way of the dwelling places of beings are called "elements" because they serve as similar bases for the beings included in those respective realms. Thus, the meaning is that there is no unincluded element.

## 3. Pariyāpannāpariyāpannavāravaṇṇanā
They are delimited by way of existence (bhava) and by way of space (okāsa). All clinging aggregates arising in that existence or space, or in others, should be understood as being included in those respective existences and spaces.

## 6. Uppādakakammaāyuppamāṇavāro
## 1. Uppādakakammavaṇṇanā
Having explained the distinctions of the aggregates and so on by way of their occurrence in elements, the sixth section beginning with "Tayo devā" is undertaken to show the distinctions of those beings who have differences in elements, the productive kamma (uppādakakamma) of those beings, and the result (vipāka) of that kamma. Indeed, the aggregates and so on are distinguished by way of the deities belonging to the three elements, by way of kammas such as giving (dāna), and by way of the clinging aggregates delimited by their respective life-spans. Some teachers say that four doṇas make one ambaṇa, and six doṇas make one ambaṇa.

## Uppādakakammavaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.
## (2.) Āyuppamāṇavaṇṇanā
"Three people also" means three groups of people are living.
"Ābhā" means beautiful radiance.
One who has glory like a gold nugget is called "kañcanapiṇḍasassirikā". In the term "subhakiṇhā", although it should be said as those mixed with beautiful radiance, the letter "ā" in "subhā" is shortened, and the final letter "ṇa" is changed to "ha", thus it is spoken as "subhakiṇhā". Alternatively, the Brahmās mixed with beautiful radiance are called "subhakiṇhā". They are as bright and beautiful as a well-polished gold mirror. In the preceding terms like "parittasubhā", these Brahmās are called "parittasubhā" because they have a small amount of beautiful bodily radiance. They are called "appamāṇasubhā" because they have immeasurable beautiful bodily radiance. Thus, the compound should be formed with the word "subha".

The meaning of the Pali text stating that there is no difference in object (ārammaṇa) and attention (manasikāra) is that at the moment of jhāna or after that moment, there is no difference in the object and attention of jhāna due to the development (bhāvanā) or adverting (āvajjana) that has a kasina object such as the limited (paritta) one. However, there is a difference in the object and attention of jhāna due to the development and adverting occurring in the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga). Indeed, by the power of access concentration (upacāra-bhāvanā) in the preliminary stage, the jhāna has various objects among the objects such as the limited earth kasina. It should be understood that there is respective attention due to the adverting that reflects on the respective kasina in the preliminary stage.
233:
The name "subhakiṇhā" is spoken by changing the final letter "ṇa" to "ha" and shortening the letter "ā". Alternatively, they are called "subhakiṇhā" because they are mixed with beautiful radiance. In the previously mentioned realms, they should be known as "parittasubhā" because these Brahmās have limited beauty, and as "appamāṇasubhā" because they have immeasurable beauty, joining the compound with the word "subha". The object and attention are spoken of in terms of the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga). At the moment of jhāna or after that, there is no difference in the object and attention of jhāna through adverting to the development of a limited kasina object and so on. The meaning is that the difference exists only through the preliminary stage development and preliminary stage adverting. Indeed, by the power of the preliminary stage access concentration, the jhāna has various objects such as the limited earth kasina. By adverting to the respective kasina in the preliminary stage, there is respective attention. Factors such as desire (chanda) exist even at the moment of absorption (appanā). Among them, "paṇidhi" (aspiration) should be understood not as craving's longing (taṇhā-patthanā), but only as desire's longing (chanda-patthanā). "Adhimokkha" is decision, and "abhinīhāra" is simply the occurrence of the mind. If one intends the factors that determine specific existences, such as the desire for existence (bhavachanda) and aspiration for existence, then the statement "they occur even in absorption" should be understood to mean they occur even after absorption has arisen. Because the object specified by weariness of perception (saññāvirāga) and so on, and the attention occurring therein, which determine the specific existence, occur only in the preliminary stage, it is said: "The object and attention are spoken of in terms of the preliminary stage."

"Vipulaphalā" means having extensive results such as peaceful happiness, long life, and beauty. They see clearly with the eye of wisdom (paññācakkhu), the physical eye (maṃsacakkhu), and the divine eye (dibbacakkhu).

According to the statement "as long as that evil kamma is not exhausted", it is said "kamma alone is the measure". The meaning is that the delimitation of life-span such as in the Abbuda hell is also made only by the power of kamma.

The absence of an opportunity to hide means that because they are always surrounded by a group of nymphs of the same kind and are crowded with sensual pleasures, there is no place devoid of those sensual pleasures.

"What determines?" means which jhāna determines the rebirth? "Nine Brahma worlds" means after purifying the nine realms such as Brahmapārisajja. "At the top" means...
234:
It means "in the Vehapphala realms." The term "noble existence" (seṭṭhabhava) implies that these are the highest existences because there is no further rebirth beyond the Vehapphala, Akaniṭṭha, and Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana realms. For this reason, they are taken as the "heads of existence" (bhavasīsa). The phrase "in these three places" is spoken with reference only to places such as Vehapphala. Considering that an Anāgāmī (Non-returner) born in the nine realms prior to Vehapphala may arise in the Immaterial Sphere (arūpadhātu), this Yamaka Pali was taught: "For some beings passing away from the Fine-material Sphere and arising in the Immaterial Sphere, seven underlying tendencies (anusaya) remain; for some, five; for some, three." This should be understood as not referring to those already born in realms such as Vehapphala.

Regarding the statement, "For Noble Disciples born in the nine Brahma worlds, rebirth occurs only there, not in lower realms," this only prohibits rebirth in lower realms. It does not prohibit rebirth within those same nine realms, in higher realms, in the Vehapphala realm, or in the Immaterial Sphere. The statement, "An Anāgāmī born in the first jhāna plane, having purified the nine Brahma worlds, attains Parinibbāna while standing at the summit," is also spoken with reference to one who ascends sequentially. Therefore, it should not be understood that this statement prohibits an Anāgāmī who has not yet reached the summit from arising in the Immaterial Sphere.

Alternatively, this commentary is spoken with reference to a Noble Disciple who, having developed the Path either in another realm or in that Fine-material realm, passes away and is born there with attachment to form (rūparāga) not yet suppressed. For this reason, the term "nibbatta" (born/arisen) is used in all such phrases as "Noble Disciples born in the nine Brahma worlds," "an Anāgāmī born in the first jhāna plane," and "Anāgāmīs born in these three places." For that Noble Disciple, since rebirth occurred there due to that attachment to form, once that attachment to form is suppressed through insight, the desire for existence will no longer occur, and the cutting off of attachment to the immaterial (arūparāga) will certainly take place. As for a worldling (puthujjana) who, having been born there, develops the Noble Path and suppresses attachment to form through immaterial jhānas, but whose desire for immaterial existence has not yet receded due to seeing the danger in the arisen existence at the time the Path arises—it should be understood that the Yamaka Pali proceeds with reference to such a person.

## The Explanation of the Lifespan is finished.
235:
## 7. Explanation of the Section on What Should Be Fully Known, etc.
"The nature characterized by transformation is matter (rūpa); the nature characterized by contact is contact (phassa)." The purification of view (diṭṭhivisuddhi) and the purification by overcoming doubt (kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi), which distinguish and grasp the general and specific characteristics, and grasp the individual characteristics in this manner, are called "full understanding of the known" (ñātapariññā). From then on, the knowledge up to the knowledge of conformity (anuloma-ñāṇa) is called "full understanding by investigation" (tīraṇapariññā). The knowledge starting from the knowledge of contemplation of rise and fall (udayabbayānupassanā-ñāṇa) up to the Path is called "full understanding by abandoning" (pahānapariññā).

In those various instances (aggregates, etc.), what should be said regarding the causes of the aggregates and so forth has already been stated in the "Section of Questioning" (pañhapucchakavāra) of the Vibhaṅga of the Aggregates (Khandha-vibhaṅga) and others. Since the roots (hetu) and so forth are included within the aggregates and so forth, it should be understood that what should be said in those various "Sections of Questioning" has already been stated.

## The Explanation of the Section on What Should Be Fully Known, etc., is finished.
## The Explanation of the Dhamma-hadaya Vibhaṅga is finished.
## Thus, the Explanation of the Obscure Meanings of the Sammohavinodanī Commentary,
## The Vibhaṅga Mūla-ṭīkā is completed.
